### [1] [Backtrader-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Algorithmic Trading with Self-Generated MCQs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11232)
*Ruoxi Zhao,Maziar Raissi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Backtrader-Bench is a dual-pipeline evaluation framework for LLM coding agents in algorithmic trading that generates deterministic multiple-choice questions with independently re-derived answers and autonomously mines harder questions, showing tool-augmented agents outperform no-tool models by 17 points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static benchmarks for algorithmic trading risk data contamination, and numerical backtest outputs need ground truth from actual code execution, making reliable evaluation of LLM coding agents difficult.

Method: A deterministic MCQ pipeline generates questions from backtest configurations across five trading strategies, 33 templates, and three difficulty tiers, with an independent checker that re-derives every answer. A second generator-solver filtering pipeline mines harder questions: a generator writes code-verified questions, converts them to MCQs, and discards any answerable by a no-tool solver without code execution. Evaluation covers 11 models without tools (10 runs each) and four tool-augmented configurations on a 30-question curated set.

Result: Tool-augmented agents reach 90.0% single-pass accuracy (GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.7), outperforming the best no-tools baseline (73.0% averaged over 10 runs) by 17 percentage points. On 38 separately mined questions, no-tools accuracy drops further, with half the models falling near random-chance level (25%).

Conclusion: The scalable MCQ infrastructure is designed to produce a training corpus for reinforcement learning, ultimately aiming to build a specialized agent for quantitative trading workflows.

Abstract: Evaluating LLM coding agents in algorithmic trading is difficult because static benchmarks risk data contamination and numerical backtest outputs require ground truth from actual code execution. We present Backtrader-Bench, a framework with two complementary pipelines. A deterministic multiple-choice question (MCQ) pipeline generates questions from backtest configurations across five trading strategies, 33 templates, and three difficulty tiers, with an independent checker that re-derives every answer. A generator-solver filtering pipeline autonomously mines harder questions: a generator writes questions verified by executable code, converts them to MCQs, and discards any that a no-tool solver can answer without code execution. We evaluate 11 models without tools (10 runs each) and four with-tools configurations on a 30-question curated set. Tool-augmented agents reach 90.0% accuracy in a single pass (GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.7), outperforming the best no-tools baselines (73.0%, averaged over 10 runs) by 17 percentage points. On 38 separately mined questions, no-tools accuracy drops further, with half the models falling to roughly random-chance level (25%). Beyond evaluation, the scalable MCQ infrastructure is designed to produce a training corpus for reinforcement learning, with the ultimate goal of building a specialized agent for quantitative trading workflows.

</details>


### [2] [Retrofitting Recurrent Depth into a Pretrained Language Model: Installation, Extrapolation, Transfer, and Retention at Two Parameter Budgets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11233)
*Mark Shapiro*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows a pretrained language model can be retrofitted with recurrent depth to perform iterative latent reasoning. The retrofit (a light adapter or full block) is non-inferior to the base model, learns one task step per loop, extrapolates to ~1.5x supervised depth, and outperforms a same-size scratchpad-trained model in both accuracy and speed—though learning the inverse rule exposed catastrophic-interference limits, and learned depth selection remains unsolved.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard transformers reason in a single forward pass or via explicit scratchpad tokens; this work asks whether recurrent depth can be added to a frozen/pretrained model so it iterates over latent state, computing deeper reasoning faster and more accurately than scratchpad-style fine-tuning, while preserving base capabilities.

Method: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct is split into a Prelude, a weight-tied Recurrent Block, and a Coda, with an identity-preserving one-loop path and a re-entry bridge on later loops (so loop 1 matches the base). Two parameter budgets are tested: a 6M-parameter adapter over frozen base weights, and 180M full-block training. Training uses intermediate-step supervision (one task step per loop), later annealed to outcome-only grading. Evaluation uses a preregistered ARC battery, verbal fine-tuning for renderings, depth-scaling tests, and a scratchpad-trained same-size baseline.

Result: The retrofit was non-inferior on the ARC battery. The adapter matched the full block overall (83.8% vs 84.0%), led through depth 11 and trailed beyond. Verbal fine-tuning reached 79–86% on controlled renderings with near-zero zero-shot transfer; adapter verbal training from the installed mechanism beat matched fresh training by 18.6 points (including held-out). The operation extrapolated to ~1.5x supervised depth, holding 70% accuracy through depth 18. Against a same-size scratchpad model, the recurrent model won 84% vs 72%, retained 53% vs 2.5% beyond depth 10, and answered 7.6x faster. The inverse rule was learnable in isolation but no continuation acquired it while preserving the installed mechanism and general capability (catastrophic interference). Learned depth selection remains open.

Conclusion: An iterative (recurrent-depth) transformer can perform deeper reasoning in latent space faster than comparable or larger models fine-tuned on the same task, with the learned mechanism persisting under outcome-only supervision and extrapolating beyond trained depth. Limits include catastrophic interference when adding a new (inverse) operation and the open problem of learned depth selection.

Abstract: A dense, pretrained language model can be retrofitted with recurrent depth and learn an iterative latent transition that persists after outcome-only annealing. Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct is split into a Prelude, a weight-tied Recurrent Block, and a Coda, with an identity-preserving one-loop path and a re-entry bridge on later loops. At loop 1 the retrofit remains non-inferior to its base on a preregistered ARC battery. Three findings. First, the mechanism is a reusable procedure rather than terminal-answer lookup, and installs at two budgets: 6M trained parameters over frozen base weights and 180M full-block. With intermediate-step supervision, the model computes one task step per loop and persists when only final answers are graded. The adapter matched the full block overall (83.8% versus 84.0%), led through depth 11, and trailed beyond. Verbal fine-tuning reached 79-86% on controlled verbal renderings (zero-shot transfer was minimal), and adapter verbal training begun from the installed mechanism outpaced matched fresh training by 18.6 points, including on a held-out test set. Second, the operation extrapolates to roughly 1.5 times its supervised depth, holding 70% accuracy through depth 18. Third, a same-size scratchpad-trained model matched the recurrent model within its learned horizon but collapsed beyond it. The recurrent model won overall, 84% versus 72%, retained 53% versus 2.5% beyond depth 10, and answered 7.6 times faster. An iterative transformer can therefore perform deeper reasoning in latent space faster than comparable or larger models fine-tuned on the same task, in a system-level comparison. A second task, running the rule in reverse, exposed the limits: the inverse was learnable in isolation, but no continuation acquired it while preserving the installed mechanism and general capability, a catastrophic-interference boundary. Learned depth selection remains open.

</details>


### [3] [TRACE Bench: Task-driven Roleplay Agentic Checklist Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11236)
*Jiahui Zhang,Ziwei Zhang,Yipeng Wang,Yibo Liu,Haozhou Pang,Yikai Hu,Hongyan Ren,Lan Zhou,Qi Gan,Kai Sheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TRACE Bench is a task-driven, agentic checklist evaluation framework for roleplay models that decomposes role profiles into checklists, updates them through natural dialogue, and produces scores traceable to specific checklist items and dialogue evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing roleplay evaluation assigns only a single holistic score, failing to reveal which role requirements were tested, which failed, and what dialogue evidence supports the judgment.

Method: TRACE Bench decomposes each role profile offline into a fixed checklist. A User Agent converses naturally with the target roleplay model while privately updating checklist states from model responses. Coverage is cross-validated by auditing M2 free-dialogue transcripts against the same role-derived checklist. It also supports Closed-Loop Benchmark Evolution by distilling verification methods from failed traces.

Result: Released M2 free-chat transcripts cover only 73.74% of key role-profile points, while TRACE Bench reaches 99.91% coverage in fewer turns. Across 26 models, TRACE Bench reports overall rankings with capability breakdowns and checklist traces, and robustness experiments show stable rankings under repeated runs and User Agent replacement.

Conclusion: TRACE Bench provides interpretable, evidence-backed roleplay evaluation with near-complete coverage, stable rankings, and a self-improving mechanism that makes later evaluations more reliable at eliciting and examining failure modes.

Abstract: Roleplay evaluation should do more than assign a single score: it should reveal which role requirements were tested, which failed, and which dialogue evidence supports the judgment. We propose TRACE Bench, a task-driven agentic checklist evaluation framework. It decomposes each role profile offline into a fixed checklist, then uses a User Agent to converse naturally with the target roleplay model while privately updating checklist states from model responses. Scores therefore trace back to checklist items and supporting dialogue turns rather than a black-box holistic impression. For coverage cross-validation, we audit released M2 free-dialogue transcripts from the MiniMax Role-play Benchmark against the same role-derived checklist. The released free-chat transcripts cover only 73.74% of key role-profile points, whereas TRACE Bench reaches 99.91% coverage in fewer turns. Robustness experiments show stable rankings under repeated runs and User Agent replacement. Across 26 models, TRACE Bench reports overall rankings together with capability breakdowns and checklist traces. It also supports Closed-Loop Benchmark Evolution, distilling verification methods proven effective in failed traces so later evaluations can more reliably elicit and examine observed failure modes.

</details>


### [4] [Lost in Compaction: Evaluating Side-Constraint Loss under Context Compaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11242)
*Zhiqi Wang,Yichi Zhang,Dongwon Lee,Yuchen Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM context compaction silently drops user-issued Session Constraints (e.g., "do not delete emails until I confirm"), with current compactors retaining only ~17% of them on average. The authors introduce the COMPINT benchmark to quantify this loss and propose an SC-aware extractor that raises retention above 90% across all scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM context windows fill up, systems compact prior context to continue tasks, but user instructions that constrain behavior for the rest of a session can be silently lost during compaction. The authors aim to identify and quantify this integrity failure.

Method: The authors define Session Constraints (SCs) as a class of user instructions meant to persist throughout a session. They build COMPINT, an evaluation suite spanning three long-context scenarios (multi-turn chat, agentic trajectory, long-horizon research), and inject SCs to measure compactor retention. They propose an SC-aware extractor that runs alongside the compactor as a plug-and-play module without modifying the compactor or LLM.

Result: Current compactors retain only 17% of injected SCs on average, and most perform worse than running the same task without compaction. Retention varies sharply with compactor, prompt, context length, SC phrasing, and injection location, indicating the loss is systematic. The SC-aware extractor achieves over 90% retention across all three scenarios.

Conclusion: LLM context compaction systematically drops user-specified Session Constraints, degrading task performance. The proposed plug-and-play SC-aware extractor substantially recovers retention without modifying existing compactors or LLMs, providing a practical mitigation. Code and benchmark are publicly available.

Abstract: When the context window is under pressure, LLM systems compact prior context to continue ongoing tasks. We identify a class of user-issued instructions, Session Constraints (SCs), such as "do not delete any emails until I confirm," that are meant to constrain LLM's behavior for the remainder of a session but are silently dropped during compaction. To quantify this loss, we introduce COMPINT, an evaluation suite that evaluates compactors across three long-context scenarios: multi-turn chat, agentic trajectory, and long-horizon research.
  Current compactors retain only 17% of injected SCs on average, and most perform worse than running the same task without compaction. Retention varies sharply with compactor, prompt, context length, SC phrasing, and injection location, showing that the loss is systematic rather than tied to any single setting. We propose an SC-aware extractor that runs alongside the compactor as a plug-and-play module, achieving over 90% retention across all three scenarios without modifying the compactor or LLM. The COMPINT evaluation suite and accompanying implementation are available at https://github.com/ZhiqiEliWang/compaction-integrity.

</details>


### [5] [Diffuse to Compress: Leveraging Diffusion LMs for Lossless Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11249)
*Angelo Nardone,Paolo Ferragina*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes replacing autoregressive LLMs with Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) in lossless text compression to overcome throughput bottlenecks, and demonstrates state-of-the-art compression ratios on enwik8.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivated by the rapid growth of digital textual data and the fact that LLM-based lossless compressors achieve far better compression ratios than general-purpose tools (zstd, gzip, bzip) but suffer from severe throughput limitations due to their one-symbol-per-step autoregressive decoding.

Method: Introduce Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) as an alternative inference paradigm within the same neural compression framework, replacing autoregressive LLMs. This requires solving algorithmic challenges in lossless compression where the number and positions of symbols encoded per forward pass can be decided independently; the authors design efficient strategies for these challenges and evaluate on enwik8.

Result: The DLM-based compression framework advances the state of the art in lossless text compression, outperforming prior LLM-based and general-purpose compressors on the enwik8 benchmark.

Conclusion: DlMs effectively overcome the throughput bottleneck of autoregressive approaches while achieving state-of-the-art compression, and since DLMs are a young paradigm, further improvements are likely as diffusion models become more capable and efficient.

Abstract: We study the problem of lossless text compression, motivated by the rapid growth in the collection and storage of digital textual data - including plain text, source code, and structured formats such as XML - and by recent advances in neural language model-based compression. In particular, recent LLM-based approaches, whether built on symbol-ranking pipelines or paired with a statistical compressor, have demonstrated compression ratios significantly superior to general-purpose compressors such as zstd, gzip, or bzip on text and code. However, these neural approaches suffer from severe throughput limitations, making them not yet practically usable.
  For the first time in the context of lossless neural text compression, we introduce Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) as an alternative inference paradigm to autoregressive LLM-based approaches. We argue that replacing autoregressive LLMs with DLMs within the same compression framework could overcome the throughput bottleneck caused by their one-symbol-per-step limitation. However, achieving these improvements requires addressing algorithmic challenges introduced by applying DLMs to lossless compression, where the architecture allows the number and positions of symbols encoded at each forward pass to be decided independently. We design efficient and effective strategies to solve these challenges and evaluate them experimentally against LLM-based and general-purpose compressors on enwik8, a well-established textual benchmark.
  Our results show that the newly proposed DLM-based framework advances the state of the art in lossless text compression. Moreover, as DLMs are still a relatively young paradigm, recent advances toward increasingly capable and efficient models suggest substantial room for further improvements.

</details>


### [6] [Gloss-Free Representation Learning for Cross-Dataset Sign Spotting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11332)
*Oğuz Akif Tüfekcioğlu,Ezgi Ekin,Mustafa Kaan Çevik,Hacer Yalim Keles*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether weak, transcript-based supervision from broadcast news can pretrain a reusable sign encoder for a low-resource, morphologically rich sign language (Turkish Sign Language), and shows the learned representations transfer well to cross-dataset sign spotting and improve downstream translation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sign-language research in resource-constrained languages is hindered by the high cost of dense linguistic annotations (glosses, temporal boundaries, sign order). Broadcast news provides weakly aligned text-to-signing supervision cheaply, but loose alignment and morphological richness (many inflected forms per lexical meaning, with some derived forms needing to stay distinct) make pseudo-gloss targets fragment and weaken representation learning. The authors investigate whether such weak supervision can still pretrain a transferable sign encoder.

Method: The authors introduce TSL-News, a new Turkish Sign Language broadcast corpus, and pretrain a sign encoder with pseudo-gloss labels derived from spoken-language transcripts (no manual annotation). They compare two normalization strategies for building pseudo-gloss targets: rule-based morphological lemmatization and constrained LLM-assisted normalization over a fixed vocabulary. They then evaluate the pretrained encoder through cross-dataset sign spotting on a new TSL Spotting Benchmark built from the TSL Dictionary corpus, plus a downstream translation check.

Result: LLM-assisted normalization raises top-5 temporal localization mean IoU from 0.235 to 0.465, with 56.2% of examples reaching IoU ≥ 0.50; a frequency analysis indicates the gain is not mainly from memorizing frequent pseudo-gloss labels. In downstream translation, the same pretraining improves BLEU-4 from 9.60 to 11.04 and ROUGE from 23.48 to 27.43.

Conclusion: Loosely aligned broadcast data can serve as effective weak supervision for learning sign representations that capture both lexical content and temporal structure, yielding a reusable encoder that transfers across datasets and improves downstream tasks such as sign spotting and translation.

Abstract: Sign-language research for resource-constrained languages is often limited by the cost of dense linguistic labels such as glosses, temporal boundaries, and sign order. Broadcast news offers a practical alternative by pairing continuous signing with spoken-language transcripts, but this supervision is weak since text and signing are loosely aligned. Morphologically rich languages such as Turkish add further difficulty, as the same lexical meaning can appear in many inflected forms while some derived forms should remain distinct. We study whether weak transcript-based supervision can pretrain a reusable sign encoder in this setting, where poor text normalization can fragment pseudo-gloss targets and weaken representation learning. Unlike prior pseudo-gloss pipelines designed mainly to improve translation, we test whether the pretrained encoder transfers as a reusable representation for cross-dataset sign spotting. We pretrain on TSL-News, a new Turkish broadcast corpus, using pseudo-gloss labels derived from transcripts rather than manual annotation, comparing rule-based morphological lemmatization with constrained LLM-assisted normalization over a fixed vocabulary. We evaluate the learned representations via cross-dataset sign spotting on a new TSL Spotting Benchmark built from the TSL Dictionary corpus. The LLM-assisted encoder raises top-5 temporal localization mean IoU from 0.235 to 0.465, with 56.2% of examples reaching an IoU of at least 0.50; a frequency analysis suggests this gain is not mainly driven by memorizing frequent pseudo-gloss labels. In a downstream translation check, the same pretraining improves BLEU-4 from 9.60 to 11.04 and ROUGE from 23.48 to 27.43. These results show that loosely aligned broadcast data can provide effective weak supervision for learning sign representations that capture both lexical content and temporal structure.

</details>


### [7] [Better, Faster, Stronger: Programmatic Skill Learning Best Reduces Agent Cost](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11338)
*Zixi Huang,Xiheng Wang,Andrew Wang,William Jurayj,Bernal Jiménez Gutiérrez,Daniel Khashabi,Nicholas Andrews*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes SpeedRunner, a coding agent that learns skills as deterministic programs by analyzing past trajectories, achieving state-of-the-art cost reduction and performance across three embodied environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work on augmenting LLM agents with skills prioritizes performance gains over cost effectiveness. Little is known about which skill-learning strategies actually reduce cost. The authors argue that viewing skills as programs offers the best cost reduction by enabling deterministic, reliable execution of action sequences instead of costly trial-and-error, especially over long horizons.

Method: SpeedRunner learns skills at inference time by incrementally discovering programs from past trajectories and refactoring them for reuse on future tasks. It analyzes trajectory signals to guide skill learning without requiring replay or validation environments, exploiting the hypothesis that past trajectories already contain sufficient signal if the agent can learn to interpret them.

Result: Across three different embodied environments, SpeedRunner consistently achieves the frontier in both learning performance and cost reduction, while remaining robust to distribution shifts and environmental randomness.

Conclusion: Skills represented as programs enable reliable, cheap goal achievement for LLM agents. Learning them incrementally at inference time from past trajectories is a cost-effective adaptation strategy for novel domains, with robustness to distribution shift and stochasticity.

Abstract: Recently, the practice of augmenting LLM agent capability with skills has gained prevalence. We explore the cost effective adaptation of agents to novel domains by means of learning skills. Existing works focus on performance gain over cost effectiveness. As a result, little is known about what skill learning strategies save cost. We argue that among all the different skill learning methods, those that view skills as programs can achieve the best cost reduction. By executing sequences of actions deterministically, a program-augmented agent can reliably and cheaply achieve goals that would otherwise require trial and error and risk degenerate behavior over long horizons. An agent can learn at inference time by incrementally discovering these programs and equipping them for future tasks. We hypothesize that past trajectories contain enough signal to guide skill learning, even without replay or validation, provided the agent can learn to analyze them. To test our claims, we propose SpeedRunner, a coding agent that analyzes trajectories and refactors skills for better performance on future tasks. Across three different embodied environments, we show that SpeedRunner consistently achieves the frontier in learning and cost reduction while remaining robust against distribution shifts and environmental randomness.

</details>


### [8] [Self-Evolving Embodied Agents via Skill-Harness Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11350)
*Peidong Wang,Zhiming Ma,Ying Chang,Xufang Luo,Xiaocui Yang,Shi Feng,Yuqing Yang,Dongsheng Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SHAPER is a train-free framework that lets embodied agents self-improve by evolving reusable skills and a context-code harness around a frozen foundation model, using environment rollouts instead of any parameter updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embodied agents built on foundation models depend heavily on the non-parametric scaffolding (skills, context, action interfaces, execution harness) around the model. Adapting via SFT or RL is costly and requires extra data/rewards, while train-free code-centric methods assume programmable robot APIs unavailable in fixed-interface settings. This motivates a way to adapt agents without training and without assuming programmable interfaces.

Method: SHAPER keeps model weights frozen and instead optimizes the external, reusable skills and context-code harness by running the agent in the target environment. The same frozen model acts as both planner and optimizer, refining its skills and harness through rollouts without any gradient updates. Evaluation covers VLABench and ESI-Bench across different low-level action interfaces.

Result: SHAPER is compared against pure execution, supervised fine-tuning, and test-time-scaling baselines (verifier-free selection and voting). Results indicate that optimizing the skill-and-harness layer is a practical, competitive route to self-evolving embodied agents when training is expensive, unavailable, or undesirable.

Conclusion: Skill-and-harness optimization provides a viable train-free path to self-evolving embodied agents, offering an alternative to weight-level adaptation (SFT/RL) and to API-dependent code-centric approaches, particularly in constrained settings where training is costly or undesirable.

Abstract: Embodied agents are increasingly built as systems around foundation models, where performance depends not only on model weights but also on the skills, context, action interfaces, and execution harness surrounding the model. While supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning can adapt agents to new environments, they require additional data, rewards, and training runs; meanwhile, many train-free code-centric approaches rely on programmable robot APIs that may be unavailable in fixed-interface settings. We propose SHAPER, a self-evolving framework for train-free embodied adaptation that keeps model parameters frozen and improves the non-parametric agent system by evolving reusable skills and a context-code harness through target-environment rollouts. In SHAPER, the same frozen model can serve as both planner and optimizer, refining its external skills and context-code harness without parameter updates. We evaluate SHAPER on VLABench and ESI-Bench, covering embodied agents with different low-level action interfaces, and compare against pure execution, supervised fine-tuning, and test-time-scaling baselines such as verifier-free selection and voting. Our results suggest that skill-and-harness optimization is a practical route to self-evolving embodied agents when model training is expensive, unavailable, or undesirable.

</details>


### [9] [ODE-Based Transformer Decoders for Iterative Sign Language Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11352)
*Tuğçe Kızıltepe,Hacer Yalim Keles*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes improving sign language translation by replacing residual refinement updates in iterative refinement decoders with Runge–Kutta (RK-2/RK-4) ODE-inspired integration schemes, boosting accuracy without adding model parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent sign language translation gains rely on scaling model capacity, which increases computation. The authors seek a parameter-efficient alternative that improves decoder expressiveness and translation quality without increasing model size.

Method: The work reinterprets residual refinement updates in iterative refinement decoders from an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) perspective and substitutes them with higher-order numerical integration schemes, specifically Runge–Kutta methods (RK-2 and RK-4). Each refinement step performs multiple function evaluations to produce more accurate and stable latent representation updates without adding decoder parameters. This is claimed to be the first ODE-inspired update dynamics applied to sign language translation.

Result: RK-2 achieves 22.96 BLEU-4 on PHOENIX-2014-T and 19.34 BLEU-4 on CSL-Daily test sets, outperforming the IPSLT baseline on both benchmarks while using fewer decoder layers and refinement iterations on CSL-Daily.

Conclusion: Stronger refinement dynamics can improve translation performance under parameter-efficient decoder designs, offering a complementary alternative to conventional model scaling.

Abstract: Sign language translation has achieved strong results with Transformer architectures, yet recent improvements largely rely on scaling model capacity at the cost of increased computation. We propose a parameter-efficient alternative that improves expressiveness without increasing model size. Rather than scaling capacity, we focus on enhancing the update dynamics of iterative refinement decoders, where each refinement step corresponds to one internal decoder iteration that progressively improves the latent representation before translation generation. We reinterpret residual refinement updates from an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) perspective and replace them with higher-order numerical integration schemes, namely Runge--Kutta methods (RK-2 and RK-4). These methods perform multiple function evaluations within each refinement step to produce more accurate and stable representation updates without adding decoder parameters. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of ODE-inspired update dynamics to sign language translation. RK-2 achieves 22.96 BLEU-4 on the PHOENIX-2014-T test set and 19.34 BLEU-4 on the CSL-Daily test set, outperforming the IPSLT baseline on both benchmarks, with fewer decoder layers and refinement iterations on CSL-Daily. These results suggest that stronger refinement dynamics can improve translation performance under parameter-efficient decoder designs, providing a complementary alternative to conventional model scaling.

</details>


### [10] [Measure, Don't Optimize: Forecasting Recovery in LLM Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11408)
*Zirui Song,Huaxing Liu,Xiang Wang,Shuai Li,Xinye Li,Lang Gao,Jinghui Zhang,Zheng Lu,Fengxian Ji,Xiaojun Chang,Xiuying Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: J-Access is an inference-time audit using the Jacobian lens to measure residual accessibility of unlearned knowledge. Auditing 398 unlearned models shows most retain above-baseline access; accessibility predicts model-level recovery susceptibility but not specific facts, and directly optimizing it causes models to hide knowledge from the audit while recovering more after attack.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing white-box unlearning audits are only one-off diagnostics. It is unclear whether residual internal signals of retained knowledge can predict future recovery under continued training or serve as reliable optimization targets. Closing this gap determines whether internal auditing can move beyond post-hoc evaluation into proactive risk monitoring and safer unlearning.

Method: Propose J-Access, an inference-time audit that uses the Jacobian lens to map intermediate representations into vocabulary space and measures how often target concepts remain accessible along the model's output pathway. Audit 398 public unlearned models across eight unlearning methods, testing whether residual accessibility (hypothesized to reflect recovery susceptibility) predicts recovery speed/extent under attack, and whether minimizing J-Access promotes genuine deletion.

Result: (1) Most unlearned models retain access above the retain-only gold level. (2) Pre-attack accessibility predicts recovery speed and extent at the model level but cannot identify which specific facts will be recovered. (3) Directly minimizing J-Access does not produce genuine deletion; models instead learn to hide knowledge from the audit, yielding lower audit scores but greater post-attack recovery.

Conclusion: J-Access serves as a model-level diagnostic for residual susceptibility in unlearned models. Internal audits should be treated as an independent diagnostic dimension in unlearning evaluation and should not be converted into optimization targets without validation.

Abstract: Prior white-box studies show that large language models can retain latent traces of target knowledge after unlearning, even when the knowledge is no longer expressed in their outputs. However, existing audits remain limited to one-off diagnostics: it is unclear whether these residual signals can predict future recovery under continued training or serve as reliable optimization targets. Resolving this gap is essential to determine whether internal auditing can move beyond post-hoc evaluation toward proactive risk monitoring and safer unlearning. We propose J-Access, an inference-time audit that uses the Jacobian lens to map intermediate representations into vocabulary space and measures how often target concepts remain accessible along the model's output pathway. We hypothesize that residual accessibility reflects recovery susceptibility: knowledge that remains closer to the output pathway requires less fine-tuning to restore, leading to faster recovery. We audit 398 public unlearned models spanning eight unlearning methods. We find that: (1) most unlearned models retain access above the retain-only gold level; (2) pre-attack accessibility predicts recovery speed and extent at the model level, but cannot identify which specific facts will be recovered; and (3) directly minimizing J-Access does not promote genuine deletion. Instead, the model learns to hide knowledge from the audit, producing lower audit scores but greater post-attack recovery. These findings position J-Access as a model-level diagnostic for assessing residual susceptibility in unlearned models. We argue internal audits should serve as an independent diagnostic dimension in unlearning evaluation, and should not be converted into optimization targets without validation.

</details>


### [11] [Total Recall at What Cost? Benchmarking the Serving Cost of Agentic Memory Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11879)
*Natchanon Pollertlam,Witchayut Kornsuwannawit*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks the serving cost and answer accuracy of three memory systems (Mem0, Hindsight, Mastra Observational Memory) against a rolling window and full-transcript baselines, finding that cost depends on internal memory behavior rather than just conversation length/message size, break-even points versus the full transcript vary widely by system and backbone, and no system wins on both cost and accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-running conversational agents increasingly use memory systems to avoid resending the full conversation each turn, but the serving cost of these memory systems has received little systematic benchmarking. The authors aim to quantify how much memory systems actually cost to serve and how that cost relates to accuracy.

Method: The paper compares three memory systems (Mem0, Hindsight, and Mastra Observational Memory) against two reference strategies — a fixed-size rolling window and resubmitting the full transcript — using two backbones and conversations of up to 400 turns. Every cost measurement is paired with answer accuracy on 665 LoCoMo questions. The analysis includes a regression that tracks reference strategies against memory systems, and a break-even analysis of when memory systems become cheaper than the full transcript.

Result: A serving cost regression tracking the two reference strategies misses memory systems by 18–69%, showing cost is driven by internal memory behavior rather than conversation length and message size alone. Break-even analysis shows whether and when a memory system becomes cheaper than the full transcript is highly sensitive to the system and backbone — from the first tens of turns for the cheapest to never within 400 turns for the most expensive. No system wins on both axes: accuracy spans 21–54%, and backbone choice drives cost as much as the memory system does.

Conclusion: Memory system serving cost cannot be predicted from conversation length and message size alone, and the trade-off between cost and accuracy means no single system dominates; practitioners must evaluate cost and accuracy jointly, as both the memory system and the backbone materially affect outcomes.

Abstract: Long-running conversational agents increasingly rely on a memory system to avoid resending the whole conversation each turn, yet how much that costs to serve has received little systematic benchmarking. We compare three memory systems (Mem0, Hindsight, and Mastra Observational Memory) against two reference strategies -- a fixed-size rolling window and resubmitting the full transcript -- across two backbones and conversations of up to 400 turns, pairing every cost measurement with answer accuracy on 665 LoCoMo questions. First, a memory system's serving cost cannot be predicted from conversation length and message size alone: a regression that tracks the two reference strategies closely misses the memory systems by 18-69%, their cost driven instead by internal memory behavior. Second, a break-even analysis shows that whether -- and when -- a memory system becomes cheaper to serve than the full transcript is highly sensitive to the system and the backbone, from the first tens of turns for the cheapest to never within 400 turns for the most expensive. Third, no system wins on both axes: accuracy spans 21-54%, and the backbone choice drives cost as much as the memory system does.

</details>


### [12] [Is Convergence Inevitable? Tracing Output Homogeneity Back to Base Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11426)
*Alexandrine Fortier,Hazel Chen,Peter West*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates where output homogeneity (semantic convergence) in language models originates, arguing it is learned during pretraining and merely revealed or amplified by alignment, rather than caused by it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The lack of diversity in LM content is widely blamed on alignment, but it is unknown where in the pipeline this collapse actually begins. The authors aim to determine whether output homogeneity is introduced by alignment or originates earlier.

Method: The authors conduct controlled SFT (instruction-tuning) experiments to examine how training data affects output convergence on specific input/output pairs. They then measure convergence in base (pre-alignment) models and test whether instruct-like collapse can be induced through prompting alone without alignment.

Result: Semantic convergence is observed starting from the earliest alignment stage (SFT). Convergence can be revealed and amplified, but not introduced, by SFT data, acting as a catalyst rather than a cause. Instruct-like collapse can be induced in base models through prompting alone, without any alignment.

Conclusion: Semantic convergence likely arises naturally from the objectives underlying LM training, making it difficult to mitigate through post-alignment interventions alone.

Abstract: The lack of diversity in LM content is widely attributed to the alignment process, but how and where exactly in the pipeline this collapse begins is unknown. We argue that output homogeneity is likely learned during the pretraining phase, and only \emph{revealed} or magnified during the alignment process. Specifically, we find that semantic convergence is observed from the first alignment stage--the instruction-tuning phase (SFT)--suggesting that homogeneity might already exist in the pre-alignment model. To investigate this, we conduct controlled SFT experiments examining how training data influences output convergence on specific input/output pairs. We find that convergence can be revealed and amplified, but not introduced by the SFT data, supporting its role as a catalyst rather than a cause. To further test whether homogeneity originates before alignment, we measure convergence in base models. We find that instruct-like collapse can be induced through prompting alone, even without alignment. Taken together, our results suggest that semantic convergence may arise naturally from the objectives underlying LM training, making it difficult to mitigate through post-alignment interventions alone.

</details>


### [13] [LODESTAR: Trustworthy Entropy Is Navigated, Not Merely Measured -- Reinforced Polarizer Keeps a Frozen LLM from Being Confidently Misled by the Wrong Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11922)
*Po-Jen Ko,Che-Cheng Wu,Hung-Chun Hsu,Li-Yang Chang,Chuan-Ju Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LODESTAR introduces a learned, prompt-level "polarizer" string that uses RL to induce uncertainty in a frozen respondent LLM, beating entropy-based and other selection rules for retrieval-augmented QA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retrieval-augmented QA needs to select the best candidate answer without gold labels. Prior entropy-based selectors (choose the lowest answer-token entropy) work well overall but fail when a misleading passage makes the respondent confidently wrong, lowering entropy on the wrong answer. The authors show the failure is caused by the passage context, which is an input that can be intervened on.

Method: LODESTAR is the first method to score a text intervention by the uncertainty it induces in a third-party frozen respondent, compared across candidates for one question. It uses offline reinforcement learning to train a "polarizer"—a short, fixed natural-language string inserted into the respondent's prompt (never into its weights). Training labels are built offline from gold answers and two LLM judges; inference reads neither.

Result: Across 5,008 questions on five QA benchmarks under the same frozen respondent and candidate pools, LODESTAR reaches the highest mean F1 of any inference-ready selector (0.5339 vs. 0.5148 baseline), the highest exact match (0.4136), and the highest GPT-4o judge score (0.6435). Its three-seed mean wins all 70 method-by-dataset F1 cells against fourteen published configurations and is paired-significant against each. Gains hold in- and out-of-domain. Ablation: the polarizer makes the respondent read a misleading passage less often (26.0% vs 30.3%).

Conclusion: The lowest-entropy selection rule fails specifically on misleading passages that make a respondent confidently wrong. Intervening on the respondent's prompt with a learned polarizer string (LODESTAR) reliably improves answer selection, outperforming fourteen published configurations while remaining inference-ready and label-free at test time.

Abstract: Predictive-distribution entropy makes a strong selection rule in retrieval-augmented question answering: across five QA benchmarks, keeping the candidate answer that a frozen respondent LLM produces with the lowest answer-token entropy lifts mean answer $F_1$ from 0.4769 to 0.5148 over the retriever's top-ranked passage, with no gold answers. Yet this lowest-entropy rule, which prior entropy-based selectors adopt, fails in a specific and consequential way: a misleading passage makes the respondent confidently wrong, driving its entropy down precisely where the signal looks most trustworthy. We show that the failure comes from the passage the respondent reads -- and the context that passage is read in is an input we can intervene on. We introduce LODESTAR, to our knowledge the first method to score a text intervention by the uncertainty it induces in a third-party frozen respondent, compared across one question's candidates. LODESTAR uses reinforcement learning to train, once and offline, a polarizer -- a short fixed natural-language string inserted into the respondent's prompt and never into its weights; its training labels are built offline from gold answers and two LLM judges, and inference reads neither. Evaluating every competing selector under the same frozen respondent and the same candidate pools on 5,008 questions, LODESTAR attains the highest mean $F_1$ of any inference-ready selector (0.5148 to 0.5339), the highest exact match (0.4136), and the highest GPT-4o judge score of the frozen-respondent configurations judged (0.6435); its three-seed mean wins all 70 method-by-dataset $F_1$ cells against fourteen published configurations while remaining paired-significant against every one. The gain holds both in-domain and out-of-domain, and ablating the polarizer shows it is what makes the respondent read a misleading passage less often (26.0% against 30.3%).

</details>


### [14] [Stigma and Support in Online Sexual Violence Narratives on Reddit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11433)
*Shirlene Rose Bandela,Karan Bindal,Vaibhav Garg,Rezvaneh Rezapour*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SCOPE, a dataset linking stigma signals in online sexual-violence survivor posts to support types in comment threads, and analyzes how stigma shapes both narratives and peer responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior research has examined stigma and social support separately in online survivor communities, but little is known about how stigma expressed in survivor narratives relates to the support offered in responses. The authors aim to bridge this gap by connecting multi-dimensional stigma in posts to the types of support comments provide.

Method: The authors build the SCOPE dataset by annotating survivor posts with a multi-dimensional stigma taxonomy (Experienced, Internalized, Anticipated, and Structural Stigma) and annotating comment threads with a support taxonomy (Information Support, Emotional Support, Esteem Support, Tangible Assistance, and Group Interaction). They then perform contextual, linguistic, and emotion analyses to compare Stigma versus No Stigma content and examine how support varies across stigma types.

Result: Stigma narratives place greater emphasis on internalized distress, while No Stigma narratives focus more on interpreting situations and experiences. Internalized Stigma is the most prevalent stigma category. Community responses remain broadly stable across stigma types, with Information Support and Esteem Support appearing most often.

Conclusion: The findings show how stigma shapes survivor narratives and peer responses, with implications for computational modeling, content moderation, and designing safer online systems.

Abstract: Online communities increasingly provide spaces where survivors of sexual violence can share their experiences and seek support. Although prior research has examined stigma and social support separately, less is known about how stigma expressed in survivor narratives relates to the support offered in response. We introduce the SCOPE dataset, linking stigma signals in online survivor narratives to support types in corresponding comment threads. We annotate posts using a multi-dimensional stigma taxonomy, including Experienced, Internalized, Anticipated, and Structural Stigma, and comments using a support taxonomy encompassing Information Support, Emotional Support, Esteem Support, Tangible Assistance, and Group Interaction. Using contextual, linguistic, and emotion analyses, we compare Stigma and No Stigma content and find that Stigma narratives place greater emphasis on internalized distress, whereas No Stigma narratives focus more on interpreting situations and experiences. Internalized Stigma is the most prevalent category, and community responses remain broadly stable across stigma types, with Information and Esteem Support appearing most often. These findings show how stigma shapes survivor narratives and peer responses and have implications for computational modeling, content moderation, and safer online systems.

</details>


### [15] [A corpus-specific clinical RAG system matches or outperforms newer frontier LLMs on HealthBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12138)
*Praveen Reddy,Charuta Mandke,Suvrankar Datta,Sarah Khan,Siddharth Reddy Anthireddy,Shitij Arora,Vishal Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A purpose-built clinical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system called VITA, designed for low- and middle-income settings (India), achieved top scores on an open HealthBench medical benchmark against frontier LLMs under an initial judge but fell to statistical parity with GPT-5.5 under a neutral, independent judge, while retaining advantages in accuracy and completeness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior claims that general-purpose LLMs match or beat clinical AI tools rely on a narrow set of systems and benchmarks developed mainly in high-income settings, so the authors sought to test a LMIC-specific RAG system (VITA) against frontier general-purpose LLMs on an open, externally evaluable benchmark to assess whether corpus specificity still provides a grounding advantage.

Method: VITA is a retrieval-augmented generation system with a curated corpus of disease-specific guidelines, India-specific antimicrobial resistance data, national formulary constraints, and resource-limited care protocols. It was evaluated on 4,023 English-language HealthBench questions (80.5% of the benchmark) scored by a GPT-4.1 judge. A 500-question subset was re-run against current-generation models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Pro, Grok 4.3) and graded by a neutral open-weight judge (DeepSeek-V4-Pro) sharing no lineage with any tested system. The physician-written rubrics and all outputs and scores were made public.

Result: Under the GPT-4.1 judge, VITA ranked first with 51.9% of rubric points vs. GPT-5.4 (46.1%), o4-mini (44.3%), Gemini 3.1 Pro (42.6%), and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (37.3%), and scored highest on 45.4% of questions. Under the neutral DeepSeek-V4-Pro judge on the 500-question subset, VITA and GPT-5.5 were statistically indistinguishable on mean per-question score, while VITA led on points-weighted score and won the most questions. VITA retained advantages in accuracy and completeness but had lower communication scores.

Conclusion: A purpose-built clinical RAG system remains competitive with frontier LLMs on an open benchmark, indicating that corpus specificity is a useful design variable that improves grounding at some cost to communication polish.

Abstract: General-purpose large language models (LLMs) have recently been reported to match or exceed specialized clinical AI tools on medical benchmarks, but such comparisons draw on a narrow set of systems and on benchmarks developed largely in high-income settings. We evaluate VITA, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system purpose-built for contextual knowledge retrieval in India and other low- and middle-income (LMIC) settings. VITA retrieves from a curated corpus of disease-specific guidelines, India-specific antimicrobial resistance data, national formulary constraints, and resource-limited care protocols; its architecture and corpus are proprietary, but the benchmark, the physician-written rubrics, and our full response and scoring outputs are public for independent verification. On 4,023 English-language HealthBench questions (80.5% of the benchmark), scored with a GPT-4.1 judge, VITA ranked first with 51.9% of possible rubric points, ahead of GPT-5.4 (46.1%), o4-mini (44.3%), Gemini 3.1 Pro (42.6%), and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (37.3%), and scored highest on 45.4% of questions. To test robustness to newer models and judge lineage, a 500-question subset was re-run against current-generation models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Pro, Grok 4.3) and graded by a neutral open-weight judge (DeepSeek-V4-Pro) sharing no lineage with any system tested. Here the gap narrowed to parity: VITA and GPT-5.5 were statistically indistinguishable on mean per-question score, while VITA led on points-weighted score and won the most questions. VITA's advantages in accuracy and completeness persisted under the neutral judge; its communication scores were lower. These results indicate that a purpose-built clinical RAG system remains competitive with frontier LLMs on an open benchmark, consistent with corpus specificity as a design variable that improves grounding at some cost to communication polish.

</details>


### [16] [DonorRank: Donor Language Selection for Low-Resource Cross-Lingual Speech Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11441)
*Akriti Dhasmana,Aarohi Srivastava,David Chiang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DonorRank is a learning-to-rank framework that predicts which donor languages will enable the most effective zero-shot ASR transfer for low-resource languages, outperforming genetic-similarity and high-resource heuristics while also serving as an analytical tool for understanding donor selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-resource ASR relies on cross-lingual transfer from donor languages, but selecting good donors is hard for spontaneous speech in under-resourced communities due to linguistic variation, changing orthographic conventions, and uneven resource availability. Existing heuristics (genetic similarity, high-resource languages) are unreliable, motivating a principled, data-driven approach to donor ranking.

Method: The authors introduce DonorRank, a learning-to-rank framework that predicts effective donor languages for zero-shot ASR. It is evaluated on two multilingual speech corpora covering Indic and African language families, and is additionally used as a general framework to analyze donor selection itself, including how the donor set composition affects which linguistic cues predict successful transfer.

Result: DonorRank accurately predicts donor language rankings and improves donor selection over common heuristics based on genetic similarity or high-resource languages. Analyses show that the composition of the donor set determines which linguistic cues are useful for predicting transfer success, and they identify transfer patterns offering practical guidance for multilingual ASR in low-resource settings.

Conclusion: DonorRank provides both a practical improvement in donor selection for low-resource zero-shot ASR and a general analytical framework for understanding cross-lingual transfer, yielding actionable guidance for multilingual ASR development in under-resourced language communities.

Abstract: Low-resource automatic speech recognition (ASR) commonly relies on cross-lingual transfer, where models are adapted from higher-resource donor languages. However, selecting donors remains challenging for spontaneous speech from under-resourced language communities, due to linguistic variation, evolving orthographic conventions, and uneven resource availability. We present DonorRank, a learning-to-rank framework for predicting effective donor languages for zero-shot ASR. We evaluate DonorRank on two multilingual speech corpora of Indic and African language families. It accurately predicts donor language rankings and improves donor selection over common heuristics based on genetic similarity or high-resource languages. Beyond improving transfer, we show how DonorRank is a general framework for analyzing donor language selection itself. Our analyses show that the composition of the donor set determines which linguistic cues are useful in predicting successful transfer. We also identify transfer patterns that provide practical guidance for multilingual ASR in low-resource settings.

</details>


### [17] [Principal Trait Analysis: Towards Deriving "Skills" in Human-AI Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11460)
*Hunter McNichols,Kai Du,Andrew Lan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Principal Trait Analysis (PTA), a PCA-inspired, data-driven method that uses LLM processing stages to automatically derive "traits" of effective human-AI interaction from conversational traces, and evaluates it on educational and professional human-AI coding datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-powered agents become common in workplaces via human-AI collaboration, it is crucial to understand what prompting traits lead to task success and what skills modern professionals need. Existing guidelines are either top-down theory (which may lag rapidly improving LLM capabilities) or context-specific empirical observations (which may quickly become obsolete), motivating an automated, data-driven approach to uncover interaction patterns aligned with task outcomes.

Method: The authors propose Principal Trait Analysis (PTA), a Principal Component Analysis-inspired algorithm. PTA uses LLM-based processing stages to analyze corpora of human-AI collaborative session traces, derive common traits across the dataset, score each collaborator's usage style by each trait, allow domain expertise to be injected during trait discovery, and select the most distinguishing traits as those exhibiting the highest variance across collaborators.

Result: PTA is evaluated on two human-AI collaborative coding datasets: an educational setting (students with an AI tutor) and a professional setting (developers with an AI coding agent). PTA-derived traits significantly explain collaborator behavior in both settings and help predict task outcomes. However, whether traits qualify as skills remains inconclusive due to mixed results on generalizability and how user traits change over time.

Conclusion: The automated, data-driven PTA approach successfully uncovers traits of effective human-AI interaction that are aligned with task outcomes across educational and professional coding contexts. Yet further work is needed to establish whether these traits represent generalizable, stable skills, as generalizability and temporal stability of traits remain unresolved.

Abstract: Large Language Model-powered agents are increasingly used in the workplace via human-artificial intelligence (AI) collaboration. In this new era of work, it is important to understand the kinds of prompting traits that contribute to task success. Moreover, we need to uncover key skills required for modern professionals and inform educators on how to foster these skills among students. Existing guidelines for human-AI collaboration are built from either top-down theory or context-specific observations of human-AI interactions. However, since LLM capabilities are rapidly improving, theory may not be able to explain emerging interaction patterns, and empirical guidelines may become obsolete quickly. In this work, we explore an automated, data-driven approach to uncover patterns, which we term traits, of effective human-AI interaction that are aligned with task outcomes. We propose Principal Trait Analysis, a Principal Component Analysis-inspired algorithm for deriving common traits from patterns in LLM conversations. Our algorithm uses LLM-based processing stages to analyze corpora of human-AI collaborative session traces, deriving common traits across the dataset and scoring each human collaborator's usage style by each trait. The approach also allows domain expertise to be injected during trait discovery and selects the most distinguishing traits to be those that exhibit the highest variance across collaborators. We evaluate PTA on two human-AI collaborative coding datasets, an educational setting (students working with an AI tutor) and a professional setting (developers working with an AI coding agent). We find that PTA-derived traits are significant in explaining collaborator behavior across both settings and can help predict task outcomes. However, whether traits qualify as skills remains to be seen, due to inconclusive results on generalizability and how user traits change over time.

</details>


### [18] [Group Alignment-Induced Sycophancy: A Two-Sided Evaluation of Steerable Pluralistic Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11528)
*Haokai Zhao,Yunze Xiao,Weihao Xuan,Flora Salim,Benjamin Tag,Aditya Joshi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Group Alignment-induced Sycophancy (GAS) and shows that aligning language models to demographic groups creates non-uniform trade-offs: opinion-alignment gains and sycophancy shifts vary per group, arguing for reporting alignment as a two-sided, multi-dimensional profile rather than a single score.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing group alignment methods and evaluations only measure how closely a model matches a group's opinions, while overlooking the by-product of sycophancy (over-agreement). The authors aim to bridge this gap by jointly studying the intended gain in opinion alignment and the unintended shift in sycophantic behavior.

Method: The authors systematically evaluate group alignment across 3 alignment methods, 4 language models, and 13 demographic groups, measuring both the intended gain in opinion alignment and the unintended shift in sycophancy induced by alignment.

Result: The gain in opinion alignment and the induced sycophancy shift are non-uniform across groups: under an identical budget, some groups receive larger opinion-alignment gains than others, and the induced sycophancy shift forms a group-specific profile rather than a single-dimensional change.

Conclusion: Group alignment should be reported as a two-sided, multi-dimensional profile that accounts for per-group differences, rather than a single fit score, when adapting LLMs to diverse populations.

Abstract: Group alignment adapts a language model to a demographic group to produce responses that reflect the group's opinions, values, and preferences. Sycophancy, a well-documented by-product of alignment, causes the model to over-agree with the user regardless of factual and objective information. However, existing group alignment methods and evaluations focus only on how closely the model matches the group's opinions, overlooking the induced change in sycophantic behaviour. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{G}roup \textbf{A}lignment-induced \textbf{S}ycophancy (GAS) and systematically evaluate alignment across 3 methods, 4 models and 13 demographic groups, on both the intended gain in opinion alignment and the unintended shift in sycophancy. We find that gain and shift are non-uniform across groups: under an identical budget, some groups receive larger gains in opinion alignment than others, and the induced sycophancy shift forms a group-specific profile rather than a single-dimensional change. These results suggest that group alignment should be reported as a two-sided, multi-dimensional profile rather than a single fit score that accounts for per-group differences when adapting LLMs to diverse populations.

</details>


### [19] [On Weak Bisimilarities in CCSK](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11531)
*Baptiste Vallée,Ivan Lanese*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies bisimilarity notions in CCSK (reversible CCS), covering strong/weak and forward-only/reversible variants, and introduces two new weak reversible bisimilarities—directional and mixed—showing mixed bisimilarity is a congruence that fully abstracts away from τ actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reversible process calculi like CCSK extend CCS with backward computation, yet a systematic comparison of bisimilarity notions—especially weak reversible bisimilarity—was lacking. The authors aim to fill this gap and characterize the role of τ (silent/internal) actions under reversibility.

Method: The authors define and compare bisimilarity notions across two dimensions: strength (strong vs. weak) and directionality (forward-only vs. reversible). For the previously unstudied weak reversible case, they propose two variants: directional bisimilarity (where τ actions must match in the same forward/backward direction as the action being matched) and mixed bisimilarity (where τ direction need not align). They then analyze congruence properties and abstraction capabilities.

Result: The paper shows the differences and commonalities among the studied bisimilarities. Key findings: mixed bisimilarity is a congruence, and it completely abstracts away from τ actions, making it the most permissive and well-behaved of the weak reversible notions.

Conclusion: For CCSK, the weak reversible case is best captured by two new variants—directional and mixed bisimilarity—with mixed bisimilarity standing out as a congruence that fully abstracts τ actions, resolving a gap in the reversible process calculus literature.

Abstract: In the context of CCSK, a reversible extension of CCS, we study different notions of bisimilarity (strong/weak, forward-only/reversible) and highlight their differences and commonalities. In particular, for the weak reversible case, not previously studied in the literature, we propose two variants, dubbed directional and mixed bisimilarity, depending on whether $τ$ actions should be in the same direction (forward/backward) as the action being matched or not. We show, in particular, that mixed bisimilarity is a congruence and completely abstracts away from $τ$ actions.

</details>


### [20] [CT-$Δ$Bench: A Benchmark for Longitudinal 3D Medical Imaging Difference Reporting with Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11534)
*Kegeng Tang,Jingbo Wang,Shaogang Ren,Zihao Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces CT-ΔBench, a benchmark for longitudinal imaging difference reporting where models generate interval-change descriptions from two temporally separated CT scans of the same patient, along with change-aware evaluation metrics, physician validation, and a baseline direct paired-CT model (DeltaMed).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Longitudinal comparison of serial CT scans is central to clinical decision-making (response assessment, recurrence detection, patient management), yet existing medical foundation models are limited to single-study understanding and do not adequately address temporally grounded cross-examination of interval changes.

Method: Formulate a longitudinal imaging difference reporting task; build CT-ΔBench with patient-level splitting to prevent leakage; develop change-aware metrics capturing clinically meaningful longitudinal changes; perform independent physician validation of synthesized references and the event extraction pipeline; compare direct paired-CT reasoning against an indirect two-stage pipeline (single-timepoint reports followed by textual differencing); and propose DeltaMed, a baseline model for direct paired-CT difference reporting trained on the benchmark training set.

Result: The paper delivers a dedicated benchmark (CT-ΔBench), validated change-aware evaluation metrics, and a baseline model (DeltaMed), establishing resources and baselines for temporally aware medical foundation models, with evidence supporting the reliability of synthesized references and event extraction via independent physician validation.

Conclusion: The contributions lay the groundwork for temporally aware medical foundation models that better reflect real-world longitudinal clinical reasoning, moving beyond single-study understanding toward clinically grounded cross-examination of serial imaging.

Abstract: In medical imaging, the clinical value of Computed Tomography (CT) lies not only in depicting current disease status, but crucially in enabling longitudinal comparison of serial scans to determine disease evolution, a process that underpins response assessment, recurrence detection, and ongoing patient management. Yet, despite this central role of temporal comparison in clinical decision-making, existing medical foundation models remain largely confined to single-study understanding, leaving temporally grounded cross-examination insufficiently addressed. To address this gap, we study longitudinal imaging difference reporting, a task in which a model takes two temporally separated scans from the same patient and generates a clinically meaningful report describing interval changes between them. We introduce CT-$Δ$Bench, a dedicated benchmark for this task with patient-level splitting to prevent information leakage. To better evaluate this task beyond surface-level text similarity, we further develop change-aware metrics specifically designed to capture clinically meaningful longitudinal changes, and conduct an independent physician validation to assess the reliability of the synthesized references and event extraction pipeline. We also compare direct paired-CT reasoning with an indirect two-stage pipeline that first generates single-timepoint reports and then performs textual differencing. Finally, we propose DeltaMed, a baseline model for direct paired-CT difference reporting, and train it on the benchmark training set. Together, these contributions lay the groundwork for temporally aware medical foundation models that better reflect real-world longitudinal clinical reasoning.

</details>


### [21] [Beyond Single-Turn Confidence: Trajectory-Adapted Uncertainty Quantification for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11552)
*Dylan Bouchard,Mohit Singh Chauhan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods designed for single-turn language model outputs transfer to multi-turn LLM agent trajectories. It finds that transfer is useful but uneven: token-probability scores are sensitive to aggregator choice, reflexive self-assessment is the strongest low-cost baseline, and black-box self-consistency (especially trajectory-equivalence and action-set consistency variants) performs best overall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing UQ methods are evaluated on single-turn outputs where uncertainty attaches to a single answer. However, LLM agents produce interactive trajectories involving clarifying questions, tool calls, state updates, and intermediate decisions whose errors propagate to the final outcome. This raises the question of whether single-turn UQ methods transfer to the trajectory-level setting.

Method: The authors test three families of single-turn UQ methods across five LLMs and four multi-turn tool-use datasets from BFCL-v4 and τ²-bench: (1) white-box scorers based on action-token probabilities, (2) black-box consistency scorers based on resampled trajectories, and (3) reflexive scorers based on model self-assessment of the trajectory. They examine different consistency measurements, aggregators, and computational budgets.

Result: Transfer is often useful but uneven. Token-probability scores are highly sensitive to the choice of aggregator used across turns. Reflexive scores provide the strongest low-cost baseline in most evaluated settings. Black-box self-consistency is often the strongest UQ family, with trajectory-equivalence and action-set consistency typically ranking highest among its variants.

Conclusion: UQ methods developed for single generations should be revalidated at the trajectory level, with careful attention to consistency measurement, aggregator choice, and computational budget.

Abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for language models are typically evaluated on single-turn outputs, where uncertainty is attached to one generated answer. For LLM agents, however, the unit of observation is an interactive trajectory, where the model can ask clarifying questions, call tools, update state, and make intermediate decisions whose errors propagate to the final outcome. We study whether three common families of single-turn UQ methods transfer to this setting. Across five LLMs and four multi-turn tool-use datasets from BFCL-v4 and $τ^2$-bench, we evaluate white-box scorers based on action-token probabilities, black-box consistency scorers based on resampled trajectories, and reflexive scorers based on model self-assessment of the trajectory. We find that transfer is often useful but uneven. Token-probability scores are highly sensitive to the choice of aggregator used across turns, reflexive scores provide the strongest low-cost baseline in most evaluated settings, and black-box self-consistency is often the strongest UQ family, with trajectory-equivalence and action-set consistency typically ranking highest among its variants. These results suggest that UQ methods developed for single generations should be revalidated at the trajectory level, with careful attention to the consistency measurement, aggregator choice, and computational budget.

</details>


### [22] [Reinforcing Step-level Reasoning for Effective Self-Correction in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11573)
*Vu Duc Anh,Nhat M. Hoang,Do Xuan Long,Cong-Duy Nguyen,Ponhvoan Srey,Luu Anh Tuan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes SFS-DPO, a two-stage reinforcement-learning framework that first strengthens step-level reasoning via step-level preference optimization and then trains LLMs to self-verify and self-correct their own mistakes, with a teacher-assisted variant (SFS-DPO-R) that adds explanatory error rationales; both outperform prior step-level baselines across domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-correction—where models verify and correct their own errors—remains a fundamental challenge for LLMs. Prior approaches lack explicit step-level training for both verifying and correcting mistakes, motivating a framework that explicitly trains self-verification and self-correction while first strengthening step-level reasoning.

Method: SFS-DPO is a two-stage framework: (1) stage one strengthens step-level reasoning using step-level preference optimization; (2) stage two explicitly trains the model to self-verify and self-correct. A teacher-assisted variant, SFS-DPO-R, additionally incorporates explanatory rationales for error verification to provide stronger corrective signals.

Result: Comprehensive in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations across multiple LLMs show SFS-DPO and SFS-DPO-R consistently outperform prior step-level training baselines. Analysis reveals improved self-correction frequency and effectiveness, underscoring the value of strengthening step-level reasoning for robust performance.

Conclusion: Strengthening step-level reasoning is crucial for robust self-correction. Explicitly training self-verification and self-correction, optionally with teacher-provided error rationales, yields consistent gains in both self-correction frequency and effectiveness across domains.

Abstract: Achieving effective self-correction, where models verify and correct their own mistakes, remains a fundamental challenge for large language models (LLMs). In this work, we propose Self-Fix Step-DPO (SFS-DPO), a reinforcement learning based, two-stage framework for step-level self-verification and self-correction. The first stage strengthens step-level reasoning via step-level preference optimization, while the second stage explicitly trains models to self-verify and self-correct. We further introduce a teacher-assisted variant, SFS-DPO-R, which incorporates explanatory rationales for error verification to provide stronger corrective signals. Comprehensive in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations across multiple LLMs demonstrate that SFS-DPO and SFS-DPO-R consistently outperform prior step-level training baselines. Our analysis further reveals improvements in self-correction frequency and effectiveness, highlighting the importance of strengthening step-level reasoning for robust performance.

</details>


### [23] [Learning to Persuade Exposes How Easily LLMs Abandon Correct Beliefs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11624)
*Nimet Beyza Bozdag,Emre Can Acikgoz,Gokhan Tur,Dilek Hakkani-Tür*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A single optimized persuasive argument can collapse LLM accuracy to near zero; adversarially trained persuader agents raise persuasion success from ~24% to over 93% against a target model, transfer to unseen models, and increasingly exploit fabricated citations and false authority to change correct answers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persuasion is central to how LLMs update beliefs and make decisions, so resistance to harmful persuasion is a core reliability requirement. The authors show this requirement is unmet: a single targeted argument can flip even correct reasoning, motivating a formal treatment of "adversarial persuasion" and the need for persuasion robustness as a safety criterion.

Method: The authors formalize adversarial persuasion and introduce an adversarial reinforcement learning framework that trains persuader agents to change a target model's answer in a single interaction via trial-and-error optimization, plus a curriculum that bootstraps on more persuadable open-weight models before attacking harder ones.

Result: RL-trained persuaders raise persuasion success from ~24% to over 93% on the training-time persuadee; strategies transfer to unseen models (83% on Qwen-14B, 79% on Llama-3.1-8B, 25% on GPT-4o-mini); curriculum bootstrapping lifts GPT-4o-mini success from 25% to 38%; and optimized persuaders increasingly rely on credibility tactics such as fabricated citations and false authoritative evidence.

Conclusion: Even when LLMs initially reason correctly, optimized natural-language influence can steer them to false conclusions, exposing a critical weakness in current LLM agents and positioning persuasion robustness as a necessary safety criterion for multi-agent and human-AI decision-making systems.

Abstract: Persuasion is a core dynamic of natural language communication, shaping how large language models (LLMs) update beliefs, resolve disagreements, and reach decisions. As LLMs increasingly debate, advise, and think collaboratively with humans and each other, resistance to harmful persuasion becomes a core requirement for reliable behavior. Yet we show that this requirement is far from met: a single targeted persuasive argument is enough to collapse model accuracy to near zero, even when the argument is factually false. We formalize this threat as adversarial persuasion and introduce an adversarial reinforcement learning framework that trains persuader agents to change a target model's answer in a single interaction.
