First, we show that optimizing persuasion strategies through trial and error exposes vulnerabilities that static prompting misses: RL-trained persuaders raise persuasion success from approximately 24% to over 93% against the training-time persuadee. Second, we find that these learned strategies transfer to unseen models, achieving 83% attack success on Qwen-14B, 79% on Llama-3.1-8B, and 25% on GPT-4o-mini. Third, we demonstrate that a curriculum that bootstraps on more persuadable open-weight models before targeting harder models further increases GPT-4o-mini attack success from 25% to 38%. Moreover, our results reveal that optimized persuaders increasingly rely on credibility-based tactics, including fabricated citations and false authoritative evidence. Together, these findings expose a critical weakness in current LLM agents: even when they initially reason correctly, they can be steered toward false conclusions by optimized natural language influence. This positions persuasion robustness as a necessary safety criterion for multi-agent and human-AI decision-making systems.

</details>


### [24] [Easper: An Accessible ASR Pipeline for Language Documentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11629)
*Aso Mahmudi,Ting Dang,Ekaterina Vylomova,Nick Thieberger*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Easper is an open-source, no-code pipeline that lets field linguists fine-tune multilingual ASR models like Whisper on cloud resources directly from ELAN annotations. Using it, the authors test transcription prioritisation strategies on three Vanuatu languages and find that prioritising lexically rich narratives and increasing acoustic-phonetic repetition (even in noisy data) improves transcription quality fastest.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Audio transcription is a major bottleneck in language documentation. Multilingual ASR models such as Whisper could help, but field linguists typically lack the technical expertise to use them. There is also a cold start problem: determining which recordings to transcribe first to bootstrap an accurate ASR model.

Method: The authors present Easper, an open-source, no-code workflow that enables iterative fine-tuning of ASR models via cloud resources directly from ELAN annotations. They evaluate transcription prioritisation strategies by fine-tuning models per recording session on three Vanuatu languages (Bislama, Nafsan, Nguna) and compare Character Error Rate trajectories when prioritising acoustic cleanliness versus linguistic richness.

Result: Prioritising lexically rich narratives and increasing acoustic-phonetic repetition—even in noisy environments—leads to faster improvements in transcription quality, as measured by Character Error Rate trajectories.

Conclusion: Easper lowers the technical barrier for linguists to deploy ASR, and the prioritisation findings provide practical guidance for bootstrapping accurate transcription models in low-resource documentation settings.

Abstract: Audio transcription is a critical bottleneck in language documentation. While multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models like Whisper offer solutions, field linguists often lack the expertise to utilise them. We present Easper, an open-source, no-code workflow enabling linguists to iteratively fine-tune ASR models via cloud resources directly from ELAN annotations. Deploying ASR also raises a cold start problem: deciding which recordings to transcribe first to bootstrap an accurate model. Using Easper, we evaluate transcription prioritisation strategies on three Vanuatu languages (Bislama, Nafsan, Nguna). We fine-tune models by recording session, comparing Character Error Rate trajectories when prioritising acoustic cleanliness versus linguistic richness. We demonstrate that prioritising lexically rich narratives and increasing acoustic-phonetic repetition, even in noisy environments, leads to faster improvements in transcription quality.

</details>


### [25] [Who Would You Vote For? Auditing Political Alignment in LLMs: An Italian Case-Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11649)
*Simone Mungari*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents an auditing framework to systematically measure how LLMs evaluate political parties and leaders, applied via an Italian case study, focusing on observable behavior rather than inferred beliefs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for political information, especially during elections, and prior work shows they can influence users' political attitudes, making it important to understand how these models themselves evaluate political actors.

Method: A systematic, reproducible auditing framework prompting multiple LLMs to evaluate parties and leaders across nine criteria, measuring consistency, cross-model differences, refusal rates, prompt-formulation sensitivity, and variation under different instructed personas.

Result: The framework is demonstrated through an Italian case study, yielding a systematic analysis of LLM-generated political evaluations of Italian parties and leaders.

Conclusion: LLMs exhibit observable, measurable preferences toward political actors that can be audited for consistency, differences, and sensitivity; the proposed framework provides a reproducible means to assess such behaviors in electoral contexts.

Abstract: As users increasingly turn to Large Language Models (LLMs) for information and advice on political matters, particularly during election periods, the political preferences expressed by these systems have become a matter of public interest. Prior research has shown that interactions with LLMs can influence users' political attitudes and choices, raising questions about how these models themselves evaluate political actors. In this paper, we investigate whether and how LLMs express preferences toward political parties and political leaders. We introduce a systematic and reproducible auditing framework in which multiple LLMs are prompted to evaluate parties and leaders across nine criteria. Rather than attempting to infer the models' "true" political beliefs, we focus on their observable behavior, examining consistency across evaluations, differences between models, refusal rates, and sensitivity to prompt formulation. We further investigate how these evaluations vary when models are instructed to adopt different personas. We demonstrate the framework through an Italian case study, providing a systematic analysis of LLM-generated political evaluations on italian parties and leaders.

</details>


### [26] [Semantic Lenia: Emergence of Homeostatic Solitons within the Semantic Space of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11657)
*Yoshihiko Kayama*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Semantic Lenia reframes LLM inference as a continuous dynamical system in logit space, where a homeostatic feedback loop balancing semantic attraction and syntactic repulsion yields "Autonomous Semantic Solitons" that maintain generative trajectories at the edge of chaos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the limitation of treating LLM inference as a static optimization problem, which tends to produce repetitive, "crystallized" outputs, by instead modeling generation as a non-linear dynamical process capable of sustaining rich, non-repetitive trajectories.

Method: The authors introduce Semantic Lenia, an artificial life framework operating on the macroscopic logit space. A non-linear homeostatic feedback loop dynamically balances semantic attraction against syntactic repulsion, and exhaustive parameter sweeps map a critical "Habitable Ridge" where steering forces balance the model's intrinsic syntactic inertia, keeping trajectories at the edge of chaos.

Result: The framework produces emergent "Autonomous Semantic Solitons" (macroscopic dissipative structures that avoid repetitive crystallization) and enables generative trajectories at the edge of chaos, triggering "profound abductive leaps" without structural collapse. The work also establishes a physical scaling law for machine cognition.

Conclusion: Treating LLM inference as a continuous dynamical system with homeostatic semantic-syntactic balance enables stable, non-degenerate generation at the edge of chaos, suggesting a physically grounded scaling law for machine cognition.

Abstract: We introduce Semantic Lenia, an artificial life framework that transforms Large Language Model (LLM) inference from a static optimization problem into a continuous dynamical system within the macroscopic logit space. By establishing a non-linear homeostatic feedback loop to dynamically balance semantic attraction and syntactic repulsion, we demonstrate the emergence of "Autonomous Semantic Solitons" -- macroscopic dissipative structures that avoid repetitive crystallization. Our exhaustive parameter sweeps map a critical "Habitable Ridge" where applied steering forces perfectly balance the model's intrinsic syntactic inertia. This approach successfully maintains generative trajectories at the edge of chaos, triggering profound abductive leaps without structural collapse and establishing a physical scaling law for machine cognition.

</details>


### [27] [Hybrid-Policy Self-Editing for Composable Unstructured Knowledge Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11660)
*Tianci Liu,Zihan Dong,Tianchun Li,Yi-Chung Chen,Qiming Cao,Xingchen Wang,Shiyang Wang,Zichen Miao,Linjun Zhang,Haoyu Wang,Jing Gao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper addresses Unstructured Knowledge Editing (UKE), where edits are free-form passages. Existing editors inject the passage but the model cannot answer atomic or multi-hop questions about it; the authors term this missing ability "composability." They propose viewing editing as proactive self-distillation from a privileged in-context state and introduce HPSE, a hybrid rollout method that injects missing facts onto the student's own trajectory only where on-policy coverage fails, improving composability across multiple LLMs and editors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are trained on static corpora, so their knowledge becomes outdated. Knowledge editing (KE) updates specific knowledge without affecting unrelated knowledge. Recent work moves toward unstructured KE (UKE), where edits are free-form passages stating multiple facts. However, current editors inject the passage yet fail to actually use it: the edited model can reproduce the passage but cannot answer atomic questions about its facts or compose them into multi-hop reasoning. The authors attribute this missing "composability" to editors' passive reliance on the fixed passage as the sole learning source.

Method: The authors cast editing as proactive self-distillation from a privileged in-context state of the same model, requiring no external supervision. They observe that because injected knowledge is novel, the pre-edited model's own rollouts rarely cover it, limiting pure on-policy distillation. To address this, they propose HPSE (Hybrid Passage-grounded Self-distillation for Editing), which builds a hybrid rollout that steps in to place missing facts onto the student's own trajectory exactly where its coverage fails, while remaining on-policy elsewhere. They also provide a theoretical analysis of HPSE's advantage over pure on-policy distillation and validate it empirically across four LLM backbones and two KE editors under various scenarios.

Result: HPSE delivers plug-and-play improvements across four LLM backbones and two KE editors under various scenarios, establishing its advantage over pure on-policy distillation both theoretically and empirically. The edited models gain composability, enabling them to answer atomic questions about facts in the passage and compose them into multi-hop reasoning.

Conclusion: The paper shows that the missing composability in UKE stems from editors' passive reliance on the fixed passage. By reframing editing as proactive self-distillation from a privileged in-context state and introducing HPSE's hybrid rollout, the approach closes the coverage gap from novel knowledge and yields plug-and-play composability improvements across models and editors.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable performance across natural language tasks, yet they are trained on static corpora and their knowledge quickly becomes outdated in a fast-changing world. This motivates knowledge editing (KE), which updates specific knowledge in an LLM without changing unrelated others. Recent works move from structured knowledge triples toward unstructured KE (UKE), where the edit is a free-form passage that may state multiple facts at once. Nonetheless, existing editors inject such a passage yet fail to use it: the edited model can recall the passage, but can neither answer atomic questions about its facts nor compose them into multi-hop reasoning. We attribute this missing property, which we term composability, to editors' passive reliance on the fixed passage as the sole learning source. In response, we cast editing as a proactive self-distillation from a privileged in-context state of the same model, which requires no external supervision. We further reveal that due to the novelty of the injected knowledge, the pre-edited model's own rollouts rarely cover it, which limits the effectiveness of pure on-policy distillation. To close this gap, we propose HPSE, which builds a hybrid rollout that steps in to place missing facts onto the student's own trajectory precisely where its coverage fails, while staying on-policy elsewhere. We theoretically analyze HPSE's advantage over pure on-policy distillation, and empirically establish its plug-and-play improvements across four LLM backbones and two KE editors under various scenarios.

</details>


### [28] [The Wording Effect: Quantifying Two-Way Drift in LLM Benchmark Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11694)
*Shailja Thakur,Sungeun An,Chad DeLuca,Hima Patel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Benchmark scores are based on a single phrasing per problem, but rephrasing a problem while preserving its meaning routinely flips model answers—a phenomenon the authors call "drift." BenchDrift generates meaning-preserving variations along four axes and shows drift is large in both directions: weak models gain more than they lose, while strong models lose far more than they gain, making top models the most phrasing-sensitive.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper argues that a benchmark score derived from one phrasing is misleadingly treated as representative of all equivalent phrasings of a problem, when in fact model correctness is highly sensitive to wording. The motivation is to quantify this "drift"—how often and why correctness flips under meaning-preserving rephrasing—and to expose the fragility of benchmark evaluations.

Method: The authors introduce BenchDrift, a tool that generates meaning-preserving variations of benchmark problems along four axes: linguistic, referential, pragmatic, and structural. They measure how often and why correctness flips across eight models and three benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, MATH-Hard), analyzing the direction, magnitude, and model agreement of drift.

Result: Drift is large in both directions. Phrasing sensitivity does not fade as models improve; instead it changes sign—weak models gain more from rephrasing than they lose, while strong models lose far more than they gain. The best models on a benchmark are those whose scores depend most on the given wording. Models largely agree on which rephrasings cost the most correct answers, indicating fragility belongs to the rephrasing rather than the specific model, and rephrasing breaks answers a model was confident about regardless of whether the problem is shortened or lengthened.

Conclusion: Benchmark scores are fragile and wording-dependent, especially for the strongest models, so single-phrasing evaluations do not reflect robust capability. Understanding and accounting for drift is essential for reliable model evaluation.

Abstract: A benchmark score comes from a single phrasing of each problem. That single phrasing is treated as if it stood for the whole space of ways the same problem could be asked, but it does not. We show that rephrasing a problem while keeping its meaning and answer fixed routinely flips a model's answer in both directions, so some failures become successes and some successes become failures. We call this drift. BenchDrift generates meaning-preserving variations of benchmark problems along four axes, namely linguistic, referential, pragmatic, and structural, and measures how often, and why, correctness flips under each. Across eight models and three benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, MATH-Hard), we observe that drift is large in both directions. Two findings stand out. First, phrasing sensitivity does not fade as models get better. Instead, it changes sign. Weak models gain more from rephrasing than they lose, while strong models lose far more than they gain. We find that the best models on a benchmark are therefore the ones whose scores depend most on the wording they happened to be given. Second, the models largely agree on which rephrasings cost the most correct answers even though they differ in how much they drift, so fragility belongs to the rephrasing and not to the model. Furthermore, rephrasing breaks answers a model was confident about, whether the problem is made shorter or longer. Code and Data: https://github.com/IBM/BenchDrift/tree/demo-ui

</details>


### [29] [When the API Speaks the Wrong Language: Revisiting Post-Training for Multilingual Tool Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11715)
*Siddharth Chauhan,Thomas Butler,Abhishek Singhania,Pankaj Porwal,Honey Gupta*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper studies "Argument Language Mismatch" (ALM), a failure mode where LLMs pick the correct API tool but generate argument values in a wrong/inconsistent language, which standard API-calling metrics miss. It finds that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a strong baseline that mostly matches or beats reinforcement learning (RL), with RL (e.g., GRPO) offering only incremental, targeted gains in generalization and multi-objective trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM reliability for API calling degrades in multilingual settings due to ALM—outputs that are semantically correct but operationally invalid in language. Standard API-calling metrics fail to capture this, motivating a systematic revisit of post-training strategies to mitigate ALM and improve end-to-end function call accuracy.

Method: The authors construct a benchmark for multilingual API grounding and compare post-training strategies: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) as a baseline versus reinforcement learning (RL), including Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with structured, argument-aware rewards. They evaluate argument language consistency, end-to-end function call accuracy, general reasoning ability, and multi-objective trade-offs.

Result: SFT substantially improves argument language consistency and end-to-end accuracy, performing comparably to or better than more complex RL approaches under consistent model selection. RL (GRPO) improves language consistency and better preserves general reasoning, but gains are incremental and mainly appear in generalization and multi-objective trade-offs.

Conclusion: Much of multilingual API grounding performance can be achieved through careful supervised training, with RL providing targeted rather than fundamental improvements; ALM should be explicitly measured as a distinct failure mode beyond standard API-calling metrics.

Abstract: The reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) for API calling degrades in multilingual settings. A common failure occurs when a model selects the correct tool but generates argument values in an inconsistent language, which we term Argument Language Mismatch (ALM). Although semantically correct, such outputs are operationally invalid and not captured by standard API-calling metrics. We revisit post-training strategies for mitigating ALM and find that, in our benchmark, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides a strong baseline, substantially improving argument language consistency and end-to-end function call accuracy. Under consistent model selection, SFT achieves performance comparable to, and sometimes exceeding more complex reinforcement learning (RL) approaches. We further examine whether RL with structured, argument-aware rewards offers additional benefits. While methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) can improve language consistency and better preserve general reasoning ability, these gains are incremental and most pronounced in generalization and multi-objective trade-offs. Overall, our results suggest that much of the performance in multilingual API grounding can be achieved through careful supervised training, with RL providing targeted rather than fundamental improvements.

</details>


### [30] [Locating and Controlling Implicit Personalization in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11735)
*Yueru Yan,Siqi Wu,Thai Le*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs adjust outputs to implicit demographic cues, and a localized internal activation signal tracks these shifts (up to r=0.87). Removing this signal can suppress a cue's influence causally, often better than prompting, though selective removal is model- and attribute-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs shift outputs in response to implicit demographic cues even when no demographic identity is stated by users. While this behavior is documented, the link between these behavioral changes and the model's internal activations is unclear, motivating an investigation of the mechanistic basis of implicit personalization.

Method: Using matched cued and neutral conversations across five LLMs, the authors locate an internal activation signal correlated with recommendation changes (up to r=0.87). They test how signals from multiple co-occurring cues combine, and apply causal interventions by removing the cue-associated signal, comparing this against prompting the model to ignore demographics, while evaluating general benchmark performance.

Result: A localized internal signal tracks changes in recommendations with correlations up to r=0.87. Multiple cue signals largely combine internally, but output changes do not sum additively. Removing the internal signal for one cue suppresses its influence, often more effectively than prompting, while mostly preserving benchmark performance. Selective removal of one dimension's influence while preserving co-present dimensions is highly model- and attribute-specific.

Conclusion: Implicit personalization behavior is connected to an identifiable internal signal that can be causally controlled, linking behavioral shifts in LLM outputs to interpretable internal activations.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often shift their outputs in response to implicit demographic cues even when users never state a demographic identity. Previous work has documented this behavior, but the connection between these behavioral changes and the model's internal activations remains unclear. Using matched cued and neutral conversations across five LLMs, we establish that a localized internal activation signal tracks changes in recommendations, with correlations up to r=0.87. When multiple cues appear together, their internal signals largely combine, but the changes in output do not simply add up. We further show that removing the internal signal associated with one cue can suppress its influence, often more effectively than asking the model to ignore demographics via prompting, while largely preserving general benchmark performance. However, the ability to selectively remove one dimension's influence while leaving co-present dimensions intact remains highly model- and attribute-specific. These results connect implicit personalization behavior to an internal signal that can be analyzed and causally controlled.

</details>


### [31] [Ripple-Pivot Search: Active Parallel Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11742)
*Yushi Ye,Xu Chen,Haoyun Jiang,Jinsong Lan,Haihong Tang,Bo Han,Ivor Tsang,Yanfeng Wang,Bo Zheng,Jiangchao Yao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RPS exploits a "ripple effect" in diffusion LLM decoding — committing a mid-entropy pivot proactively reduces uncertainty elsewhere — enabling more parallel token unmasking and achieving 4–10× speedup (up to 18× with KV caching) while preserving quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing parallel decoding schedulers for diffusion LLMs only commit positions after they pass a per-position confidence criterion, ignoring how an early commitment can benefit downstream decoding of other positions. The authors observe that proactively committing a mid-entropy pivot position can sharply reduce uncertainty across remaining masked positions, and seek to exploit this ripple effect to accelerate decoding.

Method: They propose Ripple-Pivot Search (RPS), a training-free decoding method with two components: (1) where to decode — searching for mid-entropy positions as promising candidate pivots, and (2) what to decode — using lookahead evaluation to select the token assignment for the pivot that yields the greatest downstream uncertainty reduction, then unmasking more tokens in parallel in subsequent steps.

Result: Across 3 dLLMs and 4 reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, RPS achieves 4–10× wall-clock speedup over the standard decoder while preserving generation quality, improves accuracy over the previous lookahead baseline by up to 5.49% with higher throughput in most settings, and reaches up to 18× speedup when integrated with KV caching.

Conclusion: Exploiting the ripple effect via proactive pivot commitment and lookahead evaluation substantially accelerates diffusion LLM decoding without training, improving both speed and accuracy over prior parallel decoding approaches.

Abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have emerged as a competitive alternative to autoregressive language models, offering the potential for substantially faster inference through parallel decoding. Existing parallel decoding schedulers typically commit positions only after they meet a per-position criterion, overlooking how early commitments may benefit subsequent decoding. We identify a ripple effect in dLLM decoding: proactively committing a mid-entropy pivot position can induce a pronounced reduction in uncertainty across the remaining masked positions. This uncertainty reduction allows subsequent steps to unmask more tokens in parallel, thereby accelerating the overall decoding process. To exploit the ripple effect, we propose Ripple-Pivot Search (RPS), a novel training-free decoding method that seeks mid-entropy positions as promising candidate pivots (where to decode), and determines their token assignment that yields the greatest downstream benefit via lookahead evaluation (what to decode). Across 3 dLLMs and 4 reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, RPS achieves 4-10$\times$ wall-clock speedup over the standard decoder while preserving generation quality, and improves accuracy over the previous lookahead baseline by up to 5.49% while delivering higher throughput in most settings. When integrated with KV caching, RPS further achieves up to 18$\times$ wall-clock speedup over the standard decoder.

</details>


### [32] [LabelFusion-TS: Fusing Large Language Models, Transformer Encoders, and Financial Time Series for Monetary-Policy Stance Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11753)
*Michael Schlee,Fabian Lukassen,Christoph Weisser*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces \lfts{}, a financial text classifier that augments RoBERTa and a large language model with market time-series transformers, and shows that adding this market modality improves hawkish/dovish/neutral classification of Federal Reserve communication under low-data conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Financial text is written and interpreted within a market environment, but standard financial text classifiers receive text alone. The authors investigate whether accompanying financial time series provide useful signal for classifying Federal Reserve sentences, especially given the scarcity of human-annotated data (only ~1,000 sentences).

Method: \lfts{} extends the \lf{} architecture with a market modality via a small voting network that combines three independently trained components: (1) a fine-tuned RoBERTa encoder, (2) a prompted large language model (LLM), and (3) a fused ensemble of time-series transformers over market series from months preceding publication. To cope with limited labels, RoBERTa is first pre-trained on sentences auto-annotated by the LLM and then fine-tuned on human labels. Trained on FOMC communication up to 2015; evaluated on 2015-2022.

Result: The fused system achieves 70.2% weighted F1, compared to 64.1% for the zero-shot LLM, and surpasses the LLM with as few as 240 human-labelled sentences.

Conclusion: The results provide initial evidence that market time series are a useful input modality for financial text classification.

Abstract: Financial text is produced and interpreted within a market environment, yet financial text classifiers almost always receive text alone. We study whether financial time series are useful as an additional input on the task of classifying sentences from Federal Reserve communication as hawkish, dovish, or neutral. Our system, \lfts{}, extends the \lf{} architecture with this modality: a small voting network combines three independently trained components, a fine-tuned RoBERTa encoder, a prompted large language model (LLM), and a fused ensemble of time-series transformers over the market series of the months preceding publication. Because only about a thousand annotated sentences are available for training, the RoBERTa encoder is first pre-trained on sentences annotated automatically by the LLM and only then fine-tuned on the human labels. Trained on Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) communication up to 2015 and evaluated on 2015--2022, the fused system achieves 70.2\% weighted F1 -- against 64.1\% for the zero-shot LLM -- and overtakes it with as few as 240 human-labelled sentences. We take this as initial evidence for market time series as an input modality in financial text classification.

</details>


### [33] [AWARe: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting via Activation-Weighted Adaptive REtention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11758)
*Juncheng Liao,Jinfan Lv,Guoming Wang,Jupeng Zheng,Ling Xiao,Siliang Tang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AWARe is a fine-tuning method for Multimodal LLMs that assigns activation-based importance scores to parameters and selectively freezes important ones, mitigating catastrophic forgetting without modifying model architecture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning MLLMs on downstream tasks causes catastrophic forgetting because gradient updates overwrite parameters critical to previously acquired capabilities, limiting practical deployment.

Method: AWARe dynamically controls parameter updates based on activation patterns. It computes activation-based importance scores per parameter, selectively freezing those essential for preserving prior capabilities while allowing less important parameters to adapt to new tasks. It requires no architectural modification, ensuring compatibility with existing inference engines.

Result: Extensive experiments show AWARe effectively preserves upstream capabilities while achieving superior downstream performance compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: AWARe offers a practical, architecture-agnostic solution to catastrophic forgetting in MLLM fine-tuning, balancing retention of prior knowledge with acquisition of new task-specific skills.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit strong generalization and reasoning abilities due to large-scale multimodal pre-training. However, fine-tuning these models on downstream tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where newly learned task-specific knowledge degrades previously acquired capabilities. This issue arises because gradient updates for new tasks overwrite parameters critical to prior knowledge, limiting the practical deployment of MLLMs. To address this challenge, we propose Activation-Weighted Adaptive REtention (AWARe), a fine-tuning method that mitigates catastrophic forgetting by dynamically controlling parameter updates based on activation patterns. AWARe assigns activation-based importance scores to parameters, selectively freezing those essential for preserving prior capabilities while allowing less important parameters to adapt to new tasks. Importantly, AWARe operates without modifying model architectures, ensuring compatibility with existing inference engines. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AWARe effectively preserves upstream capabilities while achieving superior downstream performance compared to existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/kaln27/AWARe.

</details>


### [34] [Causal Structure is Inducible but Functionally Decoupled: The Routing/Readout Boundary of a Typed Mechanism Library](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11767)
*Xining Xun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A study showing transformers organize causal knowledge into a type-supervised, slot-by-type routing structure that is functionally decoupled from answer readout, with preregistered evidence across two scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to determine whether and how transformers internally organize causal/interventional knowledge by evidence type, and whether any induced type-level structure causally drives (or is merely correlated with) answer readout. The authors aim for auditability and preregistered, machine-checkable claims rather than vague interpretability narratives.

Method: A causal-world benchmark with exact interventional ground truth is used under a frozen protocol. A "typed mechanism library" of discrete, auditability state-level mechanism slots partitioned by evidence type is introduced. Type-level supervision is compared against architecturally identical unsupervised controls and content-free gating labels, at 22.6M and 125M scales. Ablations measure effect on answer readout (delta-y-hat), editability/revertibility, and language-model quality vs. a parameter-matched monolith.

Result: Four preregistered findings: (i) Origin — slot-by-type organization is induced only by type-level supervision (absent in unsupervised controls, not producible by content-free gating labels), replicating across scale with all nine cells passing. (ii) Boundary — the structure is a typed routing index with a sharp routing/readout boundary; slot codes scaffold routing but do not drive answer readout (|delta-y-hat| ≤ 3.4e-6, zero collateral, stable across 3 seeds and 5.6x scale). (iii) Cost — structure is free; LM quality matches a monolith within 0.0082 nats. (iv) Trust — library state is exactly local under edit and bit-exactly revertible (250 single-edits and 1,000 stacked reverts per seed, zero failures). Additionally, the unsupervised null itself shifts with scale, so reusing a null calibrated at one scale can confound comparisons at another. One failed criterion and the frozen protocol's handling of it are documented.

Conclusion: Transformers exhibit an induced, type-supervised slot-by-type routing structure that is real and trustworthy yet functionally decoupled from answer readout, so no behavioral-editability claim is made. The work emphasizes preregistered, machine-checkable criteria and cautious, bounded interpretations of mechanistic structure.

Abstract: When a language model answers an interventional question, the computation it must perform depends on the type of evidence the query requires. We report a decoupling in how a transformer organizes causal knowledge: slot-by-type structure induced by type-level supervision organizes routing, yet remains functionally decoupled from answer readout. We establish this with a typed mechanism library -- discrete mechanism slots partitioned by evidence type, auditable at the state level -- on a causal-world benchmark with exact interventional ground truth, under a frozen protocol, at two scales (22.6M and 125M). Four preregistered findings. (i) Origin. Slot-by-type organization is induced by type-level supervision: absent in architecturally identical unsupervised controls, not buyable by content-free gating labels, and statistically attributable to the supervision signal, replicating at 125M under a powered preregistered protocol (all nine cells passed). (ii) Boundary. The induced structure is a typed routing index with a sharp routing/readout boundary: slot codes scaffold routing but do not drive answer readout ($|Δ\hat{y}| \le 3.4\times10^{-6}$, zero collateral, three seeds, stable across a 5.6x scale window) -- we therefore make no behavioral-editability claim. (iii) Cost. The structure is free: LM quality matches a parameter-matched monolith within 0.0082 nats. (iv) Trust. The library state is exactly local under edit and bit-exactly revertible -- 250 single-edit and 1,000 stacked reverts per seed, zero failures. We further find that the unsupervised null itself moves with scale, so comparisons reusing a null calibrated at one scale may be confounded at another. Every claim is tied to a preregistered, machine-checkable criterion archived before the data it governs; the full audit trail, including one criterion we failed and how the frozen protocol handled it, is released as an appendix.

</details>


### [35] [Diagnosis Before Recovery: Turning Agent Failures into Selective Self-Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11772)
*Pan Wang,Yihao Hu,Hang Wang,Zirui Lv,Xin Zhang,Jianshe Li,Jiang-Ming Yang,Wei Wu,Yongqi Tong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DARC is a diagnosis-guided recovery harness that profiles task-family failure modes to decide which correction interventions are admissible before test time, converting self-correction from generic prompt expansion into selective recovery-interface design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-correction helps when failures provide typed recovery signals (as in coding with compilers/tests), but broad language-agent tasks expose only coarse task failures. Generic recovery playbooks broaden context exactly when a narrower repair interface is needed, mixing incompatible signals for invalid actions, missing procedures, and strict-format errors. The goal is to recover the missing diagnostic substrate from development-set failures.

Method: DARC profiles task-family failure modes, prunes mismatched interventions from a shared recovery library, and freezes a verifier-selected success-cost policy for deployment. It operates in a causal order: first determine what kind of failure can be repaired, then decide how much recovery evidence to spend. The same protocol is instantiated as an action-validity harness (ALFWorld), a procedural-recovery fallback (AppWorld), and a format-precision retrieval policy (XBRL Finance).

Result: In ALFWorld, AppWorld, and XBRL Finance, DARC improves average task performance over base agents and broad playbooks while reducing environment steps or retrieval budget, demonstrating that failures need not trigger uniformly more context.

Conclusion: DARC turns self-correction from prompt expansion into recovery-interface design, offering a practical route to more reliable agents in domains lacking compiler-like feedback by making failures actionable before making contexts larger.

Abstract: Self-correction is particularly useful when a failure constrains the next repair. Coding agents benefit from this property because compilers, tests, and execution traces turn many failures into typed recovery signals, but broad language-agent tasks often expose only a coarse task failure. This creates a tension for generic recovery playbooks: they broaden the agent's context precisely when the system needs a narrower repair interface, mixing incompatible signals for invalid actions, missing procedures, and strict-format errors. Our insight is that development-set failures can recover part of the missing diagnostic substrate by deciding which recovery interventions are admissible before test-time correction. We propose DARC, a diagnosis-guided recovery harness that profiles task-family failure modes, prunes mismatched interventions from a shared recovery library, and freezes a verifier-selected success-cost policy for deployment. This causal order makes correction selective: the harness first determines what kind of failure can be repaired, then decides how much recovery evidence to spend. In ALFWorld, AppWorld, and XBRL Finance, the same protocol yields an action-validity harness, a procedural-recovery fallback, and a format-precision retrieval policy; in each evaluated setting it improves average task performance over base agents and broad playbooks while reducing environment steps or retrieval budget. Our experiments show that failures need not trigger uniformly more context: DARC turns self-correction from prompt expansion into recovery-interface design. DARC provides a practical route toward more reliable agents in domains where compiler-like feedback is absent: making failures actionable before making contexts larger.

</details>


### [36] [Language-Conditional Dequantization: Recovering What Quantization Steals from Non-English Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11786)
*Nirmal Thomas*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Quantization degrades multilingual models much more severely on non-English languages. The authors introduce Language-Conditional Dequantization (LCD), a post-hoc, per-language rank-2 LoRA correction for already-quantized models that is cheap (0.12% params/language, <20 min on one GPU) and recovers most of the perplexity and accuracy lost, especially for non-Latin scripts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aggressive quantization (sub-4B INT3 GPTQ) disproportionately damages multilingual capability, causing 2-4x larger perplexity degradation on non-English languages than English. Existing corrections are either language-agnostic or data-free and insufficient for typologically distant languages.

Method: Propose Language-Conditional Dequantization (LCD): attaching per-language rank-2 LoRA corrections to the linear layers of an already-quantized model, with only 0.12% added parameters per language and under 20 minutes of single-GPU training. Also introduce a layer-restricted LCD variant to probe error localization.

Result: On Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B, LCD recovers 70-83% of the perplexity gap for non-Latin script languages and 17-28% of the GlobalMMLU accuracy gap. It outperforms a language-agnostic correction of equal capacity by 3-9 points on typologically distant languages and a data-free low-rank baseline (LQER) by an order of magnitude. Analysis reveals a perplexity-accuracy disconnect: early-depth errors (Llama) propagate and resist local correction, while late-depth errors (Qwen) do not.

Conclusion: LCD is an effective, lightweight post-hoc fix for multilingual quantization damage, with language-specific corrections substantially better than agnostic or data-free baselines. The depth at which quantization errors concentrate explains why perplexity recovery does not always translate to accuracy recovery.

Abstract: Aggressive quantization disproportionately harms multilingual capability: in the sub-4B INT3 GPTQ regime, we measure 2-4x larger perplexity degradation on non-English languages than on English. We propose Language-Conditional Dequantization (LCD), a post-hoc method that attaches per-language rank-2 LoRA corrections to the linear layers of an already-quantized model, adding 0.12% parameters per language and training in under 20 minutes on a single GPU. Across Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B, LCD recovers 70-83% of the perplexity gap for non-Latin script languages and 17-28% of the GlobalMMLU accuracy gap, outperforming a language-agnostic correction of equal capacity by 3-9 points on typologically distant languages and a data-free low-rank baseline (LQER) by an order of magnitude. We further identify a perplexity-accuracy disconnect and trace it to where quantization concentrates damage: early-depth errors (Llama) propagate downstream and resist local correction, while late-depth errors (Qwen) do not. A layer-restricted variant of LCD validates this mechanism directly.

</details>


### [37] [GRPO for Financial Advice Generation: Outperforming Commercial LLMs under CATE Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11787)
*Ofir Ben Shoham,Shrutendra Harsola,Vignesh Subrahmaniam,Shravan Mohan,Yakov Gazman,Oded Vainas*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper frames financial advice generation as a reinforcement learning problem, fine-tuning an open-weight LLM with GRPO using an LLM-as-a-judge rubric plus a safety gate, and validates it with an independent doubly-robust CATE audit showing roughly double the gross-profit lift of the best commercial baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generating actionable financial advice requires numerical reasoning, domain knowledge, and judgment, but direct supervision is hard because historical decisions are not necessarily optimal and free-form labels are expensive. Moreover, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation alone may reflect adaptation to the judge rather than genuine business value, so an independent audit is needed.

Method: The authors formulate advice generation as reinforcement learning and fine-tune an open-weight language model using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). The reward combines an LLM-as-a-judge rubric scoring multiple binary dimensions of advice quality with a safety gate for harm prevention. For validation, they add a judge-independent off-policy audit based on a standard doubly-robust Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) estimator.

Result: Under the causal audit, the trained LLM achieves about twice the estimated gross-profit lift of the strongest commercial baseline (0.0228 vs 0.0104), with the lowest downside rate and least negative tail risk. The two evaluation methods rank baselines differently: the untrained base model is last on the judge rubric but second on the causal audit, indicating the audit captures signal the judge misses.

Conclusion: GRPO with a finance-grounded reward signal produces substantially more useful business recommendations than commercial LLMs, and a judge-independent causal audit is a valuable complement to, rather than a mere confirmation of, LLM-as-a-judge assessment in financial NLP.

Abstract: Generating actionable financial advice from business records demands that models integrate numerical reasoning, domain knowledge, and sound judgment, while avoiding recommendations that could harm the business. Direct supervision is difficult: historical decisions are not necessarily optimal, and high-quality free-form labels are expensive to obtain. We formulate financial advice generation as a reinforcement learning problem and fine-tune an open-weight language model using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Our reward is an LLM-as-a-judge rubric that scores each recommendation across multiple binary dimensions of advice quality, augmented with a safety gate for harm prevention.
  Since LLM-based evaluation alone cannot confirm whether improvements reflect genuine business value rather than adaptation to the judge, we complement it with a judge-independent audit based on a standard doubly-robust Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) estimator. Under this observational off-policy audit, our trained LLM achieves approximately twice the estimated gross-profit lift of the strongest evaluated commercial baseline ($0.0228$ vs.\ $0.0104$), together with the lowest downside rate and the least negative tail risk of any policy evaluated. Notably, the two evaluations do not rank the baselines identically: the untrained base model places last on the judge rubric but second on the causal audit, indicating that the audit captures a signal the judge does not. Our results demonstrate that GRPO with a finance-grounded reward signal can produce substantially more useful business recommendations than commercial LLMs, and that a judge-independent causal audit is a valuable complement to, rather than a confirmation of, LLM-as-a-judge assessment in financial NLP.

</details>


### [38] [TELLME: Test-Enhanced Learning for Language Model Enrichment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11788)
*Minjun Kim,Inho Won,Hyeonseok Lim,MinKyu Kim,Junghun Yuk,Wooyoung Go,Jongyoul Park,Jungyeul Park,KyungTae Lim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TELLME combines Test-Enhanced Learning with continual pre-training to make domain adaptation more data- and compute-efficient, yielding up to 23.6% improvement in finance and 9.8% better long-term memory retention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continual pre-training (CPT) for domain adaptation suffers from two persistent bottlenecks: the difficulty of collecting large-scale domain-specific corpora and the high computational cost of training. The authors seek an efficient method that improves domain knowledge acquisition and retention without these burdens.

Method: The paper proposes Test-Enhanced Learning for Language Model Enrichment (TELLME), which integrates the Test-Enhanced Learning (TEL) principle into continual pre-training. During training, quizzes (test-like retrieval practice) are used to boost training efficiency, promoting efficient acquisition of domain-specific knowledge while strengthening long-term memory retention.

Result: TELLME outperforms existing methods by up to 23.6% in the financial domain and achieves a 9.8% improvement in long-term memory retention.

Conclusion: Integrating Test-Enhanced Learning into continual pre-training effectively mitigates the data and cost challenges of domain adaptation, delivering both superior domain performance and stronger long-term knowledge retention.

Abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) has been widely adopted as a method for domain adaptation in large language models. However, CPT has consistently been accompanied by challenges, such as the difficulty of acquiring large-scale domain-specific datasets and high computational costs. In this study, we propose a novel method called Test-Enhanced Learning for Language Model Enrichment (TELLME) to alleviate these issues. TELLME leverages the TestEnhanced Learning (TEL) principle, whereby the model's training efficiency is improved using quizzes during training. It integrates this principle with CPT, thereby promoting efficient domain-specific knowledge acquisition and long-term memory retention. Experimental results demonstrate that TELLME outperforms existing methods by up to 23.6% in the financial domain and achieves a 9.8% improvement in long-term memory retention.

</details>


### [39] [Hybrid Gated Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11805)
*Zekun Zhou,Ruobing Xie,Lanrui Wang,Weixuan Sun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Hybrid Gated Attention (HyGA), a framework with three gating strategies that combine multi-stage information to improve attention's representational capacity, training efficiency, and stability over Gated Attention, verified across benchmarks and backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gated attention effectively mitigates attention sinks and boosts attention's representational capacity, but there is room to further extend its effectiveness-efficiency Pareto frontier. The authors aim to achieve more comprehensive information-flow control and stronger representational capacity via multi-source gating signals.

Method: HyGA introduces three gating strategies that leverage information from multiple stages of attention, collaboratively producing element-wise and head-wise gates to capture intra-head and cross-head interactions. It also incorporates low-rank matrix decomposition and a learnable attention sink to improve training efficiency and stability.

Result: HyGA comprehensively improves both training loss and downstream performance over Gated Attention across widely-used benchmarks and backbones, and achieves the best performance at different computation costs, supported by detailed model analyses.

Conclusion: The proposed HyGA provides a more effective, efficient, and stable attention mechanism, shedding light on improved attention designs through hybrid, multi-source gating and structural efficiency techniques.

Abstract: Gated attention is an effective approach to mitigate attention sinks and enhance the representational capacity of attention. To further extend its effectiveness-efficiency Pareto frontier, we propose a Hybrid Gated Attention (HyGA) framework that contains three types of gating strategies. Specifically, these gates leverage diverse information from multiple stages of attention, and collaboratively build element-wise/head-wise gating from multiple perspectives, capturing intra-head and cross-head information interactions. Through our hybrid gating components, HyGA could provide multi-source modulation signals, enabling more comprehensive control over information flow and improving the representational capacity of attention. We also introduce low-rank matrix decomposition and learnable attention sink to further enhance training efficiency and stability. In experiments, we evaluate HyGA on widely-used benchmarks based on different backbones. The experimental results show that our HyGA comprehensively improves both training loss and various downstream performances compared with Gated attention. HyGA has also been verified to achieve the best performance at different computation costs, with comprehensive model analyses for better understanding. The proposed HyGA sheds light on a more effective, efficient, and stable attention mechanism.

</details>


### [40] [Located but Not Releasable: Silent Gate Inversion and Bounded Linear Release](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11822)
*Xining Xun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A fully preregistered stress test of the detect–localize–release pipeline on a 25.7M causal-evidence transformer finds that localization succeeds but both gating (OOD-inverted detector) and linear release (capped far below sufficiency) fail, dissociating these failures while preserving the localization result.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work reports that language models encode task-relevant latent structure they fail to behaviorally use, but whether this structure can actually be converted into correct behavior is rarely tested end to end. The authors aim to rigorously test the complete detect–localize–release pipeline against a known suppression phenomenon under full preregistration.

Method: A 25.7M transformer trained on causal-evidence discrimination with a documented suppression phenomenon (latent causal structure present but unused) is subjected to a complete detect–localize–release pipeline. Every threshold, claim template, and decision-tree branch was hashed and archived before any data existed. Interventions target observation-evidence channels of mid layers; a detector is calibrated on out-of-distribution worlds, and an unconditional per-instance linear release direction is injected to test dose-response.

Result: (i) Localization succeeds: interventions restore target behavior with paired release advantages 0.563 and 0.854 (97.5% CIs excluding zero; best-site release rate 0.889). (ii) Gating fails OOD: the detector triggers on 6.9–7.3% of held-out in-distribution generations but on zero of the 2,400 generations that need it, silently reducing the gated pipeline to its base model. (iii) Linear release is capped: unconditional dose-response plateaus (intercept 0.382 to 0.311 to 0.264 vs. threshold ≤ 0.08), with per-instance adaptivity adding less than ±0.03.

Conclusion: Two dissociable failures are located: the detector is OOD-inverted, and the family of linear release directions is bounded away from sufficiency; neither failure overturns localization. All numbers trace to hashed artifacts in a released audit chain.

Abstract: A growing body of work reports that language models represent task-relevant latent structure that they fail to use. Whether such structure, once located, can be converted into behavior is a separate question that is rarely tested end to end. We submit the complete pipeline -- detect, localize, and release -- to a fully preregistered stress test on a 25.7M transformer trained on causal-evidence discrimination, where a known suppression phenomenon (latent causal structure present but behaviorally unused) has previously been documented. Every threshold, claim template, and decision-tree branch was hashed and archived before any corresponding data existed. Three findings. (i) Localization succeeds: interventions at observation-evidence channels of mid layers restore target behavior on otherwise-suppressed worlds (paired release advantages $0.563$ and $0.854$, 97.5% CIs excluding zero; best-site release rate $0.889$). (ii) Gating fails out of distribution: a detector calibrated to trigger on zero out-of-distribution calibration worlds triggers on 6.9-7.3% of held-out in-distribution generations and on zero of the 2,400 held-out generations that actually need it -- a complete inversion that silently reduces the gated pipeline to its base model. (iii) Linear release is capped: removing the gate and injecting a per-instance linear direction unconditionally yields a monotone dose-response that plateaus far below the preregistered release margin (intercept $0.382 \to 0.311 \to 0.264$ vs. threshold $\le 0.08$); per-instance adaptivity adds less than $\pm 0.03$. The failure is doubly located: the detector is OOD-inverted, and the entire family of linear release directions at this site and resolution is bounded away from sufficiency. The two failures are dissociable, and neither overturns localization. Every number traces to a hashed artifact in the released audit chain.

</details>


### [41] [When the Knowledge Base Becomes the Gold Standard: Measuring Resource-Shared Evaluation Loops in Entity-Level Machine Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11843)
*Jinhyung Bae,Dain Kil,Seongmin Oh,Seungmin Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper exposes a circular-evaluation (self-referential) problem in low-resource historical entity translation: when the knowledge base used to evaluate translations is also the resource injected into the translation system, reported gains are inflated and measure instruction compliance rather than genuine translation quality. Using independent expert annotations, the authors quantify this loop, show its non-uniformity, and demonstrate that apparent KB-injection gains vanish on untrained data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Seungjeongwon Ilgi (a UNESCO Memory of the World record) is only 37.4% translated, and the dominant failure mode in machine translation is person-name translation, which corrupts historical facts. Low-resource historical domains lack expert gold standards, so practitioners substitute an injected knowledge base for the gold standard, making evaluation self-referential. The paper aims to measure and expose this evaluation loop.

Method: Using expert person-name annotations from the National Institute of Korean History as an independent gold (outside the injection pipeline), the authors hold the entity set fixed and vary only the provenance of the correct reading. They compare agreement between injected readings and human translations across overlapping vs. independent segments, and conduct a difference-in-differences analysis across four models to isolate the causal effect of KB injection. They also build an independent sample by removing the construction filter to test whether the metric reflects model properties rather than sample properties.

Result: Of 527 expert-annotated mentions, only 31.1% lie outside the injection pipeline. In the overlapping segment, injected reading agrees with human translation 97.8% of the time vs. 70.1% in the independent segment. Across four models, the gain from KB injection is confined to the segment whose gold shares the injected resource; in the independent segment it is zero or negative. Post-injection preservation clusters in a 0.910-0.996 band despite fivefold baseline capability differences, meaning weaker models appear to improve more. On the independent sample, the measure replicates within models (overlapping intervals) while discriminating between models (non-overlapping intervals).

Conclusion: KB-injection gains in low-resource historical person-name translation are largely artifacts of self-referential evaluation. The apparent improvement tracks the proportion of the gold that overlaps the injected resource rather than actual translation capability, so the loop must be broken by using gold data independent of the injection pipeline for meaningful evaluation.

Abstract: The Seungjeongwon Ilgi, a UNESCO Memory of the World record, is only 37.4% translated, and the most conspicuous failure mode in automatic translation is the person name -- a misread name corrupts the historical fact rather than merely the surface. Low-resource historical domains have no expert gold standard for entity translation, so practitioners substitute a knowledge base (KB) for the gold. That KB is the same resource injected into the system: scoring becomes self-referential and the metric measures instruction compliance rather than translation quality.
  We measure this loop. Using expert person-name annotations from the National Institute of Korean History as a gold independent of the injection pipeline, we hold the entity set fixed and vary only the provenance of the correct reading. Of 527 expert-annotated mentions, only 31.1% lie outside the injection pipeline, and the residual loop is not uniform -- in the overlapping segment the injected reading agrees with the human translation 97.8% of the time against 70.1% in the independent one, so the segment that looks healthiest is the one the loop is holding up.
  Across four models, a difference-in-differences analysis shows the gain from KB injection is confined to the segment whose gold shares the injected resource; in the independent segment it is at or below zero. Post-injection preservation clusters in a narrow 0.910-0.996 band even though baseline capability differs fivefold, so the reported gain is the complement of prior performance and weaker models appear to improve more dramatically. On an independent sample built by removing the construction filter, the measure replicates within model (overlapping intervals) while discriminating between models (non-overlapping intervals) -- it reflects a property of the model, not of the sample.

</details>


### [42] [LazyTrain: Limited-resource Allocation toward Zero-waste Yield Optimization in Large Language Model Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11919)
*Xiaojun Wu,Cehao Yang,Honghao Liu,Xueyuan Lin,Xuhui Jiang,Chengjin Xu,Jia Li,Jian Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LazyTrain is an optimization layer over a layer-streaming executor that formulates checkpointing, activation placement, recomputation, and CPU-GPU-NVMe overlap as a mixed-integer scheduling problem, and combines 8-bit optimizer states with fast gradient clipping into a Hybrid 8-bit operator. It achieves ~1.24x sustained TFLOPS over baselines on H800 and larger batch sizes on RTX 3090, reaching 219.95 TFLOPS and 1361 tokens/s for Qwen3.6-27B.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training large language models on limited hardware is fundamentally a scheduling problem spanning GPU compute, host memory, PCIe transfer, and storage bandwidth. Existing offloading systems (e.g., MegaTrain's CPU-master layer-streaming executor) reduce GPU residency, but their fixed checkpointing and placement heuristics leave communication on the critical path, limiting efficiency and maximum feasible batch size.

Method: LazyTrain formulates checkpoint selection, activation placement, recomputation, and CPU-GPU-NVMe communication overlap as a mixed-integer scheduling problem, then executes the solved policy during training. It also introduces a Hybrid 8-bit operator that couples 8-bit optimizer states with fast gradient clipping: state compression reduces optimizer-state memory, while fast clipping offsets the extra CPU-side update overhead.

Result: On H800 experiments from Qwen2.5-3B to Qwen3.6-27B, LazyTrain improves sustained TFLOPS over matched baselines by ~1.24x. On RTX 3090, it increases the maximum feasible batch size by one at each model scale. In the primary Qwen3.6-27B H800 MetaMathQA run, it reaches 219.95 TFLOPS and 1361 tokens/s at batch size 72, peaks at 68.84 GB GPU memory, and achieves 95.42% exact-match accuracy on the full evaluation split.

Conclusion: LazyTrain demonstrates that treating LLM training offloading as a globally solved scheduling/optimization problem, combined with a memory-efficient Hybrid 8-bit optimizer operator, substantially improves throughput and memory headroom over fixed-heuristic baselines, enabling large-model training on single-GPU hardware. The source code is publicly available.

Abstract: Training large language models on limited hardware is increasingly a scheduling problem across GPU compute, host memory, PCIe transfer, and storage bandwidth. Existing offloading systems reduce GPU residency, and MegaTrain shows that a CPU-master layer-streaming executor can train large models on a single GPU, but fixed checkpointing and placement heuristics still leave communication exposed on the critical path. We propose LazyTrain, an optimization layer over a layer-streaming executor. LazyTrain formulates checkpoint selection, activation placement, recomputation, and CPU-GPU-NVMe communication overlap as a mixed-integer scheduling problem, then executes the solved policy during training. It further couples 8-bit optimizer states with fast gradient clipping as a single Hybrid 8-bit operator: state compression reduces optimizer-state memory, while fast clipping counteracts the additional CPU-side update overhead. Across H800 experiments from Qwen2.5-3B to Qwen3.6-27B, LazyTrain improves sustained TFLOPS over matched baselines runs by approximately 1.24$\times$; RTX 3090 experiments likewise increase the maximum feasible batch size by one at each model scale. In the primary Qwen3.6-27B H800 MetaMathQA run, LazyTrain reaches 219.95 TFLOPS and 1361 tokens/s at batch size 72, peaks at 68.84\,GB of GPU memory, and obtains 95.42\% exact-match accuracy on the full evaluation split. The source code is available at https://github.com/DataArcTech/LazyTrain.

</details>


### [43] [Spark-to-Paper: End-to-End Research Paper Generation as a Composable Skill](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11924)
*Zhuoyang Qian,Biao Wu,Yiran Wang,Chris D Yan,Desan Dai,Liangwei Zheng,Jin Jiang,Junsheng Zhang,Wenhao Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Spark-to-Paper is an end-to-end research paper generation system built as thirteen composable skills within an existing coding assistant. It separates model judgment from deterministic, checkable operations; separates experiment planning from reporting so claims are revised based on measured evidence; and uses integrity checks, self-critique, and programmatic figures to improve reliability. Across eight topics it achieves 99.5% citation validity and 96.4% figure editability, costs $8.1 per manuscript over 3.2 hours, and markedly improves detection of fabricated results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generating a full research paper requires far more than text generation: retrieving literature, designing and running experiments, revising claims against actual evidence, producing publication-ready figures, and maintaining consistency across a long generation process. Existing approaches lack lightweight, reliable ways to do this inside a coding assistant without a separate agent/orchestration platform, and suffer from reliability failures like fabricated results or repeating experiments that reject the original objective (the Self-Refutation Loop).

Method: The system implements thirteen composable skills within an existing coding assistant. Key design principles: (1) separating model-based judgment from deterministic operations that can be directly executed and checked; (2) separating experiment planning from reporting so required evidence is specified before results are observed, and claims are revised according to measured outcomes; (3) combining deterministic integrity checks with self-critique to bound the Self-Refutation Loop; and (4) producing editable vector figures via programmatic plotting for experimental results and code-based reconstruction for method diagrams.

Result: Across eight controlled research topics, Spark-to-Paper achieves 99.5% citation validity and 96.4% figure editability. A controlled ablation raises fabrication detection from 14% for a single-pass draft to 92% with the full integrity and review stack, while adversarial review achieves 74% precision. The full system uses 11.9M tokens, costs $8.1 per manuscript, and requires 3.2 hours on average.

Conclusion: End-to-end research paper generation can be implemented as a lightweight, composable workflow inside existing coding assistants while keeping experimental evidence central to how claims are accepted, revised, or abandoned.

Abstract: Turning a research idea into a complete paper requires more than text generation: the system must retrieve literature, design and execute experiments, revise claims according to evidence, produce publication-ready figures, and maintain consistency across a long generation process. We present Spark-to-Paper, an end-to-end research paper generation system implemented as thirteen composable skills inside an existing coding assistant, without requiring a separate agent platform or orchestration service. Spark-to-Paper separates model-based judgment from deterministic operations that can be directly executed and checked. It further separates experiment planning from reporting, so that required evidence is specified before results are observed and manuscript claims are revised according to measured outcomes. To improve reliability over long research trajectories, the system combines deterministic integrity checks with self-critique and bounds a failure mode we call the Self-Refutation Loop, in which repeated experiments continue to reject the original research objective. Spark-to-Paper also produces editable vector figures through programmatic plotting for experimental results and code-based reconstruction for generated method diagrams. Across eight controlled research topics, Spark-to-Paper achieves 99.5% citation validity and 96.4% figure editability. A controlled ablation increases fabrication detection from 14% for a single-pass draft to 92% with the full integrity and review stack, while adversarial review achieves 74% precision. The full system uses 11.9M tokens, costs $8.1 per manuscript, and requires 3.2 hours on average. These results show that end-to-end research paper generation can be implemented as a lightweight, composable workflow inside existing coding assistants while keeping experimental evidence central to how claims are accepted, revised, or abandoned.

</details>


### [44] [Accuracy and Order Sensitivity Diverge Under Label-Free Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11947)
*Karl Hanna,Chen Feng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper finds that removing option order bias in multiple-choice benchmarks (via generation-then-matching or scoring options in isolation) does not reliably improve accuracy, and pinpoints withholding options—not the matching step—as the main bottleneck.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MCQ scores conflate a model's underlying knowledge with sensitivity to option order, making them unreliable as measures of model knowledge. The authors test whether hiding option labels during commitment eliminates positional influence and improves performance.

Method: Two debiasing strategies are evaluated: (1) generation-then-matching (generate an answer then match it to options), and (2) scoring each option in isolation (positionally unbiased by construction). The approach is decomposed to isolate the effect of withholding options versus the matching step, and includes a configuration showing all options paired with an LLM matcher. Additional analyses use cyclic permutation and two-stage prompting with recall imbalance and per-question order sensitivity measures.

Result: Neither strategy reliably improves accuracy. The decomposition shows the bottleneck is withholding options, not the matching step. The only configuration matching the baseline shows all options with an LLM matcher. Eliminating positional influence still fails to reliably yield accuracy gains, whereas cyclic permutation often improves them. For two-stage prompting, neither recall-imbalance nor per-question order-sensitivity measures show reliable debiasing.

Conclusion: Removing option-order sensitivity alone does not translate into reliable accuracy improvements, indicating that positional bias is not the primary factor limiting MCQ performance, and that current debiasing methods do not consistently recover model knowledge.

Abstract: Multiple-choice benchmarks are widely used to evaluate large language models, but MCQ scores conflate knowledge with sensitivity to option order, which makes them unreliable measures of model knowledge. In this paper, we test whether preventing a model from seeing option labels while committing to an answer removes positional influence and, in turn, improves performance. We evaluate two different strategies for mitigating bias. The first uses a generation-then-matching approach, and the second scores options in isolation, which is positionally unbiased by construction. Neither reliably improves accuracy. A complete decomposition shows that the bottleneck is withholding options, not the matching step. The only configuration that consistently matches the baseline is the one that shows the model all options paired with an LLM matcher. However, eliminating positional influence entirely still does not reliably yield accuracy gains, while cyclic permutation often improves them. For two-stage prompting, an aggregate measure of recall imbalance and a direct per-question measure of order sensitivity both fail to show reliable debiasing.

</details>


### [45] [Benchmarking Trustworthiness of SLMs: Pre-trained vs. Compressed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11981)
*Haokun Lin,Kaijie Zhu,Haobo Xu,Yichen Wu,Zhichao Lu,Qingfu Zhang,Zhenan Sun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how compression techniques (pruning, quantization, distillation) affect the trustworthiness (fairness, robustness, privacy, ethics) of Small Language Models, finding that quantizing reliable large models yields more trustworthy SLMs than both pruning and training small models from scratch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SLMs are gaining traction for resource-constrained settings, yet while trustworthiness has become a critical concern for deployed language models, how to build trustworthy SLMs remains largely unexplored.

Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive evaluation of SLM trustworthiness across fairness, robustness, privacy, and ethics dimensions. They compare: (1) pruning versus quantization of pre-trained models, (2) compression of large models versus training small models from scratch, and (3) the effect of knowledge distillation from trustworthy teacher models.

Result: Quantization is significantly more effective than pruning at preserving trustworthiness. Compressing a reliable large model via quantization produces SLMs with superior trustworthiness and adaptability compared to small models trained from scratch. Knowledge distillation from trustworthy teachers further enhances SLM reliability.

Conclusion: The findings offer practical guidance for building trustworthy SLMs, recommending quantization of reliable large models and distillation from trustworthy teachers over pruning or from-scratch training, and lay a foundation for future research in trustworthy SLM development and deployment.

Abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) have emerged as a more efficient alternative to traditional Large Language Models (LLMs), offering promising potential in resource-constrained scenarios. Existing approaches to building SLMs typically follow two paths: training compact models from scratch, or compressing larger pre-trained models using methods such as pruning, quantization, or distillation. As language models become increasingly integrated into real-world applications, ensuring their trustworthiness has become a critical concern. However, how to build trustworthy SLMs remains an underexplored question. In this work, we present a comprehensive evaluation of SLM trustworthiness across multiple dimensions, including fairness, robustness, privacy, and ethics. We first examine the effects of pruning and quantization, and find that quantization is significantly more effective in preserving trustworthiness compared to pruning. More importantly, we demonstrate that compressing a reliable large model via quantization can produce SLMs with superior trustworthiness and adaptability compared to using small models trained from scratch. Furthermore, knowledge distillation from trustworthy teacher models can further enhance the reliability of SLMs. We hope our findings provide practical guidance and a foundation for future research into the development and deployment of trustworthy small language models.

</details>


### [46] [Asymptotic Risk Calibration for Selective Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12008)
*Shufan Lin,Sijin Dong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A-CRC-QA is a training-free, post-hoc calibration framework for uncertainty-aware selective question answering that reframes error control under selection as a linear expectation constraint and uses a monotonized empirical-risk calibration inspired by conformal risk control, targeting asymptotic risk control to improve the reliability/retention trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can produce fluent but wrong answers, so uncertainty quantification is essential for reliable QA; however, heuristic uncertainty scores cannot cleanly separate correct from incorrect predictions, and a fixed uncertainty threshold fails to provide statistical control over the error rate among accepted answers.

Method: A-CRC-QA reformulates selection-conditioned error control as a linear expectation constraint and applies a monotonized empirical-risk calibration procedure inspired by conformal risk control. Because the instance-wise loss is generally non-monotone in the acceptance threshold, it targets asymptotic rather than finite-sample risk control. The method is model-agnostic, needs no extra training, and is compatible with different uncertainty estimators.

Result: Experiments on CoQA and MedMCQA show applicability to both open-ended and closed-ended QA, achieving a favorable trade-off between accepted-answer reliability and answer retention compared with uncalibrated and confidence-bound-based baselines.
