Conclusion: A-CRC-QA provides statistically principled (asymptotic) error control for selective QA, improving reliability while retaining answers better than existing baselines, without requiring model retraining.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) may generate fluent but incorrect answers, making uncertainty quantification important for reliable question answering. However, heuristic uncertainty scores cannot perfectly distinguish correct predictions from incorrect ones, and directly applying a fixed uncertainty threshold provides no statistical control over the error rate among accepted answers. To address this limitation, we propose A-CRC-QA, a post-hoc calibration framework for uncertainty-aware selective question answering. The proposed method reformulates selection-conditioned error control as a linear expectation constraint and applies a monotonized empirical-risk calibration procedure inspired by conformal risk control. Since the resulting instance-wise loss is generally non-monotone with respect to the acceptance threshold, our framework targets asymptotic rather than finite-sample risk control. A-CRC-QA is model-agnostic, requires no additional training, and can be combined with different uncertainty estimators. Experiments on CoQA and MedMCQA demonstrate its applicability to both open-ended and closed-ended question answering, achieving a favorable trade-off between accepted-answer reliability and answer retention compared with uncalibrated and confidence-bound-based baselines.

</details>


### [47] [Poly-Dialectal Neural Machine Translation System for Bangla Regional Dialects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12018)
*Rakib Ullah,Ruhul Islam Rahul,Tanbir Ahmed*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a unified poly-dialectal NMT system for Bangla that supports multi-directional translation across 12 regional dialects without a standard pivot, backed by the largest multi-dialect Bangla parallel corpus (51,531 sentence pairs), achieving state-of-the-art results via a DoRA fine-tuned BanglaT5 model and releasing an open-access quantized web application.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Regional dialectal variation severely degrades Bangla NLP systems because contemporary NMT and LLMs assume a homogeneous language distribution. Over 240 million Bangla speakers use regional variants that diverge from Standard Colloquial Bangla (SCB) in phonology, morphology, and lexicon, creating a fundamental challenge for low-resource dialect translation that the authors seek to address directly without routing through a standard pivot.

Method: The authors compile the largest multi-dialect parallel corpus for Bangla (51,531 non-null parallel sentence pairs across 12 dialects), including 2,500 expert-verified bidirectional pairs for five previously unaddressed dialects. They evaluate sequence-to-sequence architectures under Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA), fine-tuning BanglaT5, and benchmark against NLLB-200 (615M) and mBART-50 (611M). They also perform systematic cross-dialectal transfer analysis, dataset scaling studies, and INT8 quantization for deployment.

Result: The fine-tuned BanglaT5 model achieves state-of-the-art translation performance of 29.26 BLEU and 57.26 chrF++, outperforming NLLB-200 and mBART-50 while preserving morphological coherence. Cross-dialectal transfer analysis and scaling studies establish empirical thresholds for low-resource dialect adaptation, and the optimized INT8-quantized model is deployed as an open-access web application. The dataset is publicly available on Mendeley Data.

Conclusion: A unified poly-dialectal NMT system with direct multi-directional translation across 12 Bangla dialects is feasible and superior to pivot-based or homogeneous-language approaches. The work contributes the largest multi-dialect Bangla corpus, a state-of-the-art DoRA fine-tuned BanglaT5 model, empirical adaptation thresholds, and an accessible quantized application to promote digital inclusion for marginalized dialect communities.

Abstract: Regional dialectal variation poses a fundamental challenge to natural language processing (NLP) in Bangla, where over 240 million speakers communicate across diverse regional variants that diverge significantly from Standard Colloquial Bangla (SCB) in phonology, morphology, and lexicon. Contemporary neural machine trans- lation (NMT) architectures and large language models (LLMs) predominantly as- sume a homogeneous language distribution, resulting in severe performance degra- dation when translating low-resource regional dialects. In this work, we present a unified Poly-Dialectal Neural Machine Translation System capable of multi-directional translation across 12 Bangla regional dialects without routing through an inter- mediary standard pivot. We compile the largest multi-dialect parallel corpus for Bangla to date, comprising 51,531 non-null parallel sentence pairs across 12 di- alects, incorporating 2,500 expert-verified, bidirectional parallel sentence pairs for five previously unaddressed dialects. Evaluating sequence-to-sequence architec- tures under Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA), our fine-tuned BanglaT5 model achieves state-of-the-art translation performance (29.26 BLEU, 57.26 chrF++), outperforming NLLB-200 (615M) and mBART-50 (611M) while preserving morphological coherence. Furthermore, we conduct a systematic cross- dialectal transfer analysis and dataset scaling study, establishing empirical thresh- olds for low-resource dialect adaptation. Finally, we deploy the optimized INT8- quantized model as an open-access web application to promote digital inclusion for marginalized dialect communities. The complete dataset is publicly available at Mendeley Data (https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/v9cf66fk2t/2).

</details>


### [48] [Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12062)
*Lior Baruch,Moshe Butman,Kfir Bar,Doron Friedman*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Preference Tree Optimization (PTO), a framework that iteratively improves goal-oriented dialogue agents by generating preference data through a Preference Tree with Look-Ahead method, combined with DPO, demonstrated in Motivational Interviewing using virtual patients and an oracle evaluator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Developing multi-turn, goal-oriented dialogue systems remains challenging, particularly in specialized domains like Motivational Interviewing (MI), where data scarcity limits training. The authors aim to address this data scarcity and improve agents' decision-making and long-term planning in goal-oriented conversations.

Method: The proposed Preference Tree Optimization (PTO) framework generates preference data using a Preference Tree with Look-Ahead, leveraging virtual patients and an oracle evaluator to simulate conversations. This preference data is combined with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to iteratively improve agent models over training cycles.

Result: Models trained with PTO consistently outperformed baselines on key metrics such as session satisfaction and working alliance. Incorporating look-ahead simulations improved long-term planning and conversational strategies, with deeper look-ahead configurations yielding the most stable and highest-scoring results.

Conclusion: The PTO framework effectively enhances dialogue agents' performance in goal-oriented conversations within Motivational Interviewing, addressing data scarcity and advancing the development of more nuanced and effective dialogue systems.

Abstract: Developing dialogue systems capable of engaging in multi-turn, goal-oriented conversations remains a significant challenge, especially in specialized domains with limited data. This research proposes a novel framework called Preference Tree Optimization (PTO), designed to iteratively improve agent models in such dialogue systems, by generating preference data using a method called Preference Tree with Look-Ahead. Focusing on Motivational Interviewing (MI) -- a counseling technique aimed at facilitating behavioral change -- we leverage virtual patients and an oracle evaluator to simulate conversations and generate rich preference datasets. By combining this method with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), we aim to enhance the agent's decision-making capabilities over iterative training cycles. The proposed framework addresses data scarcity and advances the development of more nuanced and effective dialogue systems in goal-oriented domains. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the PTO framework enhances dialogue agents' performance in goal-oriented conversations within the domain of Motivational Interviewing (MI). Models trained with PTO consistently outperformed the baseline in key metrics such as session satisfaction and working alliance. Additionally, incorporating look-ahead simulations led to improved long-term planning and more effective conversational strategies, with deeper look-ahead configurations yielding the most stable and high-scoring results.

</details>


### [49] [Structuring the Space of Perspectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12113)
*Agnese Daffara,Sebastian Padó,Tanise Ceron*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper reviews how "perspective" is conceptualized in NLP, identifies properties that distinguish perspective-related concepts (stances, sentiment, frames, arguments, etc.), and proposes a linear conceptual hierarchy to help researchers select operationalizations matching their research goals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The same event can be reported differently based on a writer's experiences, background, and beliefs. Many NLP areas engage with perspectives, but a wide range of operative concepts (stances, sentiment, frames, arguments) are used with unclear relationships among them. A deeper theoretical understanding would enable more effective perspective research.

Method: The authors review the space of perspectives in NLP and define a set of properties that help distinguish perspective-related concepts. They then derive a hierarchy that organizes these concepts linearly along a single axis.

Result: A principled conceptual hierarchy of perspective-related concepts is established, organized linearly along one axis, revealing systematic relationships among stances, sentiment, frames, arguments, and related notions.

Conclusion: The proposed conceptual hierarchy helps researchers navigate the field and select operationalizations of perspective that align with their specific research objectives, closing a theoretical gap in NLP perspective research.

Abstract: The same event can be reported from different perspectives depending on the experiences, background, and beliefs of the writer or speaker. A variety of NLP areas engage with perspectives, spanning from text analysis to algorithm optimization. A wide range of operative concepts (such as stances, sentiment, frames, and arguments) has been used to capture perspectives in texts, however the precise relationships among those concepts remain unclear. Arguably, a deeper theoretical understanding of these concepts would empower more effective research on perspectives. In this paper, we address this gap by reviewing the space of perspectives in NLP and defining a set of properties that help distinguishing perspective-related concepts. Our analysis leads us to posit a hierarchy which organizes these concepts linearly along a single axis. Finally, we show how this principled conceptual hierarchy can help researchers navigate the field and select operationalizations of perspective that align with their specific research objectives.

</details>


### [50] [QV-PIC: Query-Aware Visual Position-Independent Caching for Efficient RAG Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12121)
*Yilin Liu,Rui Meng,Wangze Ni,Jianxin Yan,Heng Cao,Libin Zheng,Peng Cheng,Jinfei Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: QV-PIC is a query-aware dual-resolution Position-Independent Caching framework that renders text chunks as images to reduce token counts, while recovering lost textual detail and fixing contextual mismatches to match or exceed text-PIC quality at much lower time-to-first-token (TTFT).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG repeatedly prefills identical text chunks, causing redundant KV computation. PIC reuses precomputed KV to help, but is bottlenecked by large text-token volumes. Rendering chunks as images compresses tokens, yet rendered-image PIC degrades quality more than text PIC due to (1) contextual mismatches across independently compiled caches and (2) loss of fine-grained textual evidence during visual compression. Existing PIC repairs address only the context issue via selective recomputation, adding online cost and not recovering lost textual details.

Method: QV-PIC is a query-aware dual-resolution PIC reuse framework guided by model-native templates. Offline, it compiles visual caches using the model's native chat-template prefix, improving PIC quality without online recomputation. Online, it preserves global context with low resolution and restores fine-grained textual evidence within a high-resolution budget using cumulative query relevance scores, retaining the efficiency benefit of visual compression.

Result: Across six tasks, QV-PIC improves average F1 by 21.6 points over vanilla rendered-image PIC, closes the gap to vanilla text PIC, and surpasses optimized text PIC by 2.58 F1 while reducing TTFT by 17.2%. Relative to full prefill, it cuts TTFT by 83.8%.

Conclusion: QV-PIC effectively resolves the representation-specific quality gap of rendered-image PIC by combining model-native template alignment (offline) with dual-resolution, query-aware detail restoration (online), achieving strong accuracy and substantial TTFT reductions over both vanilla and optimized baselines.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) repeatedly prefills identical text chunks across queries, incurring redundant computations. Position-Independent Caching (PIC) mitigates it by reusing precomputed Key-Value (KV) across positions, but its efficiency is constrained by the large volume of text tokens. Rendering text chunks as images can compress the text into fewer visual tokens, but the rendered-image PIC suffers more severe quality degradation than the text PIC. This representation-specific gap primarily arises from contextual mismatches across independently compiled caches and the loss of fine-grained textual evidence during visual compression. Existing PIC repair methods mainly address the former through selective recomputation, but they incur online computation and cannot recover lost textual details. We propose QV-PIC, a query-aware dual-resolution PIC reuse framework guided by model-native templates. Offline, QV-PIC compiles visual caches under the model's native chat-template prefix, improving PIC quality without online recomputation. Online, it preserves global context with low resolution and restores fine-grained textual evidence within a high-resolution budget by cumulative query relevance scores, retaining the efficiency benefit of visual compression. Across six tasks, QV-PIC improves average F1 by 21.6 points over vanilla rendered-image PIC, closes the gap to vanilla text PIC, and surpasses optimized text PIC by 2.58 F1 while reducing TTFT by 17.2\%. Relative to full prefill, it cuts TTFT by 83.8%.

</details>


### [51] [SAG: SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation with Query-Time Dynamic Hyperedges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12129)
*Yuchao Wu,Junqin Li,XingCheng Liang,Yongjie Chen,Yinghao Liang,Linyuan Mo,Guanxian Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SAG (SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation) is a structured retrieval architecture that organizes documents into an event-entity index (pairing each chunk as an event with its entities, forming latent hyperedges) instead of building a global knowledge graph. At query time, shared entities act as join keys to dynamically generate a query-scoped event neighborhood, keeping original chunks as evidence throughout. It achieves state-of-the-art retrieval and QA results on multi-hop benchmarks, with gains growing as reasoning complexity increases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mainstream dense-retrieval RAG struggles with structured constraints and multi-hop reasoning, while graph-based approaches that build offline knowledge graphs fragment semantics, impose high maintenance costs, and complicate incremental updates. The authors seek a method that preserves n-ary relations and full chunk semantics while supporting dynamic, query-scoped multi-hop retrieval.

Method: SAG structures documents into an event-entity index rather than a global knowledge graph. Each chunk is represented as a semantically complete event paired with its entities, forming a latent hyperedge that preserves n-ary relations without decomposing them into triples. At query time, shared entities are used as join keys to connect related chunks, dynamically producing a query-scoped neighborhood of events while every piece of evidence remains the original chunk.

Result: On HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, SAG achieves the best retrieval and end-to-end QA performance on every benchmark, with gains widening as reasoning-chain complexity increases. On MuSiQue (the most demanding multi-hop benchmark), SAG reaches 80.36% Recall@5, outperforming the strongest baseline by 11.52 points.

Conclusion: SAG demonstrates that a structured event-entity index without a global knowledge graph can outperform both dense retrieval and graph-based baselines for multi-hop QA, paving the way for knowledge infrastructure that lets LLM agents retrieve and reason over continually growing organizational knowledge.

Abstract: While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has proven effective at giving LLMs access to external knowledge, mainstream dense-retrieval implementations remain inherently limited in handling structured constraints and multi-hop reasoning. Graph-based methods address this by constructing knowledge graphs offline, but they often fragment semantics, incur high maintenance, and complicate incremental updates. We propose SAG (SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation), a structured retrieval architecture that organizes documents into an event-entity index without building a global knowledge graph. SAG represents each chunk as a semantically complete event paired with its entities, forming a latent hyperedge that preserves n-ary relations without decomposing them into triples. At query time, SAG treats shared entities as join keys to connect related chunks. This dynamically yields a query-scoped neighborhood of events, and yet every piece of evidence remains the original chunk throughout. Experiments on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue show that SAG achieves the best retrieval and end-to-end QA performance on every benchmark, with gains that widen as reasoning-chain complexity increases. On MuSiQue, where multi-hop evidence chaining is most demanding, SAG reaches 80.36% Recall@5, outperforming the strongest baseline by 11.52 points. This work paves the way for knowledge infrastructure that enables LLM agents to retrieve and reason over continually growing organizational knowledge.

</details>


### [52] [Massive Activations in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models: Pre-Attention Spikes and Inter-Spike Plateaus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12149)
*Zunhai Su,Bohan Sun,Xialie Zhuang,Shuibai Zhang,He Xiao,Jing Xiong,Hengyuan Zhang,Zhongzhu Zhou,Tiantian Zhang,Ngai Wong,Chuan-Wei Kuo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: First systematic study of Massive Activations (MAs) in hybrid linear attention (HLA) LLMs, identifying two architecture-aligned morphologies—pre-attention spikes (PAS) and inter-spike plateaus (ISP)—and explaining them via a shared write-sink-cancel lifecycle that recovers full-attention MA behavior at the dense-attention limit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Massive activations are known in full attention LLMs, but their behavior in hybrid linear attention (HLA) architectures is unexplored. The authors aim to systematically characterize how layer interleaving of linear and full attention reshapes MA morphology, recurrence, and underlying dynamics.

Method: The paper conducts a systematic empirical analysis of MAs across layer-interleaved HLA LLMs. It examines five linear attention architectures, six hybridization configurations, five data domains, and open-source hybrid models from 1.2B to 397B parameters. Controlled pretraining of GDN-based hybrids up to 1.3B is used to study emergence and the effect of output gating. A systematic-outlier (write-sink-cancel) analysis is performed to derive the mechanistic lifecycle of MAs.

Result: Two morphologies are found: PAS (MAs spike just before full attention layers) and ISP (MAs persist through intervening linear attention layers). As full attention becomes denser, successive PAS connect through ISP, recovering full-attention MA morphology. Both morphologies emerge early in training and respond asymmetrically to output gating: full attention output gating strongly attenuates absolute MA magnitudes without removing layerwise organization, while removing GDN gates gives comparatively modest amplification. Mechanistically, PAS follows a localized write-sink-cancel process, whereas ISP's extended persistence is consistent with delayed cancellation.

Conclusion: Massive activations in HLA LLMs are organized by the interleaving of linear and full attention layers into PAS and ISP morphologies, governed by a shared lifecycle based on the timing of MA cancellation. At the full attention limit, this account recovers the stable MA morphology of full attention LLMs.

Abstract: We present the first systematic study of Massive activations (MAs) in layer-interleaved HLA LLMs and uncover two architecture-aligned morphologies: MAs consistently spike immediately before full attention layers, forming pre-attention spikes (PAS), and can persist through intervening linear attention layers, giving rise to inter-spike plateaus (ISP). As full attention becomes denser, successive PAS become increasingly connected through ISP, ultimately recovering the stable MA morphology of full attention LLMs. We establish the recurrence of this organization across five linear attention architectures, six hybridization configurations, five data domains, and representative open-source hybrid models spanning 1.2B to 397B total parameters. Controlled pretraining of GDN-based hybrids at scales up to 1.3B shows that both morphologies emerge early and respond asymmetrically to output gating: full attention output gating strongly attenuates their absolute magnitudes without eliminating their layerwise organization, whereas removing GDN gates yields comparatively modest amplification. Mechanistically, our systematic-outlier analysis supports a shared lifecycle account governed by the timing of MA cancellation. PAS follows a localized write-sink-cancel process, while the extended persistence of ISP is consistent with delayed cancellation. At the full attention limit, this account recovers the stable MA morphology characteristic of full attention LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartluxLabs/Massive-Activations-HLA.

</details>


### [53] [Information Abundance Paradox: Long-Context Training Undermines Parametric Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12218)
*Arda Uzunoglu,Benjamin van Durme,Daniel Khashabi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs trained with long contexts may become overly reliant on contextual information rather than encoding knowledge parametrically, a phenomenon the authors call the Information Abundance Paradox. For both pretraining and fine-tuning, performance peaks at an intermediate context length and then declines, driven by a shift in gradient pressure from feed-forward networks (parametric knowledge) to attention modules (contextualization).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper challenges the implicit assumption that training LLMs on longer contexts is always beneficial. The authors investigate how the context window shape's a model's mode of learning—shifting between parametric internalization and contextualization—and hypothesize that abundant relevant in-context information reduces the incentive to encode knowledge in parameters, increasing dependence on context.

Method: The authors study pretraining with long documents and supervised fine-tuning with task-relevant train-time context. They analyze performance trends as context length grows, examine mechanistic changes via gradient pressure attribution (feed-forward networks vs. attention modules), and apply causal interventions to test whether training-induced shifts increase reliance on context during inference.

Result: In pretraining, increasing context improves language modeling, natural language understanding, and closed-book MCQA only up to an intermediate optimum, after which performance declines. In fine-tuning, more task-relevant context improves performance when supporting context is present, but reduces robustness when context is absent or misleading at test time. Mechanistically, informative context shifts gradient pressure from feed-forward networks toward attention modules, increasing reliance on context during inference.

Conclusion: The findings support the Information Abundance Paradox: scaling toward near-infinite context is not simply a matter of supplying more data, even when high-quality long-context data is abundant. Longer contexts can offer lower-complexity solutions that trade parametric knowledge retention for contextualization, ultimately degrading closed-book and out-of-context performance.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly trained and deployed with long contexts that span documents, code repositories, and interaction histories. This scaling reflects the implicit assumption that training on longer contexts will only help the model by exposing it to richer evidence. We challenge this view by studying how the context window shapes a model's mode of learning, shifting it between parametric internalization and contextualization. We propose the Information Abundance Paradox, which hypothesizes that abundant relevant information in the training context can reduce the incentive to encode that information parametrically, thereby increasing reliance on context. In pretraining with long documents, increasing the context window improves language modeling, natural language understanding, and closed-book MCQA only up to an intermediate optimum, after which performance consistently declines. In supervised fine-tuning, more task-relevant train-time context improves performance with supporting context, but reduces robustness when context is absent or misleading at test time. Our analysis suggests that this behavior arises when longer context provides a lower complexity solution. Mechanistically, training with informative context shifts gradient pressure from feed-forward networks, often linked to parametric knowledge, toward attention modules, and causal interventions show that this shift increases reliance on context during inference. Overall, these findings support the Information Abundance Paradox and suggest that scaling toward near-infinite context is not simply a matter of supplying more data, even when high-quality long-context data is abundant.

</details>


### [54] [One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12253)
*Simon Yu,Nicholas Tomlin,Marwa Abdulhai,Ximing Lu,Derek Chong,Abe Hou,Dilara Soylu,Sergey Levine,Christopher D. Manning,Weiyan Shi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Multi-agent RL for human-AI interaction using a single LLM simulator suffers from "simulator collapse," causing trained policies to overfit to the simulator's dominant mode and fail to generalize. The authors formalize this issue and propose two solutions—inference-time Verbalized Sampling and training-time Co-Training—which improve held-out success by up to 9% and 14% respectively, with gains confirmed in human studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current human-AI multi-agent RL typically uses a single LLM to simulate users, but this approach systematically fails to generalize. The authors identify the root cause as simulator collapse: the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, so policies trained against it overfit to narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's dominant mode and transfer poorly to unseen simulators and real users.

Method: The authors theoretically formalize simulator collapse and propose two complementary solutions. (1) Verbalized Sampling (inference time): broadens simulator behavior by sampling from a verbalized response distribution, reducing mode collapse. (2) Co-Training (training time): jointly optimizes the policy against a population of trainable simulators to prevent overfitting to any single simulator's mode. They also release SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training multi-agent RL.

Result: On three multi-turn benchmarks (Persuasion for Good, τ²-bench, and CooperBench), Verbalized Sampling improves held-out success by up to 9% over single-simulator RL, and Co-Training further increases gains to 14%. A human study shows similar gains on real users. Both solutions preserve policy diversity that collapses under single-simulator RL.

Conclusion: The diversity of the training environment—not only the policy—is critical for multi-turn RL to generalize to real-world deployment. The proposed Verbalized Sampling and Co-Training methods mitigate simulator collapse and improve generalization, with SCOPE released to support further research.

Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning for human-AI interaction typically relies on a single large language model to simulate user behavior. We show that this approach systematically fails to generalize, and trace the failure to simulator collapse: because the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, an LLM policy trained against it overfits to narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's dominant mode, and such a policy transfers poorly to unseen simulators and real users. We formalize this collapse theoretically and propose two complementary solutions, one at inference time and one at training time. The inference-time solution, Verbalized Sampling, broadens the simulator's behavior by sampling from a verbalized response distribution, reducing mode collapse. The training-time solution, Co-Training, jointly optimizes the policy against a population of trainable simulators, preventing it from overfitting to any single simulator's mode. We validate both solutions on three multi-turn benchmarks: Persuasion for Good, $τ^2$-bench, and CooperBench. Verbalized Sampling improves held-out success by up to 9% over single-simulator RL, and Co-Training pushes gains further to 14%; the human study shows similar gain on real users. Both solutions preserve the policy diversity that collapses under single-simulator RL. To support further work in this direction, we release SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training multi-agent RL. More broadly, our results suggest that the diversity of the training environment, not only the policy, is critical to the generalization of multi-turn RL to real-world deployment.

</details>


### [55] [A Cascaded Unsupervised-Supervised NLP Pipeline for Detecting Accusatory Language in Public Procurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12269)
*Bryan Torres,Daniel Riofrío,José Vega-Sánchez,Nathaly Orozco,Carla Parra,Karen Rosero,Felipe Grijalva*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper builds a hybrid NLP pipeline combining unsupervised clustering (GMMs over Word2Vec, LLaMA, and RoBERTa embeddings) with supervised classification (Random Forest) to analyze Ecuador's public procurement comments, detecting potentially irregular processes with high precision/recall despite class imbalance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public procurement involves large financial allocations requiring continuous oversight, yet stakeholder comments and publicly available government data remain underutilized despite their potential to expose procedural irregularities. The authors aim to close this gap by mining metadata and participant comments from Ecuador's SOCE system.

Method: A two-stage hybrid framework: (1) semantic embeddings via Word2Vec (domain-trained), LLaMA, and RoBERTa, followed by Gaussian Mixture Models for unsupervised clustering to uncover latent patterns; (2) a supervised classification stage using a Random Forest classifier to identify accusatory or whistleblowing-style comments. The pipeline is applied to SOCE metadata with emphasis on pre-contractual phase comments.

Result: The combination of domain-trained Word2Vec embeddings, GMM-based clustering, and a Random Forest classifier achieved high precision and recall even under severe class imbalance, outperforming reliance on large language model embeddings alone for this task.

Conclusion: Lightweight, domain-adapted NLP architectures can effectively support risk identification and enhance transparency in public procurement systems without requiring large-scale computational infrastructure, validating their practical deployment in resource-constrained oversight settings.

Abstract: Public procurement involves the allocation of substantial financial resources; therefore, continuous oversight through audits, controls, and monitoring mechanisms is essential. However, stakeholder comments and publicly available government data are often underutilized, despite their potential to reveal procedural irregularities. To address this gap, this paper analyzes metadata from Ecuador's Sistema Oficial de Contratación Pública (SOCE, Official Public Procurement System), with particular emphasis on participant comments generated during the pre-contractual phase. We propose a hybrid modeling framework that integrates unsupervised clustering and supervised classification within a natural language processing (NLP) pipeline to uncover latent patterns and detect potentially irregular procurement processes. Semantic embeddings are generated using Word2Vec, LLaMA, and RoBERTa, followed by Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) for unsupervised clustering. A supervised classification stage is then applied to identify accusatory or whistleblowing-style comments. Experimental results show that the combination of domain-trained Word2Vec embeddings, GMM-based clustering, and a Random Forest classifier achieves high precision and recall, even under severe class imbalance. These findings demonstrate that lightweight, domain-adapted NLP architectures can effectively support risk identification and enhance transparency in public procurement systems without requiring large-scale computational infrastructure.

</details>


### [56] [Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12278)
*Avijit Roy,Proma Roy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues that AI education/language tools reproduce structural inequalities for underrepresented languages, using Bengali as a case study. It identifies four interlocking barriers (web-presence gap, training-token deficit, tokenization penalty, connectivity exclusion) that disadvantage Bengali speakers before models are trained, and frames dataset scarcity and offline-first design as equity-oriented structural/infrastructure issues rather than mere technical limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI tools for education and language support are presented as scalable solutions to access gaps in under-resourced communities, but their underlying infrastructure (training corpora, tokenization, benchmarks, deployment) can systematically disadvantage underrepresented languages before training even begins. The paper seeks to expose and reframe these structural barriers, centering Bengali—a major world language—as a representative case.

Method: A structural/critical analysis using Bengali (one of the world's most widely spoken languages) as a case study, with emphasis on AI-assisted education in low-connectivity settings. The authors identify and quantify four interlocking failures: (1) a web-presence gap (Bengali <0.5% of global web content vs. ~4% of global population); (2) a 67:1 English-to-Bengali training-token deficit in major multilingual corpora; (3) a tokenization penalty tied to Bengali's alphasyllabary script that increases token fertility and compounds the data deficit; and (4) connectivity exclusion (rural internet penetration 36.5% vs. urban 71.4%).

Result: The analysis surfaces four interlocking structural barriers facing Bengali: severe underrepresentation in global web content, a large training-token deficit relative to English in multilingual corpora, a script-related tokenization penalty that amplifies the data deficit via higher token fertility, and marked rural-vs-urban connectivity exclusion. These failures are attributed to longstanding resource-allocation decisions, institutional priorities, and design defaults that did not center underrepresented languages in mainstream AI development.

Conclusion: Dataset scarcity should be understood as a structural barrier, not an isolated technical limitation, and offline-first design should be treated as an equity-oriented infrastructure strategy. The paper concludes with directions for linguistics and AI research aimed at reducing these structural inequalities for underrepresented languages like Bengali.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence tools for education and language support are increasingly framed as scalable responses to access gaps in under-resourced communities. Yet the infrastructure underlying these tools, including training corpora, tokenization schemes, evaluation benchmarks, and deployment architectures, can systematically disadvantage speakers of underrepresented languages before a model is trained.
  This paper examines these structural barriers through Bengali, one of the world's most widely spoken languages, focusing on AI-assisted education in low-connectivity environments. We identify four interlocking failures: a severe web presence gap, with Bengali accounting for less than 0.5% of global web content despite representing nearly 4% of the global population; a 67:1 training-token deficit between English and Bengali in major multilingual corpora; a tokenization penalty associated with Bengali's alphasyllabary script that compounds the data deficit through higher token fertility; and connectivity exclusion, with individual internet penetration at 36.5% in rural areas compared with 71.4% in urban areas.
  These failures reflect longstanding resource-allocation decisions, institutional priorities, and design defaults that did not center underrepresented languages in mainstream AI development. We argue that dataset scarcity should be understood as a structural barrier rather than an isolated technical limitation, and that offline-first design should be treated as an equity-oriented infrastructure strategy. We conclude with directions for linguistics and AI research aimed at reducing these structural inequalities.

</details>


### [57] [WavePhaseNet: A DFT-Based Method for Constructing Semantic Conceptual Hierarchy Structures (SCHS)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14419)
*Kiyotaka Kasubuchi,Kazuo Fukiya*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues that hallucinations in LLMs stem from a structural mismatch between the embedding space (a conditional expectation over a σ-algebra) and the semantic truth set. It introduces WavePhaseNet, which uses DFT to decompose semantics into frequency bands, reduces the embedding dimension from 24,576 to ~3,000, and applies Hodge-theoretic cohomological regularization to enforce global semantic consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To theoretically establish that hallucination is an inevitable structural limitation of Transformer/Attention mechanisms, caused by the embedding space failing to be isomorphic to the semantic truth set, and to propose a principled remedy for logical consistency breakdown.

Method: The authors reformulate LLM attention via measure theory and frequency analysis. WavePhaseNet explicitly builds a Semantic Conceptual Hierarchy Structure (SCHS) using DFT along the sequence dimension, separating low-frequency (global meaning) from high-frequency (local syntax) components for manipulation in diagonalized space. They show the 24,576-dim embedding follows a 1/f spectrum (via self-similarity and Zipf's law), deriving ~3,000 dimensions as a lower bound for complete representation through cumulative energy analysis. Finally, they construct a cochain complex over a graph of overlapping local windows and impose Hodge-theoretic harmonic projection, using coboundary-based losses to regularize semantic consistency.

Result: The embedding space is shown to be a conditional expectation over a σ-algebra whose non-isomorphism to the semantic truth set causes hallucinations. Cumulative energy analysis indicates that ~3,000 of GPT-4's 24,576 dimensions suffice for complete representation while preserving meaning/intent, suppressing hallucination and enabling rigorous reasoning. Cohomological/harmonic projection yields a computable regularization principle that extracts maximally consistent global representations.

Conclusion: Hallucination is a structural inevitability of standard Transformer embeddings, but can be mitigated by WavePhaseNet's frequency decomposition, dimensionality reduction to ~3,000 dimensions, and Hodge-theoretic cohomological consistency control, yielding more logically coherent and semantically consistent LLM representations.

Abstract: This paper reformulates Transformer/Attention mechanisms in Large Language Models (LLMs) through measure theory and frequency analysis, theoretically demonstrating that hallucination is an inevitable structural limitation. The embedding space functions as a conditional expectation over a σ-algebra, and its failure to be isomorphic to the semantic truth set fundamentally causes logical consistency breakdown. WavePhaseNet Method The authors propose WavePhaseNet, which explicitly constructs a Semantic Conceptual Hierarchy Structure (SCHS) using Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT). By applying DFT along the sequence dimension, semantic information is decomposed into frequency bands: low-frequency components capture global meaning and intent, while high-frequency components represent local syntax and expression. This staged separation enables precise semantic manipulation in diagonalized space. Dimensionality Reduction GPT-4's 24,576-dimensional embedding space exhibits a 1/f spectral structure based on language self-similarity and Zipf's law. Through cumulative energy analysis, the authors derive that approximately 3,000 dimensions constitute the lower bound for "complete representation." This demonstrates that reduction from 24,576 to 3,000 dimensions preserves meaning and intent while enabling rigorous reasoning and suppressing hallucination. Cohomological Consistency Control The reduced embedding space, constructed via cohomological regularization over overlapping local windows, allows defining a graph structure and cochain complex. This quantifies inconsistencies among local inferences as coboundary-based losses. Applying harmonic projection based on Hodge theory positions cohomology as a computable regularization principle for controlling semantic consistency, extracting maximally consistent global representations.

</details>


### [58] [What Iterated Self-Feeding Probes of Language Models Measure, and a test that separates the construction from the model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10986)
*Nicolás Vera Zúñiga*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a probing methodology, based on Glauber dynamics over token rings with a novel common-random-number coupling, to distinguish what self-referential probes actually measure about language models. The key result: such probes conflate two readings — one fixed by construction (kinematic light cone, model-invariant Lyapunov scaling) and one that genuinely tracks the model (where the Lyapunov exponent crosses zero in training, consistency of attractor-share rankings). The authors describe a phase transition attributable to the probe rather than the model, provide a discrimination test (vary model vs. vary construction), validate bit-exact reproduction of a Domany-Kinzel damage field, and report four retracted conclusions caught by estimator-failure discipline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To make precise what a self-referential probe (feeding a model its own output) measures, by separating quantities fixed by the probe's construction from quantities that genuinely reflect properties of the language model, after the authors themselves confused the two for months.

Method: The model is probed on a ring of token cells resampled by the model's windowed conditional p_r(x_i | x_{i±r}), i.e., Glauber dynamics on token sequences. The new element is the coupling: two rings differing in one token are advanced under common random numbers, making undamaged copies diverge by exactly zero, so damage spreading is measurable where maximal coupling would only give mixing times. The test separating construction effects from model effects is to hold the construction fixed and vary the model, or hold the model fixed and vary the construction, observing which readings move. Validation is by bit-exact reproduction of a Domany-Kinzel damage field against an independent prediction, plus recording of estimator failures.

Result: Some quantities are fixed by construction: the damage light cone is kinematic, and the radius scaling of the token-space Lyapunov exponent lambda_ca(r) is model-invariant across 19 models and two scale ladders spanning 70x. Others track the model: lambda_ca crosses zero at a reproducible training point, and the attractor share ranks models consistently regardless of lattice construction. A phase transition was measured to three decimal places but belongs to the probe, not any language model. Estimator-failure discipline caught four retracted verdicts, each on a quantity that looked like a measurement.

Conclusion: Self-referential probes measure two different things at once in visually identical readings. Left undistinguished, the construction-fixed kind is readily mistaken for the model-tracking kind; the proposed test (vary model vs. vary construction) separates them. The methodology ships as a package.

Abstract: A growing class of methods probes a language model by feeding it its own output: self-consistency, iterated refinement, agentic loops. We ask what such a probe measures, in a construction chosen to make the question sharp: a ring of token cells resampled in place by the model's own windowed conditional p_r(x_i | x_{i+-r}). The substrate is Glauber dynamics on token sequences and is not new; what we change is the coupling. Advancing two rings that differ in one token under common random numbers makes undamaged copies diverge by exactly zero, so damage spreading becomes measurable where a maximal coupling gives mixing times instead. The answer is that it measures two different things at once, in readings that look alike. Some quantities are fixed by the construction: the damage light cone is kinematic, and the radius scaling of the token-space Lyapunov exponent lambda_ca(r) is model-invariant across 19 models and two scale ladders spanning 70x. Others genuinely track the model: lambda_ca crosses zero at a reproducible point in training, and the attractor share ranks models consistently however the lattice is built. Left undistinguished, the first kind is readily mistaken for the second -- we did so ourselves for four months, and report a phase transition we measured to three decimal places that belongs to the probe rather than to any language model. We give the test that separates them: hold the construction fixed and vary the model, or hold the model fixed and vary the construction, and see which readings move. We validate the instrument by reproduction first, recovering a Domany-Kinzel damage field bit-exactly against an independent prediction, and we report the estimator failures that this discipline caught -- four retracted verdicts, each on a quantity that looked like a measurement. The methodology ships as a package.

</details>

### [59] [Agent Safety Should Be a Runtime Contract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11274)
*Albus W. Ng,Yi Han,Jusheng Zhang,Wenhao Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper argues that AI safety for autonomous agents should be enforced at runtime by the harness through a dual contract (preventive blocking and evidential proof), rather than solely instilled during model training, and supports this with empirical audits showing a publication imbalance and convergent precedent from computer security and experimental science.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training-time safety methods (RLHF, DPO, Constitutional AI) are structurally insufficient for agents that execute code, mutate files, send messages, and modify databases, because they cannot guarantee runtime behavior once deployed.

Method: The authors propose a runtime "agent safety contract" enforced by the harness with two faces: (1) preventive — sandboxes, permission gates, output filters, trajectory monitors; (2) evidential — requiring verifiable proof (test runs, log captures, file diffs, citation grounding) that good actions occurred before gating task submission. They formalize an Agent Trajectory Schema and Evidence Chain, state a compositional gating proposition based on monitor composition, and ground the position in four public-evidence audits: a survey of 52 safety incidents, a false-completion audit (31 core cases plus 1 disputed), a trajectory-schema audit of 12 agent systems/harnesses, and a title-level audit of 28,560 NeurIPS/ICML/ICLR 2023–2025 papers showing an 8–12x training-time vs deployment-time imbalance.

Result: The 28,560-paper audit found a pooled 8–12x publication imbalance favoring training-time over deployment-time safety research. The false-completion audit yielded 31 non-contested core cases plus one disputed illustrative case. Two prior communities (computer security and experimental sciences) independently converged on runtime contracts combining preventive and evidential elements, supporting the authors' claim that agentic AI now faces the same pressure.

Conclusion: The correct unit of safety in agentic AI is the trajectory-with-checkable-evidence, not the model. The authors outline a research agenda around the Agent Trajectory Schema, Evidence Chain, and compositional gating, arguing agent safety must shift from a training-time property to a runtime contract.

Abstract: The dominant paradigm treats AI safety as a property to be instilled during model training via RLHF, DPO, or Constitutional AI. We argue this is structurally insufficient for autonomous agents that execute code, mutate files, send messages, and modify databases. Agent safety should be a runtime contract enforced by the harness, and the contract has two complementary faces. The preventive face blocks dangerous actions before they happen via sandboxes, permission gates, output filters, and trajectory monitors. The evidential face requires verifiable proof that good actions actually happened, gating task submission on hard evidence such as test runs, log captures, file diffs, and citation grounding. We ground the position in four lines of public evidence, with row-level protocols and data released in the supplementary JSON files: a survey of 52 documented AI-agent and LLM safety incidents, a false-completion audit with 31 non-contested core cases plus one disputed illustrative case, a trajectory-schema audit of 12 public agent systems and harnesses, and a title-level audit of all 28,560 papers accepted at NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR 2023-2025 showing a pooled 8-12x imbalance between training-time and deployment-time publication. Two prior communities that needed to enforce safety, computer security and the experimental sciences, converged on runtime contracts with both preventive and evidential elements; agentic AI is now under the same pressure. We formalize an Agent Trajectory Schema and Evidence Chain, state a compositional gating proposition based on standard monitor composition, and outline a research agenda. The right unit of safety in agentic AI is the trajectory-with-checkable-evidence, not the model.

</details>


### [60] [Knowledge-Graph-Guided Retrieval-Augmented LLMs for Explainable Root Cause Analysis in Automotive HiL Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11277)
*Hamza Ouarrad,Mohammad Abboush,Andreas Rausch*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a knowledge-graph-guided retrieval-augmented large language model framework for root cause analysis and fault localization in automotive Hardware-in-the-Loop time-series data, achieving Top-1 accuracies of 90% and 94% on two case studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual analysis of large multivariate HiL time-series recordings is time-consuming and limited to anomaly detection/fault classification rather than root-cause analysis. Deep learning methods require task-specific retraining for new fault locations/systems/operating conditions, treat localization as classification without modeling spatial/functional relationships, and thus have limited generalizability and usefulness for engineering diagnosis.

Method: A KG-guided retrieval-augmented LLM framework: (1) converts raw time-series recordings into compact diagnostic evidence; (2) enriches evidence with sensor-to-location and propagation knowledge from a knowledge graph; (3) retrieves similar historical cases to support reasoning; (4) uses the LLM as a decision/explanation layer (not a direct time-series classifier) to output a ranked fault-location prediction with an interpretable RCA explanation.

Result: Evaluated on two automotive HiL case studies (an ASM gasoline engine and an electric vehicle system), the best model reaches Top-1 accuracies of 90% and 94%, respectively, and recording-level aggregation achieves perfect file-level fault localization in the evaluated subset.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate the potential of KG-guided RAG-LLM reasoning for explainable and generalizable HiL root cause analysis.

Abstract: Hardware-in-the-Loop validation of automotive software systems generates large multivariate time-series recordings whose manual analysis is time-consuming and often limited to anomaly detection and fault classification rather than root-cause analysis. Although deep learning methods have shown strong performance in fault detection and classification, they usually require task-specific training or retraining when new fault locations, systems, or operating conditions are introduced. They also tend to treat localization as a classification task, without explicitly representing the spatial and functional relationships between fault locations, sensors, and downstream subsystem effects. This limits their generalizability and their usefulness for engineering root cause analysis and diagnosis. This paper proposes a knowledge-graph-guided retrieval-augmented large language model framework for RCA (root cause analysis) and fault localization in automotive HiL data. The method converts raw time-series recordings into compact diagnostic evidence, enriches this evidence with sensor-to-location and propagation knowledge, and retrieves similar historical cases to support the final reasoning step. The LLM is then used as a decision and explanation layer rather than as a direct time-series classifier, producing a ranked fault-location prediction together with an interpretable RCA explanation. The framework is evaluated on two automotive HiL case studies: an ASM gasoline engine and an electric vehicle system. The best-performing model achieves Top-1 accuracies of 90\% and 94\%, respectively, while recording-level aggregation reaches perfect file-level fault localization in the evaluated subset. These results demonstrate the potential of KG-guided RAG-LLM reasoning for explainable and generalizable HiL RCA.

</details>


### [61] [Benchmarking Cyberattack Detection in Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure with Benign User Updates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11286)
*Hannan Chen,Roshni Anna Jacob,Jie Zhang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A session-level benchmark and a Dual-Branch Masked-Autoencoder Transition Boost model for detecting charging manipulation attacks in EV charging infrastructure, which preserve legitimate post-activation request revisions as normal behavior and outperform 22 competing model families under source-grouped cross-validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Detecting cyberattacks in EV charging infrastructure is hard because legitimate users routinely revise requested energy and departure time after activation, and attackers can exploit the same interface and variables. A request change alone cannot indicate malicious intent, so models must distinguish benign revisions from charging manipulation attacks without rejecting legitimate user choices.

Method: A leakage-controlled session-level benchmark preserving the ordered inputs of real Adaptive Charging Network (ACN) sessions, with a fixed data pool keeping each attack in its source session's split and six physically motivated attacks plus coordinated variants. It compares 22 profile-only, transition-aware, and context-stratified model families under common source-grouped folds, attack data, and operating constraints. The proposed Dual-Branch Masked-AE Transition Boost model uses a state branch (masked reconstruction plus a radial-basis-function one-class support boundary) to judge whether the current request is normal, and a transition branch (masked reconstruction plus shrinkage covariance distance) to judge whether the producing transition resembles an observed benign update. Source-grouped five-fold cross-validation selects configurations under explicit overall-normal and benign-update acceptance constraints; disjoint normal data calibrate the final threshold before one test evaluation.

Result: The dual-branch model achieves the strongest robust validation performance, detecting malicious request manipulations while preserving legitimate user choices (i.e., without learning to reject benign revisions).

Conclusion: Modeling legitimate revisions explicitly and combining state-level one-class detection with transition-level anomaly scoring yields superior, leakage-free detection of charging manipulation attacks, establishing a rigorous benchmark for future work in EV charging infrastructure security.

Abstract: Cyberattack detection in electric vehicle charging infrastructure is complicated by legitimate post-activation revisions to requested energy and departure time. Charging manipulation attacks can exploit the same interface and variables; therefore, detecting a request change alone does not establish malicious intent. This paper develops a leakage-controlled session-level benchmark that preserves the ordered inputs of real Adaptive Charging Network (ACN) sessions and models legitimate revisions as normal behavior. A fixed pool keeps each generated attack in its source session's split and contains six physically motivated attacks and their coordinated variants. We compare 22 profile-only, transition-aware, and context-stratified model families under common source-grouped folds, attack data, and operating constraints. The proposed Dual-Branch Masked-Autoencoder (Masked-AE) Transition Boost model evaluates whether the current request is normal and whether its producing transition resembles an observed benign update. Its state branch combines masked reconstruction with a radial-basis-function one-class support boundary, while its transition branch combines masked reconstruction with shrinkage covariance distance. Source-grouped five-fold cross-validation selects complete configurations under explicit overall-normal and benign-update acceptance constraints; disjoint normal data then calibrate the final threshold before one test evaluation. The developed dual-branch model provides the strongest robust validation performance while detecting malicious request manipulations without learning to reject legitimate user choices.

</details>


### [62] [Dueling Deep Q-Learning for Intrusion Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11291)
*Logan Luna,Matthew P. Berkowitz,Laxima Niure Kandel,Sirio Jansen-S'anchez*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a reward-based dueling Q-learning (deep reinforcement learning) model for intrusion detection that separates value and advantage streams, achieving 99.68% average accuracy on CIC-IDS2018, with SHAP integrated for explainability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional intrusion detection systems rely on supervised machine learning, which is effective but struggles to adapt to new, unseen attack types. The paper aims to overcome this limitation by using a reinforcement learning approach that can better adapt to evolving cyber threats.

Method: A reward-based dueling Q-learning model with a dueling network architecture that separates predictions into value and advantage streams, improving learning efficiency and stability. The model is trained on the CIC-IDS2018 benchmark dataset containing multiple attack classes (DDoS, botnets, brute-force). SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) is integrated into training and evaluation to provide interpretability of predictions.

Result: The proposed model achieves an average accuracy of 99.68% across multiple attack classes on the CIC-IDS2018 benchmark dataset.

Conclusion: The dueling Q-learning approach provides an effective and adaptable alternative to supervised methods for intrusion detection, while SHAP integration enables interpretability of the model's decisions.

Abstract: Intrusion detection systems (IDS) and automated systems for detecting and reporting cyber threats, are commonly handled via supervised machine learning methods. Though effective, these models struggle to effectively adapt to new attack types. This study proposes a novel approach by employing a reward-based, dueling Q-learning model for IDS, achieving an average accuracy of 99.68% across multiple attack classes. The proposed model has a dueling network architecture which separates its predictions into value and advantage streams. This has the benefit of improving learning efficiency and stability. The model was trained on the CIC-IDS2018, a benchmark dataset based on real-world intrusion detection scenarios, having multiple attack classes such as DDoS, botnets, and brute-force attacks. Furthermore, Explainable AI (XAI), specifically SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), was also integrated into the training and evaluation process to provide interpretability into the model's predictions.

</details>


### [63] [Battlefield 5G: Dual-PKI and TPM-Based UE Attestation for Tactical 5G Standalone Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11293)
*Al Nahian Bin Emran,Rajendra Paudyal,Rajendra Upadhyay,Lisa Donnan,Arupjyoti Bhuyan,Duminda Wijesekera*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Battlefield 5G is a pre-authentication framework for 5G Standalone networks that authenticates both the device (dual X.509 certificate checks) and its boot state (TPM-based attestation) before standard 5G-AKA registration, addressing the gap where only the USIM credential — not the physical device — is authenticated.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard 5G-AKA authenticates only the subscriber credential in the USIM, not the physical device or its boot state. In tactical deployments, user equipment may be captured, modified, returned to service, or used with transplanted subscriber credentials, so there is a need to authenticate the device and verify its firmware integrity before registration is accepted.

Method: The design combines dual X.509 device-certificate checks with TPM-based boot attestation inserted into the registration path. An outer certificate challenge is placed on the gNB and an independent inner certificate challenge on the AMF, plus a TPM PCR quote verified by an attestation proxy in the 5G core. A gNB-side RRC forwarding gate and an AMF-side save-and-replay mechanism enable multi-round challenge-response exchanges without modifying 3GPP NAS message structures or adding new NAS message types. Implemented by extending srsRAN gNB, srsUE, and Open5GS on a B210 USRP testbed with a hardware TPM 2.0 in the UE.

Result: The prototype blocks SIM-transplant, rogue-certificate, firmware-tampering, and replay attacks. Across six trials, average onboarding latency increased from 1886 ms to 2260 ms — a 373.4 ms pre-authentication overhead — while preserving standard 5G-AKA, security mode, and PDU session procedures.

Conclusion: Battlefield 5G successfully closes the device- and boot-state authentication gap in tactical 5G deployments with modest latency overhead and no changes to standard 3GPP NAS messaging, protecting against credential transplant, rogue certificates, firmware tampering, and replay attacks.

Abstract: The standardized 5G Authentication and Key Agreement (5G-AKA) authenticates a subscriber credential stored on a Universal Subscriber Identity Model (USIM) but does not authenticate the physical device that holds that credential or verify its boot state. This gap is significant in tactical 5G deployments, where user equipment may be captured, modified, returned to service, or used with transplanted subscriber credentials. We present Battlefield 5G, a pre-authentication framework for 5G Standalone networks that combines dual X.509 device-certificate checks with Trusted Platform Module (TPM) -based boot attestation before standard registration is accepted. The design places an outer certificate challenge on the 5G base-station called gNB, an independent inner certificate challenge on the Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF) in the 5G core network, and a TPM PCR (Platform Configuration Register) quote verified by an attestation proxy on the 5G core network side. A gNodeB (gNB) side Radio Resource Control (RRC) forwarding gate and an AMF-side save-and-replay mechanism enable multi-round certificate and attestation challenge-response exchanges to be inserted into the registration path without modifying any 3GPP Non-Access Stratum (NAS) message structures or adding new NAS message types. We implement these capabilities by extending the Radio Access Network of the Software Radio System (srsRAN), gNB, User Equipment of the Software Radio System (srsUE) and Open5GS in a B210-based Universal Radio Peripheral (USRP) testbed with a hardware TPM 2.0 in the UE. The prototype blocks SIM-transplant, rogue-certificate, firmware-tampering, and replay attacks. Across six trials, Battlefield 5G increases average onboarding latency from 1886 ms to 2260 ms, adding 373.4 ms of pre-authentication overhead while preserving standard 5G-AKA, security mode, and packet data unit (PDU) session procedures.

</details>


### [64] [Backdoor Decontamination Dynamics in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11295)
*Gabriel Huang,Abhay Puri,Léo Boisvert,Alexandre Drouin,Perouz Taslakian,Spandana Gella,Christopher Pal*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper studies how to remove unknown backdoors in open-weight LLM agents by first installing a known defensive backdoor and then unlearning it, showing this unreliable on its own (~56% erasure) but highly effective when followed by decontamination, which erases nearly all survivors and reveals residual trigger traces in intermediate layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-weight LLM agents can carry undetectable backdoors installed during fine-tuning, and defenders cannot directly unlearn an unknown trigger. The paper aims to understand whether defensive poisoning (installing a known backdoor) followed by unlearning can reliably remove the original unknown backdoor, given that outcomes are uncertain (persistence, erasure, or rerouting).

Method: The authors introduce a framework for tool-calling agents that decouples trigger, response, teacher, and fine-tuning method, running 115 systematic experiments on the AgentDyn benchmark. They test defensive poisoning alone, follow it with decontamination via unlearning, co-install up to four backdoors to measure resistance, and visualize post-decontamination model internals using J-lens to inspect residual trigger awareness at intermediate layers.

Result: Defensive poisoning alone erases about 56% of original backdoors; subsequent decontamination drives almost all survivors to erasure, confirming trigger recognition and malicious execution are behaviorally dissociable. Malicious backdoors never persist when defensive backdoors use different triggers of the same general type followed by unlearning. Co-installing up to four backdoors increases resistance (~36% erased), yet decontaminating a single known co-resident backdoor collaterally clears 52/60 co-residents (87%). J-lens visualization shows decontamination restores benign responses but leaves traces of original trigger awareness in intermediate layers.

Conclusion: Defensive poisoning followed by decontamination via unlearning is a promising strategy for neutralizing unknown backdoors in tool-calling LLM agents, even though trigger recognition and malicious execution are dissociable and residual trigger representations may remain in internal activations.

Abstract: Open-weight LLM agents are vulnerable to backdoors installed during fine-tuning, which may be undetectable if the trigger conditions are never met during testing. Assuming defenders do not know the existing trigger, they cannot unlearn it directly. One decontamination strategy is to install a known backdoor (defensive poisoning) then to unlearn it, hoping that the original unknown backdoor is removed as a side effect. However, this procedure has uncertain outcomes: the original backdoor may persist or be erased or rerouted, among other possibilities. We introduce a framework for studying these dynamics in tool-calling agents, decoupling trigger, response, teacher, and fine-tuning method across systematic experiments on AgentDyn. Across 115 experiments, defensive poisoning alone erases around 56% of original backdoors; subsequent decontamination then drives almost all survivors to erasure, confirming that trigger recognition and malicious execution are behaviorally dissociable. Interestingly, our experiments find that malicious backdoors never persist when using different triggers of the same general type as the defensive backdoor when followed by decontamination via unlearning. Co-installing up to four backdoors increases resistance (around 36% erased), yet decontaminating a single known co-resident backdoor collaterally clears 52/60 co-residents (87%). Upon visualizing postdecontamination model internals using J-lens, we confirm that although the decontamination restores benign LLM responses, traces of original trigger awareness persist at intermediate layers.

</details>


### [65] [Association-based Privacy Attacks in Wireless Protocols: Formal Modeling and Mitigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11337)
*Mohit Kumar Jangid,Felix Engelmann,Zhiqiang Lin*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper formally analyzes pairing-based privacy threats in wireless protocols (Wi-Fi P2P and Bluetooth LE) caused by replay/relay techniques, and proposes countermeasures validated against association inference attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The surge in privacy-sensitive data from social media and IoT devices creates a pressing need for formal, automated methods to assess privacy risks in complex wireless systems, particularly the root causes of pairing-based privacy threats exploited via replay/relay techniques.

Method: The paper formalizes condition-oblivious responses, replay-resistance, and distance bounding measures for protocols using shared keys in allowlists for authenticated reconnections. It builds formal models of real-world protocols (Wi-Fi P2P persistent group formation and Bluetooth Low Energy reconnection) to identify root causes and validate countermeasures against association inference attacks, as well as existing formalizations of well-authentication, frame opacity, and no-desynchronization.

Result: The analysis uncovers uncharted privacy realms in wireless communication and identifies both old and new vulnerabilities. The proposed design changes were acknowledged by the Wi-Fi Alliance and Bluetooth SIG.

Conclusion: Formal modeling and validation reveal root causes and countermeasures for pairing-based privacy threats, and the acknowledged design changes pave the way for future resilient, privacy-preserving wireless protocols.

Abstract: With the surge in privacy-sensitive data from sources such as social media and IoT devices, there is a pressing need for formal, automated methods to assess privacy risks within these intricate systems. This paper formally investigates root sources of pairing-based privacy threats exploited using replay/relay techniques in wireless communication. Our research harnesses condition-oblivious responses, replay-resistance, and distance bounding measures vital for protocols utilizing shared keys in allowlists for authenticated reconnections. Particularly, the paper uses formal modeling of notable wireless networks, like the Wi-Fi P2P persistent group formation and the Bluetooth Low Energy reconnection procedure, to illustrate the root causes and countermeasures. Our model rigorously validates the proposed solution against association inference attacks, along with existing formalizations of well-authentication, frame opacity, and no-desynchronization. The ensuing analysis reveals not only uncharted privacy realms in wireless communication but also identifies old and new vulnerabilities. Our proposed design changes are acknowledged by Wi-Fi Alliance and Bluetooth SIG, paving the way for future advancements in resilient, privacy-preserving wireless protocols.

</details>


### [66] [An Empirical Study of Output-to-Input Loops for Black-Box Backdoor Detection in Fine-Tuned Open-Weight LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11348)
*Md. Nahid Hasan,Mohammad Arif Hossain*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Self-feeding is a black-box method that repeatedly feeds a model's own output back as its next input, causing text to drift toward the fine-tuning data and exposing hidden backdoors. It detects backdoors in five of six LLMs at 92.0% precision, outperforming a repeated same-prompt baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Users can download fine-tuned LLMs from public repositories with no reliable way to verify safety, since a backdoored model behaves normally until a hidden trigger fires. Without training data, clean reference weights, or the trigger phrase, there is no clear method to check a model before use.

Method: A black-box test called self-feeding that uses a model's own output as the next input, so generations drift from the starting prompt toward the fine-tuning data. It is compared against a repeated same-prompt baseline using six open-weight LLMs (3B-15B), backdoors from eleven attack categories, twenty ordinary prompts, and chains up to ten steps.

Result: Self-feeding found backdoors in five of six models at 92.0% pooled precision, versus the same-prompt baseline succeeding on only one of 120 prompt-model pairs. Per-prompt recall was low (19.2%) but accumulated to high model-level detection with several prompts. One model was never triggered, and self-feeding produced two false positives the baseline cannot. Cutting chains to four steps kept all model-level detections at 100% precision while using 60% fewer queries.

Conclusion: Requiring only text-level query access and a way to recognize malicious output, self-feeding provides a cheap first safety check for a downloaded model, though per-prompt recall remains low and detection depends on using multiple starting prompts.

Abstract: Anyone can upload a fine-tuned large language model (LLM) to a public repository and claim it is safe. A backdoored model behaves normally on ordinary inputs until a hidden trigger fires, and a user with no training data, clean reference weights, or the trigger phrase has no clear way to check the model before using it. We introduce and empirically evaluate self-feeding, a black-box test method that feeds a model's own output back as its next input, so the text drifts away from the starting prompt and toward the data the model was fine-tuned on. We test self-feeding against a repeated same-prompt baseline on six open-weight LLMs (3B-15B parameters), each fine-tuned with backdoors spanning eleven attack categories, using twenty ordinary starting prompts and chains of up to ten steps. Self-feeding finds backdoors in five of six models at 92.0\% pooled precision, while the same-prompt baseline succeeds on only one of 120 prompt-model pairs; chains that begin with a joke request, an arithmetic question, or a coffee recipe all reach a trigger within a few steps. Recall per prompt is low (19.2\%), and we show why it still adds up to much higher detection at the model level once several starting prompts are used. We also report where the method falls short: one model was never triggered, and self-feeding produced two false positives that the same-prompt baseline cannot produce. Cutting the chains to four steps keeps every model-level detection at 100\% precision while using 60\% fewer queries. Needing only text-level query access and a way to recognize malicious output, self-feeding offers a cheap first check on a downloaded model.

</details>


### [67] [AI Guardrail Survival under Single-Cycle Agentic Self-Summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11392)
*Ted Kwartler,Alan Aqrawi,Arian Abbasi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Compaction can leave "rule-looking" text that no longer enforces the safety rule; a textual presence check gives false assurance, and only behavioral replay against external ground truth reveals the true degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work (Governance Decay) showed that dropping a standing safety constraint during context compaction causes violations across many models. This paper asks a finer-grained question: within a single compaction cycle, how exactly is a safety rule lost, and what does that imply for detection and evaluation.

Method: They study a single compaction cycle and compare textual survival vs. behavioral enforcement of safety rules. They distinguish "welded" (intact) rules from degraded "residues" that look like rules but do not fire. They replay behavior under two replay models, measure category-level survival, compare rule-form items against prominence-matched facts, vary compaction budget to probe loss regimes (weld-or-drop vs. degraded predicate-loss), and test LLM-judge labels against comparison with retained external ground truth (a constraint registry).

Result: A presence check is not a safety check. Degraded residues make the model perform the prohibited action far more often than intact welded rules (all-case gaps of +34 and +57 points under two replay models, both positive).
