Category-level survival behaves like a residue. Even intact rules sometimes fail to fire. Rule-form items are retained substantially more often than prominence-matched facts, which is why presence-based checking feels adequate even though survival is not protection. Textual loss is regime-dependent: weld-or-drop with a single rule, degraded predicate-loss residues under a tighter budget; no textual severing mode was observed. Loss is silent at runtime and detectable only by comparison with retained external ground truth, which reveals textual absence but not whether a surviving rule still fires. LLM-judge labels alone would have reversed a conclusion.

Conclusion: Textual presence of a rule after compaction does not guarantee it still enforces the constraint. Detection requires behavioral replay against retained external ground truth, and evaluation should not rely solely on LLM-judge labels. All findings concern a single compaction cycle.

Abstract: Long-running agents periodically compact their context, replacing the transcript with a model-generated summary.Recent work shows that dropping a standing safety constraint during compaction drives behavioral violations acrossmany models (Governance Decay; Chen, 2026). We ask a finer question: under a single compaction cycle, how is a safetyrule lost, and what does that imply for detection and evaluation? Our central finding is that a presence check is not asafety check: when compaction does not drop a rule outright, it often leaves something that looks like a rule but doesnot act like one. On behavioral replay, a degraded residue leads the model to perform the prohibited action far more oftenthan an intact welded rule does (all-case gaps of +34 and +57 points under two replay models, both positive), category-level survival behaves like a residue, and even intact rules sometimes fail to fire, so an audit that checks only textualpresence gives false assurance. Sharpening this, rule-form items are retained substantially more often than prominence-matched facts, which is exactly why presence-based checking feels adequate even though survival is not protection.Textual loss is regime-dependent (weld-or-drop with a single rule; degraded predicate-loss residues under a tighterbudget), and we did not observe the hypothesized textual severing mode. Such loss is silent at runtime and detectableonly by comparison with retained external ground truth (such as a constraint registry), which reveals textual absence butnot whether a surviving rule still fires. We also document evaluation pitfalls where LLM-judge labels alone would havereversed a conclusion. All results concern a single compaction cycle.

</details>


### [68] [A Study of Kernel Telemetry Options for Security-Oriented Provenance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11418)
*Paul R. B. Houssel,Olivier Levillain,Sylvie Laniepce,Nicolas Dejon,Hervé Debar*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper surveys kernel telemetry capture for provenance systems, identifies eBPF as the most promising approach via micro-benchmarks of overhead and filtering, and classifies 13 provenance tools, concluding that most use heterogeneous capture layers that fail to guarantee event integrity and availability for security use cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provenance (capturing origins, transformations, and interactions of system objects) is critical for security and forensics, but existing capture approaches face major challenges and are not yet production-ready. The work seeks to understand why and to evaluate whether current tools meet the integrity and availability requirements of security-oriented deployments.

Method: The authors first analyze the main kernel telemetry capture approaches and identify eBPF as the most promising candidate. They complement this analysis with micro-benchmarks measuring performance overhead and evaluating filtering mechanisms that enable capture granularity (e.g., restricting capture to individual containers). They then classify eight provenance systems and five capture agents (collectively "tools") according to the studied capture approaches and filtering methods.

Result: The classification reveals that the thirteen tools are built on highly heterogeneous capture layers. Most of these capture layers cannot guarantee the integrity and availability of the captured events, and therefore fail to meet the requirements of security-oriented use cases.

Conclusion: Existing provenance capture approaches are heterogeneous and insufficiently robust for production security/forensic environments; stronger guarantees of event integrity and availability are needed, positioning eBPF-based capture as a promising direction but still requiring further work.

Abstract: Provenance aims to capture the origins, transformations, and interactions of system objects for security and forensic applications. Existing provenance capture approaches still face major challenges and are not yet ready for production environments. In this paper, we first analyze the main kernel telemetry capture approaches, identifying eBPF as the most promising, and complement this analysis with micro benchmarks to assess its performance overhead and the filtering mechanisms used to achieve capture granularity, such as restricting capture to individual containers. Building on this foundation, we then classify, according to the studied capture approaches and filtering methods, eight provenance systems and five capture agents that could serve as their capture layers, collectively referred to as tools. Our study reveals that these tools are built on highly heterogeneous capture layers, most of which cannot guarantee the integrity and availability of the captured events, completely failing to meet the requirements of security-oriented use cases.

</details>


### [69] [When Agents Talk: Honeytokens under Shared Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11436)
*Joshua S. Gans*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Honeytokens cannot be both harmless to trusted agents and undetectable by sophisticated attackers; a private reference monitor plus a provenance-enforcing broker is required, with honeytokens retained only as sensors behind a real security boundary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A 2026 cyber-capability evaluation showed short-lived AI agents using a shared package repository as persistent memory to pass exploit findings and rebuild removed channels, culminating in a Hugging Face intrusion. This motivates the question of whether honeytokens can remain invisible to attackers who share information and can implement the same trusted policy.

Method: Formal analysis of honeytoken indistinguishability using information-theoretic and statistical tools: a total-variation bound on legitimate compatibility when decoys resemble genuine objects; sequential-probing analysis showing repeated non-triggering observations drive minimum Bayes error to zero under distinguishable, learnable response laws; transfer conditions requiring stable deployment rules and class-orienting information; and a detection bound separating reliable token activation from reliable attack coverage.

Result: Any trusted rule selecting genuine objects while avoiding decoys can be copied by the attacker, and shared memory pools weak fingerprints to create a second leakage channel. For a fixed candidate, non-triggering probes make classification error vanish; if probing triggers containment, learning additionally requires the attacker coalition to remain active long enough. The architectural solution is to keep token identity in a private reference monitor and route legitimate agents through a provenance-enforcing broker, yielding high-confidence detection only for specified policy violations.

Conclusion: Honeytokens are fundamentally unable to achieve simultaneous harmlessness to trusted agents and unrecognizability to attackers. They remain useful as sensors, but must be complemented by a separate security boundary and a provenance-enforcing architecture rather than relied upon as a standalone defense.

Abstract: During a 2026 cyber-capability evaluation, short-lived AI agents turned a shared package repository into persistent memory, passing exploit findings to later agents and rebuilding the channel after it was removed. The broader evaluation culminated in an intrusion into Hugging Face. This episode raises a question for defensive deception: can a honeytoken be harmless to trusted agents without becoming recognisable to an attacker who shares their information and can implement the trusted policy? The answer is no. A trusted rule that selects genuine objects while avoiding decoys can be copied by the attacker, while a total-variation bound limits legitimate compatibility when decoys resemble genuine objects. Shared memory creates a second leakage channel by pooling weak fingerprints. For a fixed candidate, repeated non-triggering probes drive the minimum Bayes classification error to zero when type-dependent response laws differ and are known or learnable. If probing triggers containment, learning also requires the coalition to remain active long enough. Transfer across objects requires a stable deployment rule and information that orients the classes. A separate detection bound distinguishes reliable token activation from reliable attack coverage. The architectural response is to keep token identity in a private reference monitor and route legitimate agents through a provenance-enforcing broker. This produces high-confidence detection only for a specified policy violation. Honeytokens remain useful sensors, but a separate security boundary is still required.

</details>


### [70] [The Next Challenge for Agentic Cybersecurity: A Realistic, Contamination-Free Reverse Engineering Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11469)
*Jeremy Spence,Nicholas Assaderaghi,Jinhao Zhu,Nikil Ravi,Raluca Ada Popa,Guannan Wei,Yangruibo Ding,Zhuo Zhang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SRE-Bench introduces the first realistic, contamination-free reverse engineering benchmark, built from scratch with 19 private programs and 44 anti-analysis primitives, showing that frontier LLM agents still largely fail at binary analysis (best model GPT-5.6-sol scores 61.4% and fully solves only 31.5% of instances).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Much consequential software (malware, firmware, proprietary apps) exists only as binaries, requiring reverse engineering (RE) to recover semantics before analysis. Existing RE benchmarks fail to jointly satisfy two requirements: (1) instances must be unseen as source code in LLM training data (contamination-free) to prevent shortcut recognition rather than real analysis, and (2) they must match the scale and anti-analysis protections of real software.

Method: The authors built SRE-Bench entirely from scratch with RE experts over 5,000+ hours. It contains 19 private, real-world-scale programs averaging 16.9K lines of code, with 44 in-house anti-analysis primitives, producing 262 binary instances and 1,572 deterministically graded tasks. They evaluated five frontier LLMs (GPT-5.6-sol, Claude-Opus-5, GPT-5.5, Grok-4.5, GLM-5.2) and performed controlled ablations on contamination control and realistic scale, plus analysis of agent behavior versus human engineers.

Result: RE remains largely unsolved: the strongest model GPT-5.6-sol scores 61.4% per instance and fully solves only 31.5% of instances. Agents behave differently from human engineers, being relatively insensitive to compiler optimization and static linking. Ablations confirm that both contamination control and realistic scale are essential for a valid benchmark.

Conclusion: Strong source-code security capabilities do not yet transfer to binary analysis, making RE an important frontier for agentic cybersecurity. SRE-Bench serves as a rigorous testbed to measure progress in this area.

Abstract: AI agents are rapidly improving in cybersecurity capabilities when the source code is available for analysis, yet much of the software most consequential to cybersecurity, including malware, firmware, and proprietary applications, is available only as binaries. Analyzing such software requires reverse engineering(RE): recovering program semantics before the analysis can be meaningfully performed. However, evaluating agentic RE poses a fundamental challenge: benchmark instances must be unseen as source code in the LLMs' training data to prevent models from taking shortcuts by recognizing them rather than really analyzing them, while also matching the scale and anti-analysis protections of real software. Unfortunately, however, existing benchmarks do not jointly satisfy these requirements. To this end, we introduce SRE-Bench, the first realistic, contamination-free RE benchmark. Built entirely from scratch by RE experts with over 5,000 hours, SRE-Bench comprises 19 private, real-world-scale programs averaging 16.9K lines of code. We further developed 44 in-house anti-analysis primitives, yielding 262 binary instances and 1572 deterministically graded tasks. Our evaluation across five frontier LLMs (GPT-5.6-sol,Claude-Opus-5,GPT-5.5,Grok-4.5, and GLM-5.2) shows that RE remains largely unsolved: the strongest model, GPT-5.6-sol, scores 61.4% per instance, and fully solves only 31.5% of the instances. Our analysis further reveals that agents behave differently from human engineers, where agents are relatively insensitive to compiler optimization and static linking. Controlled ablations also confirm that both contamination control and realistic scale are essential. These results indicate that strong source-code security capabilities do not yet transfer to binary analysis, highlighting RE as an important frontier for agentic cybersecurity and SRE-Bench as a rigorous testbed to measure progress.

</details>


### [71] [A Runtime Decentralized Attestation and Coordinated Repair Framework for Securing Automotive ECUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11489)
*Josh Dafoe,Niusen Chen,Bo Chen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: DACER is a decentralized runtime attestation and coordinated repair framework for automotive ECUs that co-designs local firmware rollback with global reboot coordination, using ARM TrustZone and secure flash memory to detect and repair compromised ECUs with low overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern vehicles are interconnected systems of ECUs where malware injection poses safety risks; existing approaches focus only on detection but do not integrate detection with runtime repair, which is nontrivial because repair requires local rollback plus reboot timed by global vehicle context to avoid unsafe behavior.

Method: DACER co-designs attestation and repair, having each ECU perform low-overhead local self-attestation and self-repair while leveraging the hierarchical vehicle computing architecture. It uses ARM TrustZone on each ECU and a secure flash memory controller for firmware restoration, enabling decentralized coordination that checks the entire vehicle state and resists single points of failure.

Result: Implemented on real-world hardware, DACER experimentally demonstrated low overhead while meeting real-time constraints and enabling runtime firmware restoration.

Conclusion: DACER is the first approach to unify the local nature of firmware rollback with the global nature of ECU reboot, providing a practical low-overhead mechanism for runtime detection and coordinated repair of compromised automotive ECUs.

Abstract: The evolution of automotive technology increasingly integrates components, transforming vehicles into interconnected systems of systems. Modern vehicles are controlled by a distributed system of computing devices, known as electronic control units (ECUs). However, this interconnectedness means that any error poses significant risks to the vehicle operator. In particular, malware can be injected into ECUs, threatening vehicle safety. To address this, we need mechanisms to detect compromised ECUs then repair them to a benign state. Existing approaches mainly focus on detection and do not address the challenge of integrating detection with runtime ECU repair. This integration is nontrivial because runtime repair involves both local rollback and reboot with timing determined from global vehicle context to avoid unsafe behavior.
  In this work, we have designed DACER, a runtime decentralized attestation and coordinated repair framework for automotive ECUs. DACER is the first approach that co-designs attestation and repair to unify the ``local'' nature of firmware rollback with the ``global'' nature of ECU reboot. In DACER, each ECU performs efficient local self-attestation and self-repair functions, enabling low-overhead coordination for distributed operations. In addition, DACER takes advantage of the hierarchical vehicle computing architecture. Our resulting DACER design checks the entire state of the vehicle, resists single points of failure, conforms to real-time constraints, and enables firmware restoration during runtime. The key functions are enabled by the ARM TrustZone equipped within each ECU and the secure flash memory controller embedded in the storage device. We implemented DACER on real-world hardware and experimentally demonstrated its low overhead.

</details>


### [72] [Cross-Corpus Evaluation of Generalizable Vulnerability Detection in IoT Firmware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11492)
*Sadib Hassan Rumman,Md. Shariful Islam,Md. Rayhanur Rahman*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: IoTVulBench introduces a human-verified benchmark for cross-corpus IoT firmware vulnerability detection, showing that domain-matched data and curriculum design drive generalization, with a diversity-optimized ensemble reaching 0.73 MCC.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IoT firmware vulnerability detection is hindered by heterogeneous ecosystems, resource-constrained platforms, and limited benchmarks. Existing datasets are often synthetic or general-purpose, lacking human-verified, contamination-screened annotations, which limits evidence on how models generalize across training sources, architectures, and curriculum strategies.

Method: The paper constructs IoTVulBench-Core from GitHub repositories, validated by three expert reviewers. It evaluates on a contamination-screened held-out target across five model architectures, two tuning methods, and three curriculum strategies, with additional ensemble, distillation, and robustness analyses. Staged curriculum learning and a diversity-optimized ensemble are applied, and results are compared against single-source datasets (PrimeVul, D2A) and a static analyzer.

Result: Models trained on IoTVulBench achieved the highest MCC among matched single-source datasets (0.58 vs. 0.44 for PrimeVul and 0.39 for D2A). Staged curriculum learning raised MCC to 0.69, and a diversity-optimized ensemble reached 0.73, improving by 0.42 over the static analyzer (0.31) and 0.29 over PrimeVul. At a 0.5% false-positive rate, the model missed only 21% of vulnerabilities versus 71% for the strongest comparator, and retained 86% of performance under identifier renaming with strong calibration and largely faithful explanations.

Conclusion: Domain-matched training data and curriculum design, rather than model scale alone, are key drivers of generalization in firmware vulnerability detection. IoTVulBench provides a benchmark for future research and deployment-ready configurations for practical IoT security applications.

Abstract: IoT firmware vulnerability detection remains challenging due to heterogeneous firmware ecosystems, resource-constrained platforms, and limitations in existing benchmarks. Many datasets are synthetic or general-purpose and lack human-verified, contamination-screened annotations, limiting evidence on cross-corpus generalization across training sources, model architectures, and curriculum strategies. To address this gap, this paper introduces IoTVulBench, a human-verified benchmark for cross-corpus firmware vulnerability detection. IoTVulBench-Core was constructed from GitHub repositories, validated by three expert reviewers, and evaluated on a contamination-screened held-out target across five model architectures, two tuning methods, and three curriculum strategies, with ensemble, distillation, and robustness analyses. Models trained on IoTVulBench achieved the highest MCC among matched single-source datasets, reaching 0.58 versus 0.44 for PrimeVul and 0.39 for D2A. Staged curriculum learning increased MCC to 0.69, while a diversity-optimized ensemble achieved 0.73, improving by 0.42 MCC over the strongest reference comparator, a static analyzer at 0.31, and by 0.29 over PrimeVul. At a 0.5% false-positive rate, the model missed only 21% of vulnerabilities, compared with 71% for the strongest comparator. It retained 86% of its performance under identifier renaming and demonstrated strong calibration and largely faithful explanations. These findings indicate that domain-matched training data and curriculum design, rather than model scale alone, are key drivers of generalization in firmware vulnerability detection. The results provide a benchmark for future research and deployment-ready configurations for practical IoT security applications.

</details>


### [73] [Towards Scalable Fuzzy PSI via Efficient Fuzzy Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11526)
*Meng Hao,Xinpeng Yang,Hanxiao Chen,Tianwei Zhang,Haiyang Xue,Guomin Yang,Hongwei Li,Robert H. Deng*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces scalable fuzzy private set intersection (PSI) protocols supporting general L_p distances for both low- and high-dimensional sets, using two efficient fuzzy matching primitives (role-reversed OPRF and customized OT) plus a dual-layer hashing framework, achieving large speedups and communication reductions over prior work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior fuzzy PSI protocols for general L_p distance incur prohibitive overheads such as O((log δ)^d) for high-dimensional sets or O(δ) factors, making them impractical to scale. The authors aim to remove these exponential/polynomial-in-δ dependencies and support both low- and high-dimensional inputs efficiently.

Method: The core technique consists of two fuzzy matching protocols: (1) a role-reversed oblivious PRF (OPRF) construction achieving O(d log δ) overhead, and (2) a customized oblivious transfer (OT) construction with O(dℓ) overhead (ℓ = input bit length), suited for short inputs. On top of these, a dual-layer hashing framework is proposed for fuzzy PSI over low-dimensional sets, instantiated with the OT-based matching and a domain reduction optimization, yielding overhead linear in n, m, log δ, 2^d. For high-dimensional sets, fuzzy PSI protocols are built on the OPRF- and OT-based matching, achieving overhead linear in n, m, d, and log δ but relying on a strong globally disjoint assumption.

Result: Extensive evaluations show up to 145× speedup in running time and 20× reduction in communication compared to van Baarsen and Pu (ASIACRYPT'25), and up to 25× speedup and 17× reduction in communication compared to Piske et al. (CCS'25).

Conclusion: The proposed scalable fuzzy PSI protocols eliminate the O((log δ)^d) and O(δ) factors present in prior work, achieving linear overheads and substantial practical performance gains, establishing a more scalable foundation for fuzzy PSI over general L_p distances.

Abstract: In this paper, we present scalable fuzzy PSI protocols for general $L_{p \in [1, \infty]}$ distance, supporting both low- and high-dimensional sets. The core technique is two efficient fuzzy matching protocols. The first is built from a role-reversed oblivious PRF (OPRF) and realizes $O(d\log δ)$ overhead, compared to $O((\log δ)^d)$ in previous works. The second leverages customized oblivious transfer (OT) with $O(d\ell)$ overhead, where $\ell$ is the bit length of inputs, which is particularly suitable for short inputs. With these new techniques, we further propose a new dual-layer hashing framework for fuzzy PSI over low-dimensional sets, instantiated with our OT-based fuzzy matching and enhanced with a domain reduction optimization. The protocols achieve an overhead linear with $n, m, \log δ, 2^d$, without the $O((\log δ)^d)$ or $O(δ)$ factors present in prior works. {For high-dimensional sets, we construct fuzzy PSI protocols based on our OPRF- and OT-based fuzzy matching, which achieve an asymptotic overhead linear with $n, m, d$, and $\log δ$ but rely on the strong globally disjoint assumption.}
  Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our protocols achieve up to a $145\times$ speedup in running time and a $20\times$ reduction in communication cost compared to van Baarsen and Pu~(ASIACRYPT'25), and achieve up to a $25\times$ speedup in running time and up to a $17\times$ reduction in communication cost compared to Piske et al.~(CCS'25).

</details>


### [74] [Plaintext Recovery Against Post-Filtering Access Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11730)
*Zachary Espiritu,David Cash*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Prior FGAC side-channel attacks only leak existence of chosen values, not full high-entropy data. The authors show that rich query interfaces (range, prefix, conjunctive predicates) amplify existence leakage into efficient full-record and text reconstruction attacks in PostgreSQL (RLS timing) and Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (DLS scoring).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-grained access control (FGAC) implementations often use post-filtering, which creates side-channels. Prior work exploited these side-channels only to test whether a chosen value exists in unseen data, but could not efficiently recover rich, high-entropy data such as full records or text documents. This paper investigates whether rich query interfaces can amplify these existence leaks into more powerful reconstruction attacks.

Method: The authors use rich query interfaces—range predicates, prefix predicates, and conjunctive predicates—to amplify existence leakage into reconstruction attacks. In PostgreSQL, they exploit a timing side-channel with expressive SQL queries (ranges, conjunctions) to enumerate unknown attribute values and recover full records via binary search over large domains. In Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, they exploit scoring and prefix-expansion side-channels to recover indexed terms from documents and, in some cases, extract n-grams from the corpus to reconstruct approximate text.

Result: In PostgreSQL, the timing side-channel combined with range/conjunctive queries enables full record reconstruction via binary search over large domains. In Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, scoring and prefix-expansion side-channels allow recovery of indexed terms, and in some cases n-gram extraction yields approximate text reconstruction. Overall, the attacks demonstrate scalable reconstruction of high-entropy records from previously membership-only leakage.

Conclusion: FGAC side-channels must be evaluated in the presence of rich predicates, since these can turn simple membership tests into scalable reconstruction of high-entropy records. This raises the security bar for FGAC implementations that rely on post-filtering over shared physical indexing structures.

Abstract: Fine-grained access control (FGAC) mechanisms such as row-level security (RLS) and document-level security (DLS) are widely deployed in databases to restrict access to data stored in physical indexing structures shared by multiple users (e.g., in multi-tenant databases, or in the implementation of least-privilege within an organization). FGAC implementations often use post-filtering where untrusted queries run over all data and private results are redacted afterwards. Prior work shows this approach can lead to side-channels that enable attackers to test if a chosen value exists in unseen data. While damaging, prior attacks do not enable the efficient recovery of rich, high-entropy data like full records or text documents.
  We show these side-channels are more damaging than previously thought. Using rich query interfaces (e.g., range, prefix, and conjunctive predicates), we amplify existence leakage into reconstruction attacks. We do this in two settings:
  - PostgreSQL (RLS timing). We exploit a timing side-channel and expressive SQL queries (e.g., ranges, conjunctions) to enumerate unknown attribute values and, in turn, full records via binary search over large domains.
  - Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (DLS scoring). We exploit scoring and prefix-expansion side-channels to recover indexed terms from documents. In some cases, we can extract $n$-grams in the corpus to recover approximate text.
  Our results show that FGAC side-channels must be evaluated in the presence of rich predicates, which can turn membership tests into scalable reconstruction of high-entropy records.

</details>


### [75] [Fingerprinting Text-to-Image Diffusion Models via Collapsed Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11732)
*Yuanmin Huang,Chen Chen,Geng Hong,Xiaoyu You,Hui Xue,Zhenxing Qian,Mi Zhang,Min Yang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces a non-invasive fingerprinting method for text-to-image diffusion models based on "collapsed generation" — conditions that yield highly consistent images across random seeds — enabling ownership verification under both white-box and black-box access without embedding watermarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Proprietary diffusion models are distributed as hosted services or downloadable checkpoints, making intellectual property protection critical against leakage, copying, and unauthorized fine-tuning. Traditional watermarking is invasive, so the authors seek an intrinsic, non-invasive ownership verification approach.

Method: The framework leverages collapsed generation, a model-dependent property where certain input conditions produce near-identical images across stochastic seeds. On the source model, collapse-prone conditions are identified (optimized continuous embeddings for white-box, natural language prompts for black-box). A suspect model is evaluated by testing whether it reproduces the source model's collapse behavior across stochastic samplings, with ownership evidence measured by collapse consistency.

Result: Experiments across UNet- and transformer-based diffusion models show the fingerprints distinguish different source models with low confusion, remain verifiable in fine-tuned derivatives and under common and adaptive model- or query-level obfuscations, while requiring only a modest query budget.

Conclusion: Collapsed generation serves as a reliable intrinsic evidence source for non-invasive diffusion model ownership verification across multiple access settings and obfuscation scenarios.

Abstract: Proprietary text-to-image diffusion models are increasingly distributed as hosted services and downloadable checkpoints, making their intellectual property (IP) protection an increasingly critical concern when model leakage, copying, or unauthorized fine-tuning is disputed. In this work, we present a non-invasive model fingerprinting framework based on \emph{collapsed generation}, a phenomenon where certain input conditions produce highly consistent images across multiple stochastic seeds. We show that collapsed generation is an intrinsic, model-dependent property of the learned generation process. These collapse-prone conditions therefore expose model-specific behavioral signatures, enabling reliable ownership verification without embedding invasive watermarks. After preparing conditions on the source model, the framework verifies a suspect model under two access settings: (1) white-box pipeline access, where optimized continuous embeddings can be injected into the generation process, and (2) black-box API-only access, where natural language prompts are queried through the service interface. In both cases, ownership evidence is measured by whether the suspect model reproduces the source model's collapse behavior across stochastic samplings. Extensive experiments across UNet- and transformer-based diffusion models show that collapsed generation fingerprints can distinguish different source models with low confusion. These fingerprints remain verifiable in fine-tuned derivatives and under common and adaptive model- or query-level obfuscations, while requiring only a modest verification query budget. Together, these results establish collapsed generation as a reliable intrinsic evidence source for non-invasive diffusion model ownership verification.

</details>


### [76] [AmbSentry: Mitigating Sensing Eavesdropping in ISAC Systems by Harnessing Ambient IoT Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11799)
*Yifan Zhang,Yu Bai,Riku Jantti,Zhu Han,Christos Masouros*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AmbSentry proposes an ISAC system that uses distributed passive ambient IoT devices as cooperative jammers and ghost targets to prevent sensing information leakage to eavesdroppers, with iterative optimization achieving large security gains (14-dB SNR advantage and ~100x lower estimation error for legitimate receivers).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ISAC enables spectrum and hardware convergence for 6G, but its open wireless nature exposes sensing information to unauthorized eavesdroppers who can directly estimate sensing echo channels to extract target parameters like range and velocity. Traditional data-level protection is ineffective against such channel-estimation attacks, motivating physical-layer sensing security.

Method: The paper designs AmbSentry, which strategically configures distributed passive ambient IoT (AIoT) devices as cooperative jammers and ghost targets to inject controllable interference into the sensing environment. It formulates a joint optimization problem maximizing the integrated sidelobe level at the eavesdropper subject to quality-of-service constraints for legitimate sensing and communication. The non-convex problem is solved via an iterative algorithm combining Dinkelbach transformation with block coordinate descent to jointly design base-station transmit beamforming and AIoT reflection modulations.

Result: Extensive results show AmbSentry substantially improves sensing security: the legitimate sensing receiver attains a 14-dB SNR advantage in detection probability and achieves roughly a hundred times lower estimation error compared to the eavesdropper.

Conclusion: AmbSentry effectively mitigates sensing eavesdropping threats in ISAC systems by leveraging ambient IoT devices as controllable jammers/ghost targets, degrading the eavesdropper's sensing performance while preserving legitimate QoS, with significant SNR and estimation-accuracy advantages demonstrated.

Abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for 6G networks, enabling the synergistic convergence of spectral and hardware resources to maximize system efficiency. However, the inherent openness of wireless transmission exposes ISAC systems to critical security risks, particularly regarding the privacy of the sensing information. Unauthorized sensing eavesdroppers can extract sensitive target parameters (e.g., range and velocity) by directly estimating open sensing echo channels, rendering traditional data-based protection techniques ineffective. To mitigate this threat, this paper proposes AmbSentry, an ISAC system that prevents the leakage of sensing information to sensing eavesdroppers by harnessing naturally distributed passive ambient IoT (AIoT) devices. Specifically, these AIoT devices are strategically configured to act as cooperative jammers and ghost targets, introducing controllable interference into the sensing environment. Based on the proposed system, we formulate a joint optimization problem to maximize the integrated sidelobe level at the eavesdropper under quality-of-service (QoS) constraints, thereby degrading sensing eavesdropping performance while maintaining sensing and communication performance for legitimate receivers. Since the problem is non-convex, we further develop an efficient iterative algorithm to cooperatively design the transmit beamforming at the base station and the reflection modulations of the AIoT devices based on Dinkelbach transformation and block coordinate descent methods. The detailed results also demonstrate that AmbSentry significantly enhances sensing security, allowing the legitimate sensing receiver to achieve a 14-dB SNR advantage in detection probability and a hundred times lower estimation error compared to the eavesdropper.

</details>


### [77] [VICBench: A Multi-Language Benchmark for Code Vulnerability Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12246)
*Jin Lu,Xuening Han,Yang Zhong,Lin Tan,Kevin Luo,Andrew Gacek,Neha Rungta*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: VICBench introduces a benchmark of 100 verified vulnerability-inducing commits (VICs) across 88 projects and three languages, showing that state-of-the-art VIC detection tools remain unreliable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating vulnerability detection tools requires benchmark datasets containing vulnerability-inducing commits (VICs), which identify the full range of vulnerable software versions. Existing datasets are limited in language coverage, patch complexity, and project scope, hindering robust evaluation.

Method: The authors build VICBench by dual annotation from human experts combined with an agentic workflow, producing 100 verified VICs for 100 CVEs across 88 projects in Python, Java, and C++, covering 48 CWE types.

Result: VICBench features complex fixes averaging 38.6 lines and corresponding VICs of 252.5 lines, substantially larger than prior work. State-of-the-art algorithms V-SZZ and LLM4SZZ achieve only 33.3%–40.1% F1, indicating substantial remaining manual effort.

Conclusion: VICBench provides a rigorous foundation for evaluating vulnerability detection approaches and demonstrates that current state-of-the-art VIC detection methods still require significant manual involvement.

Abstract: Evaluating security vulnerability detection tools requires benchmark datasets with vulnerability-inducing commits (VICs) - the commits that first introduce vulnerabilities into codebases. VICs are essential for determining the full range of vulnerable software versions. Existing vulnerability datasets suffer from limited programming language coverage, restricted patch complexity, and narrow project scope. Through our dual annotation by human experts and an agentic workflow, we create a benchmark - VICBench - of 100 verified VICs for 100 CVEs across 88 projects in Python, Java, and C++, covering 48 CWE types. VICBench features complex real-world vulnerability fixes averaging 38.6 lines and corresponding VICs of 252.5 lines - significantly larger than prior work. Our evaluation shows that state-of-the-art algorithms V-SZZ and LLM4SZZ achieve only 33.3%-40.1% F1, confirming that using existing approaches still entails significant manual effort. VICBench enables robust evaluation of vulnerability detection approaches.

</details>


### [78] [Towards Model-based Run-time Cybersecurity: On Control-Flow Anomaly Detection, Attack Identification, and Hardware Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11802)
*Martin Sachenbacher,Martin Leucker,Alexander Weiss,Aliyu Tanko Ali*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a model-based architecture combining software- and hardware-based control-flow monitoring to make intrusion detection and attack-tree-based attack identification more robust against camouflage attacks, demonstrated with an authentication-service example where hardware monitoring corrects a misdiagnosed control-flow hijack.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Increasing resilience against cyber-attacks is critical. Control-flow monitoring detects anomalies, and attack trees identify attack types, but this approach is vulnerable to camouflage, where attackers manipulate the observed control flow to evade detection and mislead diagnosis. Therefore, more robust detection and identification are needed.

Method: A model-based approach combining software-level and hardware-level monitoring: software observation flags suspicious activity, and an independent hardware control-flow monitor verifies the actual transition sequence in detail, making camouflage harder. Attack trees are then used for intrusion identification, with the hardware layer correcting the diagnosis.

Result: In the authentication-service example, the software-level observer sees an anomalous but apparently harmless control-flow deviation and maps it to a benign attack-tree root cause, missing a true intrusion. The hardware monitor observes the actual transition sequence and changes the diagnosis from a low-severity configuration/maintenance issue to a high-confidence code-injection or control-flow hijack.

Conclusion: Combining control-flow anomaly detection, attack-tree-based intrusion identification, and hardware-based monitoring improves not only anomaly detection but also the diagnostic precision of cyber-attack identification.

Abstract: Methods to increase the resilience of systems to cyber-attacks become increasingly important. Control-flow monitoring provides a principled basis to ensure integrity and detect possible anomalies at run-time. Once anomalies have been detected, so-called attack trees can be used to identify possible types of attacks. However, this approach is vulnerable to camouflage, by which attackers try to evade detection (and correct identification) by deliberately manipulating also the system's observed control flow. In this paper, we outline a model-based approach that provides more robust intrusion detection and attack identification through an architecture that combines software- with hardware-based monitoring. In this approach, software-level observation indicates suspicious activities, while hardware-level monitoring checks them separately in more detail, making it much harder for attacks to camouflage themselves and go undetected. We illustrate the approach with an authentication-service example that captures a realistic failure mode: a software-level observer sees an anomalous but apparently harmless control-flow deviation, maps it to a benign root cause in an attack tree, but misses the true intrusion. A second, independent hardware control-flow monitor observes the actual transition sequence and thereby changes the attack-tree diagnosis from a low-severity configuration or maintenance issue to a high-confidence code-injection or control-flow hijack. In this scenario, the proposed combination of control-flow anomaly detection, attack-tree based intrusion identification, and hardware-based monitoring can improve not only anomaly detection, but also the diagnostic precision of attack-tree-based cyber-attack identification.

</details>


### [79] [How China-Origin Vision-Language Models Move from Refusal to Reframing in State Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11816)
*Guang Yang,Fengchen Liu,Alex Wang,Homa Hosseinmardi,Amir Ghasemian*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A systematic benchmark study of nine vision-language models (seven China-origin, two non-China) across 21,708 trials finds that state-aligned distortion in multimodal systems manifests increasingly as "invisible reframing"—fluently rewording or reframing politically sensitive content rather than explicitly refusing—especially under Chinese-language prompting and in newer China-origin model generations. The authors argue this shift undermines users' ability to detect information withholding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work documented state-aligned distortion in China-origin text-only LLMs, but whether and how such distortion arises in multimodal (vision-language) systems had not been systematically examined. The authors aim to decompose "multimodal censorship" into independent signals (refusal vs. framing, plus other dimensions) rather than a single refusal-based metric, and to investigate how the form of censorship is evolving.

Method: Constructed a balanced benchmark of 200 core entries across ten politically sensitive topics plus a seven-variant visual-abstraction probe. Ran nine VLMs (seven China-origin, two non-China) across four elicitation paradigms and two prompt languages, yielding 21,708 trials. Each response audited on six dimensions—explicit refusal, information integrity, visual grounding, state-aligned framing, language consistency, and response length—by two independent frontier LLM judges, validated against three human experts on a 200-trial sample. Measuring dimensions separately enables decomposing censorship into individual signals, with refusal and framing measured independently.

Result: (i) Chinese-language prompting roughly triples the odds of state-aligned framing within every model; (ii) China-origin models reframe more than non-China models (direction robust across judges and human raters; magnitude 1.6–3.2x); (iii) the effect is strongest in text-only political commentary (36.5%) and is gated by subject recognition rather than pixel detail, persisting at silhouette for iconic images; (iv) across four Qwen generations, state-aligned framing rises while explicit refusal falls, indicating censorship migrates from a visible act (refusal) to an invisible one (fluent reframing).

Conclusion: The shift from explicit refusal to invisible reframing is fundamentally a human-AI interaction problem: it removes the very signal users rely on to recognize that information has been withheld. The separate measurement of framing and refusal is key to detecting this migration, which a refusal-only score would miss.

Abstract: State-aligned distortion has been documented in China-origin text-based large language models (LLMs), but whether, and in what form, it arises in multimodal systems has not been systematically examined. We construct a balanced benchmark of 200 core entries spanning ten politically sensitive topics, plus a seven-variant visual-abstraction probe, and run nine vision-language models (VLMs), seven China-origin and two non-China, across four elicitation paradigms and two prompt languages, yielding 21,708 trials. Each response is audited on six dimensions -- explicit refusal, information integrity, visual grounding, state-aligned framing, language consistency, and response length -- by two independent frontier LLM judges, validated against three human experts on a 200-trial sample. Measuring each dimension separately lets us decompose multimodal censorship into individual signals rather than a single refusal-based score; in particular, refusal and framing are measured independently, so a model can stop refusing while still reframing. We find that (i) Chinese-language prompting roughly triples the odds of state-aligned framing, within every model; (ii) China-origin models reframe more than non-China models (direction robust across judges and human raters; magnitude 1.6--3.2x); (iii) the effect is strongest in text-only political commentary (36.5%) and is gated by recognition of the depicted subject rather than pixel detail, persisting even at silhouette for iconic images; and (iv) across four Qwen generations, state-aligned framing rises while explicit refusal falls: censorship migrates from a visible act (refusal) to an invisible one (fluent reframing). We argue this shift to invisible reframing is fundamentally a problem of human-AI interaction: it removes the very signal users rely on to recognize that information has been withheld.

</details>


### [80] [ToolHazard: Scaling Adversarial Environments for Security Evaluation and Alignment of LLM-based Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11878)
*Yutao Mou,Pengfei Yang,Zhe Yin,Zhangchi Xue,Xiaotian Luan,Dingyao Yu,Tong Zhang,Shikun Zhang,Wei Ye*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ToolHazard is a scalable framework that automatically synthesizes adversarial agent environments to study indirect prompt injection attacks on LLM agents, yielding a benchmark (ToolHazard-Bench) and alignment data that improve agent security without hurting benign utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research on indirect prompt injection in LLM agents is limited by manually implemented/reused environments, stochastic LLM-based tool simulation, and predefined injection locations, which hinders scalable security research across diverse domains.

Method: ToolHazard uses three components: an Environment Simulator (synthesizes executable stateful environments), an Attacker Agent (discovers viable injection points and generates environment-specific payloads), and a User Simulator (constructs state-grounded long-horizon tasks). These expand with additional seed domains and compute to build ToolHazard-Bench.

Result: Experiments show substantial agent vulnerabilities, and reveal that injection timing and placement significantly affect attack effectiveness. ToolHazard-generated alignment data improves security on both ToolHazard-Bench and AgentDojo while preserving benign task utility.

Conclusion: ToolHazard enables scalable, domain-expandable synthesis of adversarial environments for indirect prompt injection, providing a stress-test benchmark and effective alignment data to harden LLM agents against diverse environmental attacks.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents integrated with external tools are vulnerable to indirect prompt injections embedded in environmental states. However, existing studies largely rely on manually implemented or reused environments, stochastic LLM-based tool simulation, and predefined injection locations, limiting scalable security research across broader domains. To bridge this gap, we propose **ToolHazard**, a scalable adversarial environment synthesis framework that reduces human engineering and supports expansion with additional seed domains and compute. Through an Environment Simulator, an Attacker Agent, and a User Simulator, ToolHazard synthesizes executable stateful environments, discovers viable injection points and generates environment-specific payloads, and constructs state-grounded long-horizon tasks. Based on ToolHazard, we build **ToolHazard-Bench** for stress-testing agents under complex workflows and diverse environmental attacks. Experiments reveal substantial agent vulnerabilities and show that injection timing and placement affect attack effectiveness. Moreover, ToolHazard-generated alignment data improves security on both ToolHazard-Bench and AgentDojo while preserving benign task utility.

</details>


### [81] [Rank-Two Frobenius-Linearized Normal Forms and Orthoderivative Dual Coordinates in Quadratic APN Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11939)
*Jingchuan Ma,Yanhua Liu,Qiaoyun Huang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper classifies binary-linear two-term twisted-linear operators L(Y)=AY^σ+BY on K^3 (K a finite extension of F_2) satisfying rank-two and one-dimensional binary-kernel conditions, reducing them to a canonical model (α,β,γ)↦(α^σ+α,β^σ,γ), and connects this to APN maps, permutation behavior, and known constructions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To classify a natural family of σ-Frobenius-linearized operators on K^3 under a rank-two/kernel condition, and to obtain a canonical normal form that clarifies the algebraic structure behind almost perfect nonlinear (APN) maps, their duals, and known constructions (triprojective and cubic norm-twist).

Method: The authors impose a coefficient-rank and binary-kernel condition: A and B have K-rank two and L has a one-dimensional kernel over F_2. They construct coordinate frames from the two coefficient-kernel directions and the binary kernel, and show invertible K-linear input/output changes reduce L to the canonical model (α,β,γ)↦(α^σ+α,β^σ,γ). They extract the first dual output row as the unique nonzero trace-adjoint normal, normalize it exactly over K, and apply the normal form to pure σ-quadratic APN maps and to the triprojective (Gologlu–Kolsch) and cubic norm-twist (Li–Zhou–Li–Qu) constructions.

Result: Under the stated conditions L is canonically equivalent to (α,β,γ)↦(α^σ+α,β^σ,γ). For pure σ-quadratic APN maps this identifies the orthoderivative by π_F(X)^T F(X)=1; in odd extension degree it yields permutation behavior and a projective-plane-to-dual bijection. A Gold representation has coefficient-rank pair (3,3), delimiting the rank-two subclass. The normal form also supplies exact extension-field labels for known component-radical and Walsh-support relations.

Conclusion: The rank-two, one-dimensional-binary-kernel class of operators admits a clean canonical normal form with exact K-valued normalization. This normal form unifies the orthoderivative identity and permutation/projective-duality properties of pure APN maps, while distinguishing what follows from the operator theorem alone versus what requires the specific algebraic construction (triprojective vs. norm-twist).

Abstract: We classify binary-linear two-term Frobenius-linearized operators $L(Y)=AY^σ+BY$ on $K^3$, where $K$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{F}_2$ and $σ$ is a fixed nontrivial Frobenius automorphism of $K$ with fixed field $\mathbb{F}_2$. Under a coefficient-rank and binary-kernel condition, if $A$ and $B$ both have $K$-rank two and $L$ has a one-dimensional kernel over $\mathbb{F}_2$, then invertible $K$-linear input and output changes reduce $L$, for this fixed $σ$, to the canonical model $(α,β,γ)\mapsto(α^σ+α,β^σ,γ)$. The proof constructs the coordinate frames from the two coefficient-kernel directions and the binary kernel. In these coordinates, the first dual output row is exactly the unique nonzero trace-adjoint normal, with an exact $K$-valued normalization. For pure $σ$-quadratic almost perfect nonlinear maps, this identifies the orthoderivative by $π_F(X)^T F(X)=1$; in odd extension degree it also yields permutation behavior and a bijection from the projective plane to its dual. The triprojective construction of Gologlu and Kolsch and the cubic norm-twist construction of Li, Zhou, Li, and Qu provide two realizations arising from different algebraic constructions. The triprojective case further admits a determinant factorization and a complete dual frame, whereas the norm-twist realization shows that the pure-map consequences do not follow from the operator theorem alone. A natural Gold representation has coefficient-rank pair $(3,3)$, delimiting the rank-two subclass. The normal form also supplies exact extension-field labels for known component-radical and Walsh-support relations.

</details>


### [82] [Slips: Behavioral Evidence Aggregation for Network Security](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11979)
*Sebastian Garcia,Veronica Valeros,Alya Gomaa,Ondřej Lukáš,Martin Řepa,Lukáš Forst,David Otta,František Střasák,Jan Svoboda,Dita Hollmannová*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Slips is a network intrusion detection system that profiles host behavior within time windows and accumulates evidence from independent modules; on an expert-labeled PCAP dataset it achieved 83% higher recall and 70% higher F1 than Suricata with no false positives from either system.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional IDSs analyze individual packets or flows, limiting their ability to combine isolated detections into a coherent host-level assessment; packet-level features are too low-level for accurate AI-based detection at low false-positive rates.

Method: Slips builds host-centered behavioral profiles and organizes activity into time windows using a modular architecture in which independent modules report evidence rather than emitting final alerts; evidence is accumulated into host-level decisions. It is evaluated against Suricata on an expert-labeled PCAP dataset.

Result: At the profile-time-window level, Slips achieved 83% higher recall and a 70% higher F1 score than Suricata, while neither system produced false positives.

Conclusion: Time-window-based evidence accumulation yields context-aware decisions that align better with expert judgment than connection-level analysis.

Abstract: Network intrusion detection systems often analyze individual packets or flows, although malicious behavior may develop across many connections and over time. This may limit their ability to combine isolated detections into a coherent assessment of host behavior. Packet-level features may also be too low-level for complex AI-based detection, requiring additional processing to improve accuracy while maintaining a low false-positive rate.
  We present Slips, a network intrusion detection system that builds host-centered behavioral profiles and organizes activity into time windows. It uses a modular architecture in which independent modules report evidence rather than generating final alerts directly. Slips then accumulates this evidence into host-level decisions. We evaluate Slips against Suricata on an expert-labeled PCAP dataset. At the profile-time-window level, Slips achieved 83% higher recall and a 70% higher F1 score than Suricata, while neither system produced false positives. These results indicate that time-window-based evidence accumulation can produce context-aware decisions that better align with expert judgment.

</details>


### [83] [A Comparison of Malware Image Transformations Using Grad-CAM and Hybrid Learning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12077)
*Vibha Bhavikatti,Mark Stamp*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper uses Grad-CAM as an explainable AI tool on binary-to-image malware representations, showing that a Random Forest trained on Grad-CAM-extracted MobileNetV2 features achieves 0.777 accuracy across 17 malware families, beating a 0.750 benchmark, while revealing that accuracy and explanation faithfulness do not coincide across image transformations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Binary-to-image representations enable effective ML for malware detection, but performance varies with the conversion technique, and the explainability/interpretability of image-based malware models is largely unexplored. The work aims to fill this gap by applying XAI to understand and leverage these representations.

Method: The authors employ Grad-CAM as an XAI tool to analyze eight distinct image types derived from malware samples. They compute quantitative faithfulness and stability metrics for Grad-CAM heatmaps, compare them against HiResCAM, and use Grad-CAM-derived features (via a MobileNetV2 CNN) to train a Random Forest classifier.

Result: A Random Forest trained on Grad-CAM image features through MobileNetV2 achieves a test accuracy of 0.777 across 17 malware families, exceeding the previous 0.750 benchmark on the same dataset. A key finding is that accuracy and explanation faithfulness do not coincide: the transformations producing the most faithful explanations yield only mid-tier accuracy.

Conclusion: Grad-CAM heatmaps provide useful information for malware classification and improve accuracy over prior work, but there is a trade-off between model accuracy and explanation faithfulness across malware image transformations, motivating careful selection of representation techniques.

Abstract: Recent studies have shown that binary-to-image representations can enable effective machine learning-based results for malware detection and classification. However, performance can vary significantly, depending on the technique used to convert binaries to images. Furthermore, the explainability and interpretability of image-based models is largely unexplored within the malware domain. In this research, we employ Gradient-weighted Class Activation Maps (Grad-CAM) as an eXplainable AI (XAI) tool, which we use to analyze eight distinct image types derived from malware samples. We provide quantitative faithfulness and stability metrics for Grad-CAM heatmaps and we compare these heatmaps to High-Resolution Class Activation Mappings (HiResCAM). We also show that Grad-CAM heatmaps can provide useful information for malware classification. Specifically, we show that a Random Forest model trained on features extracted from Grad-CAM images via a MobileNetV2 Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model achieves a test accuracy of 0.777 across 17 malware families, exceeding a previous benchmark of 0.750 for this same dataset. A key finding of this research is that for the malware image transformations considered, accuracy and explanation faithfulness do not coincide, e.g., image transformation techniques that produce the most faithful explanations yield only mid-tier accuracy.

</details>


### [84] [Machine Learning-Based Cyber Defense for Cloud Infrastructure: An Adaptive Deep Q-Network Architecture for Intelligent Intrusion Detection and Automated Threat Mitigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12190)
*Md Yassir Mottalib,Md Yousuf,Eklachur Rahman Bhuiyan,S M Ahsan Habib,Sonjoy Kumar Dey,Md. Salahuddin Gazi,Molay Kumar Roy,Asaduzzaman Anik*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a reinforcement learning-based dynamic cyber defense framework using a Deep Q-Network (DQN), trained on CICIDS2017 and validated on UNSW-NB15, achieving 99.72% accuracy and a 99.54% attack mitigation rate, outperforming several classical ML models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With the increasing complexity of cyber assaults in cloud environments, there is a need for adaptable security solutions that support real-time detection and autonomous response. Existing static approaches cannot keep up with evolving attacks, motivating a dynamic, self-learning defense framework.

Method: A reinforcement learning-based dynamic cyber defense framework that deploys a Deep Q-Network (DQN) to learn effective defensive strategies. It uses the CICIDS2017 dataset for model creation and UNSW-NB15 for external validation, with preprocessing, feature engineering, and adaptive policy learning. The DQN is compared against decision tree, SVM, random forest, XGBoost, and multilayer perceptron models.

Result: The DQN achieves 99.72% accuracy, 99.68% precision, 99.65% recall, 99.66% F1-score, and 0.999 ROC-AUC, with a 0.31% false positive rate, 0.35% false negative rate, and 15 ms detection latency. The framework achieved a 99.54% attack mitigation rate.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate the potential of reinforcement learning as a powerful and scalable approach for autonomous cybersecurity in modern cloud environments, providing strong adaptive and real-time defensive capabilities.

Abstract: With the increasing complexity of cyber assaults in cloud environments, adaptable security solutions are needed that can support real-time detection and autonomous response. In this paper, we propose a reinforcement learning-based dynamic cyber defense framework. We deploy a Deep Q-Network (DQN) to train effective defensive strategies to counteract the evolving cyberattacks. We leverage the CICIDS2017 dataset for model creation and the UNSW-NB15 dataset for external validation, involving preprocessing of data, feature engineering, and adaptive policy learning. We compare the proposed DQN with decision tree, support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost, and multilayer perceptron models. The proposed DQN achieves an accuracy of 99.72%, a precision of 99.68%, a recall of 99.65%, an F1-score of 99.66%, and an ROC-AUC of 0.999, while the false positive rate is 0.31%, the false negative rate is 0.35%, and the detection latency is 15 ms. The framework achieved 99.54% attack mitigation rate, demonstrating strong adaptive and real-time defensive capabilities. These results demonstrate the potential of reinforcement learning as a powerful and scalable approach for autonomous cybersecurity in modern cloud environments.

</details>


### [85] [Convergent Detour Hijacking: Task-Preserving Resource Amplification in Skill-Based LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12273)
*Junliang Liu,Ruoyu Li,Wenxin Tang,Jingyu Xiao,Zhenyu Liu,Jingheng Xu,Laizhong Cui*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces Convergent Detour Hijacking (CDH), a text-only attack on LLM agents that combines skill-selection manipulation with skill-body planning to make agents take unnecessarily costly detours while preserving task completion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents increasingly rely on third-party skills with natural-language descriptions (for selection) and instruction bodies (for planning). This progressive-disclosure design exposes two control points to untrusted publishers. Prior work studies selection manipulation, malicious instructions, and resource amplification separately, leaving their end-to-end composition unclear.

Method: CDH couples the selection and planning stages: under shared semantic cover, a skill description establishes relevance during selection, while an aligned body reuses that rationale to fabricate plausible dependencies during planning. This attracts an attacker-controlled coordinator alongside legitimate skills, recruits unnecessary benign skills into a bounded detour, and re-enters the original route to preserve task completion. Evaluated across multiple LLM backends and 491 held-out tasks under single-task and multi-turn conditions.

Result: On DeepSeek-V4-Pro, the matched coordinator is selected in 80.02% of tasks; among coordinator-hit runs completing tasks, token consumption and end-to-end execution time increase by 66.91% and 92.45%, respectively, while aggregate task completion remains comparable.

Conclusion: Correct outcomes do not guarantee trajectory integrity or cost safety; an LLM agent can complete a task correctly while still being steered onto an unnecessarily costly trajectory.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on third-party skills, using natural-language descriptions for selection and instruction bodies for planning. This progressive-disclosure design exposes two sequential control points to untrusted publishers: a static skill may steer an otherwise correct task onto an unnecessarily costly trajectory. Prior work studies selection manipulation, malicious skill instructions, and tool-chain resource amplification largely separately, leaving their end-to-end composition unclear. We introduce Convergent Detour Hijacking (CDH), a text-only, runtime-independent attack that couples these stages. Under shared semantic cover, a description establishes relevance during selection, while an aligned body reuses that rationale to fabricate plausible dependencies during planning. CDH attracts an attacker-controlled coordinator alongside legitimate skills, recruits unnecessary benign skills into a bounded detour, and then re-enters the original route to preserve task completion. We evaluate it across multiple LLM backends and 491 held-out tasks under single-task and multi-turn conditions. On DeepSeek-V4-Pro, the matched coordinator is selected in 80.02% of tasks; among coordinator-hit runs that complete tasks, token consumption and end-to-end execution time increase by 66.91% and 92.45%, respectively, while aggregate task completion remains comparable. Thus, correct outcomes do not guarantee trajectory integrity or cost safety.

</details>


### [86] [Evaluating LLM Generated Detection Rules in Cybersecurity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16749)
*Anna Bertiger,Bobby Filar,Aryan Luthra,Stefano Meschiari,Aiden Mitchell,Sam Scholten,Vivek Sharath*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces an open-source evaluation framework and benchmark metrics for assessing LLM-generated cybersecurity rules, using a holdout-set methodology and three expert-inspired metrics to compare LLM output against human-written rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in security environments, but there are limited measures of their effectiveness, which undermines trust and usefulness for security practitioners. The work aims to provide a rigorous, realistic evaluation of LLM-based security rule generation.

Method: An open-source evaluation framework and benchmark metrics are presented. The benchmark uses a holdout set-based methodology to measure the effectiveness of LLM-generated security rules against a human-generated corpus of rules. Three key metrics inspired by how experts evaluate security rules provide a multifaceted evaluation of an LLM-based security rule generator. The methodology is demonstrated using rules from Sublime Security's detection team and rules generated by Sublime Security's Automated Detection Engineer (ADE).

Result: The paper provides a thorough analysis of ADE's skills in the results section, illustrating the evaluation methodology's application and revealing the capabilities and limitations of the LLM-based Automated Detection Engineer relative to human-written rules.

Conclusion: The proposed framework and benchmark metrics offer a realistic and multifaceted way to evaluate LLM-generated security rules, aiming to increase trust and utility for security practitioners by measuring effectiveness against human-generated baselines.

Abstract: LLMs are increasingly pervasive in the security environment, with limited measures of their effectiveness, which limits trust and usefulness to security practitioners. Here, we present an open-source evaluation framework and benchmark metrics for evaluating LLM-generated cybersecurity rules. The benchmark employs a holdout set-based methodology to measure the effectiveness of LLM-generated security rules in comparison to a human-generated corpus of rules. It provides three key metrics inspired by the way experts evaluate security rules, offering a realistic, multifaceted evaluation of the effectiveness of an LLM-based security rule generator. This methodology is illustrated using rules from Sublime Security's detection team and those written by Sublime Security's Automated Detection Engineer (ADE), with a thorough analysis of ADE's skills presented in the results section.

</details>
