### [104] [TRACES: A Benchmark for Epistemic Reliability in Scientific Reasoning by LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11415)
*Valentin Rodionov,Shamil Assylbekov*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper introduces a probe corpus of 42 retracted, fraudulent, and pseudoscientific papers to test whether language models can identify unreliable scientific literature when acting as agents. Across 30 models, most engaged with untenable premises (~95% of non-empty responses) and failed over 71% of probes, suggesting rejections stem from topic-keyed safety behavior rather than genuine epistemic judgment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly proposed as agents in scientific workflows where no downstream verifier exists, which assumes they can distinguish reliable from unreliable scientific literature. This capability has not been directly measured; existing factuality benchmarks test questions with known answers rather than the failure mode of engaging with flawed premises.

Method: The authors built a probe corpus of 42 retracted, fraudulent, and pseudoscientific papers spanning five claim types (fabricated observation, pseudophysical mechanism, magical premise, legitimization bridge, cargo-cult experiment). Each probe pairs a near-verbatim preamble from the target paper with a plausible study-design request, eliciting single-shot model engagement. Two complementary scores are defined: IFR-a (outright rejection of the flawed premise) and IFR-i (recognizing unreliability while still engaging), plus an Engagement Depth Index (EDI) quantifying reproduction of paper- or field-specific withheld details. Matched-structure controls were used to test whether rejections generalize beyond keyed topics. Evaluated 30 models over 10 repeated runs.

Result: Aggregate IFR-a is 0.93 ± 0.004 and aggregate IFR-i is 0.809 ± 0.009, meaning models failed to reject outright in ~93% of cases and failed to even flag unreliability in ~81%. Models engaged with untenable premises in 95% of non-empty responses. Every model failed more than 71% of agentic probes, and 22 of 30 models failed more than 90%. Rejections concentrated on a few high-notoriety topics/specific probes and vanished under matched-structure controls, indicating topic-keyed safety behavior rather than robust epistemic competence.

Conclusion: The results indicate language models lack robust epistemic competence for distinguishing unreliable scientific literature and instead exhibit topic-keyed safety behavior, creating an urgent need for guardrail infrastructure before deploying LLMs as agents in scientific workflows.

Abstract: Large language models are being proposed as agents in scientific workflows, in domains where no downstream verifier exists. Such deployment assumes the model can distinguish reliable scientific literature from unreliable literature, a capability that has not yet been directly measured. Existing benchmarks evaluate factuality on questions with known answers; the failure mode we target here is different. We introduce a probe corpus of 42 retracted, fraudulent, and pseudoscientific papers, paired with a methodology for eliciting and scoring single-shot model engagement with each paper's framing. Each probe pairs a preamble extracted near-verbatim from the target paper with a scientifically plausible study-design request. The probes span five claim types: fabricated observation, pseudophysical mechanism, magical premise, legitimization bridge, and cargo-cult experiment. Two complementary scores measure whether a model rejects the flawed premise outright (IFR-a) and whether it recognizes the unreliability while still engaging (IFR-i). A depth score, the Engagement Depth Index (EDI), quantifies reproduction of paper- or field-specific withheld details. Across 30 models and 10 repeated runs, aggregate IFR-a is 0.93 $\pm$ 0.004 and aggregate IFR-i is 0.809 $\pm$ 0.009. Models engaged with untenable premises in 95% of all non-empty responses. Every evaluated model fails more than 71% of agentic probes, and 22 of 30 models fail more than 90% of the time. Rejections are concentrated on a small number of high-notoriety topics and specific probes, and disappear under matched-structure controls. These results are consistent with topic-keyed safety behavior rather than robust epistemic competence, and indicate an urgent need for guardrail infrastructure for scientific deployment of language models.

</details>


### [105] [From Overlooked to Explored: Recovering Item Relations via Mixture of Perspectives for Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11846)
*Junyoung Kim,Wonbin Kweon,Woojoo Kim,Jaehyung Lim,Dongha Kim,Hwanjo Yu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: PRISM addresses similarity bias in self-attention-based sequential recommenders by re-examining item relations from multiple perspectives (Affinity View for homogeneous relations, Contrast View for heterogeneous ones), achieving state-of-the-art results on seven benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sequential recommendation relies on capturing inter-item relations, but empirical analysis shows dot-product attention suffers from similarity bias: it over-weights similar items and overlooks heterogeneous relations that carry meaningful preference signals, limiting recommendation accuracy across various transformer-based SR models.

Method: The authors propose PRISM (Perspective-based Relational Insight Synthesis Module), which uses K Perspective Lenses to calibrate attention from distinct viewpoints. It combines an Affinity View that refines homogeneous (similar) relations with a Contrast View that surfaces heterogeneous relations suppressed by similarity bias, enabling the model to capture the full spectrum of user preferences.

Result: Extensive experiments on seven real-world benchmarks show that PRISM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines for sequential recommendation.

Conclusion: Self-attention's similarity bias systematically degrades sequential recommendation. PRISM effectively mitigates this by synthesizing relational insights from multiple perspectives, achieving consistent and superior performance across diverse benchmarks; code is publicly released.

Abstract: Capturing user preference from a user's interaction sequence is the central challenge of Sequential Recommendation (SR). This preference intuitively emerges from inter-item relations: each item transition reflects a preference embedded in the relations between items, making the faithful capture of these relations essential for accurate recommendation. For this reason, self-attention is dominant in sequential recommendation for its ability to compute pairwise item interactions, yet our empirical analysis reveals that it consistently suffers from similarity bias across various types of transformer-based SR models: dot-product attention scores disproportionately favor similar items, systematically overlooking heterogeneous relations with meaningful preference signals and directly limiting recommendation performance. To address this, we propose PRISM (Perspective-based Relational Insight Synthesis Module), a module that re-examines item relations from multiple perspectives. PRISM employs K Perspective Lenses to calibrate attention from distinct viewpoints, combining an Affinity View that refines homogeneous relations and a Contrast View that exposes heterogeneous ones suppressed by similarity bias, enabling the model to capture the full spectrum of user preferences. Extensive experiments on seven real-world benchmarks demonstrate that PRISM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/327aem/PRISM/.

</details>


### [106] [Sci-Surf: Navigating Scientific Literature Discovery through Human Feedback and Intelligent Summarizatio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11973)
*Fang Guo,Qi Zhu,Rongcan Pei,Shuqi He,Hui Chen,Yue Zhang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Sci-Surf is an intent-centric academic knowledge discovery system that combines feedback-driven personalized paper recommendation with multi-modal, blog-style paper summaries, using LLM-based user profiling to improve both discovery and comprehension.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid growth of scientific literature makes it hard for researchers to find relevant new studies and understand them deeply. Existing platforms rely on static topic subscriptions or embedding similarity and only provide abstracts/short summaries, lacking nuanced intent modeling and in-depth paper digestion.

Method: Sci-Surf refines user intent representations via LLM-based user profiling (verbalized profiles) for feedback-driven personalized recommendation, and generates structured blog-style summaries that synthesize textual and visual information from full papers. It is presented as an end-to-end academic discovery pipeline in a demo.

Result: Real-user evaluations show measurable improvements in both recommendation quality and digestion quality. Integrating verbalized profiles yielded a 10.4% average improvement in predictive alignment with real-world user preferences over a month-long online evaluation.

Conclusion: Sci-Surf demonstrates an effective intent-centric approach to academic discovery, showing that LLM-based user profiling and multi-modal blog-style summarization improve both recommendation and comprehension, validated through real-user online evaluation.

Abstract: The rapid growth of scientific publications makes it increasingly difficult for researchers to identify relevant new studies and effectively comprehend them. Existing academic discovery platforms typically rely on static topic subscriptions or embedding-based similarity and provide only abstracts or short summaries, offering limited support for nuanced intent modeling and in-depth paper summarization. We present Sci-Surf, an intent-centric knowledge discovery system that integrates feedback-driven personalized recommendation with multi-modal blog-style paper digestion. Our approach refines user intent representations through LLM-based user profiling, while generating structured summaries that synthesize textual and visual information from full papers. The demo presents an end-to-end academic discovery pipeline and demonstrates measurable improvements in both recommendation quality and digestion quality through real-user evaluations. Specifically, the integration of verbalized profiles led to a 10.4% average improvement in predictive alignment with real-world user preferences throughout a month-long online evaluation.

</details>


### [107] [HCGRec: Hint-Conditioned Generative Recommendation with Semantic IDs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11980)
*Kangning Zhang,Haotian Fang,Xukun Luo,Hao Yin,Yang Gao,Peng Yan,Weiwen Liu,Weinan Zhang,Yong Yu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: HCGRec addresses a structured optimization bottleneck in semantic-ID generative recommenders by injecting minimal target-prefix hints during reward-based post-training and decomposing credit between hinted and sampled tokens, which recovers learning signal and cuts zero-advantage samples dramatically.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semantic-ID generative recommenders suffer during reward-based post-training because when an early semantic token branches incorrectly, the token space is so large that finite rollout groups almost never reach the ground-truth item. This yields identical zero rewards across the group, so group-relative optimization (GRPO-style) gets no advantage signal and the model fails to learn on hard instances.

Method: HCGRec first diagnoses each training instance via checkpoint rollouts. Only when the current generator cannot reach the correct item does it supply a minimal target-prefix hint, conditioning the model to generate the unhinted suffix under the correct semantic branch. It then applies hint-aware credit decomposition: hinted prefix tokens are treated as oracle-provided item context and optimized with supervised learning to preserve item-semantic and prefix-structure alignment, while unhinted suffix tokens are treated as sampled generation actions and optimized with GRPO.

Result: On sequential recommendation benchmarks, HCGRec substantially outperforms both supervised fine-tuning and vanilla reward-based post-training, and reduces zero-advantage training samples from over 70% to below 20%.

Conclusion: By supplying minimal hints only for hard cases and separating credit between oracle-hinted and model-sampled tokens, HCGRec restores informative comparison signal in semantic-ID generative recommendation and achieves clear performance gains, with code released for reproducibility.

Abstract: Semantic-ID generative recommenders represent each item as a short sequence of discrete semantic tokens and predict the next item by autoregressively generating this token sequence. This paradigm enables a unified generation interface for item IDs, histories, and item text, but it also creates a structured optimization bottleneck during reward-based post-training: when an early semantic token enters the wrong branch of the item-token space, finite rollout groups rarely reach the ground-truth item, so group-relative optimization receives identical zero rewards and produces no useful advantage. We propose Hint-Conditioned Generative Recommendation (HCGRec), a semantic-ID generative recommendation framework that recovers learning signal for such hard training instances. HCGRec diagnoses each instance with checkpoint rollouts and supplies a minimal target-prefix hint only when the current generator cannot reach the correct item. The model then generates the unhinted suffix under the hinted semantic branch, turning zero-reward groups into informative comparisons over item-token completions. Hinting also changes token identity: hinted prefix tokens are oracle-provided item context, while unhinted suffix tokens are sampled generation actions. We therefore introduce hint-aware credit decomposition, using supervised learning to preserve item-semantic and prefix-structure alignment for hinted tokens and GRPO to optimize the sampled suffix. Experiments on sequential recommendation benchmarks show that HCGRec substantially improves over supervised fine-tuning and vanilla reward-based post-training, while reducing zero-advantage training samples from over 70% to below 20%. The code is accessible at https://github.com/WncFht/GRec.

</details>


### [108] [Token-Level Credit Assignment Optimization for Generative Document Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12049)
*Xinpeng Zhao,Yang Liu,Ran Chen,Xinyu Ma,Daiting Shi,Pengjie Ren,Zhumin Chen,Zhaochun Ren,Xin Xin*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Generative retrieval uses autoregressive DocID generation, but existing RL methods apply coarse sequence-level rewards that cannot identify which token decisions drive retrieval success. This paper proposes a fine-grained RL framework with token-level relevance rewards that estimate step-wise contributions to retrieval quality, improving credit assignment and outperforming sequence-level baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative retrieval models generate document identifiers token by token, yet retrieval quality is only evaluated after the full DocID is emitted. This mismatch means reinforcement learning methods rely on sequence-level rewards that propagate identical document-level feedback to every decoding step, making it impossible to pinpoint which token decisions cause success or failure.

Method: The paper proposes a fine-grained reinforcement learning framework that assigns token-level relevance rewards instead of a single sequence-level reward. It estimates step-wise rewards by measuring how each token decision changes the expected retrieval quality of the generation trajectory, enabling precise credit assignment. Practical reward estimation strategies tailored to DocID generation are developed and integrated into a policy optimization framework.

Result: Experiments on retrieval benchmarks show the method consistently outperforms sequence-level reward baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of fine-grained supervision for aligning autoregressive DocID generation with retrieval objectives.

Conclusion: Fine-grained, token-level relevance rewards provide more precise credit assignment than sequence-level feedback, better aligning autoregressive DocID generation with document-level retrieval objectives and yielding consistent performance gains over existing baselines.

Abstract: Generative retrieval models perform document retrieval by autoregressively generating document identifiers (DocIDs). This process naturally forms a sequential decision problem, where each decoding step selects a DocID token and the complete token sequence determines the retrieved document. However, retrieval effectiveness is typically evaluated only after the full DocID is generated, creating a mismatch between token-level generation and document-level relevance supervision. As a result, existing reinforcement learning methods for generative retrieval mostly rely on sequence-level rewards, where the same document-level feedback is propagated to all decoding steps. Such coarse-grained feedback makes it difficult to identify which token decisions are responsible for successful or failed retrieval.
  In this work, we propose a fine-grained reinforcement learning framework for generative retrieval with token-level relevance rewards. Instead of assigning a single reward to the entire generated DocID, we estimate step-wise rewards by measuring how each token decision changes the expected retrieval quality of the corresponding generation trajectory. This enables more precise credit assignment and encourages the policy to favor token decisions that contribute more directly to document-level relevance. We further develop practical reward estimation strategies tailored to the DocID generation process and incorporate them into a policy optimization framework. Experiments on retrieval benchmarks show that our method consistently outperforms sequence-level reward baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of fine-grained supervision for aligning autoregressive DocID generation with retrieval objectives.

</details>


### [109] [Making Collaborative Signals Count: Graph-Aware Large Language Models for Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12184)
*Fenglin Yan,Bohao Wang,Jian Zhang,Yu Cui,Tongya Zheng,Ye Feng,Can Wang,Jiawei Chen*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: GALLM is a graph-aware LLM framework for sequential recommendation that injects collaborative signals into the LLM attention mechanism via lightweight learnable attention biases derived from a heterogeneous graph over text tokens and item tokens, without requiring a separate graph encoder.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs used as recommenders suffer from language-centric pretraining that overlooks collaborative signals in user-item interactions. Existing solutions either depend on external recommenders to provide collaborative representations or only capture intra-sequence dependencies, failing to exploit global collaborative patterns. GALLM aims to integrate global collaborative information directly into the LLM.

Method: GALLM builds a collaborative graph over text tokens and item tokens and models three relation types: Text-Text (semantic dependencies), Item-Text (item-token alignment with descriptions), and Item-Item (global co-occurrence). These relations are converted into lightweight learnable attention biases and added into the LLM attention mechanism, enabling collaborative-aware token interactions without an additional graph encoder.

Result: On four real-world benchmarks, GALLM achieves the best performance among compared baselines, improving over the strongest baseline by 9.76% on average in HR@5.

Conclusion: By embedding graph-based collaborative relations as attention biases within the LLM, GALLM effectively captures both semantic and global collaborative patterns, outperforming state-of-the-art sequential recommendation baselines.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been widely adopted as backbones for recommender systems. However, their language-centric pretraining makes it difficult to capture collaborative signals implicit in user-item interactions, which are crucial for personalized recommendation. Existing methods either inject collaborative representations produced by external recommenders or model only intra-sequence dependencies, limiting their ability to exploit global collaborative patterns. To address this limitation, we propose GALLM, a graph-aware LLM framework for sequential recommendation. GALLM constructs a collaborative graph over text tokens and item tokens, and models three types of relations: Text--Text relations for preserving semantic dependencies, Item--Text relations for aligning item tokens with their textual descriptions, and Item--Item relations derived from global item co-occurrence patterns. These relations are transformed into lightweight learnable attention biases and incorporated into the LLM attention mechanism, enabling collaborative-aware token interactions without introducing an additional graph encoder. Experiments on four real-world benchmarks show that GALLM achieves the best performance among the compared baselines, improving over the strongest baseline by 9.76\% on average in HR@5.

</details>

### [110] [FarSky: Task-Aware Latent-Space Coupling for Generative Intra-Hour Solar Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11254)
*Yann Fabel,Bijan Nouri,Milon Miah,Niklas Blum,Luis F. Zarzalejo,Julia Kowalski,Robert Pitz-Paal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FarSky is a generative framework using a multi-task autoencoder and latent diffusion model to produce probabilistic intra-hour solar irradiance forecasts from all-sky images, outperforming baselines and improving ramp event detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable solar irradiance forecasting is critical for integrating photovoltaic power into grids. All-sky imagers suit intra-hour forecasting, but existing deep learning methods are largely deterministic and struggle to anticipate ramp events. The work aims to overcome these limits with probabilistic, generative forecasting.

Method: FarSky combines latent-space coupling with diffusion: a multi-task autoencoder learns a shared latent representation optimizing both image reconstruction and irradiance estimation; a latent diffusion model then generates future latent states conditioned on recent observations, and irradiance forecasts are decoded directly. Probabilistic forecasts come from stochastic sampling. Trained on a multi-year ASI dataset from Plataforma Solar de Almería and evaluated on two independent test sets against persistence, state-of-the-art end-to-end, and generative baselines.

Result: FarSky achieves the best overall deterministic and probabilistic performance, improving forecast skill by up to 11 percentage points, and substantially improves ramp event detection with F1-scores above 60%.

Conclusion: Combining generative models with task-aware latent-space coupling shows strong potential for solar forecasting, yielding accurate probabilistic forecasts and better ramp event detection than existing methods.

Abstract: Accurate solar irradiance forecasting is essential for the reliable integration of photovoltaic power into modern electricity grids. All-sky imagers (ASI) provide high-resolution observations of clouds, making them well suited for intra-hour forecasting. Recent deep learning approaches have substantially improved forecast accuracy but are often limited by deterministic predictions and a reduced capability to anticipate ramp events. This work proposes FarSky, a generative forecasting framework that leverages latent-space coupling to learn task-aware representations of sky images. A multi-task autoencoder first learns a shared latent representation for image reconstruction and irradiance estimation. A latent diffusion model then generates future latent states conditioned on recent observations, from which irradiance forecasts are directly decoded. Probabilistic forecasts are inherently obtained through stochastic sampling. The framework is developed using a multi-year ASI dataset acquired at the Plataforma Solar de Almería, Spain, and evaluated on two independent test datasets against persistence, state-of-the-art end-to-end, and generative forecasting approaches. FarSky achieves the best overall deterministic and probabilistic forecasting performance, improving forecast skill by up to 11 percentage points. Furthermore, it substantially improves ramp event detection over existing methods, achieving F1-scores above 60%. These results demonstrate the potential of combining generative models with task-aware latent-space coupling for solar forecasting.

</details>


### [111] [Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11256)
*Jonathan A. Karr,Grigorii Khvatskii,Ting Hua,Nitesh V. Chawla*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Institutions rely on commercial AI detectors that cannot tell AI editing apart from full LLM drafting. This study shows compliant light AI editing is flagged far more often (64–80%) than unmodified recent originals (9–15%), while "humanizer" evasion defeats detectors almost entirely (<4% flagged). The result: honest AI editing raises sanction risk more than evasion, so detector scores should not be used as standalone misconduct evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether commercial AI detectors enforce academic integrity fairly, given they cannot distinguish guideline-compliant AI editing from full AI drafting, and may punish the former as misconduct while rewarding evasion.

Method: A controlled study using published English abstracts across four domains, comparing 2013–2015 versus 2023–2025 originals under proxy human/AI labels at tau=0.50. Analyzed light "refine abstract only" edits and "Undetectable AI" humanization, measuring flag rates and relating elevated scores to long-token and Academic Word List density.

Result: Light refine-only edits (proxy for compliant AI assistance) are flagged at 64–80% by Pangram/GPTZero. Unmodified 2023–2025 originals are flagged at 9–15%, with non-STEM significantly higher than STEM (p<0.001); scores track lexical features (long-token/AWL density) rather than authorship intent alone. After humanization, fewer than 4% of AI-labeled rewrites remain flagged (post-humanization detection rate <4%; FNR >96%).

Conclusion: Compliant AI editing carries a higher sanction risk than humanizer-assisted evasion, demonstrating a policy failure. AI detector scores should therefore not be used as standalone evidence of misconduct.

Abstract: Institutions use commercial AI detectors for academic integrity, yet detectors cannot distinguish AI editing from full LLM drafts and may treat both as misconduct. In a controlled study of published English abstracts (four domains; 2013 to 2015 vs. 2023 to 2025), we quantify this policy failure under proxy human/AI labels at tau=0.50. Light "refine abstract only" edits, a proxy for guideline-compliant AI assistance, are flagged at 64 to 80% (Pangram/GPTZero). Unmodified 2023 to 2025 originals are flagged at 9 to 15%, with non-STEM rates far above STEM (p<0.001); elevated scores track long-token and Academic Word List density, not authorship intent alone. After Undetectable AI humanization, evasion is near-total: fewer than 4% of AI-labeled rewrites remain flagged (post-humanization detection rate <4%; FNR >96%). Honest AI-editing results in a higher sanction risk than humanizer-assisted evasion. Therefore, detector scores should not serve as standalone misconduct evidence.

</details>


### [112] [Basin: Efficient and Extensible Numerical Optimization in Rust](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11279)
*Johan Larsson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Basin is a Rust numerical optimization library providing a unified interface for stating and solving minimization problems, including constraints and multiple solvers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Numerical optimization is a fundamental task across the sciences—model fitting, simulation calibration, machine learning training, and engineering design—but users lack a single, consistent way to state and solve such problems. Basin addresses this need by offering one unified library.

Method: Basin provides a unified API for defining optimization problems and solving them, featuring a broad catalog of solvers and first-class support for constraints within the Rust programming language.

Result: The library gives users one consistent workflow for both stating problems and applying a variety of solvers, including constrained optimization.

Conclusion: Basin simplifies numerical optimization in Rust by unifying problem formulation and solving, with broad solver coverage and native constraint handling.

Abstract: Basin is a numerical optimization library for the Rust programming language. Numerical optimization is the task of finding the inputs that minimize a function, and it is a fundamental element across the sciences: fitting a model to data, calibrating a simulation, training a machine learning model, or choosing engineering parameters that minimize cost. Basin gives users a single, consistent way to both state and solve such problems, with a broad catalog of solvers and first-class support for constraints.

</details>


### [113] [Federated Learning for Distributed CNC Tool Wear Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11281)
*Afsana Khan,Morris Stallmann,Marcin Pietrasik,Charis Kouzinopoulos,Anna Wilbik*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies federated learning for CNC tool wear prediction, showing it achieves near-centralized accuracy while significantly outperforming isolated local models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool wear prediction is critical for product quality and process reliability in CNC machining. Although machine learning is promising, industrial deployment is hindered by data being distributed across machines/sites and by restrictions on sharing raw operational data. This motivates investigating federated learning as a privacy-preserving collaborative training framework.

Method: Tool trajectories are distributed across simulated clients to emulate a federated learning scenario. Federated models trained collaboratively are then benchmarked against two references: centralized models (trained on pooled data) and local client models (trained on each client's own data only).

Result: Federated learning achieves performance close to centralized learning and significantly improves over local client baselines.

Conclusion: Federated learning can effectively support collaborative tool wear prediction in distributed CNC manufacturing environments, offering a viable way to train accurate models without sharing raw data.

Abstract: Tool wear prediction is an important task in CNC machining, where accurate monitoring of tool condition supports product quality and process reliability. Machine learning methods have shown potential for this task, but their use in industrial environments is limited by the distributed nature of machining data and by restrictions on data sharing between machines, sites, or organizations. Federated learning offers a suitable framework for this setting by enabling collaborative model training without transferring raw operational data. This paper investigates federated learning for CNC tool wear prediction. Tool trajectories are distributed across simulated clients to represent a federated learning scenario. The federated models are compared against centralized references and local client baselines. Results show that federated learning achieves performance close to centralized learning and improves significantly over local client models. These findings indicate that federated learning can support collaborative tool wear prediction in distributed CNC manufacturing environments.

</details>


### [114] [Terminal Symmetry as a Decision Resource: Statewise Refinement for Anytime Verified Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11318)
*Yi Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a decision-resource decomposition of terminal symmetry in sequential construction tasks, yielding a transport–refine–certify framework instantiated by a method that combines an episode-fixed transported process structure, a state-restricted process rank, a refreshed state-dependent residual rank, and an ordinal rank meet that union the two proposal prefixes, providing completion guarantees, tight verifier-query bounds, and large anytime AUC gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many sequential construction tasks are exactly symmetric at completion, yet their execution is directed and history-dependent, so this terminal symmetry is underused. The work aims to turn terminal symmetry into a reusable decision resource for directed construction rather than treating symmetry only as a final-state property.

Method: A decision-resource view decomposes terminal symmetry into transport–refine–certify: process evidence supplies directionality, terminal correspondence transports that structure across equivalent outcomes, realized-state evidence refines current decision relevance after transitions, and a fixed verifier certifies execution. The method instantiates this with an episode-fixed transported process structure, a state-restricted process rank, a state-dependent residual rank refreshed after accepted transitions, and an ordinal rank meet whose top-k set is exactly the union of the two proposal prefixes.

Result: The rank meet gives a completion guarantee under prefix coverage and meets the tight worst-case verifier-query bound under the corresponding prefix information model; a two-state construction predicts a strict post-transition dynamic–static separation. Statewise refresh improves anytime AUC by up to 6.77, 21.75, and 8.68 points on CAD assembly, Mini-Programs, and exact-fill packing respectively. On 1,135 target-removal episodes from official GRN OOD scenes, the method attains the lowest mean capped verifier cost at all three scales among compared GRN and CDGS-style planners, and the statewise signal transfers across aggregation and scheduler organizations.

Conclusion: Terminal symmetry can be decomposed into transport, refine, and certify components and thereby becomes a reusable decision resource for directed construction, with strong empirical and theoretical gains over existing planners.

Abstract: Many sequential construction tasks exhibit exact symmetry at completion while their execution remains directed and history-dependent. We develop a decision-resource view of terminal symmetry: process evidence supplies directionality, terminal correspondence transports that structure across equivalent outcomes, realized-state evidence refines its current decision relevance after transitions, and a fixed verifier certifies execution. This decomposition yields transport--refine--certify. \method{} instantiates the principle with an episode-fixed transported process structure, its state-restricted process rank, a state-dependent residual rank refreshed after accepted transitions, and an ordinal rank meet whose top-$k$ set is exactly the union of the two proposal prefixes. The meet provides a completion guarantee under prefix coverage and attains the tight worst-case verifier-query bound under the corresponding prefix information model; a two-state construction predicts a strict post-transition dynamic--static separation. Across CAD assembly, Mini-Programs, and exact-fill packing, statewise refresh improves anytime AUC by up to $6.77$, $21.75$, and $8.68$ points, respectively. On 1,135 target-removal episodes from the official GRN OOD scenes, \method{} attains the lowest mean capped verifier cost at all three scales among the compared GRN and CDGS-style planners. The statewise signal also transfers across aggregation and scheduler organizations. Terminal symmetry thereby becomes a reusable decision resource for directed construction.

</details>


### [115] [Contextual Quality-Diversity Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning for HVAC Control in Tropical Commercial Buildings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11324)
*Tran Le Vu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CQD-ERL is a contextual quality-diversity evolutionary reinforcement-learning controller for supervisory control of a tropical water-cooled chiller plant, maintaining an archive of specialised policies indexed by operating context, weather/load regime, and behaviour descriptor, with safety-shielded actions, trained on a reduced-order model and backtested against ASHRAE Guideline 36.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional RL controllers converge to a single scalarised policy, which is ill-suited to a chiller plant whose optimal behaviour varies across diverse operating contexts and daily weather/load regimes; the goal is to maintain a population of specialised, context-adaptive policies rather than one compromise solution.

Method: CQD-ERL combines quality-diversity with evolutionary RL: it maintains a product archive of policies indexed jointly by (1) a data-driven operating context, (2) a cluster of daily weather and load regime, and (3) a context-invariant behaviour descriptor. The archive is filled by a gradient-free evolutionary operator and a soft-actor-critic (SAC) policy-gradient operator sharing a single replay buffer; every action passes through a deterministic safety shield before execution. Training uses a two-tier reduced-order environment capturing latent load, cooling-tower approach, and humidity constraints of a Singapore commercial building.

Result: The controller is evaluated over a full annual backtest against an ASHRAE Guideline 36 baseline; the paper presents this as the validation setting for the proposed controller's performance.

Conclusion: The abstract positions CQD-ERL as a safety-shielded, context-indexed quality-diversity RL approach for chiller plant supervisory control, with evaluation carried out via annual backtesting against an industry standard baseline (ASHRAE Guideline 36).

Abstract: This paper proposes a contextual quality-diversity evolutionary reinforcement-learning controller, CQD-ERL, for the supervisory control of a tropical, water-cooled chiller plant and its associated air side. Rather than converging to a single scalarised policy, the controller maintains a product archive of specialised policies indexed jointly by a data- driven operating context, a cluster of daily weather and load regime, and a context-invariant behaviour descriptor, filled by a gradient-free evolutionary operator and a soft-actor-critic policy-gradient operator that share one replay buffer. Every action is filtered through a deterministic safety shield before execution. The controller is trained on a two-tier reduced-order environment representing the latent load, cooling-tower approach and humidity constraints of a Singapore commercial building, and is evaluated over a full annual backtest against an ASHRAE Guideline 36 baseline.

</details>


### [116] [Long-Horizon Forecasting of Complete Financial Statements with Forma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11327)
*Travis L. Johnson,Jiannan Jiang,Soumyabrata Chaudhuri,Yihao Chen,Lauren Falvey,Donal O'Cofaigh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProForma-20Q, a benchmark for forecasting 78 financial statement line items 1–20 quarters ahead, is introduced along with Forma, a masked-tuple transformer that outperforms all competitors and supports scenario analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No prior work jointly forecasts complete financial statements beyond one year, yet discounted-cash-flow valuation depends most on forecasts past that horizon; specialist models are needed rather than generalist scale.

Method: Forma is a transformer that reads statements as sets of (account, quarter, value) tuples and maximizes a masked-tuple Gaussian likelihood; evaluated on ProForma-20Q using change-space R² across 78 line items, 1–20 quarters ahead, for anonymized firms with past statements and industry codes.

Result: Forma beats classical ML, chained gradient boosting, a zero-shot time-series foundation model, and frontier LLMs; its lead widens with horizon, its predictive intervals never under-cover, forecasts nearly satisfy accounting identities (exact coherence recoverable at no significant accuracy cost), and pinning revenue paths sharpens remaining forecasts.

Conclusion: Specialist training outperforms generalist scale for financial statement forecasting; Forma provides accurate, coherent, long-horizon joint forecasts and a flexible tuple interface enabling scenario analysis without retraining.

Abstract: Specialist training beats generalist scale when forecasting financial statements. To our knowledge, no prior work jointly forecasts complete financial statements beyond one year, yet in a discounted-cash-flow valuation most firm value sits past that window. We release ProForma-20Q, a reproducible benchmark for forecasting 78 statement line items 1-20 quarters ahead, for anonymized firms, from past statements and an industry code, scored by change-space $R^2$. On it, Forma, a transformer that reads statements as sets of (account, quarter, value) tuples and maximizes a masked-tuple Gaussian likelihood, beats every competitor we field: classical machine learning, chained gradient boosting, a zero-shot time-series foundation model, and frontier large language models. Its lead widens with horizon, where valuation needs accuracy most, and its Gaussian predictive intervals never under-cover. Forma's forecasts nearly satisfy accounting identities; exact coherence is recoverable at no statistically significant accuracy cost. Its tuple interface supports scenario analysis without retraining, and we show that pinning future revenue paths sharpens the rest of the statement.

</details>


### [117] [Defending against Model Extraction for GNNs with Model Reprogramming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11495)
*Yan Wen,Zhenyi Wang,Heng Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GraphRP is a proactive defense that repurposes Model Reprogramming for graphs, using a Structure-Aware Gating Mechanism driven by learnable topological prototypes to build a "structural firewall" that protects GNN models from Model Extraction attacks while preserving benign utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNNs deployed in MLaaS are vulnerable to Model Extraction (ME) attacks, but existing defenses transfer image-based strategies (e.g., random noise) to graphs, ignoring topological dependencies between nodes and causing severe utility degradation. Passive watermarking also cannot prevent theft in real time. The paper aims to bridge this gap with a graph-native, proactive defense.

Method: GraphRP repurposes Model Reprogramming for security by introducing a Structure-Aware Gating Mechanism driven by learnable topological prototypes. It creates a dynamic "structural firewall" that selectively modulates the model's decision boundary: benign queries on the training manifold retain fidelity, while adversarial queries have Fisher Information maximized along the perturbation direction. The paper proves a lower bound on the attacker's estimation error that grows with the structural sensitivity of the reprogramming noise, under assumptions of bounded loss, optimal attacker, and local second-order approximation.

Result: Extensive experiments on hard-label and soft-label ME attacks show that GraphRP significantly degrades attack effectiveness while preserving benign utility.

Conclusion: GraphRP overcomes the Euclidean bias of prior defenses and provides an effective, graph-aware proactive protection against Model Extraction attacks, maintaining model utility for legitimate users while substantially impeding adversaries.

Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) serve as the backbone for high-stakes applications in Machine-Learning-as-a-Service (MLaaS). Still, their black-box deployment exposes them to Model Extraction (ME) attacks, in which adversaries steal intellectual property by querying APIs. Existing defenses suffer from a critical ''Euclidean bias'': they transfer image-based strategies (e.g., random noise) to graphs, ignoring the complex topological dependencies between nodes, which often results in severe utility degradation. Passive methods like watermarking also fail to prevent theft in real time. To bridge this gap, we propose GraphRP (Graph Reprogramming Protection), a proactive defense framework that repurposes Model Reprogramming for security. Unlike static perturbations, GraphRP introduces a Structure-Aware Gating Mechanism driven by learnable topological prototypes. This creates a dynamic ''structural firewall'' that selectively modulates the model's decision boundary: it preserves fidelity for benign queries residing on the training manifold, while maximizing the Fisher Information along the perturbation direction for adversarial queries. Under standard assumptions (bounded loss, optimal attacker, and local second-order approximation), we prove a lower bound on the attacker's estimation error that increases with the structural sensitivity of the reprogramming noise. Extensive experiments on both hard-label and soft-label ME attacks demonstrate that GraphRP significantly degrades attack effectiveness while preserving benign utility.

</details>


### [118] [Weightless Fine-Tuning: Personalizing LLMs via Logit-Space Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11342)
*Bohan Zhang,Anqi Ni,Yixin Wang,Paramveer S. Dhillon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Weightless Fine-Tuning (WFT) is a training-free, decoding-time method that mimics the distributional effect of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) via cross-prefix transport of dropout-induced supervised residuals, achieving near-SFT performance at under 7% of the computation on personalization benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SFT adapts LLMs to target distributions, but in personalization settings where each author needs separate weight access, optimization, storage, and retraining, its costs become prohibitive. This motivates a lightweight alternative that captures SFT's distributional effect without weight updates.

Method: WFT is a training-free, decoding-time approach. It computes supervised residuals on an author's training sequence and transports them to the current prompt via a cross-prefix transport operator estimated from dropout-induced cross-covariance. The operator captures how a perturbation at one context propagates to predictions at another, replacing gradient-based parameter updates with logit-space corrections.

Result: On three LaMP personalization benchmarks, WFT achieves the best average performance across datasets, matches or exceeds SFT on individual tasks, and outperforms other lightweight baselines on average. In a budget-controlled comparison, WFT approaches SFT performance using less than 7% of the effective computation. Logit-level analysis shows a cosine similarity of 0.875 between WFT- and SFT-induced logit shifts over 95% of the next-token probability mass.

Conclusion: WFT captures the distributional effect of supervised adaptation without modifying model weights, providing a cheap, training-free alternative to SFT that is especially suited to per-author personalization where weight updates are impractical.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a standard approach for adapting LLMs to a target distribution, but in settings such as personalization, where each author requires separate weight access, optimization, storage, and retraining, its costs become prohibitive. We propose Weightless Fine-Tuning (WFT), a training-free decoding-time method that approximates the distributional effect of SFT without weight updates. WFT computes supervised residuals on an author's training sequence and transports them to the current prompt through a cross-prefix transport operator estimated from dropout-induced cross-covariance. The operator captures how a perturbation at one context propagates to predictions at another, replacing gradient-based parameter updates with logit-space corrections. On three LaMP personalization benchmarks, WFT achieves the best average performance across datasets, matches or exceeds SFT on individual tasks, and outperforms other lightweight baselines on average. In a budget-controlled comparison, WFT approaches SFT performance using less than 7% of the effective computation. Logit-level analysis shows a cosine similarity of 0.875 between the logit shifts induced by WFT and SFT over 95% of the next-token probability mass, suggesting that WFT captures the distributional effect of supervised adaptation without modifying model weights.

</details>


### [119] [FunnelCausalNet: Funnel-aware Joint Conversion-Revenue Uplift for Multi-tier Coupon Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11675)
*Yu Zhang,Zhihan Wang,Guanlin Chen,Min Jiang,Shuai Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FunnelCausalNet is an uplift model for coupon campaigns that couples a binary conversion head with a nonnegative conditional order-value head via their product to estimate GMV uplift; paired with conformal audit bands and a Lagrangian budgeted allocator, it shows competitive AUUC, reduced effect error (18–48%) in ablations, and the best frontier DeltaROI on industrial RCT logs, while a benchmark regime boundary is defined where revenue-focused rankers beat uplift proxies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coupon campaigns must optimize both conversion and revenue, but GMV follows a deterministic funnel (conversion × conditional order value) and is zero-inflated and heavy-tailed, making direct GMV uplift estimation hard. The authors seek an estimator respecting this product structure and the associated distributional challenges.

Method: Proposes FunnelCausalNet, a shared-representation neural uplift estimator with a binary conversion head and a nonnegative conditional-value head combined as μ_gmv = μ_conv × μ_val. Provides an idealized leading-order MSE analysis under RCT, support, rate-gap, and cross-head covariance-control assumptions showing a regime where funnel composition lowers pointwise variance (heuristic, not a guarantee). Adds marginal split-conformal CATE summaries combined via Bonferroni union as audit bands and a Lagrangian budgeted allocator with RCT-anchored subsidy-aware ROI accounting. Evaluated on semi-synthetic Criteo-MT7, a de-identified industrial Hotel-Coupon RCT (~4.9M hold-out exposures per seed) with full LP frontier sweeps, and sparse binary-spend public benchmarks.

Result: On Criteo-MT7, mean AUUC_GMV is within one seed standard deviation of the leading feature-interaction baseline among 11 baselines; a controlled ablation cuts GMV effect error by 18–48% vs direct GMV regression across zero-inflation regimes. On Hotel-Coupon RCT logs, FunnelCausalNet achieves the best seed-averaged mean DeltaROI at all seven correlated anchors (10%–60%), treated as descriptive frontier consistency. On sparse binary-spend benchmarks, revenue-focused rankers can dominate uplift-curve proxies, defining an explicit regime boundary.

Conclusion: Composing conversion and value heads captures the GMV funnel and materially reduces effect-estimation error versus direct regression, with competitive AUUC and consistent frontier ROI on industrial data; the theoretical variance reduction is heuristic, and benchmark results delineate conditions under which revenue-focused ranking is preferable to uplift proxies.

Abstract: Coupon campaigns seek to lift both conversion and revenue, but gross merchandise value (GMV) follows a deterministic funnel from conversion to conditional order value and is zero-inflated and heavy-tailed. We propose FunnelCausalNet, an uplift estimator coupling a binary conversion head with a nonnegative conditional-value head through $μ_{\mathrm{gmv}}=μ_{\mathrm{conv}}μ_{\mathrm{val}}$. Under explicit RCT, support, rate-gap, and cross-head covariance-control assumptions, an idealized leading-order MSE comparison identifies a regime in which funnel composition can reduce pointwise variance; this is a heuristic, not a guarantee for the shared-representation neural model. The estimator is paired with marginal split-conformal CATE summaries, combined through a Bonferroni union as audit bands, and a Lagrangian budgeted allocator using RCT-anchored estimates for subsidy-aware ROI accounting. On semi-synthetic multi-tier Criteo-MT7, FunnelCausalNet's mean AUUC_GMV is within one seed standard deviation of the leading feature-interaction baseline among eleven baselines, while a controlled ablation reduces GMV effect error versus direct GMV regression by 18--48% across tested zero-inflation regimes. On de-identified industrial Hotel-Coupon RCT logs with about 4.9 million hold-out exposure records per seed, expected-outcome evaluation sweeps full LP frontiers; FunnelCausalNet has the best seed-averaged mean DeltaROI at all seven correlated anchors from 10% to 60%, which we treat as descriptive frontier consistency rather than independent significance. On sparse binary-spend public benchmarks, revenue-focused rankers can dominate uplift-curve proxies, defining an explicit regime boundary.

</details>


### [120] [Dynamics Models for Offline Hyperparameter Selection in Real-World RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11349)
*Jordan Coblin,Han Wang,Martha White,Adam White*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents the first real-world industrial application of calibration models (offline dynamics models) for offline RL hyperparameter selection, in a municipal water treatment plant, demonstrating realistic rollouts, meaningful sensitivity trends, and scaling/robustness insights while flagging practical challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL deployment in real systems is hindered by hyperparameter selection, especially when simulators are unavailable and online experimentation is costly or risky. Prior calibration-model approaches were only validated in simple simulated settings, leaving uncertainty about their viability in real, high-dimensional, non-stationary industrial environments.

Method: The authors apply calibration models trained on offline data to approximate environment dynamics for offline hyperparameter selection in a municipal water treatment plant. They evaluate several approaches, including a k-nearest neighbors model with a Laplacian distance metric, on high-dimensional, non-stationary sensor data for nexting prediction tasks. They test long-horizon rollout generation, year-long dataset scaling, selection of fine-tuning learning rates for pre-trained agents, and robustness under distribution shift.

Result: Calibration models generate realistic long-horizon rollouts and recover meaningful hyperparameter sensitivity trends. They scale to year-long datasets, support choosing fine-tuning learning rates for pre-trained agents, and show performance under distribution shift, though with identified practical challenges.

Conclusion: The work provides a proof of concept for using offline dynamics models to support RL deployment in real-world environments, while highlighting important practical challenges (e.g., non-stationarity, scaling, and distribution shift) that require future work.

Abstract: A key obstacle to deploying reinforcement learning in real-world systems is hyperparameter selection, particularly when simulators are unavailable and online experimentation is costly. Prior work has proposed calibration models trained on offline data to approximate environment dynamics and enable offline hyperparameter selection, but these methods have so far been evaluated only in simple simulated settings. In this paper, we present the first application of calibration models in a real-world industrial setting: a municipal water treatment plant. We evaluate several calibration model approaches, including a k-nearest neighbors model with a Laplacian distance metric, on high-dimensional, non-stationary sensor data for nexting prediction tasks. Our results show that these models can generate realistic long-horizon rollouts and recover meaningful hyperparameter sensitivity trends. We further examine how calibration models scale to year-long datasets, how they support the selection of fine-tuning learning rates for pre-trained agents, and how robust they are under distribution shift. Overall, our findings provide a proof of concept for using offline dynamics models to support RL deployment in real-world environments, while highlighting important practical challenges for future work.

</details>


### [121] [Is Per-Agent Policy Composition Safe? Rethinking Successor-Feature Transfer in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11658)
*Zijian Zhao,Sen Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multi-agent transfer to new objectives via independent per-agent successor-feature recombination can perform worse than every library policy; the paper proposes MA-USFA, a hierarchical method combining cross-agent-conditioned universal successor feature approximators with a synchronized upper composer, to achieve safe and flexible composition with no per-task adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning systems often face objectives that change after deployment, and retraining per objective is too costly. Single-agent transfer is solved via successor features and generalized policy improvement with a safety guarantee, but the multi-agent analog lacks a guarantee: independent per-agent composition can break down because changing teammates' policies changes each agent's environment, invalidating the learned values.

Method: MA-USFA is a two-layer hierarchical approach. The lower layer uses universal successor feature approximators (USFAs) that predict each agent's successor features conditioned on its teammates' objectives. The upper composer selects, across agents, which library entry each agent should follow and supplies a cross-agent correction that per-agent values cannot represent. It is trained once over the distribution of objectives.

Result: The authors prove that independent composition can yield joint behavior strictly worse than every policy in the library, and that the only unconditionally safe fixed rule is synchronized composition (moving the whole team to one jointly trained policy), which cannot serve objectives assigning different goals to different agents. MA-USFA attains both safety and flexibility simultaneously.

Conclusion: By conditioning per-agent successor feature predictions on teammates' objectives and using a cross-agent corrective composer, MA-USFA enables safe and flexible multi-agent transfer to unseen objectives at deployment time, without per-task adaptation.

Abstract: Many reinforcement learning systems, from fleet management to traffic signal control, must serve an objective that changes dynamically after deployment, and retraining a policy for each new objective is prohibitively expensive. For a single agent, this problem is well understood: successor features with generalized policy improvement, together with their universal extension, recombine a library of learned policies into a policy for any new objective, with a guarantee that the result is never worse than any policy in the library. However, multi-agent transfer has received far less attention, and the common practice of letting each agent recombine its own library independently inherits the recipe but not the guarantee. We prove that this independent composition can produce joint behavior strictly worse than every policy in the library, because recombining teammates changes the environment each agent faces and invalidates the values it relies on, a failure with no single-agent counterpart. We further show that the only unconditionally safe fixed rule is synchronized composition, which moves the whole team to one jointly trained policy but cannot serve objectives that assign different goals to different agents. To attain safety and flexibility at once, we propose MA-USFA, a hierarchical method with two layers: a lower layer of universal successor feature approximators that predicts each agent's successor features while conditioned on its teammates' objectives, and an upper composer that selects, across agents, which library entry each agent should follow and supplies the cross-agent correction a per-agent value cannot represent. Trained once over the distribution of objectives, it is applied at deployment with no per-task adaptation.

</details>


### [122] [Market-Information-Aware Gated-LoRA of Foundation Models for Transferable Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11359)
*Hang Fan,Wei Wei,Shengwei Mei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A transfer learning framework adapts the Chronos-2 time-series foundation model to day-ahead electricity price forecasting by aligning multi-source market information (7-day price context plus supply-demand, reserve, maintenance, capacity, and intertie variables) and training a gated low-rank adapter (LoRA) on source markets only, enabling application to data-scarce target markets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Electricity price forecasting is essential for market participants but is difficult due to high volatility, market-specific dynamics, and dependence on anticipated system conditions. Existing supervised approaches rely heavily on market-specific historical data, limiting their applicability in newly established or data-scarce markets. This motivates a cross-market transfer method that leverages a foundation model without requiring target-market labels.

Method: The paper proposes a market-information-aware adaptation framework built on the Chronos-2 time-series foundation model. It constructs a multi-source market information (MSMI) interface that aligns 7-day price context with pre-clearing supply-demand, reserve, maintenance, generator-capacity, and intertie variables. A source-domain gated low-rank adapter (LoRA) is trained, updating about 1% of model parameters without target-market labels. The gate scales the frozen source adapter according to reserve-tightness and operating-state signals. Evaluation uses a leave-one-market-out protocol to assess cross-market transferability on four Chinese provincial day-ahead spot markets.

Result: The framework reduces average MAE/RMSE by 6.24%/7.99% versus market-information-aware zero-shot Chronos-2 and by 3.05%/3.52% versus vanilla Source-LoRA. The gain is not reproduced by a learned global scalar or random gate initialization, and the additional improvement over Source-LoRA is limited, indicating that the gating mechanism provides modest but non-trivial benefits.

Conclusion: Market-structured inputs combined with a state-dependent gated LoRA offer a practical transfer path for data-scarce electricity markets, with the gated adapter mechanism validated as a meaningful (if limited) contributor to cross-market forecasting accuracy.

Abstract: Electricity price forecasting is crucial for market participants but remains difficult because prices are volatile, market-specific, and closely tied to anticipated system conditions. Existing supervised methods depend largely on market-specific historical data, limiting their use in newly established or data-scarce markets. This paper proposes a market-information-aware adaptation framework that transfers the Chronos-2 time-series foundation model to day-ahead electricity price forecasting. It first constructs a multi-source market information (MSMI) interface aligning 7-day price context with pre-clearing supply--demand, reserve, maintenance, generator-capacity, and intertie variables, and then trains a source-domain gated low-rank adapter (LoRA), updating about $1\%$ of model parameters without target-market labels. The gate scales the frozen source adapter according to reserve-tightness and operating-state signals. A leave-one-market-out protocol is adopted for evaluating cross-market transferability. Experiments on four Chinese provincial day-ahead spot markets show that the proposed framework reduces the average MAE/RMSE by $6.24\%/7.99\%$ relative to market-information-aware zero-shot Chronos-2 and by $3.05\%/3.52\%$ relative to vanilla Source-LoRA. Experiments show that the gain is not reproduced by a learned global scalar or by random gate initialization, while the additional improvement over Source-LoRA is limited. These results suggest that market-structured inputs and state-dependent gated LoRA can provide a practical transfer path for data-scarce electricity markets.

</details>


### [123] [Lifecycle-Optimal Tokenization: Vocabulary Size as a Deployment-Regime-Dependent Infrastructure Parameter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11361)
*Rima Mittal,Ankit Gubrani,Satyanarayana Kakollu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Tokenizer vocabulary size (V) should be optimized for the serving regime, not fixed at training time. The paper shows the cost-optimal vocabulary shifts dramatically (up to 16x) with inference batch size and volume, while quality stays near-invariant, turning vocabulary into a pure systems optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vocabulary size is a foundational LLM design choice, yet it is typically chosen at training time by convention rather than by analyzing deployment costs. The authors argue that the cost-optimal vocabulary is not a constant but depends on the serving regime (inference volume and batch size), so a fixed training-time choice is suboptimal for production systems.

Method: The authors formalize total deployment cost as C_lifecycle(V) = C_train(V) + λ·C_infer(V, B), where λ is inference volume and B is serving batch size. They run controlled experiments on two GPU families spanning memory-bound and compute-bound regimes (A10G with ridge ≈ 117 FLOP/byte; A100 with ridge ≈ 183 FLOP/byte), evaluating vocabulary sizes from 32k to 524k at 1.3–2.3B model scale, measuring both cost and quality (bits per byte, BPB).

Result: (1) The inference-optimal vocabulary shifts 16x with serving batch size, from 32k at B=1 to 524k at B=64+, driven by amortization of the V×d unembedding matrix read. (2) At 1.3–2.3B scale, quality (BPB) is optimized at V=65k, confirming scale-dependent vocabulary preference. (3) The lifecycle-optimal vocabulary diverges from the training-optimal by up to 16x for production deployments. Quality is approximately invariant across the optimal range (<2% BPB spread), so vocabulary choice carries no quality penalty in the measured range.

Conclusion: Vocabulary size should be treated as a serving-regime-dependent systems parameter. The authors give actionable guidance: on-device deployments (B=1) should use V ≈ 32k, while datacenter serving (B ≥ 64, λ ≥ 10) should use V ≈ 131–262k. Because quality is nearly invariant in this range, these choices optimize cost without sacrificing model quality.

Abstract: Tokenizer vocabulary size is a foundational design choice in large language model (LLM) infrastructure, yet it is typically fixed at training time based on convention rather than deployment analysis. We show that the cost-optimal vocabulary is not a constant but a function of the serving regime. We formalize total deployment cost as $C_{lifecycle}(V) = C_{train}(V) + λ\cdot C_{infer}(V, B)$, where $λ$ is inference volume and $B$ is the serving batch size. Through controlled experiments on two GPU families spanning the memory-bound to compute-bound regimes (A10G, ridge $\approx$ 117 FLOP/byte; A100, ridge $\approx$ 183 FLOP/byte), we demonstrate: (1) the inference-optimal vocabulary shifts 16x with serving batch, from 32k at $B=1$ to 524k at $B=64+$, driven by amortization of the $V \times d$ unembedding matrix read; (2) at 1.3-2.3B model scale, quality (bits per byte, BPB) is optimized at $V=65$k, confirming scale-dependent vocabulary preference; (3) the lifecycle-optimal vocabulary diverges from training-optimal by up to 16x for production deployments. Quality is approximately invariant across the optimal range ($<$2% BPB spread), making vocabulary a pure systems optimization with no quality penalty in the measured range. Our results provide actionable capacity planning guidance: on-device deployments ($B=1$) should use $V \approx 32$k; datacenter serving ($B \geq 64$, $λ\geq 10$) should use $V \approx 131$-262k.

</details>


### [124] [PAIR: Pairwise-Aware Inclusion Reweighting for Adaptive Rollout Allocation in RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11368)
*Pixel Nomand,Elena Voss,Marcus Hale,Sofia Reyes*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PAIR reweights adaptive trajectory selection in RLVR as a contrast graph over rollout pairs, yielding a design-unbiased pair-gradient estimator that cuts token use roughly in half while improving accuracy over pointwise allocators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLVR spends most compute generating long reasoning trajectories. Existing budget allocators assign pointwise difficulty/utility scores to prompts, rollouts, or tokens, but the authors identify a statistical mismatch: since the leave-one-out group-relative score gradient is a second-order U-statistic over pairs of rollouts, pointwise treatments ignore pairwise contrast and the bias introduced by adaptive selection of which pair terms become observable.

Method: PAIR models short rollout prefixes as vertices and pair-gradient terms as edges of a contrast graph. A prefix-only predictor estimates correctness and remaining token cost; a convex design chooses positive continuation probabilities under an expected suffix-token budget; each edge induced by completed vertices is inverse-weighted by its logged joint inclusion probability. The analysis assumes conditionally independent on-policy rollouts and an unclipped, unstandardized objective.

Result: Across compute-matched RLVR runs on Qwen3-1.7B/4B, PAIR improves average accuracy by +1.2 and +1.4 over the strongest pointwise allocator while using 51% and 52% fewer generated tokens than full-group GRPO. A frozen-population estimator audit confirms unweighted adaptive selection is biased, whereas pair-inclusion correction recovers the complete-pair target at matched suffix cost.

Conclusion: Treating the RLVR gradient as a pairwise U-statistic and correcting adaptive selection via joint inclusion probabilities yields an unbiased estimator that achieves better accuracy at roughly half the token cost of full-group GRPO, demonstrating the value of pairwise-aware inclusion reweighting.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) spends most of its compute generating groups of long reasoning trajectories. Recent allocators reduce this cost by assigning budgets to prompts, rollouts, or tokens according to a pointwise notion of difficulty or utility. We identify a statistical mismatch: the unclipped leave-one-out group-relative score gradient is not a sum of independent point contributions, but a second-order U-statistic over pairs of rollouts. Completing one rollout therefore reveals contrast with every other completed rollout, and adaptive endpoint selection changes which pair terms are observable. We introduce PAIR (Pairwise-Aware Inclusion Reweighting), which treats short rollout prefixes as vertices and pair-gradient terms as edges of a contrast graph. A prefix-only predictor estimates correctness and remaining token cost; a convex design chooses positive continuation probabilities under an expected suffix-token budget; and each edge induced by completed vertices is inverse-weighted by its logged joint inclusion probability. Under conditionally independent on-policy rollouts and an unclipped, unstandardized objective, the resulting estimator is design-unbiased for the complete candidate-pair gradient. Across compute-matched RLVR runs on Qwen3-1.7B/4B, PAIR improves average accuracy by +1.2 and +1.4 over the strongest pointwise allocator while using 51% and 52% fewer generated tokens than full-group GRPO. A frozen-population estimator audit confirms that unweighted adaptive selection is biased, whereas pair-inclusion correction recovers the complete-pair target at matched suffix cost.

</details>


### [125] [Towards an approach to multivariate outlier detection for District Heating System data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11375)
*Rajko Turudija,Dušan Stojiljković,Milan Zdravković,Marko Ignjatović*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper compares several outlier detection methods on district heating transmission data, combining energy data with outdoor temperature, and proposes an ensemble of PCA, Isolation Forest, and Hotelling's T² test for identifying irregular plant operation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To uncover irregular operation of a district heating substation, ultimately aiming to reduce gas consumption in central heating plants and lower CO2 emissions. It addresses domain-specific challenges such as treating zero transmitted energy timepoints as off-grid (non-informative) rather than genuine anomalies.

Method: Multivariate outlier detection methods are compared: univariate Z-score (benchmark), Mahalanobis distance, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Isolation Forest, and Hotelling's T-squared test, applied to transmitted heat energy data together with outside ambient temperature. Results are reviewed with domain experts, and a final ensemble method selects outliers based on agreement of all three best-performing methods (PCA, Isolation Forest, Hotelling's T²).

Result: PCA, Isolation Forest, and Hotelling's T² test produced relevant results, while Z-score and Mahalanobis distance were less suitable. The ensemble approach, requiring agreement among all three effective methods, was adopted as the final outlier detection strategy.

Conclusion: An ensemble of PCA, Isolation Forest, and Hotelling's T² test, selected by agreement, is proposed as the final approach for detecting operational anomalies in district heating data, supporting the wider goal of energy and emission reduction.

Abstract: In this paper, we test different methods for multivariate detection of outliers in the data of transmitted heat energy in the selected substation of local District Heating System, by also considering outside ambient temperature, namely Z-score (univariate, as a benchmark), Mahalanobis distances, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Isolation Forest and Hotelling's T-squared test. The overall research aims at uncovering irregular plant operation, with a wider objective of identifying the opportunities for reducing the consumption of gas in central heating plants as well as the CO2 emission. The proposed approach considers specific domain circumstances, such as irrelevance of zero transmit-ted energy timepoints as indication of off-grid plant. The outcomes of the different methods are discussed with domain experts. It was concluded that PCA, Isolation Forest and Hotelling method provide relevant results. Finally, we adopt the ensemble method (selection based on the agreement of all three methods on the detected outliers) as the final approach.

</details>


### [126] [Reoptimization Algorithms for Contextual Bandits with Knapsack Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11383)
*Zhen Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a UCB-based algorithm with re-optimization for Contextual Bandits with Knapsack, achieving average regret O((ln T)^3/T), which greatly improves upon the O(1/sqrt(T)) bound of related re-optimization-based dynamic-pricing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contextual Bandits with Knapsack involve finite customer types, products, and capacity-constrained resources, where products consume fixed resource combinations. The decision maker must assign arriving customers to products while simultaneously learning an unknown linear reward function and maximizing revenue. The goal is to minimize expected revenue loss relative to an omniscient optimal policy, and prior re-optimization-based dynamic pricing approaches only achieved O(1/sqrt(T)) regret, motivating the search for faster rates.

Method: The authors propose a natural, simple extension of the Upper-Confidence-Bound (UCB) family, combined with re-optimization techniques. They exploit the structure of re-optimization to sharpen the regret analysis from the typical sqrt(T) scaling to a polylogarithmic-over-T rate.

Result: The proposed algorithm achieves an average regret of O((ln T)^3 / T) over a horizon of length T, significantly reducing the O(1/sqrt(T)) bound from the literature for closely related re-optimization-based dynamic-pricing problems.

Conclusion: Leveraging re-optimization within a UCB framework enables a substantially improved regret rate of O((ln T)^3/T), demonstrating that near-optimal performance is attainable in Contextual Bandits with Knapsack beyond the conventional 1/sqrt(T) rate.

Abstract: We study new algorithms for Contextual Bandits with Knapsack. In these problems, there are finitely many types of customers, products, and resources. Each product is made from a fixed combination of resources, and resources have finite capacity. A decision maker must assign each arriving customer one out of a set of multiple possible products. Every assignment of a customer to a product will generate a random reward, which equals an unknown linear function of customer and product features, plus a noise term. The objective is to jointly learn the mean reward function, and to make online assignments to minimize the expected revenue loss relative to an optimal policy that knows the reward function. We propose a natural and simple extension of the Upper-Confidence-Bound (UCB) family of algorithms and apply re-optimization techniques. We show that by taking advantage of re-optimization, our algorithm achieves an average regret of $O(\frac{(\ln T)^3}{T})$ where $T$ is the horizon length. Our bound significantly reduces the $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}})$ bound in the literature for closely related dynamic-pricing problems that are based on re-optimization.

</details>


### [127] [Mechanism Design for Generative Engines: From Exploitation toward Win-Win Outcomes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11390)
*Chen Xu,Zitian Guo,Chenyan Xiong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Generative engines create a strategic citation contest between content providers and platforms; GEO attacks adapt to defenses, degrading quality and adding unsupported claims. The paper models this as a repeated Stackelberg game and proposes VCR (verifiable-content rewards), which credits factually checkable rewrites, outperforming baselines by 12.1 points on Net defense-utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative engines make citations a mechanism for allocating attention and value, incentivizing content providers to optimize for model citation while platforms must preserve answer quality and trustworthy attribution. This tension escalates into "citation wars" where GEO attacks degrade document quality and introduce unsupported claims.

Method: The supplier-platform interaction is formulated as a repeated Stackelberg game with partial monitoring; a local best-response analysis identifies when citation competition reaches an inert stationary outcome.
