Based on this, the authors propose VCR, a platform-creator mechanism that rewards rewrites surfacing checkable factual substance in addition to penalizing suspicious rewrites. Experiments are conducted on three benchmarks.

Result: VCR consistently achieves the largest Net defense-utility score, outperforming the strongest baseline by an average of 12.1 percentage points, and yields a win-win outcome under the empirical equivalence criterion.

Conclusion: By aligning creator incentives with answer trustworthiness through verifiable-content rewards, the VCR mechanism mitigates citation wars and produces a win-win equilibrium between platforms and content providers.

Abstract: Generative engines are reshaping the web ecosystem by making citations a key mechanism for allocating attention, attribution, and downstream value. This creates a strategic tension: content providers are incentivized to optimize for model citation, while platforms must preserve answer quality and trustworthy attribution. We show that this tension can escalate into citation wars. In repeated simulations, state-of-the-art generative engine optimization (GEO) attacks adapt to conventional defenses by producing citation-seeking rewrites that degrade document quality and introduce unsupported claims. To study this problem, we formulate the supplier--platform interaction as a repeated Stackelberg game with partial monitoring. A local best-response analysis identifies when citation competition approaches an inert stationary outcome. Motivated by this finding, we propose a platform--creator mechanism called VCR based on verifiable-content rewards. Rather than only penalizing suspicious rewrites, the platform also credits rewrites that surface checkable factual substance, aligning creator incentives with answer trustworthiness. Experiments on three benchmarks show that VCR consistently achieves the largest Net defense-utility score, outperforming the strongest baseline by an average of 12.1 percentage points, and produces a win--win outcome under our empirical equivalence criterion.

</details>


### [128] [Unmasking Toxic Mimicry in Medical Offline Reinforcement Learning for ICU Sepsis Management via Counterfactual Clinical Audits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11410)
*Hangqi Ren,Junyi Liao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Counterfactual Clinical Audit (CCA) framework to stress-test offline RL agents on ICU data, revealing that a Medical Decision Transformer exhibits unsafe "Toxic Mimicry" (e.g., reducing vasopressors as lactate rises), while a Historical Causal Transformer with causal shielding maintains physiologically sound behavior despite standard metrics failing to distinguish them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard offline-RL evaluation metrics (MSE and FQE) only measure behavioral imitation and cannot detect Toxic Mimicry—a failure mode where agents copy harmful clinical patterns such as withdrawing treatment during comfort-care transitions. There is a need to bridge the gap between statistical fit and clinical safety when deploying RL for ICU treatment optimization.

Method: The authors propose the Counterfactual Clinical Audit (CCA) framework, which stress-tests RL agents via physiological perturbations (counterfactual interventions) anchored in Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) guidelines. Using the MIMIC-III database, they audit two agents: a Medical Decision Transformer (MedDT) and a Historical Causal Transformer (HCT-RL) that combines Causal Action Shielding, propensity-based importance weighting, and Conservative Q-Learning.

Result: CCA found that MedDT paradoxically decreases vasopressor dosage as lactate levels escalate, contradicting sepsis resuscitation guidelines, whereas HCT-RL maintains physiologically consistent responses. Standard metrics (MSE/FQE) failed to surface this discrepancy, exposing a systemic misalignment between statistical fit and clinical safety.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate that counterfactual audits are a necessary evaluation standard for medical RL, as conventional fit-based metrics cannot guarantee clinically safe policies. The work supports integrating guideline-anchored counterfactual testing into the evaluation pipeline for offline RL in healthcare.

Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) offers considerable promise for optimizing ICU treatment decisions, yet standard evaluation metrics Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) assess only behavioral imitation and cannot detect Toxic Mimicry, a failure mode in which agents replicate harmful patterns such as treatment withdrawal during comfort-care transitions. Using the MIMIC-III database, we propose the Counterfactual Clinical Audit (CCA) framework, which stress-tests RL agents through physiological perturbations anchored in Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) guidelines. We audit a Medical Decision Transformer (MedDT) and a Historical Causal Transformer (HCT-RL), the latter employing Causal Action Shielding, propensity-based importance weighting, and Conservative Q-Learning. CCA reveals that MedDT paradoxically reduces vasopressor dosage as lactate escalates, contradicting resuscitation guidelines, while HCT-RL maintains physiologically consistent responses. These findings expose a systemic misalignment between statistical fit and clinical safety, supporting counterfactual audits as a necessary evaluation standard for medical RL.

</details>


### [129] [Diffusion-Based Data-Driven Assortment Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11419)
*Junyi Liao,Xiaohui Jiang,Zhengwei Tong,Ethan X. Fang,Vahid Tarokh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a model-agnostic assortment optimization framework using guided discrete diffusion, where assortments are binary vectors and a learned reverse diffusion process performs stochastic search with reward-guided transitions, avoiding combinatorial enumeration while remaining robust to model misspecification and generating diverse near-optimal solutions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assortment optimization is typically solved with parametric choice models (e.g., MNL), which are tractable but sensitive to model misspecification and struggle to capture complex customer behavior. The authors aim to develop a model-agnostic method that avoids explicit combinatorial enumeration and performs well even when the assumed model is misspecified.

Method: The authors represent assortments as binary vectors and perform stochastic search via a learned reverse diffusion process (guided discrete diffusion). A reward-guided mechanism biases local transitions using estimates of expected revenue, balancing exploration and exploitation during generation. This generative approach avoids explicit enumeration and is agnostic to the underlying choice model.

Result: Empirically, the framework consistently identifies high-quality assortments, remains robust under model misspecification, and often recovers near-optimal solutions in high-dimensional settings. The generative nature of diffusion also produces diverse high-performing assortments, offering flexibility beyond a single deterministic solution.

Conclusion: Generative modeling via guided discrete diffusion is a scalable and robust paradigm for combinatorial optimization in data-driven decision-making, outperforming or matching parametric-choice-model approaches while providing robustness and solution diversity.

Abstract: Assortment optimization is a fundamental problem in revenue management, typically addressed using parametric choice models such as the multinomial logit (MNL) and its variants. While these models enable tractable formulations, their performance is sensitive to model misspecification and often struggles to capture complex customer behavior. In this paper, we propose a model-agnostic framework for assortment optimization based on guided discrete diffusion. We represent assortments as binary vectors and perform stochastic search via a learned reverse diffusion process, avoiding explicit combinatorial enumeration. To incorporate decision objectives, we introduce a reward-guided mechanism that biases local transitions using estimates of expected revenue. This allows the method to effectively balance exploration and exploitation during generation. Empirically, we show that the proposed approach consistently identifies high-quality assortments and remains robust under model misspecification, often recovering near-optimal solutions in high-dimensional settings. Moreover, the generative nature of diffusion enables the production of diverse high-performing assortments, offering flexibility beyond a single deterministic solution. These results highlight the potential of generative modeling as a scalable and robust paradigm for combinatorial optimization in data-driven decision-making.

</details>


### [130] [Analysis of Federated Aggregation under Model Poisoning and Backdoor Attacks: A Reconstructed Cross-Dataset and Cross-Architecture Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11423)
*Soumya Mazumdar,Vineet Kumar Rakesh,Tapas Samanta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper reconstructs a 500-cell evaluation matrix to compare five federated aggregation methods under clean and three attack conditions, finding Trimmed Mean best on clean accuracy and Krum best under sign-flipping and Gaussian attacks, while auditing metric and scaffold provenance reveals important limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robust comparisons of federated aggregation methods require jointly accounting for predictive performance, threat definitions, metric semantics, and execution provenance; prior comparisons failed to do so comprehensively, motivating a careful reconstruction and audit of the experimental matrix.

Method: A 500-cell seed-1 evaluation matrix was reconstructed across five aggregation methods (including Trimmed Mean and Krum), five datasets, five architectures, and four conditions (clean, sign-flipping, Gaussian, BadNets). Execution logs were verified: 454 original runs and 36 repaired/rerun executions succeeded, plus 10 clean SVHN cells supported by summary-only provenance. Analyses included macro-mean accuracy, within-task rank, matching to 21 fully-provenanced task pairs, and audits of the BadNets metric implementation and the FedPARETO scaffold.

Result: Trimmed Mean achieved the highest clean macro-mean accuracy (76.02%) and the lowest mean within-task rank (1.70). Krum attained the highest recorded accuracy under both sign-flipping and Gaussian configurations. Rankings were unchanged when restricted to the 21 fully-provenanced task pairs. The BadNets metric counts every triggered input, so it measures Triggered Target-Label Rate (TTLR) rather than a conventional target-excluding attack success rate. The FedPARETO scaffold can pair predictive summaries of an uncorrupted local model with aggregation weights applied to a separately corrupted update.

Conclusion: Because exact attack and configuration lineage is incomplete and each cell has a single identified seed, the findings are descriptive comparisons within the recorded configurations rather than statistical estimates or universal robustness claims.

Abstract: Robust comparisons of federated aggregation methods require joint consideration of predictive performance, threat definitions, metric semantics, and execution provenance. A 500-cell seed-1 evaluation matrix was reconstructed across five aggregation methods, five datasets, five architectures, and four recorded conditions: clean, sign-flipping, Gaussian, and BadNets. Successful execution logs were identified for 454 original runs and 36 repaired or rerun executions, whereas 10 clean SVHN cells were supported by summary-only provenance. Trimmed Mean achieved the highest clean macro-mean accuracy (76.02%) and the lowest mean within-task rank (1.70). Krum attained the highest recorded accuracy under both sign-flipping and Gaussian configurations. These relative rankings remained unchanged when analysis was restricted to 21 task pairs for which original successful logs were available for every method-condition combination. Audit of the supplied BadNets metric implementation established that every test input is triggered prior to target-label counting; consequently, the retained metric represents Triggered Target-Label Rate (TTLR) rather than a conventional target-excluding attack success rate. An audit of the supplied FedPARETO scaffold further identified a pathway in which predictive summaries may characterize an uncorrupted local model while the aggregation weight is applied to a separately corrupted update, introducing a potential discrepancy between reported predictive outcomes and the updates used for aggregation. The canonical matrix contains a single identified seed for each cell, and exact attack and configuration lineage is incomplete. Accordingly, the findings should be interpreted as descriptive comparisons within the recorded configurations and not as statistical estimates or universal claims regarding robustness.

</details>


### [131] [Click2Poly: A VLM for vector mapping buildings and walls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11424)
*Nicolas Girard,Jawher Ben Abdallah,Arno Gobbin,Liuyun Duan,Sacha Lepretre*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Click2Poly is a QGIS plugin that extends the Florence-2 VLM to let users edit building and wall vector layers via clicks, accelerating manual post-extraction quality control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate vector mapping of buildings and walls is essential for geospatial applications but labor-intensive. Deep learning extraction still falls short of cartographic standards, requiring human quality control and correction of complex cases. The goal is to speed up this manual step.

Method: Click2Poly extends the Florence-2 Vision Language Model (VLM) to respond to user clicks by directly editing building or wall vector layers. It is implemented as a QGIS plugin and integrates into a human-in-the-loop workflow.

Result: Click2Poly speeds up manual editing of building and wall vector layers in a real-world production environment.

Conclusion: A human-in-the-loop AI assistant that leverages a VLM and click-based interaction can effectively accelerate the manual editing stage of building/wall vector mapping to meet cartographic standards.

Abstract: Accurate vector mapping of buildings and walls is critical for geospatial applications but remains a labor-intensive process. While recent deep learning methods have improved automatic extraction, in order to meet cartographic standards they always require a human to perform quality control and fix complex cases in the extraction. We present Click2Poly, a human-in-the-loop AI assistant designed to speed up this manual step. Extending the Florence-2 Vision Language Model (VLM), Click2Poly responds to user clicks by editing the building or wall vector layer directly. Implemented as a QGIS plugin, Click2Poly speeds up the manual editing of building and wall vector layers in a real-world production environment.

</details>


### [132] [Three Tokens Force Exponential Feature Rank in Nonnegative Kernel Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11427)
*Vicente Opazo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper establishes an exponential separation between full (dense softmax) attention and single-head kernel (sketch) attention, showing that kernel attention needs 2^Ω(m) features to solve a simple three-token Min-IP task while dense softmax solves it with m-dimensional scores, and generalizes bound to sketch models with finite alphabets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To formally characterize and quantify the expressive (representational) gap between full attention, which can attend to every token pair, and kernel attention, which compresses the sequence into a fixed-dimensional sketch, by exhibiting tasks where this distinction becomes exponentially large.

Method: The authors identify the first context length where two competing candidates must be distinguished, reduce attention to Min-Inner-Product (Min-IP) over Boolean inputs, and prove lower bounds via combinatorial/analytic arguments for single normalized nonnegative kernel-attention heads. They also extend the analysis to deterministic multihead multilayer sketch models whose cross-token channels have finite alphabets, proving a transcript lower bound linear in the number of independent answers and logarithmic in alphabet size.

Result: Rank-one normalized kernel attention solves all sequences of length at most two exactly on Boolean Min-IP; any single normalized nonnegative kernel-attention head achieving error strictly below 1/2 on all three-token sequences requires 2^Ω(m) features, even with arbitrary finite-dimensional tokenwise values and query-dependent affine readout, while dense softmax needs only m-dim scores and constant temperature. The lower bound survives position-dependent token maps and a causal final query and approaches the exact 2^m-feature realization as context grows. Transcript lower bounds are linear in the number of independent answers and logarithmic in alphabet size.

Conclusion: Kernel (sketch) attention is exponentially weaker than full dense attention on a minimal three-token task, and this gap is robust to position-dependent maps, causal queries, and finite-alphabet multihead multilayer sketch variants, sharpening our understanding of the representational cost of sketch-based token mixing.

Abstract: Full attention exposes every token pair, whereas kernel attention compresses a sequence into a fixed-dimensional sketch. We show that this distinction becomes exponential at the first context length containing two competing candidates. On Min-IP over Boolean inputs, rank-one normalized kernel attention solves every sequence of length at most two exactly. In contrast, any single normalized nonnegative kernel-attention head that succeeds on all three-token sequences with error strictly below $1/2$ requires $2^{Ω(m)}$ features, even with arbitrary finite-dimensional tokenwise values and an arbitrary query-dependent affine readout. Dense softmax solves the same task with $m$-dimensional scores and constant temperature. The conclusion survives position-dependent token maps and a causal final query. As context length grows, the lower bound approaches the exact $2^m$-feature realization. Separately, for deterministic multihead, multilayer sketch models whose cross-token channels have finite alphabets, we prove a transcript lower bound linear in the number of independent answers and logarithmic in their alphabet size.

</details>


### [133] [AutoGrable: What Is a Good Graph for a Table?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11431)
*Tamara Cucumides,Floris Geerts*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoGrable is a criterion-based, model-free method that automatically converts tables and relational databases into graphs for GNNs by scoring candidate column subsets via a label-alignment risk, without training any graph model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Applying GNNs to tabular/relational data requires a graph construction (choosing nodes, edges, relations), which is currently done by hand, by schema heuristics, or by training a model on every candidate and keeping the best. The paper seeks a cheap, principled, model-free criterion for deciding which construction is good for a given task.

Method: Uses the minimal table-to-graph abstraction (each row is a node) and observes that a message-passing GNN bounded by 1-WL sees a construction only as a partition of rows into colour-refinement classes. A construction is "good" if that partition separates rows with different labels and does not split rows sharing one. For incidence constructions the partition is fixed by the selected columns; candidate column subsets are scored by a label-alignment risk: the held-out risk of the best predictor constant on the partition's blocks, penalised by an occupancy term measuring how thinly blocks are populated. The score materialises no graph and trains no GNN, enabling greedy, cheap search over column subsets and returning a "grable" for single tables and foreign-key schemas.

Result: Experiments show the score discards a large fraction of candidate graphs while retaining the best; AutoGrable recovers the label-generating columns on controlled tasks; it outperforms fixed, random, and task-aware constructors on real tasks under a fixed predictor; and it is the only compared method that can decline to build a graph when none helps.

Conclusion: AutoGrable provides an effective, model-free graph construction procedure for tabular/relational data, offering both predictive performance and the ability to abstain from building a graph when it would not help.

Abstract: Graph learning presupposes a graph, and tables and relational databases do not come with one. Applying a GNN to them requires deciding which entities become nodes, which of them to connect, and through which relations---a decision made by hand, by schema heuristics, or by training a model on every candidate graph and keeping the best. We give a criterion that requires no trained graph model. In the minimal table-to-graph abstraction each row is a node, so a message-passing GNN, bounded by 1-WL, sees a construction only as a partition of the rows into colour-refinement classes: a construction is good for a task when that partition separates rows with different labels and does not split rows that share one. AutoGrable turns this criterion into a construction procedure. For incidence constructions the partition is fixed by the selected columns, so building a graph reduces to choosing them, and we score a candidate subset by a label-alignment risk: the held-out risk of the best predictor constant on its blocks, penalised by an occupancy term measuring how thinly the blocks are populated. The score materialises no graph and trains no GNN, so AutoGrable can search the space of subsets greedily and cheaply, and returns the resulting grable for single tables and for foreign-key schemas alike. Our experiments show that over a space of candidate graphs the score discards a large fraction while retaining the best; that AutoGrable recovers the columns that generate the label on controlled tasks and outperforms fixed, random, and task-aware constructors on real tasks under a fixed predictor; and that it is the only method compared that can decline to build a graph when none helps.

</details>


### [134] [Variational Parameter Calibration with Physics-Aware Latent-Space Surrogates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11435)
*Qiyao Zhou,Xujia Zhu,Pierre Joli,Yu Cong,Sibo Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a physics-aware, autoencoder-based latent-space framework that provides a differentiable reduced-order surrogate for both forward flow-field prediction and variational parameter estimation, and shows that a physics-aware end-to-end formulation improves parameter calibration under realistic, noisy/partial measurement settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forward and inverse modeling of parametric dynamical systems needs surrogates that are simultaneously accurate for state prediction and informative for parameter calibration, but a systematic end-to-end differentiable approach that couples deep-learning reduced-order surrogates with variational parameter estimation is still lacking.

Method: An autoencoder-based latent-space framework that maps physical parameters to predicted flow fields through a latent representation. During offline training, observable supervision encourages the latent variables to retain parameter-correlated information; the online inverse problem is solved in parameter space via the surrogate-induced observation operator.

Result: On two CFD benchmarks, reconstruction accuracy alone is insufficient for inverse modeling; observable supervision improves case-level separability and temporal organization of latent representations. Under noisy, low-resolution, randomly masked, and block-wise partial observations, the framework reduces calibration error and variability compared to standard surrogates.

Conclusion: An end-to-end differentiable, physics-aware latent-space surrogate enables robust variational parameter estimation in reduced-order forward/inverse modeling, outperforming standard surrogates under realistic measurement conditions.

Abstract: Forward and inverse modeling of parametric dynamical systems requires surrogate models that are not only accurate for state prediction, but also informative for parameter calibration. However, a systematic end-to-end differentiable formulation for coupling deep-learning-based reduced-order surrogates with variational parameter estimation remains underdeveloped. In this work, we introduce a physics-aware neural-network-based latent-space framework for reduced-order forward modeling and variational parameter estimation. The proposed autoencoder-based approach yields a differentiable surrogate that maps physical parameters to predicted flow fields through a latent representation. The observable supervision is used during offline training to encourage the latent variables to retain information correlated with system parameters, while the online inverse problem is solved in the parameter space through the surrogate-induced observation operator. The method is evaluated on two computational-fluid-dynamics benchmarks. The results show that reconstruction accuracy alone is insufficient for inverse modeling, owing to the lack of end-to-end differentiability or physics awareness for variational parameter calibration. Quantitative latent-space analysis further shows that observable supervision improves case-level separability and temporal organization of latent representations. Experiments with realistic measurement settings, including noisy, low-resolution, randomly masked, and block-wise partial observations, demonstrate the robustness of the proposed framework and show that it generally reduces calibration error and variability compared with the standard surrogate models.

</details>


### [135] [XGBoost "is all you need": the case of forecasting transmitted heat energy in District Heating Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11446)
*Milan Zdravković*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares XGBoost and LSTM for forecasting transmitted heat energy in District Heating Systems, finding that XGBoost consistently outperforms LSTM while also requiring less computation, which lowers cost and carbon footprint.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore scenarios in which conventional machine learning algorithms outperform deep learning networks in time series forecasting, and to quantify the associated benefits in terms of computational cost and environmental impact in energy systems.

Method: A comparative experimental study using a real-world District Heating System dataset, applying XGBoost (conventional ML) versus LSTM (deep learning) for time series forecasting of transmitted heat energy, with analysis of error distributions and computational demands.

Result: XGBoost consistently outperforms LSTM on this forecasting task. The performance gap is explained by error distribution analysis showing LSTM produces larger errors in intervals with less available data. Conventional ML also reduces computational demands, yielding cost savings and a smaller carbon footprint.

Conclusion: Conventional ML methods like XGBoost can be preferable to deep learning (LSTM) for certain time series forecasting tasks in District Heating Systems, offering both superior accuracy and lower computational and environmental costs.

Abstract: This paper presents a comparative study of two distinct approaches, XGBoost and Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM), for forecasting transmitted heat energy in District Heating Systems (DHS). The objective is to explore scenarios in which conventional ML algorithms demonstrate better performance over deep learning networks in time series forecasting and the associated benefits in terms of computational cost and environmental impact. The study focuses on a real-world DHS dataset. Through experimentation and analysis, it is demonstrated that XGBoost consistently outperforms LSTM in this specific forecasting task. The difference is explained by the error distribution illustrating that LSTM makes more significant errors in the intervals of less data availability. The reduced computational demands of conventional ML approaches not only result in cost savings but also minimize the carbon footprint associated with data analysis tasks in energy systems.

</details>


### [136] [PAC-Bayes Beyond Parameter Space: Behavioral Equivalence, Z-Information, and Exact Complexity Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11465)
*Vasant G. Honavar,Satish Kumar Keshri,Neil Ashtekar,Zehao Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper decomposes the classical PAC-Bayes KL divergence into a behavior-selection term (complexity of the predictive behavior distribution) and a realization-level term (expected conditional KL within fibers of behaviorally equivalent configurations). It defines "Z-information" as the negative of the latter and shows the behavior term admits an exact variational characterization attained by a fiber-symmetrized posterior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predictive risk depends only on the predictive behavior induced by a hypothesis, not on its internal realization. In over-parameterized systems many distinct configurations induce identical behavior, yet the classical PAC-Bayes KL divergence does not separate uncertainty over predictive behavior from variation among behaviorally equivalent realizations.

Method: Formalize behavioral equivalence via a measurable behavior map and use measure disintegration to decompose probability measures on the configuration space into a distribution over predictive behaviors plus conditional distributions over behavioral fibers. This yields an exact decomposition of the classical PAC-Bayes KL divergence into a behavior-selection term and a realization-level expected conditional KL term. Define Z-information as the negative realization-level contribution, and derive a variational characterization of the behavior-selection term as the minimum KL among all posteriors inducing the same predictive-behavior distribution.

Result: The classical PAC-Bayes KL divergence decomposes exactly into a behavior-selection term and a realization-level (expected conditional KL) term. The behavior-selection term is the minimum KL divergence over all posteriors inducing the same behavior distribution, attained by a canonical fiber-symmetrized representative. Symmetry, behavior-preserving directions, fiber geometry, and invariance under fiber-preserving perturbations all emerge naturally from the behavior-map structure.

Conclusion: Predictive behavior, rather than internal configuration, is the natural object of PAC-Bayes complexity; the classical KL divergence over-accounts by including redundant realization-level variation, and this redundancy is exactly captured and removable via the behavior-map decomposition and the fiber-symmetrized representative.

Abstract: PAC-Bayes theory provides generalization guarantees by controlling the Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence between posterior and prior distributions over a chosen hypothesis representation. However, predictive risk depends only on the predictive behavior induced by a hypothesis, not on the particular internal realization that implements that behavior. In over-parameterized systems, many distinct configurations induce identical predictive behavior, yet the classical PAC-Bayes KL divergence does not distinguish uncertainty over predictive behavior from variation among behaviorally equivalent realizations.
  We show that this distinction induces an exact structural decomposition of classical PAC-Bayes complexity. We formalize behavioral equivalence through a measurable behavior map and use measure disintegration to decompose probability measures on the configuration space into a distribution over predictive behaviors and conditional distributions over behavioral fibers. This yields an exact decomposition of the classical PAC-Bayes KL divergence into a behavior-selection term and a realization-level term given by an expected conditional KL within fibers.
  We define Z-information as the negative of this realization-level contribution: the exact gap between the KL divergence and the complexity of uncertainty over predictive behavior alone. We further show that the behavior-selection term admits an exact variational characterization: it is the minimum KL divergence among all posteriors inducing the same distribution over predictive behaviors, attained by a canonical fiber-symmetrized representative.
  Finally, we show that symmetry, behavior-preserving directions, fiber geometry, and invariance under fiber-preserving perturbations arise naturally from the same behavior-map structure. Together, these results identify predictive behavior as the natural object of PAC-Bayes complexity.

</details>


### [137] [Dual-Primal Graph VAEs for Noisy Label Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11473)
*Patrick Stinson,Nikolaus Kriegeskorte*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a graph VAE with GAT-based message passing on a crowdsourced dataset graph (and its dual) that treats ground-truth labels as latent variables, achieving unsupervised label inference and state-of-the-art crowdsourcing benchmark results, with extensions to incorporate side information from neural classifiers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Crowdsourced labels are noisy, and inferring ground truth is a key problem. Neural methods avoid the restrictive generative-model assumptions of classical Bayesian approaches, but existing neural models still rely on fairly simple generative models or require pseudo-labels/synthetic data to train the aggregate classifier. A fully unsupervised, graph-based alternative is needed.

Method: A graph VAE architecture where the decoder and encoder apply GAT-based message passing on the adjacency graph of a crowdsourced dataset and its dual graph, respectively. Ground-truth labels are treated as latent variables, enabling unsupervised representation learning without a separate classifier. The approach is extended by augmenting the crowdsourcing graph with side information such as classifier representations to boost test-time performance.

Result: The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on crowdsourcing benchmarks, and incorporating side information from neural network classifiers trained on noisy labels substantially boosts their classification performance at test time.

Conclusion: Graph VAE with GAT-based message passing provides a flexible, unsupervised framework for crowdsourced label aggregation, generalizing to include side information and outperforming prior methods.

Abstract: Inferring the ground-truth from noisy crowdsourced labels is an important theoretical and practical problem. Neural network-based methods offer an alternative to classical Bayesian models which require specifying a family of generative models used for inference. However, current models either still rely on fairly simple generative models for inference or require pseudo-labels or synthetic data to train the aggregate classifier. We propose a graph VAE architecture in which the decoder and encoder use GAT-based message passing on the adjacency graph of a crowdsourced dataset and its dual, respectively. The ground-truth labels are treated as latent variables, enabling unsupervised representation learning without needing to train a separate classifier. We show our model achieves state of the art performance on crowdsourcing benchmarks. We then demonstrate the generality of our approach by showing how the original crowdsourcing graph can be augmented to incorporate side information such as representations from neural network classifiers trained on the noisy labels to substantially boost their classification performance at test time.

</details>


### [138] [Convergence Guarantees of Gradient Descent for Neural Networks via Generalized Lipschitz Smoothness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11479)
*Siqiao Mu,Diego Klabjan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proves convergence guarantees for gradient descent on arbitrary-width/depth feedforward neural networks under only Lipschitz smoothness, Lipschitz continuity, and linear boundedness of activations and Lipschitz smoothness of the loss. It derives a generalized Lipschitz smoothness condition, establishes a descent lemma, and shows the minimum squared gradient norm converges to zero at rate O(1/T^{1/L}).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide convergence guarantees for gradient descent on general feedforward neural networks without restrictive assumptions on initialization, dataset, width, or depth, thereby extending guarantees beyond common frameworks (e.g., overparameterization or specific initialization schemes) to broadly used activations such as linear, tanh, softplus, and sigmoid.

Method: The authors leverage the observation that Lipschitz properties of activation functions are partially preserved under repeated composition, yielding a novel generalized Lipschitz smoothness condition: the change in gradient is bounded by the change in parameters multiplied by polynomial terms of the parameter norms at both endpoints. This condition applies to both the model and the loss, producing a descent lemma where loss decreases whenever the learning rate is sufficiently small relative to parameter norms. Bounding parameter norm growth then yields convergence of the minimum squared gradient norm to zero.

Result: For an L-layer feedforward neural network with Lipschitz smooth, Lipschitz continuous, and linearly bounded activations and a Lipschitz smooth loss (e.g., mean-squared error), gradient descent achieves convergence of the minimum squared gradient norm to zero in T iterations at rate O(1/T^{1/L}), regardless of width, depth, initialization, or dataset.

Conclusion: Gradient descent provably converges for general feedforward networks under mild, widely satisfied assumptions, with a convergence rate O(1/T^{1/L}) for the minimum squared gradient norm, establishing theoretical guarantees that hold across common architectures and activations without special initialization or data constraints.

Abstract: We establish convergence guarantees of gradient descent for general feedforward neural networks of arbitrary width or depth, with no special requirements on the initialization or dataset. We only assume that the activation functions are Lipschitz smooth, Lipschitz continuous, and linearly bounded--- properties that hold for linear, tanh, softplus, and sigmoid activation functions. For the loss function, we require that it is Lipschitz smooth in the model outputs, which is true for mean-squared error. The key theoretical insight is that the Lipschitz properties of the activation functions are partially preserved even through repeated compositions, leading to a novel generalized Lipschitz smoothness condition where the change in gradient is upper bounded by the change in the parameter space, multiplied by polynomial terms of the parameter norms at both endpoints. This type of condition holds for both the model function and the loss function, enabling a descent lemma where the loss decreases as long as the learning rate is small enough with respect to the parameter norms. By ensuring that the parameter norms do not grow too quickly to infinity, we prove that the minimum squared gradient norm converges to zero in $T$ iterations at rate $O(1/T^{1/L})$ for an $L$-layer neural network.

</details>


### [139] [HyperFix: Combinatorial Nonlinear Correction for Task Vector Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11499)
*Hyo Seo Kim,Ren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HyperFix is a lightweight hypernetwork that predicts subset-conditioned nonlinear weight-space corrections for task vector merging, trained once on small subsets and generalizing to larger ones without per-subset tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing task vector merging methods rely on scalar tuning for a specific subset of tasks, which requires repeated tuning whenever the subset changes and restricts merging to linear rescaling. The authors aim to support varying task subsets efficiently while enabling nonlinear corrections.

Method: The paper formulates merging across varying task subsets as a combinatorial correction problem and proposes HyperFix, a lightweight hypernetwork that predicts subset-conditioned nonlinear corrections in weight space. It is trained once on singleton, pair, and triple subsets from a task bank and generalizes to larger subsets without per-subset optimization. A local perturbation analysis bounds the residual correction beyond linear merging and motivates learning from small task updates.

Result: Experiments across diverse benchmarks show that HyperFix outperforms existing task vector merging methods while reducing tuning cost.

Conclusion: HyperFix provides an effective, low-cost alternative to per-subset scalar tuning, improving merging performance through learned nonlinear corrections and demonstrating strong generalization to larger task subsets.

Abstract: Task vectors enable model merging without joint retraining. In practice, the subset of task vectors to be merged may vary, but many existing methods use scalar tuning for a particular subset, requiring repeated tuning across subsets and restricting task vector merging to linear rescaling. We therefore formulate merging across varying task subsets as a combinatorial correction problem and introduce HyperFix, a lightweight hypernetwork that predicts subset-conditioned nonlinear corrections in weight space. Trained once on singleton, pair, and triple subsets from a task bank, HyperFix generalizes to larger subsets without per-subset optimization. Our local perturbation analysis bounds the residual correction beyond linear merging and motivates learning it from small task updates. Experiments across diverse benchmarks show that HyperFix outperforms existing task vector merging methods while reducing tuning cost.

</details>


### [140] [RelShap: Relationally Consistent Shapley Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11508)
*Seungeun Lee,Joao Fonseca,Julia Stoyanovich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RelShap is a framework that integrates relational constraints and data provenance into Shapley value computation, yielding relationally valid feature attributions with reduced runtime via functional-dependency-induced equivalence classes, while remaining compatible with Kernel SHAP, Monte Carlo, and Leverage SHAP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard ML pipelines flatten relational data into single tables, discarding structural constraints. Shapley value-based attributions assume feature independence and thus evaluate the model on impossible feature combinations, producing misleading explanations. Existing conditional methods fail to leverage relational structure/provenance.

Method: RelShap incorporates relational constraints and data provenance into Shapley value computation, restricting both background data and coalition evaluation to relationally valid configurations. It is estimator-agnostic and composes with Kernel SHAP, Monte Carlo, and Leverage SHAP without changing their sampling/weighting properties. Functional dependencies induce equivalence classes over coalitions, exploited for runtime reduction without altering Shapley values, with a combinatorial characterization of expected speedup.

Result: Across multiple datasets, models, and estimators, RelShap yields explanations more faithful to the data-generating process and correctly identifies the dominant feature in controlled settings where Conditional SHAP and ManifoldShap do not.

Conclusion: RelShap provides relationally valid, estimator-agnostic Shapley explanations that outperform existing conditional/manifold-based methods on faithfulness and correctness, with provable runtime savings from functional dependencies; code is publicly available.

Abstract: Machine learning pipelines commonly flatten relational data into single-table representations, discarding structural constraints. Widely used Shapley value-based feature attributions then rely on feature independence, evaluating the model on combinations that could never arise in the underlying data, producing misleading explanations. We propose RelShap, a framework that incorporates relational constraints and data provenance into Shapley value computation, restricting both background data and coalition evaluation to relationally valid configurations. The framework is estimator-agnostic and composes with Kernel SHAP, Monte Carlo, and Leverage SHAP without altering their sampling or weighting properties. Functional dependencies further induce equivalence classes over feature coalitions, which RelShap exploits to reduce runtime without changing Shapley values; we provide a combinatorial characterization of the expected speedup. Experiments across multiple datasets, models, and estimators show that RelShap produces explanations that are more faithful to the data-generating process, correctly identifying the dominant feature in controlled settings where existing methods, including Conditional SHAP and ManifoldShap, do not. Our code is available at: https://github.com/duneag2/relshap.

</details>


### [141] [Let it Cook: Learning to Wait in Sequential Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11511)
*Christopher Watson,Arjun Krishna,Dinesh Jayaraman,Rajeev Alur*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces "learning to wait" for sequential decision making, where an agent learns when to pause sensing and actions to save resources without hurting task performance, using reinforcement learning with lexicographic objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agents in sequential decision making usually observe and act every timestep, but many tasks have periods where constant monitoring and control are unnecessary. Allowing the agent to wait during these periods conserves resources (e.g., sensing/energy) or frees attention for other tasks, without sacrificing task performance such as total completion time.

Method: The authors formalize "learning to wait" as minimizing the frequency of sensing and decision making without sacrificing task performance. They propose training a "waiting policy" that decides where and how long to wait, committing to a wait action for a set number of timesteps while forgoing sensing. The approach uses reinforcement learning with lexicographically ordered objectives to jointly optimize task performance (primary) and waiting/minimizing sensing (secondary).

Result: Experiments across 4 discrete-state household tasks and 3 continuous-state environments show the approach successfully learns waiting behaviors and can adapt pre-trained policies to wait where appropriate. Different tasks permit different amounts of waiting, but the approach consistently finds solutions with significant waiting, sometimes waiting for over 50 percent of the task duration.

Conclusion: The proposed learning-to-wait framework effectively identifies opportunities to pause sensing and control, achieving substantial waiting (sometimes over 50% of task duration) while maintaining task performance. It works across both discrete and continuous environments and can be applied to pre-trained policies, offering a resource-efficient alternative to acting at every timestep.

Abstract: In sequential decision making, an agent typically observes its environment and acts at every timestep. However, such active participation may not always be necessary; tasks such as brewing coffee include periods that are served equally well by letting the environment evolve without constant monitoring and control. During such periods, the agent could simply wait to conserve its resources, or redirect its attention to another task. We capitalize on these opportunities by training a "waiting policy" that decides where and how long to wait. This involves forgoing sensing to commit to a wait action, representing a deliberate pause for a set number of timesteps. We formalize "learning to wait" as minimizing the frequency of sensing and decision making without sacrificing task performance (e.g., the total amount of time to complete a task). To train a waiting policy, we propose an approach that employs reinforcement learning with lexicographically ordered objectives. In experiments across 4 discrete-state household tasks and 3 continuous-state environments, we show that our approach successfully learns waiting behaviors, and can adapt pre-trained policies to wait where appropriate. While different tasks permit different amounts of waiting without sacrificing task performance, our approach consistently finds solutions with significant waiting, sometimes waiting for over 50 percent of the task duration.

</details>


### [142] [FLARE++: Low-rank attention with dynamic attention routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11519)
*Vedant Puri,Yongjie Jessica Zhang,Levent Burak Kara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FLARE++ is a low-rank attention architecture that replaces learned, static latent queries with input-conditioned dynamic queries built by reusing the model's own encoder, keeping O(NM) linear complexity while improving accuracy on PDE surrogates and Long Range Arena.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full self-attention is a strong token mixer for PDE surrogates on irregular domains, but its quadratic O(N^2) cost prevents scaling to high-resolution problems. Latent-attention models like FLARE reduce cost by routing N tokens through M learned queries, but those queries are fixed parameters shared across all inputs, limiting adaptability to each specific input.

Method: FLARE++ introduces dynamic token routing while retaining FLARE's low-rank factorization and O(NM) complexity. It reuses FLARE's encoder to build routing queries: learned latent seeds trigger one extra encode call that gathers the N input tokens into M input-conditioned queries, which then govern compression and redistribution of the tokens. The entire routing operation is expressed using only standard scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) calls. A multi-GPU context-parallel implementation shards input tokens across devices without gathering the full token sequence on any single device.

Result: FLARE++ is competitive on standard PDE surrogate benchmarks, outperforming fixed-query FLARE by 24% on average, and gains 2.3 points of average accuracy on Long Range Arena.

Conclusion: Making latent queries input-conditioned via FLARE's own encoder removes the restriction of fixed learned queries, preserving linear complexity and explicit low-rank structure while substantially improving performance across PDE surrogate tasks and Long Range Arena.

Abstract: Full self-attention is a strong token mixer for PDE surrogates on irregular domains, but its quadratic cost limits its use on high-resolution problems. Efficient latent-attention models such as the Fast Low-rank Attention Routing Engine (FLARE) avoid that cost by routing all N tokens through M << N learned latent queries, but those queries are parameters: once trained, the same learned query templates serve every input. We remove this restriction with FLARE++, a low-rank attention architecture with dynamic token routing. FLARE++ reuses FLARE's own encoder to build its routing queries: learned latent seeds drive one extra encode call that gathers the N input tokens into M input-conditioned queries, and those queries then determine how the same tokens are compressed and redistributed. This preserves FLARE's explicit low-rank factorization and linear O(NM) complexity, and expresses the complete routing operation with standard scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) calls alone. We also provide a multi-GPU context-parallel implementation that shards input tokens across devices without ever gathering the full token sequence on one of them. FLARE++ is competitive across a set of standard PDE surrogate benchmarks, improving on fixed-query FLARE by 24% on average, and it gains 2.3 points of average accuracy on Long Range Arena.

</details>


### [143] [Hierarchical Federated Transfer Learning in Digital Twin-Based Vehicular Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11532)
*Qasim Zia,Saide Zhu,Haoxin Wang,Zafar Iqbal,Yingshu Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a Hierarchical Federated Transfer Learning (HFTL) framework for Digital Twin-based Vehicular Ad hoc Networks (DT-VANET) to overcome data heterogeneity and sparsity, using vehicle-type clustering, cloud/cluster-level update algorithms, and a data quality scoring mechanism to improve global model accuracy and resist malicious vehicles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated Learning in DT-VANET preserves data privacy but suffers from data heterogeneity and data sparsity among vehicles, leading to suboptimal global model accuracy for different vehicle types. A more effective training approach is needed to handle these challenges.

Method: The authors combine Federated Transfer Learning (FTL) with vehicle-type-based clustering and propose HFTL. They construct a DT-VANET framework with two algorithms: one for cloud server model updates and one for intra-cluster federated transfer learning. A data quality score-based mechanism is also designed to mitigate the influence of malicious vehicles on the global model. Experiments are conducted on real-world datasets across multiple performance metrics.

Result: Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed HFTL framework effectively improves global model accuracy and efficiency compared to baseline approaches, while the data quality score mechanism protects the global model from malicious vehicles.

Conclusion: HFTL combined with vehicle-type clustering and a data quality scoring mechanism successfully addresses data heterogeneity and sparsity in DT-VANET, yielding higher global model accuracy and robustness against malicious vehicles, as validated by experiments.

Abstract: In recent research on the Digital Twin-based Vehicular Ad hoc Network(DT-VANET), Federated Learning (FL) has shown its ability to provide data privacy. However, Federated learning struggles to adequately train a global model when confronted with data heterogeneity and data sparsity among vehicles, which ensure suboptimal accuracy in making precise predictions for different vehicle types. To address these challenges, this paper combines Federated Transfer Learning (FTL) to conduct vehicle clustering related to types of vehicles and proposes a novel Hierarchical Federated Transfer Learning (HFTL). We construct a framework for DT-VANET, along with two algorithms designed for cloud server model updates and intra-cluster federated transfer learning, to improve the accuracy of the global model. In addition, we developed a data quality score-based mechanism to prevent the global model from being affected by malicious vehicles. Lastly, detailed experiments on real-world datasets are conducted, considering different performance metrics that verify the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithm.

</details>


### [144] [Robust Ambiguity Detection (RAD) From Model- and Feature-Space Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11541)
*Manya Singh,Mark T. Keane,Arjun Pakrashi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Robust Ambiguity Detection (RAD) framework, which quantifies predictive ambiguity in machine learning models using two complementary metrics—Model-Space Consistency and Feature-Space Consistency—combined as the RAD Score-Pair and visualized via the RAD Plot.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine learning models should remain predictively consistent under permissible variations, such as replacing a model with a functionally equivalent one or applying minor admissible input perturbations. When such changes significantly alter predictions, the prediction is ambiguous, and models should abstain or flag these cases—especially in high-stakes decision-making. However, ambiguity is difficult to identify once a model is deployed.

Method: The RAD framework quantifies predictive ambiguity using two complementary consistency metrics: Model-Space Consistency and Feature-Space Consistency. These scores form the RAD Score-Pair and are visualized through the RAD Plot, offering an interpretable characterization of ambiguity sources. RAD is evaluated on synthetic datasets with controlled overlap and real-world datasets where ambiguity cannot be directly inspected. A downstream application ranks samples by RAD Pareto-Rank and abstains from predicting the most ambiguous ones.

Result: RAD provides an interpretable characterization of the sources of ambiguity and suggests actions users may take. In a downstream rejection-based application, abstaining from the most ambiguous samples (ranked by RAD Pareto-Rank) achieves performance comparable to existing rejection-based approaches.

Conclusion: The RAD framework offers an effective, interpretable way to detect and quantify predictive ambiguity, supporting abstention or flagging of ambiguous predictions and performing comparably to existing rejection methods in downstream applications.

Abstract: Machine learning models should be robust, in the sense of remaining predictively consistent under permissible variations. A model's predictions should ideally remain unchanged when it is replaced by a functionally equivalent one, or when its inputs are subject to minor, admissible perturbations. If such changes alter a prediction significantly, then the prediction is "ambiguous" with respect to the model. Models should abstain from making such ambiguous predictions and/or should flag them for human inspection, especially in high-stakes decision-making scenarios. However, in practice, such ambiguity is not easy to identify once a model is deployed. Here, the Robust Ambiguity Detection (RAD) framework is advanced for quantifying predictive ambiguity using two complementary metrics: Model-Space Consistency and Feature-Space Consistency. These two scores, the RAD Score-Pair, visualised through the RAD Plot, provide an interpretable characterisation of the sources of ambiguity and the actions a user may consider in response. RAD is evaluated on synthetic datasets with systematically controlled overlap, as well as several real-world datasets where the level of ambiguity cannot be directly inspected. Finally, we demonstrate a downstream application of RAD where samples are ranked by their RAD Pareto-Rank and the most ambiguous are abstained from prediction, achieving performance comparable to existing rejection-based approaches.

</details>


### [145] [Certifying What Helps Customer-Return Timing: A Screen-and-Confirm Test for Conditioning Signals, and Why Decay Is Nearly Enough](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11555)
*Sang Su Lee,Vineeth Loganathan,Shishir Dash,Vijay Raghavan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a screen-and-confirm protocol and a model-free predictability ceiling to rigorously test whether added covariates actually improve temporal-point-process timing. Applying it to customer-return data, it certifies that continuous-time decay suffices and most conditioning signals are redundant or harmful.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Customer-return and TPP modeling increasingly add rich signals (LTV, category, recency/frequency, geography), but there is no credible way to distinguish "feature X doesn't help" from "the method was too weak to find the signal." The authors want a trustworthy, checkable basis for claiming that conditioning signals do (or do not) improve event-timing likelihood.

Method: Two contributions: (i) a screen-and-confirm protocol using a positive control that plants a coupling of known strength and verifies the model recovers it, so a real-data null can be read as "no signal" rather than "weak method" (validated for categorical and continuous encodings and on clock-driven NYC taxi data); (ii) a model-free ceiling on point-predictability showing that only a single-digit percentage of gap variance is explainable by any covariate (returns are near-memoryless).

Result: On three public benchmarks (Amazon, Taobao, RetailRocket) and a real marketplace (Thumbtack), the inter-event clock (continuous-time decay) is nearly sufficient; added conditioning is statistically null on public benchmarks (at most 0.06 NLL) and null to mildly harmful on the marketplace. The paper also documents read-out/leakage pitfalls that were hit and retracted.

Conclusion: The contribution is not the finding that decay helps, but the tools that turn "conditioning doesn't help" into a checkable, certified statement, supported by an honest account of evaluation pitfalls.

Abstract: Practitioners enrich customer-return models with ever more signals (lifetime value, category, recency/frequency, calendar, geography), and the temporal-point-process (TPP) literature follows suit with covariate- and external-covariate-conditioned intensities. But does any of it improve the timing, and how would you know? A null ("feature X doesn't help") is only meaningful if the model could have found a signal. We make two contributions--a method and a measurement--to answer this credibly. (i) A screen-and-confirm protocol that certifies whether a candidate signal improves a TPP's event-timing likelihood: a positive control plants a coupling of known strength and confirms the model recovers it, so a real-data null can be read as "no signal" rather than "weak method." The control is validated for categorical and continuous encodings, and on a real clock-driven dataset (NYC taxi hour-of-day). (ii) A model-free ceiling quantifying how little of customer-return timing is point-predictable at all (a single-digit percentage of gap variance from any covariate; returns are near-memoryless). With these we certify a clean result on three public benchmarks (Amazon, Taobao, RetailRocket) and a real marketplace (Thumbtack): the inter-event clock--continuous-time decay, long known to beat frozen-intensity models--is nearly sufficient, and the conditioning the field keeps adding is redundant or harmful on top of it (statistically null on the public benchmarks, at most 0.06 NLL; null to mildly harmful on the marketplace). We do not claim to discover that decay helps; our contribution is the tools that turn "conditioning doesn't help" into a checkable, certified statement--plus an honest-evaluation account of the read-out/leakage pitfalls we hit and retracted.

</details>


### [146] [When Offline Evaluation Misleads: A Diagnostic Protocol for Reward and Policy Selection in Delayed-Feedback Contextual Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11560)
*Sang Su Lee,Vineeth Loganathan,Shishir Dash,Vijay Raghavan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A diagnostic protocol for contextual multi-armed bandit (CMAB) reward/policy candidates under delayed feedback, screening on alignment and learnability before trusting offline lift estimates; validated on a public OPE benchmark, a synthetic generator, and a deployed marketplace push system.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalized marketing with CMABs optimizes a proxy reward because the true north-star metric (downstream conversion) is observed only after weeks, too late for online learning. Standard offline checks (batch off-policy estimates, marginal arm-discrimination tests, confidence intervals) can be systematically misleading under delayed feedback, and teams lack a principled way to decide whether a bandit is worth its complexity over a single best message.

Method: An ordered diagnostic protocol that screens a reward-and-policy candidate on two axes before trusting reported lift: (1) alignment - whether optimizing the reward moves the north-star metric - and (2) learnability - whether the bandit can identify the reward-optimal policy. The protocol is validated on a public off-policy-evaluation benchmark and a controllable synthetic generator, then illustrated on a deployed large-marketplace push system with five arms and one split.

Result: Two recurring lessons emerge: (N1) a single offline number can mis-rank rewards because a denser reward signal gives the bandit more to learn from, so rewards that look tied in a static estimate diverge once learning happens online; (N2) if the best single message cannot be identified in advance, a per-user policy partly just avoids betting on the wrong arm - appearing like personalization but actually reflecting robustness, so a "personalization premium" is easily overstated. In the deployed system, evidence is directional rather than powered.

Conclusion: The contribution is methodological rather than algorithmic: an ordered diagnostic protocol, the two lessons it surfaces (denser rewards pull apart under learning; apparent personalization can be robustness), and the end-to-end experience of applying the protocol to a delayed-feedback CMAB.

Abstract: Personalizing marketing messages with contextual multi-armed bandits (CMABs) drives real business value, yet the objective that ultimately matters - a downstream conversion - is observed only weeks later, too late to drive online learning. Teams therefore train the bandit on a fast proxy reward, and separately must judge whether a contextual bandit is worth its complexity over sending one best message. Settling both decisions with the usual offline checks - a batch off-policy estimate, a marginal arm-discrimination test, a confidence interval - can mislead systematically under delayed feedback. We give an ordered diagnostic protocol that screens a reward-and-policy candidate on two axes, alignment (does optimizing the reward move the north-star?) and learnability (can the bandit identify the reward-optimal policy?), before trusting any reported lift. We validate it where the truth is known - a public off-policy-evaluation benchmark and a controllable synthetic generator - and illustrate it on a deployed large-marketplace push system (where, with five arms and one split, the evidence is directional rather than powered). Two lessons recur. (N1) A single offline number can mis-rank rewards: a denser reward signal gives the bandit more to learn from, so rewards that look tied in a static estimate pull apart once learning happens online. (N2) If you cannot tell in advance which single message is best, a per-user policy partly just avoids betting on the wrong one - that looks like personalization but is really robustness, so a "personalization premium" is easily overstated. Our contribution is methodological rather than algorithmic: the ordered protocol, the two lessons it surfaces, and the end-to-end experience of applying it to a delayed-feedback CMAB.

</details>


### [147] [Sparse and robust geometric twin support vector machine via asymmetric RoBoSS loss function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11567)
*Kai Qi,Xinji Huang,Hongchun Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes aRSGTSVM, a novel $l_1$-norm penalized geometric twin SVM with an asymmetric, robust, bounded, sparse and smooth (aR) loss function. It handles feature selection, label noise, and feature noise, solved via proximal gradient descent, and is validated on synthetic, UCI, and stock index tracking tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world training data often contains redundant features plus label and feature noise, undermining standard SVM (which uses $l_2$-norm penalty and hinge loss), making it unable to select significant features and sensitive to noise.

Method: The authors propose an asymmetric, robust, bounded, sparse and smooth (aR) loss function combined with an $l_1$-norm penalized geometric twin SVM (aRSGTSVM) for both classification and regression. The $l_1$-norm penalty enables feature selection; the aR loss mitigates label noise and improves stability to zero-mean feature noise (resampling noise) near the boundary hyperplanes. They conduct a robustness analysis using the influence function and solve the nonconvex, nonsmooth optimization with a fast, stable proximal gradient descent algorithm.

Result: Experiments on synthetic and UCI datasets show aRSGTSVM outperforms related state-of-the-art methods. Applied to index tracking on different China stock market indices, it achieves satisfactory performance.

Conclusion: aRSGTSVM effectively combines feature selection with robustness against label and feature noise, and is competitive across classification, regression, and practical index tracking applications.

Abstract: In real-world scenarios, the training data usually contains redundant features, label noise and feature noise, which provide severe challenges for the efficiency of machine learning methods. Since standard support vector machine (SVM) adopts $l_2$-norm penalty and hinge loss function, it lacks the ability of selecting significant features and is sensitive to noise. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel asymmetric, robust, bounded, sparse and smooth (aR) loss function for $l_1$-norm penalized geometric twin SVM (aRSGTSVM) to handle classification and regression tasks. The $l_1$-norm penalty can achieve the feature selection. The proposed aR loss function can not only effectively mitigate the impact of label noise, but also significantly enhance the stability to resampling noise, i.e., the zero-mean feature noise around the boundary hyperplanes. Furthermore, a statistical analysis of the robustness of aRSGTSVM was also conducted using the influence function. Since aRSGTSVM involves nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization, we develop a fast and stable proximal gradient descent based solving algorithm. Compared with related state-of-the-art methods, experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed aRSGTSVM on both synthetic and UCI datasets. Furthermore, we apply aRSGTSVM to index tracking tasks, where results for tracking the different indices in the China stock market show that it can achieve satisfactory performance.

</details>


### [148] [RECAST: A Machine-Learning Framework for Correction and Super-Resolution of Coarse-Grid PDE Solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11572)
*Maryam Reza,Farbod Faraji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RECAST is a machine-learning framework that corrects coarse-grid numerical PDE trajectories and reconstructs fine-grid states, reducing time-averaged relative error by 50-92% across six 1D PDE systems while enabling grids coarsened by 8-16x with 1000-step closed-loop rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coarse-grid numerical solvers reduce computational cost for time-dependent PDE simulation, but under-resolution degrades both the trajectory accuracy and spatial fidelity of the solution. The work aims to restore lost accuracy while retaining the low-cost coarse-grid evolution.

Method: RECAST integrates two learned components: (1) correction of the coarse-grid state within the numerical time-stepping loop, and (2) super-resolution reconstruction of the corresponding fine-grid state from the corrected coarse-grid history. The framework is evaluated on six one-dimensional PDE systems (transport, diffusion, dispersion, reaction, wave dynamics) with 8-16x spatial coarsening and 1000-step closed-loop rollouts from unseen initial conditions.

Result: RECAST remains closely aligned with fine-grid reference solutions, reducing time-averaged relative error by approximately 50-92% versus uncorrected coarse-grid solvers. It generalizes to unseen PDE parameter values and achieves lower error and better long-horizon agreement over 5000-step rollouts compared with a contemporary coarse-correction architecture.

Conclusion: Learned correction and reconstruction enable substantially coarser PDE evolution without the corresponding loss of solution fidelity, offering a proof-of-concept route toward machine-learning acceleration of higher-dimensional numerical simulations across science and engineering.

Abstract: Coarse-grid numerical solvers can substantially reduce the computational cost of time-dependent PDE simulation, but under-resolution often degrades both the trajectory and the spatial fidelity of the solution. We introduce RECAST (Recurrent Error Correction And Super-resolution of coarse-grid Trajectories), a machine-learning framework designed to restore this lost accuracy while retaining coarse-grid evolution. RECAST combines learned correction within the numerical time-stepping loop with reconstruction of the corresponding fine-grid state from the corrected coarse history. We evaluate the framework on six one-dimensional PDE systems spanning transport, diffusion, dispersion, reaction, and wave dynamics, using spatial grids coarsened by factors of 8-16 and 1000-step closed-loop rollouts from unseen initial conditions. Across the test cases, RECAST remains closely aligned with the fine-grid reference solutions and reduces time-averaged relative error by approximately 50-92% compared with the corresponding uncorrected coarse-grid solvers. Additional tests show generalization to unseen PDE parameter values, while comparison with a contemporary coarse-correction architecture shows that RECAST achieves lower error and better long-horizon agreement with the fine-grid reference over 5000-step rollouts. These results demonstrate that the learned correction and reconstruction capabilities of RECAST can enable substantially coarser PDE evolution without the corresponding loss of solution fidelity, providing a proof-of-concept route toward machine-learning acceleration of higher-dimensional numerical simulations across science and engineering.

</details>


### [149] [Dion3: Full-Stack Orthogonal Updates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11612)
*Noah Amsel,Jack Zhang,Kwangjun Ahn,Ali Naeimi,Austin Feng,Berlin Chen,Tri Dao,John Langford*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Dion3 is a revised Muon optimizer that reduces overhead across the stack—faster orthogonalization via Gram Newton-Schulz, symmetric CuteDSL kernels, megabatching to cut communication, and a row-subset update rule—achieving up to 6x faster step time while matching or improving Muon's loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Muon's cubic-time Newton-Schulz orthogonalization creates significant overhead, which is compounded by communication costs under weight sharding, eroding Muon's benefits in many settings. The goal is to eliminate this overhead at every level of the stack.

Method: Dion3 introduces three components plus an update-rule change: (1) a Gram Newton-Schulz algorithm to lower the FLOP cost of orthogonalization; (2) CuteDSL kernels that exploit symmetry to accelerate it; (3) a megabatching strategy to reduce communication overhead; and (4) a modified update rule that orthogonalizes only a fraction of the momentum matrix's rows at each step, improving on the compressed Dion variant in both speed and performance.

Result: Dion3 matches or improves on Muon's achieved loss while reducing optimizer step time by up to 6x. It also improves on Dion in both speed and performance.

Conclusion: Dion3 successfully addresses Muon's computational and communication overhead, offering a drop-in replacement (available via the dion package on GitHub) that maintains or improves loss while substantially accelerating optimizer step time.

Abstract: The Muon optimizer incurs a significant overhead cost due to its cubic-time Newton-Schulz orthogonalization step. When weights are sharded, communication overhead compounds this computational cost, eroding the benefits of Muon in many settings. We present Dion3, a revision of Muon that targets this overhead at every level of the stack. Our Gram Newton-Schulz algorithm reduces the FLOP cost of orthogonalization, our CuteDSL kernels accelerate it by exploiting symmetry, and our megabatching strategy reduces communication overhead. Moreover, we propose a simple change to the update rule that cuts costs even further: selecting only a fraction of the momentum matrix's rows to orthogonalize at each step. This update rule improves on Dion (another "compressed" version of Muon), in both speed and performance. Overall, Dion3 matches or improves on the loss achieved by Muon but reduces optimizer step time by up to 6x. Dion3 is available via the dion package (https://github.com/microsoft/dion) as a drop-in replacement for Muon.

</details>


### [150] [A Local Sinkhorn Framework for Conditional Distribution Reconstruction of Multidimensional Random Fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11613)
*Mingtao Xia,Qijing Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a local Sinkhorn divergence framework for reconstructing the conditional distributions of multidimensional random fields. It uses debiased Sinkhorn divergence as a differentiable, efficient local matching objective to train stochastic neural networks, and provides generalization error bounds that characterize the bias–efficiency trade-off governed by the regularization parameter. The approach offers a scalable alternative to exact local optimal transport for uncertainty quantification and probabilistic scientific machine learning, and numerical experiments show it balances reconstruction accuracy, computational efficiency, and scalability better than competing loss functions and frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Exact local optimal transport for conditional distribution reconstruction of multidimensional random fields is computationally expensive and difficult to scale. There is a need for a differentiable, statistically efficient, and scalable distribution-matching objective to train stochastic neural networks for uncertainty quantification and probabilistic scientific machine learning, while retaining geometric fidelity in capturing multidimensional dependence.

Method: The authors propose a local Sinkhorn divergence framework that applies debiased (entropy-regularized) Sinkhorn divergence as a local distribution-matching loss to train stochastic neural networks. They derive theoretical generalization error estimates that explicitly link the regularization parameter to the trade-off between approximation bias and statistical efficiency, enabling scalable conditional distribution reconstruction of multidimensional random fields.

Result: The framework yields a scalable, differentiable alternative to exact local optimal transport. Numerical examples comparing the proposed loss against other loss functions for training SNNs, and against other machine-learning-based uncertainty quantification frameworks, show that the method achieves an effective balance between reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency while maintaining good scalability for multidimensional stochastic systems.

Conclusion: The proposed local Sinkhorn divergence framework provides a practical compromise between geometric fidelity, statistical efficiency, and computational scalability. It is well-suited for uncertainty quantification and probabilistic scientific machine learning, improving reconstruction accuracy and efficiency for multidimensional random field models compared to existing approaches.
