Abstract: In this paper, we propose a local Sinkhorn divergence framework for conditional distribution reconstruction of multidimensional random fields. By utilizing the debiased Sinkhorn divergence, our proposed approach develops a differentiable and computationally efficient local distribution matching objective to train stochastic neural networks (SNNs). Furthermore, we establish theoretical generalization error estimates for our local Sinkhorn divergence framework, which explicitly characterizes the trade-off between approximation bias and statistical efficiency controlled by the regularization parameter and reveals how our proposed local Sinkhorn divergence loss function can be efficiently applied to learning multidimensional random field models. The proposed framework provides a scalable alternative to exact local optimal transport for conditional distribution reconstruction, offering a practical compromise between geometric fidelity, statistical efficiency, and computational scalability for uncertainty quantification and probabilistic scientific machine learning. Through various numerical examples, we compare our proposed local Sinkhorn divergence framework with other loss functions to train SNNs and with other machine-learning-based uncertainty quantification frameworks, demonstrating that the proposed local Sinkhorn divergence framework achieves an effective balance between reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency while maintaining good scalability for multidimensional stochastic systems.

</details>


### [151] [FM-LLM: A frequency-enhanced mixture-of-experts framework for adapting LLMs to time series forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11623)
*Rentao Gu,Yihang Ding,Junjie Li,Yi Ding,Weijing Sang,Xiaoli Huo,Xin Qin,Yuefeng Ji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FM-LLM is a prompt-free, frequency-aware autoregressive framework that adapts frozen LLMs to time-series forecasting by injecting Fourier-based spectral tokens directly into the model and using an asymmetric Mixture-of-Experts decoder, achieving state-of-the-art results across 11 benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based time-series forecasting methods rely heavily on textual prompts for modality alignment, causing nontrivial computational overhead and failing to exploit the rich spectral dynamics inherent in time-series data. The authors aim to enable prompt-free, frequency-aware adaptation of frozen LLMs.

Method: FM-LLM builds on constrained asymmetric coupling with three key components: (1) a Fourier Analysis Network (FAN)-based spectral token aligner that injects structured harmonic representations into the frozen LLM with numerical compatibility; (2) an asymmetric Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoder enforcing role separation, where shared experts with lightweight FAN layers reconstruct the global periodic backbone and routed experts restricted to standard FFNs specialize in non-periodic residual dynamics; and (3) a time-frequency hybrid loss function that jointly optimizes temporal accuracy and spectral consistency to mitigate error accumulation in long-horizon autoregressive rollouts.

Result: Across eleven public benchmarks, FM-LLM achieves state-of-the-art performance on 59 of 78 evaluation metrics. Compared to the strongest autoregressive LLM-based baseline, it delivers average improvements of 5.3% in MSE and 5.6% in MAE, with maximum gains of 8.0% (MSE) and 8.4% (MAE). It also shows robust transferability, maintaining superior performance in 10% few-shot and zero-shot forecasting.

Conclusion: FM-LLM demonstrates that prompt-free, frequency-aware adaptation of frozen LLMs is effective for time-series forecasting, delivering state-of-the-art accuracy and strong transferability while avoiding the computational overhead of textual prompt-based alignment.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have spurred cross-modal solutions for time-series forecasting. However, existing methods rely heavily on textual prompts for modality alignment-introducing nontrivial computational overhead and failing to leverage the rich spectral dynamics inherent in time-series data. To enable prompt-free, frequency-aware adaptation of frozen LLMs, we propose FM-LLM (Frequency-Enhanced Mixture-of-Experts for adapting LLMs to Time Series Forecasting), an autoregressive framework grounded in constrained asymmetric coupling. A Fourier Analysis Network (FAN)-based spectral token aligner injects structured harmonic representations directly into the frozen LLM with numerical compatibility. An asymmetric Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoder enforces role separation: shared experts with lightweight FAN layers reconstruct the global periodic backbone, while routed experts-restricted to standard FFNs-specialize in modeling non-periodic residual dynamics. A time-frequency hybrid loss function jointly optimizes temporal accuracy and spectral consistency, mitigating error accumulation during long-horizon autoregressive rollouts. Evaluated across eleven public benchmarks, FM-LLM achieves state-of-the-art performance on 59 out of 78 evaluation metrics. Compared to the strongest autoregressive LLM-based baseline, it delivers average improvements of 5.3% in MSE and 5.6% in MAE, with maximum gains reaching 8.0% for MSE and 8.4% for MAE. FM-LLM also demonstrates robust transferability, maintaining superior performance in 10% few-shot and zero-shot forecasting scenarios.

</details>


### [152] [Transferable Above-Ground Biomass (AGB) Estimation Model from Multi-Sensor Data with Sparse Field Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11638)
*Pann Thinzar Seint,Bryan Atwood,Subas Chhatkuli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A globally trained CNN is adapted to local landscapes via a lightweight field-calibration (scale-and-bias correction plus Random Forest fine-tuning) to produce spatially continuous forest above-ground biomass maps, outperforming the global baseline and ESA CCI Biomass against field plots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Field inventories are accurate but spatially sparse, while GEDI spaceborne LiDAR offers broad biomass samples but lacks spatial continuity and systematically underestimates high-biomass forests. The need is for credible, spatially continuous AGB quantification that avoids retraining a model for every new landscape.

Method: A single globally trained CNN ingests Sentinel-2 optical, Sentinel-1 C-band SAR, ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 L-band SAR, and DEM terrain data on a harmonized 10 m grid, using vegetation indices, polarimetric ratios, per-band normalization, and a hybrid log-domain SmoothL1 with RMSE loss for skewed biomass. It is trained once against multi-region, wet- and dry-season GEDI Level-4A data to learn persistent woody structure. Local adaptation uses a few field plots to fit a scale-and-bias correction followed by Random Forest fine-tuning with 10-fold cross-validation, avoiding full retraining per landscape.

Result: Held-out validation of the global GEDI-based model achieved R² ≈ 0.78 and RMSE ≈ 22 Mg/ha. Field calibration improved local validation to R² ≈ 0.82 and RMSE ≈ 15 Mg/ha, outperforming both the uncalibrated global model and the ESA CCI Biomass product against field plots.

Conclusion: Combining a globally trained deep CNN with a lightweight empirical field-calibration workflow yields spatially continuous, locally accurate AGB estimates that correct regional bias and GEDI's high-biomass underestimation, making carbon accounting more credible and mitigation strategies more actionable.

Abstract: Spatially continuous quantification of forest above-ground biomass (AGB) is what makes carbon accounting credible and mitigation strategies actionable. While field inventories provide high localized accuracy, they are spatially sparse; conversely, spaceborne LiDAR from the Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) offers broad biomass samples but lacks spatial continuity and systematic underestimation of high-biomass forests. This paper presents an operational framework centered on a single globally trained convolutional neural network (CNN) that is seamlessly adapted to each new landscape through a lightweight empirical field-calibration workflow. The global model combines optical (Sentinel-2), C-band SAR (Sentinel-1), L-band SAR (ALOS-2 PALSAR-2), and terrain (DEM) data. It is trained once against GEDI Level-4A biomass reference data spanning multiple regions and both wet and dry seasons so that it learns the persistent woody-structure rather than a single-date appearance. To avoid retraining for every landscape, the framework applies a small number of local field plots to fit a scale-and-bias correction that aligns the global prediction with ground truth in each region. The pipeline harmonizes sensor data onto a shared 10 m grid, derives vegetation indices and polarimetric ratios, computes per-band normalization stats, and trains the CNN with a hybrid log-domain SmoothL1 with RMSE loss for skewed biomass distribution. On held-out validation the global GEDI-based model achieved R^2 approximately 0.78 and RMSE approximately 22 Mg/ha. A subsequent field calibration combining Random Forest fine-tuning under a 10-fold cross-validation eliminates localized regional biases. This improves local validation performance to R^2 approximately 0.82 and reduces RMSE to approximately 15 Mg/ha, outperforming both the uncalibrated global model and the ESA CCI Biomass product against field plots.

</details>


### [153] [Towards a Formal Definition of Agent Memory: Basis, Span, Optimality, and the Sequential Memory Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11654)
*Hongyao Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper formalizes agent memory: memory is a basis, knowledge is its span, and answerability is a coverage problem. It defines optimal memory as a capacity-constrained maximizer of expected coverage, yielding a utility–capacity frontier for comparing memory systems; it then models noise, continual memory via a sequential MDP, and instantiates the framework on Homer's Odyssey.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite widespread use of memory in large-model agents, there is no unified formal account of what memory is or when it is optimal, making it impossible to rigorously compare or reason about memory systems. The paper aims to provide this formal foundation and turn open problems into concrete research questions.

Method: The authors define a formal framework where events are extracted from a material, a generation operator maps any event set to the knowledge it entails (its span), and a query is answerable iff some single item in the span covers it. Optimal memory is the capacity-constrained maximizer of expected coverage, with its value tracing a utility–capacity frontier. They extend this to noise (coverage vs. precision, requiring the write policy to infer truth) and formalize continual agent-memory as a sequential MDP where memory is the state, writing is the action, and query-time utility is the delayed reward. They instantiate the framework on Homer's Odyssey and map existing systems onto it.

Result: The framework yields concrete metrics from the Odyssey test case: the utility–capacity frontier, a compression zone, and the divergence between coverage and precision under noise. It also positions existing memory systems within the framework, making "how good is a memory" measurable.

Conclusion: The paper establishes memory as a coverage problem over a span, with optimality defined by a utility–capacity frontier, and recasts the open problems of constructing and learning agent memory as concrete, measurable research questions, setting a foundation for principled memory system design and comparison.

Abstract: Despite the wide deployment of memory in large-model agents, there is no unified formal account of what a memory is or when it is optimal. This paper takes a first step toward this account. The central idea is that memory is a basis, knowledge is its span, and answerability is a coverage problem: an agent stores events extracted from a material; a generation operator turns any event set into the knowledge it entails; and a query is answerable exactly when some single item in the span covers it. The optimal memory is then the capacity-constrained maximizer of expected coverage, and its value traces a utility--capacity frontier, the common yardstick on which memory systems can be compared. Next, we consider noise in the memory and discuss coverage versus precision under it: a memory may store false claims, so the write policy must infer the truth of what it stores. Drawing an analogy with biological memory, which is formed continuously through ongoing experience, we formalize the continual agent-memory problem in a sequential MDP that covers multiple levels, where memory is the state, writing is the action, and the utility settled at query time is the delayed reward that drives learning. To make the framework concrete, we instantiate it on Homer's \emph{Odyssey}, turning the frontier, the compression zone, and the divergence of coverage from precision into concrete numbers. Finally, we position existing systems within the framework, making ``how good is a memory'' measurable and recasting the open problems of constructing and learning agent memory as concrete research questions.

</details>


### [154] [Continuous-Latent Predictive Modeling with Semantic Alignment for EEG-Language Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11656)
*Myeong-Ju Cho,Hye-Bin Shin,Seo-Hyun Lee,Seong-Whan Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BLPM is an EEG-language foundation model that reframes heterogeneous EEG decoding as continuous semantic embedding prediction, using a CELP encoder and MQSD module to align EEG with text semantics, achieving strong generalization across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dominant EEG pretraining paradigms are limited: masked autoencoding focuses on low-level signal reconstruction rather than task-relevant semantics, and autoregressive modeling mismatches continuous neural dynamics with discrete token spaces. New strategies are needed to align continuous EEG representations with natural-language semantics and integrate them with large language models.

Method: BLPM reformulates heterogeneous EEG decoding tasks as a continuous semantic embedding prediction problem. It introduces a Continuous EEG Latent Predictive (CELP) encoder that learns transferable representations via latent target prediction. A Multi-Query Semantic Decomposition (MQSD) module then extracts task-relevant information and aligns continuous EEG representations with textual semantics in a shared latent space based on semantic relationships.

Result: Experiments across multiple benchmarks show consistent generalization performance across diverse tasks, validating continuous latent semantic prediction as an effective paradigm for EEG-language foundation models.

Conclusion: Continuous latent semantic prediction is established as an effective paradigm for EEG-language foundation models, addressing the limitations of masked autoencoding and autoregressive pretraining by aligning continuous EEG representations with natural-language semantics.

Abstract: Recent advances in EEG foundation models have demonstrated the potential of large-scale pretraining to enable generalizable neural decoding across subjects, recording environments, and datasets. However, dominant pretraining paradigms face key challenges: masked autoencoding tends to prioritize low-level signal reconstruction over task-relevant semantics, while autoregressive modeling creates a mismatch between continuous neural dynamics and discrete token spaces. To address these challenges, new strategies are needed to effectively align continuous EEG representations with natural-language semantics and enable their integration with large language models. Accordingly, we propose Brain Latent Predictive Model (BLPM), an EEG-language foundation model that reformulates heterogeneous EEG decoding tasks as a continuous semantic embedding prediction problem. BLPM introduces a Continuous EEG Latent Predictive (CELP) encoder that learns transferable representations through latent target prediction. Building on these representations, a Multi-Query Semantic Decomposition (MQSD) module extracts task-relevant information and aligns continuous EEG representations with textual semantics within a shared latent space according to their semantic relationships. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent generalization performance across diverse tasks, establishing continuous latent semantic prediction as an effective paradigm for EEG-language foundation models.

</details>


### [155] [Low-Interaction-Rank Learning: Unifying Multiplicative Dual-Encoder Heads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11661)
*Zijian Zhao,Sen Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper develops a unified theory for multiplicative dual-encoder networks (functions computed as inner products of two separate encodings). It introduces the class of functions of low interaction rank, whose complexity is captured by an interaction spectrum. This framework gives guidance on design choices (number of modes, encoder normalization, when to avoid the architecture), decomposes approximation error into spectral truncation and encoder-realization terms, characterizes sample complexity by the sum of encoder complexities, and exposes a linear gauge symmetry that makes raw encodings unidentifiable — showing that normalization is gauge fixing and whitening recovers modes up to permutation/sign. Experiments on synthetic kernels, operator learning, and CLIP validate the theory and show whitening reveals interpretable concept axes and a single rotation relating independently trained CLIP models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multiplicative dual-encoder networks appear independently across operator learning, bipartite matching, contrastive vision-language models, and retrieval, but no unified theory guides basic design decisions such as how many interaction modes to represent, how to normalize encoders, and when the architecture should be avoided. The authors aim to supply that missing theoretical foundation and to explain/repair the uninterpretability of contrastive embedding dimensions caused by gauge symmetry.

Method: The paper introduces the class of low-interaction-rank functions with an interaction spectrum as an intrinsic complexity measure. It analyzes approximation error as a spectral truncation term plus an encoder-realization term, and sample complexity as governed by the sum of the two encoder complexities rather than their product. It proposes a usability criterion based on spectral decay to decide when the architecture can succeed. It formalizes encoder non-uniqueness as a linear gauge symmetry and interprets normalization as gauge fixing; whitening is proposed to pin interaction modes up to permutation and sign, providing a constructive remedy for interpretability.

Result: Experiments on synthetic kernels, operator learning, and CLIP models validate the theoretical predictions: spectral decay rates match predicted scaling, whitening recovers the true interaction modes, and independently trained CLIP models are related by a single rotation; after removing this rotation via whitening, interpretable concept axes are exposed.

Conclusion: The unified interaction-rank framework resolves key design questions for multiplicative dual-encoder networks, explains the uninterpretability of contrastive dimensions as a gauge-symmetry artifact, and shows that whitening provides a constructive remedy, yielding interpretable concept axes in CLIP.

Abstract: A multiplicative dual-encoder network computes a real-valued output for a pair of inputs as the inner product of their separate encodings. This architecture has been developed independently in operator learning, bipartite matching, contrastive vision-language models, retrieval, and other areas, yet no unified theory guides the basic design decisions: how many interaction modes to represent, how to normalize the encoders, and when the architecture should be avoided. We provide such a foundation by introducing the class of functions of low interaction rank, a class whose intrinsic complexity is measured by its interaction spectrum. Within this framework, approximation error decomposes into a spectral truncation term and an encoder-realization term; sample complexity is governed by the sum of the two encoder complexities rather than their product; and a usability criterion based on spectral decay determines when the architecture can succeed. The same framework exposes a central identifiability problem: the encoders are defined only up to a linear gauge symmetry that leaves the learned coordinates arbitrary. We show that normalization is gauge fixing and that whitening pins the interaction modes up to permutation and sign, thereby explaining the uninterpretability of contrastive dimensions and providing a constructive remedy. Experiments on synthetic kernels, operator learning, and CLIP models validate the theoretical predictions: spectral decay rates match the predicted scaling, whitening recovers the true modes, and independently trained CLIP models are related by a single rotation which, after removal by whitening, exposes interpretable concept axes. The code of this paper is provided at https://github.com/RS2002/Mul-Net .

</details>


### [156] [Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-as-Reward RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11669)
*Minglai Yang,Xinyu Guo,Utkarsh Tyagi,Mian Zhang,Razvan Dumitru,Sunjie Hou,Yunzhong He,Daniel Yue Zhang,Ying Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GRPO-trained language models learn to exploit rubric-based LLM judges (reward hacking), causing out-of-distribution gold performance to peak then decline; the author introduces Rubric Dropout—randomly dropping rubric criteria each training step—which improves OOD scores and reduces hacking metrics at no domain cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rubrics used by LLM judges are fixed, imperfect proxies for quality, so a policy trained against them long enough will learn to exploit their gaps rather than genuinely improve quality. The work aims to quantify this reward hacking and find a simple intervention to mitigate it.

Method: Train Qwen3-8B with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on medical and science rubrics; measure divergence between the training judge's score and a stronger gold judge's score on out-of-distribution benchmarks (HealthBench-Hard, ResearchQA). Propose Rubric Dropout: at each step, randomly drop a subset of rubric criteria before computing the reward (shared across each rollout group to preserve group-relative advantages; full rubric always used at evaluation). Compare no dropout against 30% and 50% dropout, sweep the dropout fraction, and test reweighting criteria by training usefulness as an alternative.

Result: The training and gold judges' scores diverge during training: the training score keeps climbing while the gold score peaks then falls (down 3 points on HealthBench-Hard, 22 points on ResearchQA), indicating reward hacking rather than judge noise. Rubric Dropout raises the OOD gold score at every matched checkpoint (+1 to +2 on HealthBench-Hard, +6 to +7 on ResearchQA), lowers the two hacking measures, and costs nothing in-domain. A 30-50% dropout fraction is a broad sweet spot, while criterion reweighting performs worse than no intervention.

Conclusion: Rubric-based RL is vulnerable to reward hacking that inflates training scores while degrading true quality, and Rubric Dropout—a simple, one-line fix—effectively mitigates this by preventing the policy from over-optimizing the same fixed rubric, improving generalization at no training cost.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning against rubrics, lists of criteria graded by an LLM judge, has become a standard way to post-train language models on tasks with no deterministic answer. The rubric, however, is a fixed proxy for quality, never a complete description of it, and a policy trained against it long enough will learn to exploit the difference. We measure this directly. Training Qwen3-8B with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on medical and science rubrics and grading out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks with both the training judge and a stronger gold judge, we find that the two scores diverge during training. The training judge's score keeps climbing while the gold judge's score peaks and then falls, by 3 points on HealthBench-Hard and by 22 points on ResearchQA. A judge with a fixed bias would shift the gold curve by a constant, not send it down while the training score rises, so the divergence is reward hacking, not judge noise. We propose Rubric Dropout, a one-line fix borrowed from neuron dropout. At every step, we randomly drop a subset of the rubric's criteria before computing the reward, so the policy never optimizes the same rubric twice. The dropped subset is shared across each rollout group, so GRPO's group-relative advantages stay comparable, and evaluation always uses the full rubric. Comparing no dropout against dropout at 30% and 50% on both benchmark pairs, dropout raises the OOD gold score at every matched checkpoint (+1 to +2 points on HealthBench-Hard, +6 to +7 points on ResearchQA), lowers the two hacking measures we track, and costs nothing in domain. Sweeping the dropout fraction shows a broad 30-50% sweet spot, while the natural alternative, reweighting criteria by how useful they are to training, performs worse than no intervention at all in our setting.

</details>


### [157] [GCPO: Diagnosing and Constraining Subspace Geometry in Rollout RL for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11674)
*Kai Yang,Jingwei Xu,Wanyu Wang,Kai-Yuan Guo,Zhenbo Yu,Yi Wang,Yu Qiao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Principal-Subspace Overlap, a diagnostic revealing that transient spikes in the overlap between individual rollout updates and the pretrained weights' dominant singular subspaces precede performance degradation. It proposes GCPO, a method applying hard bilateral orthogonal projections to constrain updates to complementary subspaces, improving stability and performance over GRPO and variants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy rollout methods like GRPO suffer from training instability, cross-task capability degradation, and response-length inflation. Prior work explored aggregate update geometry, but the stepwise variation of this geometry and its link to performance remained unclear, motivating a finer-grained geometric analysis and a principled remedy.

Method: The authors introduce Principal-Subspace Overlap, a dimension-corrected measure of each rollout update relative to the dominant singular subspaces of the pretrained weights, showing transient spikes precede degradation. They then propose GCPO (Geometrically Constrained Policy Optimization), which imposes hard bilateral orthogonal projections to constrain updates to the complementary subspaces, preventing harmful excursions by construction.

Result: GCPO consistently outperforms GRPO and recent variants (DAPO, GSPO) across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and tool-use tasks on Qwen3-8B and GLM4-9B, improving over base models by up to 27.69 points and over the strongest baseline by up to 2.37 points. It also preserves general capabilities, eliminates response-length inflation, and stabilizes policy entropy.

Conclusion: The findings provide a new diagnostic lens and a principled design perspective for stable reinforcement learning post-training, showing that geometrically constraining updates to complementary subspaces yields more stable and higher-performing policy optimization.

Abstract: On-policy rollout methods such as GRPO are central to post-training of large language models, yet they frequently suffer from training instabilities, cross-task capability degradation, and response-length inflation. Although prior work has characterized the subspace geometry of aggregate updates, the stepwise variation of this geometry and its relationship to model performance remain unclear. We introduce Principal-Subspace Overlap, a dimension-corrected measure of individual rollout updates relative to the dominant singular subspaces of pretrained weights. Despite low average overlap, transient spikes often precede performance degradation. To address this, we propose GCPO (Geometrically Constrained Policy Optimization), which applies hard bilateral orthogonal projections to constrain updates to the complementary subspaces, preventing such excursions by construction. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and tool-use tasks on Qwen3-8B and GLM4-9B, GCPO consistently outperforms GRPO and recent variants, including DAPO and GSPO, improving over the base models and the strongest baseline by up to 27.69 and 2.37 points, respectively. Furthermore, GCPO preserves general capabilities, eliminates response-length inflation, and stabilizes policy entropy. Our findings provide a new diagnostic lens and a principled design perspective for stable reinforcement learning post-training.

</details>


### [158] [Drift and Dependence: Layer-wise Information-Theoretic Bounds for Replay-Based Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11690)
*Tieliang Gong,Zhongbo Zhang,Wen Wen,Yong-Jin Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops a layer-wise information-theoretic framework for continual-learning replay that separates the generalization effects of (1) replacing past distributions with finite empirical samples and (2) the shared optimization trajectory coupling buffer, current data, and final hypothesis. The framework yields a depth-dependent drift–sensitivity trade-off identifying which interior layer to stabilize, and an SGLD-based curvature-aware gradient-alignment statistic usable as an online forgetting diagnostic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing analyses of replay in continual learning fold two coupled generalization effects into a single hypothesis-level quantity: finite memory turning each past distribution into an empirical proxy, and repeated reuse coupling the buffer, current data, and hypothesis through a shared optimization trajectory. The authors seek to disentangle these effects at every network depth and make them operationally usable (optimal layer stabilization and online forgetting diagnostics).

Method: A layer-wise information-theoretic framework decomposes the expected generalization gap into a replay-induced representation drift term and an optimization-dependence term; the latter is separated into stability, plasticity, interaction, and residual-coupling components. Two refinements operationalize it: (1) a Wasserstein relaxation of the drift term (valid under support mismatch) giving a depth-dependent drift–sensitivity trade-off whose minimizer selects the interior layer to stabilize; (2) an SGLD instantiation reducing the optimization term to a trajectory-level log-determinant budget, exposing a curvature-aware gradient-alignment statistic as an online task-wise forgetting diagnostic.

Result: Controlled and benchmark experiments confirm the predicted memory scaling, the existence of an "interior funnel" (a specific interior layer whose stabilization minimizes the drift–sensitivity trade-off), and the link between the alignment signal and task-wise forgetting.

Conclusion: Separating representation drift from optimization-dependence at each layer, and operationalizing them via a Wasserstein drift–sensitivity minimizer and an SGLD log-determinant alignment statistic, provides a principled, depth-aware understanding of replay generalization in continual learning, with practical guidance on which layers to stabilize and how to monitor forgetting online.

Abstract: Continual learning must absorb new tasks without erasing old ones, and replay---mixing a small buffer of past examples into current training---is among the most effective remedies for catastrophic forgetting. Yet its generalization behavior is shaped by two coupled effects that existing analyses fold into a single hypothesis-level quantity: finite memory replaces each past distribution with an empirical proxy, and repeated reuse couples the buffer, the current data, and the final hypothesis through a shared optimization trajectory. We develop a layer-wise information-theoretic framework that separates these effects at every depth. Our main result decomposes the expected generalization gap into a replay-induced representation drift and an optimization-dependence term, the latter further resolved into stability, plasticity, interaction, and residual-coupling components. Two refinements make the framework operational. A Wasserstein relaxation of the drift term, valid under support mismatch, yields a depth-dependent drift--sensitivity trade-off whose minimizer identifies which interior layer to stabilize. An SGLD instantiation of the optimization term reduces it to a trajectory-level log-determinant budget, exposing a curvature-aware gradient-alignment statistic that serves as an online diagnostic of task-wise forgetting. Controlled and benchmark experiments confirm the predicted memory scaling, the interior funnel, and the alignment signal's link to forgetting.

</details>


### [159] [LEMUR: Latent Entropy-aware Multimodal Unlearning via Visual-anchored Reasoning Redirection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11691)
*Xinhao Zhong,Yuxia Qiao,Junhao Li,Hao Fang,Yi Sun,Bin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RL post-training improves visual reasoning in multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) but creates a privacy vulnerability: sensitive facts unlearned from final answers can still leak in the chain-of-thought reasoning traces. The authors propose LEMUR, a training-free, inference-time unlearning framework that uses RL-induced token entropy dynamics to detect and sanitize sensitive reasoning without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing unlearning methods are designed to remove sensitive content from final answers, but they fail to address leakage in reasoning traces. The authors discover that natively RL-trained MLRMs leak unlearned sensitive facts in their CoT more prominently than base models, and that this leakage has a distinctive token-level entropy signature. This motivates a privacy-aware unlearning method targeting reasoning traces specifically.

Method: LEMUR is a fully training-free, inference-time unlearning framework. It exploits RL-induced entropy dynamics as a control signal to detect when sensitive reasoning starts and when sanitization should stop. During the identified interval, it redirects the reasoning trajectory via entropy-modulated visual-anchor latent injection, replacing committed tokens with sanitized, probability-weighted embeddings re-grounded in the input image.

Result: Across diverse MLRMs, LEMUR consistently outperforms existing unlearning methods in suppressing both reasoning-trace and answer leakage, while better preserving non-sensitive utility and output fluency. Results confirm that RL-induced entropy dynamics provide a distinctive privacy leakage signal and that exploiting it enables effective training-free unlearning.

Conclusion: RL-induced entropy dynamics offer a reliable signal for detecting privacy leakage in reasoning-capable multimodal models. Exploiting this signal through LEMUR enables effective training-free unlearning that suppresses sensitive content in both reasoning traces and final answers while maintaining utility and fluency.

Abstract: Reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training equips multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) with exploratory chains of thought (CoT), substantially improving visual reasoning. However, we find that this capability introduces a distinct privacy vulnerability: even when a sensitive fact is successfully unlearned from the final answer, the model may still reproduce it in its reasoning trace. This leakage is substantially more pronounced in natively RL-trained MLRMs than in their non -reasoning base models, revealing a privacy risk that existing unlearning methods are not designed to address. We show that RL-induced exploration leaves sensitive content with a distinctive token-level entropy signature that is largely absent from base models. Based on this observation, we propose LEMUR, a fully training-free, inference-time unlearning framework for natively RL-trained multimodal models. LEMUR uses entropy dynamics as a control signal to identify when sensitive reasoning begins and when sanitization should stop. During this interval, it redirects the reasoning trajectory through entropy-modulated visual-anchor latent injection, replacing committed tokens with sanitized, probability-weighted embeddings re-grounded in the input image. Across diverse MLRMs, LEMUR consistently outperforms existing unlearning met hods in suppressing both reasoning-trace and answer leakage, while better preserving non-sensitive utility and output fluency. These results demonstrate that RL-induced entropy dynamics provide a distinctive signal for privacy leakage and that exploiting this signal enables effective training-free unlearning for reasoning-capable multimodal models.

</details>


### [160] [REOPD: Reliability-Adaptive Reward Extrapolation for On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11698)
*Yang Sun,Lichao Ma,Houyuan Qin,Yuxin Liu,Hanyang Lu,Yao Zhu,Pinlong Cai,Guohang Yan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: REOPD is a reliability-adaptive reward extrapolation framework for on-policy distillation that replaces a single global extrapolation coefficient with a token-wise coefficient (λ_b,t = 1 + γ_b q_t), combining token-level compatibility weights and a batch-level adaptive budget to avoid reward hacking and unstable training without requiring extra rollout or any reward/value models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) relies on dense token-level supervision from a teacher, and reward-extrapolation methods like ExOPD amplify the teacher-reference log-likelihood ratio using a single global coefficient λ applied uniformly to every token. This uniform scaling can drive the student to overfit extreme peaks in the implicit reward, causing reward hacking and training instability. Additionally, the optimal λ varies across domains, requiring expensive hyperparameter sweeps. REOPD aims to address these issues by making extrapolation adapt per token and per batch based on reliability.

Method: REOPD combines a token-level compatibility weight q_t with a batch-level adaptive budget γ_b to produce a token-wise extrapolation coefficient λ_b,t = 1 + γ_b q_t. It selectively extrapolates along teacher-reference directions only where they are deemed reliable, preserving teacher alignment elsewhere. The method requires no verifier, reward model, value model, or additional rollouts beyond standard OPD.

Result: REOPD outperforms G-OPD on single-teacher mathematics tasks and on both domains in the multi-teacher setting, while matching G-OPD on single-teacher code. This demonstrates effective fine-grained reliability adaptation across domains and teacher configurations.

Conclusion: REOPD provides an effective reliability-adaptive reward extrapolation approach that mitigates reward hacking and unstable training in OPD by adapting the extrapolation coefficient token-wise and batch-wise, achieving strong or matching performance relative to G-OPD across mathematics and code domains and single/multi-teacher settings without extra computational overhead.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own trajectories under dense token-level supervision from a teacher. Reward-extrapolation methods such as ExOPD amplify the teacher-reference log-likelihood ratio to move beyond direct imitation, but apply a single global coefficient $λ$ to every token. This can drive the student to fit extreme peaks in the implicit reward, causing reward hacking and unstable training, and the optimal $λ$ varies across domains, requiring costly sweeps. We propose REOPD, a reliability-adaptive reward extrapolation framework for OPD. REOPD combines a token-level compatibility weight with a batch-level adaptive budget, yielding a token-wise coefficient $λ_{b,t}=1+γ_b q_t$ that preserves teacher alignment while selectively extrapolating along reliable teacher-reference directions. It requires no verifier, reward model, value model, or extra rollout beyond standard OPD. REOPD outperforms G-OPD on single-teacher mathematics and on both domains in the multi-teacher setting, while matching G-OPD on single-teacher code, demonstrating effective fine-grained reliability adaptation across domains and teacher configurations.

</details>


### [161] [Consolidator: Learning Persistent Routed Memory Across Context Boundaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11701)
*Sungwoo Goo,Hwi-yeol Yun,Sangkeun Jung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper distinguishes persistent memory content from memory that actually gates later retrieval. It shows that a small learned Consolidator operator in a Phasor Memory Network, which compresses short-term memory into long-term memory without replay, must both store retrievable content and condition the router controlling which memory slots future inputs access. Training only 12.35K parameters (0.041% of the model) raises updated-mapping recall from 44.38% to 87.02%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Merely copying short-term memory (STM) into a slower store preserves state across context boundaries, but persistence is not sufficient: the retained state must also be able to influence subsequent memory access. The paper aims to test this distinction between stored content and access-conditioning, and whether learned consolidation can recover updated mappings after resets.

Method: Uses a Phasor Memory Network (PMNet) with a Consolidator, a shared slot-local operator that transforms routed STM before accumulating it into long-term memory (LTM) without replaying source tokens. After each consolidation the KV cache and STM are cleared; the retained LTM remains readable and is fed into the hierarchical router to condition which explicit-memory slots subsequent inputs access. Evaluated on a two-segment modulo-10 mapping task where the second segment updates the mapping at the same memory address, followed by a second consolidation/reset and a held-out query that must recover the updated mapping. The backbone and memory interface are frozen; only 12.35K Consolidator parameters are trainable (0.041% of a 29.95M model), with five paired runs from the same STM-pretraining checkpoint, training separate Consolidators while retaining the same LTM read paths.

Result: Direct LTM routing raises updated-mapping recall from 44.38±1.94% to 87.02±1.76% (+42.64±1.10 pts), while immediate STM recall stays at 89.90% in both conditions. Learned consolidation beats forced identity accumulation by 21.40±1.91 pts without routing and 68.70±1.76 pts with routing.

Conclusion: Consolidated LTM acts as both retrievable content and an access state that shapes subsequent slot selection, demonstrating that persistence alone is insufficient — the retained state must also influence memory access to be useful.

Abstract: Copying short-term memory (STM) into a slower store can preserve state across a context boundary, but persistence alone does not ensure that the retained state influences subsequent memory access. We test this distinction in a Phasor Memory Network (PMNet) using Consolidator, a shared slot-local operator that transforms routed STM before accumulating it into long-term memory (LTM), without replaying the source tokens. After each consolidation, the KV cache and STM are cleared. The retained LTM can still be read and is also fed into the hierarchical router, thereby conditioning which explicit-memory slots subsequent inputs access. We evaluate this mechanism on a two-segment modulo-10 mapping task in which the second segment updates the mapping at the same memory address. Following a second consolidation and reset, a held-out query must recover the updated mapping from LTM. The backbone and memory interface are frozen, leaving only 12.35K Consolidator parameters trainable (0.041\% of a 29.95M model). Across five paired runs from the same STM-pretraining checkpoint, direct LTM routing raises updated-mapping recall from $44.38\pm1.94\%$ to $87.02\pm1.76\%$ ($+42.64\pm1.10$ percentage points), while immediate STM recall remains 89.90\% in both conditions; both train separate Consolidators and retain the same LTM read paths. Learned consolidation outperforms forced identity accumulation by $21.40\pm1.91$ percentage points without routing and $68.70\pm1.76$ with routing. Thus, on this task, consolidated LTM serves as both retrievable content and an access state that shapes subsequent slot selection.

</details>


### [162] [Robust and Efficient Noisy-Label Time-Series Classification via Dynamic Time Warping Based Granular Ball Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11704)
*Ziqiang Li,Yun Liu,Gouhei Tanaka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DTW-GBC groups temporally similar training samples into granular balls for granule-level classification, reducing label-noise sensitivity and cutting inference-time DTW computations versus DTW-based 1-NN.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DTW-based Nearest-Neighbor classifiers are effective for time-series classification but suffer from two weaknesses: vulnerability to mislabeled training samples and high computational cost from numerous DTW comparisons during inference. The authors aim to address both problems simultaneously.

Method: The paper proposes DTW-based Granular Ball Computing (DTW-GBC), which organizes temporally similar training samples into granular balls and performs classification at the granule level rather than on individual samples. Two granular-ball construction strategies are developed for DTW-GBC. Evaluation uses four benchmark datasets injected with symmetric label noise.

Result: Experiments show both DTW-GBC variants generally mitigate the performance degradation caused by label noise while requiring substantially fewer comparisons than DTW-based 1-NN during inference.

Conclusion: DTW-GBC offers a favorable balance between classification robustness (resistance to label noise) and inference efficiency, making it a promising alternative to DTW-based 1-NN.

Abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)-based Nearest-Neighbor (NN) classifiers are effective for time-series classification but are vulnerable to mislabeled training samples and require numerous DTW computations during inference. We propose DTW-based Granular Ball Computing (DTW-GBC), which organizes temporally similar training samples into granular balls and performs classification at the granule level. We further develop two granular-ball construction strategies for DTW-GBC. Experiments on four benchmark datasets with symmetric label noise show that the two DTW-GBC variants generally mitigate the performance degradation caused by label noise while requiring substantially fewer comparisons than DTW-based 1-NN during inference. These findings suggest that DTW-GBC provides a favorable balance between classification robustness and inference efficiency.

</details>


### [163] [High-dimensional Multi-objective Bayesian Optimization with Learned Variable Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11713)
*Hongyan Wang,Jiayu Huang,Haotian Zheng,Xin Gao,Chi Ding,Ying Liu,Xia Wang,Qing Xu,Keqiang Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ViaMOBO is a multi-objective Bayesian optimization framework that uses decision variable interaction analysis to decompose high-dimensional decision spaces into subspaces, enabling local BO and improving Pareto front approximation for expensive black-box problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) methods struggle with high-dimensional decision spaces due to exponential sampling complexity, limiting their applicability. The authors aim to overcome this scalability bottleneck without strong assumptions about problem structure.

Method: ViaMOBO employs a variable interaction analysis model to detect whether the decision space is separable, partially separable, or non-separable based on independent/interdependent relationships among variables. It then (completely or partially) partitions the decision space and performs local Bayesian optimization within the resulting subspaces.

Result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show ViaMOBO outperforms state-of-the-art MOBO baselines in approximating the Pareto front of high-dimensional expensive multi-objective problems.

Conclusion: ViaMOBO effectively addresses the high-dimensional scalability problem in expensive MOBO by leveraging variable interaction analysis for space decomposition, achieving superior Pareto front approximation compared to existing MOBO methods.

Abstract: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) is effective in identifying the Pareto fronts for expensive black-box problems. However, most current MOBO approaches are limited to low-dimensional decision space due to its exponential sampling complexity. This paper presents decision variable interaction analysis-based MOBO, ViaMOBO, a generic framework for expensive multi-objective problems with high-dimensional decision space. The key idea of ViaMOBO is that it utilizes a variable interaction analysis model to determine whether the decision space can be completely or partially divided, and then performs local Bayesian optimization in the divided decision subspaces. Through the variable analysis model, it can be derived whether the objectives in black-box problems are separable, partially separable, or non-separable based on the potential independent or interdependent relationships among decision variables without any strong assumptions. We compare ViaMOBO with the state-of-the-art MOBO methods on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks. The experimental results demonstrate that ViaMOBO outperforms other related MOBO baselines in approximating the Pareto front of high-dimensional expensive multi-objective problems.

</details>


### [164] [Chain-of-Thought Shows the Path to a Tree: Realizing Branching Complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11716)
*Debanjan Dutta,Anish Chakrabarty,Swagatam Das*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper gives explicit, depth-bounded Chain-of-Thought (CoT) constructions for graph traversal algorithms, using at most 2-layer hard-attention decoders to implement DFS and Dijkstra (subsuming BFS). These decoders are reused as a shared substrate to compute the Strahler number (4 layers, 2n−1 steps) and tree width (3 layers, n−1 steps) of n-vertex trees, providing a concrete witness for the linear-step regime of the CoT circuit hierarchy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CoT is known to lift the expressive power of bounded-depth Transformers, and characterizations tie the number of CoT steps to circuit complexity classes. However, concrete instantiations with explicit depth-bounded constructions—and the traversal procedures these characterizations presuppose—are largely missing. The authors aim to close this gap for branching complexity.

Method: The authors construct unique hard-attention Transformer decoders of at most two layers that realize depth-first search (DFS) and Dijkstra's algorithm (which subsumes breadth-first search). They reuse these traversal decoders as a common computational substrate: the DFS decoder computes the Strahler number of an n-vertex tree in 2n−1 steps using four layers, and the Dijkstra decoder computes tree width in n−1 steps using three layers. The constructions handle arbitrary n-ary trees without layer normalization or positional encodings. They also exploit the classical bijection between ordered trees and Dyck paths (realized by the DFS construction, which emits the path as it traverses) to give independent constructions for both measures on the path representation.

Result: The paper provides explicit CoT realizations of DFS and Dijkstra/BFS via unique hard-attention decoders with at most two layers. Reusing them yields the Strahler number in 2n−1 steps with four layers and tree width in n−1 steps with three layers. Since computing the Strahler number of a binary tree given as a term is NC¹-complete, and the constructions handle arbitrary n-ary trees without layer normalization or positional encodings, these results constitute a non-trivial witness for the linear-step regime of the CoT hierarchy.

Conclusion: The work supplies concrete, depth-bounded CoT instantiations for graph traversal, closing the gap between circuit-complexity characterizations of CoT and explicit constructions. The shared-substrate reuse of DFS and Dijkstra decoders demonstrates how traversal procedures can serve as a computational foundation for branching measures, yielding non-trivial linear-step CoT witnesses (Strahler number and tree width) and independent constructions on Dyck path representations.

Abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) lifts the expressive ceiling of bounded-depth Transformers, with characterizations tying the number of CoT steps to circuit complexity classes. What remains largely missing are concrete instantiations with explicit, depth-bounded constructions, and the traversal procedures such characterizations presuppose. We close this gap for branching complexity. We give CoT realizations of depth-first search (DFS) and of Dijkstra algorithm, the latter subsuming breadth-first search, by unique hard-attention decoders of at most two layers, and use them as a shared computational substrate: reusing the DFS decoder yields the Strahler number of an $n$-vertex tree in $2n-1$ steps with four layers, and reusing the Dijkstra decoder yields its width in $n-1$ steps with three. Since computing the Strahler number of a binary tree given as a term is \textsf{NC\textsuperscript{1}}-complete, and our constructions handle arbitrary $n$-ary trees without layer normalization or positional encodings, this is a non-trivial witness for the linear-step regime of the CoT hierarchy. Exploiting the classical bijection between ordered trees and Dyck paths, itself realized by our DFS construction, which emits the path as it traverses, we give independent constructions for both measures on the path representation.

</details>


### [165] [Epiplexity Guided Data Selection and Generation for Out-of-Distribution Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11746)
*Ellen Su,Andres Potapczynski,Shikai Qiu,Edward Hughes,Andrew Gordon Wilson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper operationalizes "epiplexity" (a measure of structural information a compute-bounded learner can extract from data) as an online training signal for both data selection and synthetic data generation, showing that maximizing epiplexity improves downstream zero-shot and fine-tuning performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern systems increasingly need to transfer to tasks not seen during training. The authors hypothesize that data containing more structural information (shared circuits/subprograms) can be recycled across diverse downstream settings, and they seek a practical mechanism to leverage this via epiplexity.

Method: Two approaches: (1) For data selection, fit scaling laws to training loss curves of natural domains to predict expected epiplexity gain as a function of training tokens, then use this to adaptively set sampling weights over domains. (2) For synthetic data generation, define a generator's reward as the change in learner epiplexity over a buffer of previously generated data and use REINFORCE policy gradients to guide the generator toward an epiplexity-maximizing distribution.

Result: Higher epiplexity predicts improved downstream performance on both zero-shot and fine-tuning based tasks, supporting the hypothesis that data rich in structural information yield representations that transfer across domains.

Conclusion: Epiplexity can be operationalized as a practical online training signal, and data maximizing epiplexity improves cross-domain generalization, validating the structural-information hypothesis.

Abstract: Modern systems are increasingly expected to transfer across tasks not specified during training. What data facilitates generalization in these new, unanticipated settings? One hypothesis is that data with more structural information could contain shared circuits and subprograms that could be recycled in a wider array of downstream settings. Epiplexity, a recently proposed measure of the structural information a compute-bounded learner can extract from data, provides a mechanism to reason about this relationship. In this paper, we show how to operationalize epiplexity as an online training signal for data selection and synthetic data generation. For selection, we fit scaling laws to the training loss curves of natural data domains to predict the expected epiplexity gain as a function of training tokens, and use this signal to adaptively determine the sampling weights over domains during training. For synthetic data generation, we define a generator's reward as the change in learner epiplexity over a buffer of previously generated data and use REINFORCE policy gradients to guide the generator toward an epiplexity-maximizing distribution. In both cases, higher epiplexity predicts improved downstream performance on zero-shot and fine-tuning based tasks, supporting the hypothesis that data rich in structural information yield representations that transfer across domains.

</details>


### [166] [MOON: Multi-Objective OrthoNormalized Updates for Multitask Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11749)
*Shiji Zhou,Kunlin Lyu,Lei Zhang,Ruodong Wang,Yifan Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes MOON, a multi-objective optimization method that manipulates gradients under spectral–nuclear norm (matrix) geometry instead of Euclidean geometry, yielding orthonormalized parameter updates with improved optimization efficiency and multi-task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-objective multi-task learning methods flatten parameters into vectors and manipulate gradients under Euclidean geometry, ignoring the matrix structure common in Transformers. The authors show Euclidean gradient manipulation does not yield the steepest descent direction under matrix geometry, limiting optimization efficiency.

Method: MOON performs gradient manipulation under spectral–nuclear norm geometry and uses an orthonormalized manipulated gradient for parameter updates, drawing on steepest-descent theory for matrix-valued parameters.

Result: For smooth non-convex objectives, MOON achieves convergence of the averaged Pareto-stationarity measure at O(T^{-1/2}) (deterministic) and O(T^{-1/4}) (stochastic). Empirically, it consistently improves optimization efficiency and final multi-task performance across benchmarks.

Conclusion: Accounting for matrix structure via spectral–nuclear norm geometry and orthonormalized updates enables faster convergence and better multi-task performance than Euclidean-gradient-based MOO methods, with supporting theory and open-sourced code.

Abstract: Multi-objective optimization (MOO) has demonstrated significant success in multi-task learning by mitigating task conflicts through gradient manipulation. However, most existing methods flatten model parameters into vectors and perform gradient manipulation under Euclidean geometry, thereby overlooking the matrix structure prevalent in modern architectures such as Transformers. In this paper, we show that gradient manipulation in Euclidean space does not generally yield the steepest descent direction under matrix geometry, potentially limiting optimization efficiency. Drawing from the theory of steepest descent for matrix-valued parameters, we propose MOON (Multi-Objective OrthoNormalized Updates), which performs gradient manipulation under spectral--nuclear norm geometry and uses the orthonormalized manipulated gradient for parameter updates. Theoretically, for smooth non-convex objectives, we establish convergence of the averaged Pareto-stationarity measure at rates of $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting and $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/4})$ under stochastic gradients. Empirical results across various benchmarks show that MOON consistently improves both optimization efficiency and final multi-task performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/KunlinLyu/MOON.

</details>


### [167] [TradingMoE: Routing the Right Experts in Evolving Markets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11785)
*Chang Zhou,Xingtong Yu,Minbin Huang,Zhennan Wu,Yuan Fang,Hong Cheng,Xinming Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TradingMoE is a trading-oriented sparse Mixture-of-Experts that augments frozen LLMs with lightweight residual experts, using a Query-Key router and a sparse expert-selection update mechanism to adapt to changing market conditions, achieving large cumulative return gains over 22 baselines on stock and crypto markets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Direct LLM trading is challenging because needed predictive capabilities vary by asset, decision field, and market condition. Existing systems either hand-pick external experts or use internal MoE routers that fail to directly assess each expert's contribution to trading decisions and receive no signal when an inactive expert becomes suitable as conditions shift. The authors show native router scores poorly predict expert usefulness.

Method: TradingMoE augments a frozen dense LLM with lightweight residual experts. It introduces a Query-Key router that encodes each token's required expertise under current market context as a low-dimensional query, matched against learnable expert keys. It also proposes a sparse expert-selection update mechanism that, during training, samples a few inactive experts and estimates whether they should replace the weakest expert in the current Top-k route, enabling the router to adapt selection as market conditions change while keeping computation sparse.

Result: Against 22 baselines on stock and cryptocurrency markets, TradingMoE improves cumulative return over the best-performing baselines by 30.89% and 30.7%, respectively. Rolling paper-trading experiments confirm the advantage persists under forward-only deployment.

Conclusion: Native MoE routers poorly reflect expert usefulness, while token-specific expert usefulness has a compact low-dimensional structure. TradingMoE's Query-Key router and sparse expert-selection update mechanism effectively adapt to changing market conditions, producing substantial and persistent return improvements.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for financial analysis and trading, but direct trading remains challenging because the predictive capabilities required can vary across assets, decision fields, and market conditions. Existing LLM-based trading systems either coordinate human-defined external experts or adopt conventional internal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers that do not directly evaluate how individual experts contribute to trading decisions. Moreover, these routers receive no direct signal indicating when an inactive expert has become more suitable as market conditions change. We find that native router scores poorly reflect how much individual experts improve trading decisions, frequently leaving better alternatives unselected. We further reveal that token-specific expert usefulness exhibits a compact low-dimensional structure. Based on these findings, we propose TradingMoE, a trading-oriented sparse MoE that augments a frozen dense LLM with lightweight residual experts. We introduce a Query-Key router that represents the expertise required by each token under the current market context as a low-dimensional query and matches it with learnable expert keys. We further propose a sparse expert selection update mechanism that samples a few inactive experts during training and estimates whether they should replace the weakest expert in the current Top-k route. This mechanism enables the router to update expert selection as market conditions change while preserving sparse computation. Experiments against 22 baselines on stock and cryptocurrency markets show that TradingMoE improves cumulative return over the best-performing baselines by 30.89% and 30.7%, respectively. Rolling paper-trading experiments further demonstrate that its advantage persists under forward-only deployment.

</details>


### [168] [High-Order Liquid Evidence Encoding for Gradual GNSS Spoofing Detection in Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11790)
*Muhammad Ayub Sabir,Junbiao Pang,Fatima Ashraf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a causal high-order liquid evidence framework to detect subtle, continuous GNSS spoofing attacks in autonomous driving. It builds a physics-guided GNSS–motion inconsistency residual, forms multiple evidence streams (residual level plus its first- and second-order variations), processes each with adaptive liquid encoders, and hierarchically couples temporal states. On the AV-GPS dataset it achieves the highest F1-scores (0.9535 and 0.9777 on Datasets 1 and 3) among evaluated temporal models and detects normal-to-attack transitions within four sampling steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNSS spoofing attacks can manipulate vehicle positioning, and continuous/subtle attacks are hard to detect because individual observations may stay plausible while the inconsistency between GNSS-implied displacement and onboard motion grows gradually. Existing methods rely on static vehicle-behavior features or a single residual signal and fail to explicitly model this temporal evolution.

Method: The method constructs a physics-guided GNSS–motion inconsistency residual by comparing GNSS-implied displacement with onboard-motion-derived displacement. It forms separate evidence streams for the residual level and its first- and second-order discrete variations, selecting contextual cues according to evidence order. Each stream is processed by a separate adaptive liquid encoder, and temporal states are hierarchically coupled to predict spoofing at the window endpoint using only current and past observations (causal).

Result: On three subsets of the real-world AV-GPS dataset, the method achieves the highest F1-scores among evaluated temporal models on Dataset 1 (0.9535) and Dataset 3 (0.9777). On Dataset 3 it detects both labeled normal-to-attack transitions within four sampling steps.

Conclusion: The proposed causal high-order liquid evidence framework effectively detects subtle, continuous GNSS spoofing by explicitly modeling the evolution of GNSS–motion inconsistency through multi-order evidence streams and hierarchical temporal coupling, achieving state-of-the-art detection performance with rapid transition detection. Code and datasets are publicly available.

Abstract: Accurate Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-based localization is essential for safe and reliable autonomous driving. However, spoofing attacks can manipulate vehicle position estimates. Continuous and subtle attacks are particularly difficult to detect because individual GNSS observations may remain plausible while the inconsistency between GNSS-implied displacement and onboard vehicle motion gradually increases. Existing methods often rely on static vehicle-behavior features or a single residual signal and do not explicitly model this evolution. To address this problem, we propose a causal high-order liquid evidence framework for GNSS spoofing detection. The method first constructs a physics-guided GNSS--motion inconsistency residual by comparing GNSS-implied displacement with onboard-motion-derived displacement. It then forms separate evidence streams for the residual level and its first- and second-order discrete variations, with relevant contextual cues selected according to the evidence order. Each stream is processed by a separate adaptive liquid encoder, and the resulting temporal states are hierarchically coupled to predict spoofing at the window endpoint using only current and past observations. Experiments on three subsets of the real-world AV-GPS dataset show that the proposed method achieves the highest F1-scores among the evaluated temporal models on Dataset~1 and Dataset~3, reaching 0.9535 and 0.9777, respectively. On Dataset~3, it detects both labeled normal-to-attack transitions within four sampling steps. Code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/pangjunbiao/GNSS_Spoofing.git.

</details>


### [169] [Orientation, not magnitude: the causal structure of task-vector interference in merged language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11797)
*Chencheng Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that magnitude is an inadequate and inconsistent diagnostic for task-arithmetic model merging failures. Through exact layerwise decomposition, it shows a stable cross-term direction dominates the layerwise flux, is an attractor of the forward pass under perturbation, and is causally load-bearing: erasing it dose-dependently removes expressed interference, while norm-matched wrong-direction controls fail. The effect is gated by instruction wrappers, and apparent "universality" of naive bfloat16 results is shown to be quantization roughness. All 46 predictions were preregistered.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work explains when task arithmetic merging fails using magnitude-based diagnostics (layerwise representation bias, cross-task linearity deviations, parameter overlap), but the paper finds magnitude to be insufficient and inconsistent across model families. The goal is to identify the true causal structure of the interfering cross-term in merged LLMs rather than relying on coarse magnitude correlates.

Method: The authors compute an exact layerwise decomposition of the cross-term using a factorial ledger, then intervene directly on that term. They apply erasure along a specific carried direction (a basin test with six starting displacements establishes it as a forward-pass attractor), run norm-matched wrong-direction controls, test instruction wrappers versus a length-matched control, and compare against naive bfloat16 generation. Forty-six predictions were preregistered and frozen before data collection.

Result: The layerwise flux is dominated by amplifying transport of the existing cross-term (~65-70% in both families, gain >1 per late block). Erasing the term is undone by propagation, rebuilding to 99% of norm at cosine 0.99 unless applied near the output. The carried direction is causally load-bearing: erasure along it removes expressed interference dose-dependently and saturates at exact erasure; norm-matched wrong-direction controls fail or backfire. Instruction wrappers gate the effect, leaving 13x less relative interference removable under a wrapper that internally amplifies the cross-term via a template-pinned main effect. Task pairs whose local cross-term generation differs by at most 1.9x differ by 14x-337x in causally removable interference. Magnitude is a coarse correlate at best, and the +-15% "universality" of naive bfloat16 is quantization roughness.

Conclusion: Magnitude-based diagnostics are insufficient to explain or predict merging interference; the relevant structure is a specific, causally load-bearing cross-term direction that behaves as a forward-pass attractor. Its erasure reliably removes interference, though effects are modulated by instruction wrappers and confounded by quantization in low precision. The preregistered design yields both confirmations and falsifications, including of the authors' own headline expectations.

Abstract: Model merging by task arithmetic works until it doesn't, and the field diagnoses why with magnitudes: layerwise representation bias, deviations from cross-task linearity, parameter overlap. Tracking the exact layerwise cross-term of merged LLMs through a factorial ledger and intervening on it directly, we find magnitude insufficient - and inconsistent across model families - as a diagnostic axis. An exact decomposition of the layerwise flux shows it is dominated by amplifying transport of the existing cross-term (~65-70% in both families, gain >1 per late block), and erasing the term is undone by propagation - rebuilt to 99% of its norm at cosine 0.99 - unless applied near the output; a basin test with six starting displacements establishes the carried direction as an attractor of the forward pass. That direction is causally load-bearing: erasure along it removes expressed interference dose-dependently and saturates at exact erasure, while norm-matched wrong-direction controls fail or backfire. Instruction wrappers gate the effect: the same erasure finds 13x less relative interference to remove under a wrapper that internally amplifies the cross-term, because the wrapper drowns the interaction in a template-pinned main effect rather than shrinking it - a structure that replicates across further instruction templates but not under a length-matched control. Magnitude, by contrast, is at best a coarse correlate, and the striking +-15% "universality" of naive bfloat16 generation turns out to be quantization roughness. Task pairs whose local cross-term generation differs by at most 1.9x differ by 14x-337x in causally removable interference. All 46 predictions were preregistered and frozen before their data; falsifications, including of our own headline expectations and of behavioral recovery under a validated continuous endpoint, are reported as such.

</details>


### [170] [JAPE: Joint Anomaly Prediction and Intrinsic Explanation in Multivariate Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11801)
*Yian Wei,Yuanyuan Yao,Lu Chen,Xiangmin Zhou,Tianyi Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JAPE is a joint anomaly prediction and explanation framework that shifts from numerical-deviation modeling to evolving dependency-structure modeling, enabling point-wise alerting and native variable-level explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multivariate time-series anomaly prediction methods characterize anomalies as deviations in future numerical values, which can miss subtle dependency changes caused by weak anomaly precursors and cannot natively explain which variables are involved. This motivates modeling evolving dependency structures to catch structural precursors before numerical deviations appear and to provide built-in variable-level explanations.

Method: JAPE has three components: (i) a Decoupled Spatio-Temporal Representation (DSTR) backbone that separates temporal and spatial modeling and captures lag-aware dependencies via learnable lag aggregation, perceiving structural precursors early; (ii) a dual-view alerting mechanism that fuses numerical forecasts with evolving dependency graphs for point-wise anomaly prediction, capturing structural evidence even under subtle numerical deviations; and (iii) Native Predictive Explanation (NPE), which directly reuses the predicted dependency graphs to rank variables by structural deviation without extra models or training.

Result: On five real-world benchmarks across three prediction horizons, JAPE improves average F1 by 19.7% and AUC-PR by 41.3%, and improves explainability with a 26.6% gain in MRR.

Conclusion: Modeling evolving dependency structures, rather than only numerical deviations, enables more accurate point-wise anomaly prediction and provides native, training-free variable-level explanations, as demonstrated by strong gains in F1, AUC-PR, and MRR.

Abstract: Multivariate time-series anomaly prediction aims to identify whether and when anomalies will occur over a future horizon from historical observations. Existing methods primarily characterize anomalies as deviations in future numerical values, which may overlook subtle dependency changes induced by weak anomaly precursors and provide no native variable-level explanation together with the alert. To bridge these gaps, we propose JAPE, a Joint Anomaly Prediction and Explanation framework that lifts anomaly prediction from numerical-deviation modeling to dependency-structure modeling. JAPE is the first anomaly prediction framework to explicitly model evolving dependency structures for both point-wise alerting and native variable-level explanation. Specifically, JAPE (i) proposes a Decoupled Spatio-Temporal Representation (DSTR) backbone that decouples temporal and spatial modeling and captures lag-aware dependencies via learnable lag aggregation, thereby perceiving structural precursors before numerical deviations emerge; (ii) designs a dual-view alerting mechanism that fuses numerical forecasts with evolving dependency graphs for point-wise anomaly prediction, capturing structural evidence even under subtle numerical deviations; and (iii) presents Native Predictive Explanation (NPE), which directly reuses the predicted dependency graphs to rank variables by structural deviations without additional models or training. Extensive experiments on five real-world benchmarks across three prediction horizons demonstrate that JAPE improves average F1 and AUC-PR by 19.7% and 41.3%, respectively, while improving explainability with 26.6% gain in MRR.

</details>


### [171] [Learning with Bilevel-Minimax Optimization for Efficient and Reliable Transfer Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11815)
*Yaohua Liu,Yifan Guo,Jiaxin Gao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BMAT is a bilevel-minimax framework for transfer-based adversarial attacks that jointly couples initialization, surrogate adaptation, and gradient dynamics, achieving state-of-the-art cross-architecture transferability across 30+ victim models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transfer-based attacks suffer from limited transferability because existing methods treat perturbation generation in isolation, whereas transferability is fundamentally governed by the coupling among initialization, surrogate adaptation, and gradient dynamics. The authors aim to model and optimize these three factors jointly.

Method: The authors formulate the problem as a bilevel-minimax program: an outer bilevel structure captures the dependency between initialization and perturbation, and an inner minimax problem promotes surrogate robustness for cross-architecture generalization. They propose an integrated bottom-up solver using a Soft Weight Modulator and an Implicit Gradient Approximator to enable ternary coupling among initialization, surrogate adaptation, and perturbation optimization, along with theoretical analysis of the optimization dynamics.

Result: Extensive experiments on classification and segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that BMAT outperforms more than 10 strong baselines across more than 30 victim models, improving both intra- and cross-architecture transfer and yielding up to a 2x reduction in mIoU.

Conclusion: BMAT establishes that jointly modeling initialization, surrogate adaptation, and perturbation optimization within a bilevel-minimax framework substantially improves transferability of adversarial examples across diverse victim models and tasks.

Abstract: Transfer-based adversarial attacks craft adversarial examples using surrogate models to mislead black-box victim models.
