Beyond perturbation generation, transferability is fundamentally governed by the coupling of initialization, surrogate adaptation, and gradient dynamics. We revisit this challenge from a bilevel-minimax perspective and propose BMAT (Bilevel-Minimax Adversarial Transfer). The bilevel formulation captures the dependency between initialization and perturbation, while the inner minimax problem promotes surrogate robustness for cross-architecture generalization. Algorithmically, we develop an integrated bottom-up solver that combines a Soft Weight Modulator and an Implicit Gradient Approximator to enable ternary coupling among initialization, surrogate adaptation, and perturbation optimization. We further provide theoretical insights into the optimization dynamics of the proposed bilevel-minimax framework. Extensive experiments on classification and segmentation benchmarks show that BMAT outperforms more than 10 strong baselines across more than 30 victim models, improving both intra- and cross-architecture transfer and yielding up to a 2x reduction in mIoU. Code is available at https://github.com/callous-youth/BMAT.

</details>


### [172] [Towards Understanding On-Policy Distillation through the Lens of Test-Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11829)
*Xinmu Ge,Zizhuo Zhang,Yu Huang,Jianing Zhu,Lin Yuan,Wanli Gu,Weichang Wu,Weiran Huang,Xiaolu Zhang,Bo Han,Jun Zhou,Jiangchao Yao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: On-policy distillation (OPD) appears to improve LLM reasoning mainly by boosting sampling efficiency, not by truly expanding reasoning capability; under large sampling budgets (pass@K with large K) the pre-OPD base model catches up or overtakes the OPD model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Challenge the common belief that OPD enables a student model to genuinely acquire new reasoning capabilities from a stronger teacher, and instead test whether observed gains reflect real capability expansion or merely better sampling efficiency.

Method: Analyze several OPD variants under test-time scaling by varying the sampling budget K, comparing performance with pass@K (best-of-K) and avg@K (average accuracy). Track pass@K dynamics during OPD training, and perform a problem-level solvability analysis using pass@1024 as the criterion to count transitions between solvable and unsolvable problems.

Result: OPD models keep superior avg@K across budgets, but their pass@K advantage shifts to the pre-OPD base model as K grows. During training, OPD progressively raises small-K performance while lowering the large-K boundary. Using pass@1024, OPD makes more previously solvable problems unsolvable than it makes previously unsolvable problems solvable.

Conclusion: OPD functions as an "illusory distillation": apparent gains stem mainly from improved sampling efficiency rather than from acquiring genuinely new reasoning capabilities from the teacher.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as a promising post-training technique for enhancing LLM reasoning. It is commonly believed to enable the student model to distill knowledge from a stronger teacher model, thereby expanding capabilities beyond the pre-OPD base model. In this study, we examine this view through the lens of test-time scaling by varying the sampling budget K and evaluating performance with pass@K and avg@K. Specifically, across several OPD variants, we observe that OPD-trained models maintain superior avg@K performance across sampling budgets, while the advantage in pass@K gradually shifts to the pre-OPD base models as K increases. These results suggest that OPD primarily improves sampling efficiency rather than consistently expanding the student's reasoning capability boundary. The pass@K dynamics throughout OPD training further reveal a progressive shift toward stronger small-K performance at the expense of the large-K capability boundary. Furthermore, a problem-level solvability analysis using pass@1024 as the criterion reveals an asymmetry: OPD causes more previously solvable problems to become unsolvable than previously unsolvable problems to become solvable. Together, these findings suggest that, from the perspective of capability expansion, OPD behaves more like an "illusory distillation": its apparent gains arise primarily from improved sampling efficiency rather than from acquiring genuinely new reasoning capabilities from the teacher.

</details>


### [173] [Kernel Methods for Learning Operators with Multiple Inputs and Outputs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11831)
*Adrien Weihs,Chunyang Liao,Jingmin Sun,Hayden Schaeffer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a general kernel-based encoder-decoder framework for operator learning that separates observation, representation, learning, and reconstruction, and instantiates it as KernelMO for multi-input, multi-output operator learning with competitive accuracy and lower cost than neural operators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning mappings between infinite-dimensional objects (operators) is a central challenge in scientific machine learning. Existing neural operator and deep learning approaches are computationally expensive in training and inference. The authors aim to develop a mathematically tractable, closed-form, and lightweight alternative that scales well to multi-input, multi-output operator learning settings.

Method: The authors introduce a kernel-based encoder-decoder framework that decouples observation, representation, learning, and reconstruction stages. They develop it for multi-input, multi-output operators mapping between products of distinct function spaces. The framework yields kernel methods with closed-form training and inference. They further specialize it via KernelMO, a family of kernel methods with complementary operator-valued and product-space formulations.

Result: Approximation theory shows that even as the number of inputs and outputs grows, the convergence rate is governed by the most difficult constituent approximation problem rather than the total problem dimension. Across five families of parametric PDEs, the proposed methods achieve competitive or state-of-the-art predictive accuracy while reducing training and inference costs compared to neural operator architectures and deep learning models.

Conclusion: The kernel-based framework offers an efficient and lightweight alternative to neural operators for operator learning, combining mathematical tractability, closed-form solvability, and computational efficiency, with strong empirical performance across multiple PDE families.

Abstract: Learning mappings between infinite-dimensional objects is a central challenge in scientific machine learning. We introduce a general kernel-based encoder-decoder framework for operator learning that separates observation, representation, learning, and reconstruction. We develop this framework for multi-input, multi-output operator learning, where operators map between products of potentially distinct function spaces. Our approximation theory shows that, although the number of inputs and outputs can increase, the convergence rate is governed by the most challenging constituent approximation problem rather than the overall problem dimension. The framework leads to practical kernel methods with closed-form training and inference, combining mathematical tractability with computational efficiency. We further specialize the approach to multiple operator learning by introducing KernelMO, a family of kernel methods with complementary operator-valued and product-space formulations. Across five families of parametric partial differential equations, the proposed methods achieve competitive or state-of-the-art predictive accuracy while reducing training and inference costs relative to neural operator architectures and deep learning based models, offering an efficient and lightweight alternative.

</details>


### [174] [Air Quality Station Simulation via LSTM and Attention-Based Modelling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11839)
*Alexander Kostadinov,Petar O. Hristov,Dessislava Petrova-Antonova*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SATADL is a deep-learning model that forecasts multiple-hour-ahead air-quality, enabling it to act as a virtual proxy for a failed measurement station, and it outperforms baseline models across 48-hour simulation windows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Urban air quality monitoring depends on reliable, uninterrupted station operation, but hardware faults and blackouts cause data unavailability that degrades analyses; the motivation is to simulate an unresponsive station's measurements until service is restored.

Method: The authors propose SATADL, a deep-learning architecture that extracts information from different aspects of the data to infer complex relations and produce multi-hour-ahead forecasts. Its components are examined in detail, and it is used to simulate PM10 concentrations during hypothetical 48-hour failures of one station, benchmarked against baseline and published deep learning models across four sets of stations worldwide.

Result: SATADL performs better than baseline and published deep learning models across different prediction windows, measured by both coefficient of determination and root mean squared error, particularly for simulating PM10 over failure periods up to 48 hours.

Conclusion: SATADL demonstrates suitability as a virtual proxy station, providing reliable multi-hour-ahead air-quality forecasts to simulate measurements of an unresponsive station until its operation is restored.

Abstract: Poor air quality in urban areas is driven by a complex chain of processes and presents a significant public health concern. To better understand and control the mechanisms that determine air quality, cities deploy networks of measurement stations, and launch initiatives for collecting denser data about the concentration of pollutants in the atmosphere. Extracting insights from the stations relies on their reliable and uninterrupted operation. However, hardware is susceptible to faults and black- outs that may result in data unavailability, which affects the overall quality of analyses. In this paper, we present a deep-learning model, called SATADL, which can infer complex relations and output multiple-hour-ahead air-quality forecasts. The goal of the model is to simulate the mea- surements of an unresponsive station until its operation is restored. The architecture of the model, which allows it to extract information from different aspects of the data, is described in detail and a careful examination of all of its components is provided. We demonstrate the performance of SATADL on four sets of air quality stations from around the world, by using it to simulate the concentration of PM10 for periods of hypothetical failures of one of the measurement stations, lasting for as long as 48 hours. A selection of baseline and published deep learning models were trained and used as a benchmark. The results show that SATADL per- forms better across different prediction windows, for both coefficient of determination and root mean squared error, demonstrating its suitability as a virtual proxy station.

</details>


### [175] [Small-Scale Experiments: Are We There Yet?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11859)
*Nicholas Lourie,Kyunghyun Cho,Karen Ullrich,Sanae Lotfi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Scaling laws can be recovered at small scales (e.g., 4M parameters) provided hyperparameters are extensively tuned; the failure of small-scale extrapolation is a hyperparameter-sensitivity problem, not a model-size problem. The authors reveal why tuning gets easier with scale (the hyperparameter loss surface becomes lower dimensional) and propose a new methodology for model-centric research, demonstrated by recovering the known result that pre-normalization beats post-normalization in transformers as they grow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scaling laws promised cheap, small-scale experiments to guide large-model design, but after six years they remain unreliable, and researchers concluded sizable models are unavoidable. The authors aim to show this is a hyperparameter confound, not inherent, and to make small-scale experiments trustworthy again.

Method: The authors ablate the standard scaling-law recipe, showing that well-tuned hyperparameters dominate all other ingredients, and analyze how hyperparameter sensitivity fades with scale and why the hyperparameter loss surface becomes lower dimensional as scale grows. They then synthesize these insights with prior literature into a new methodology for model-centric research, applying it to the transformer normalization placement question using only small-scale experiments.

Result: Small models are highly sensitive to hyperparameters, but this sensitivity decreases with scale; scaling laws only emerge on the fully tuned frontier. With sufficient tuning, scaling laws are observable even at 4M parameters, though extrapolation remains statistically limited. Applying the methodology, small-scale experiments recover the large-scale finding that pre-normalization outperforms post-normalization as transformers scale.

Conclusion: Scaling laws' long-awaited promise can be delivered at small scale with the right tools and a better understanding of hyperparameter sensitivity; the key is extensive, well-tuned hyperparameter search rather than avoiding small models. This enables faster, cheaper model-centric experimentation.

Abstract: Scaling laws promised cost-effective experiments; six years later, they have yet to fully deliver. Instead, researchers have found them unreliable at small scales (starting at 4M parameters) and concluded that sizable models cannot be avoided. We show this is not the case: the confounding factor is hyperparameters. Small models are highly sensitive, but hyperparameter sensitivity fades with scale. This small-scale sensitivity makes scaling laws easy to miss because they only emerge on the fully tuned frontier, and reaching that frontier requires an extensive search far beyond what most ever run. By ablating the basic scaling law recipe, we show well-tuned hyperparameters matter more than any other ingredient. Further, we reveal why those hyperparameters become easier to find: as scale increases, the hyperparameter loss surface becomes lower dimensional. Nevertheless while scaling laws exist in small models, extrapolation hits statistical limitations. A holistic approach is required. Synthesizing our insights with the recent literature, we develop a new methodology for model-centric research and demonstrate it on a question that once took the field years to settle: where to place normalization layers in the transformer architecture. From small-scale experiments, we recover the large scale result: pre-normalization works better as models grow in size. With the right tools and a better understanding, small-scale experiments can deliver on scaling laws' long-awaited promise.

</details>


### [176] [Forward and Inverse Virtual Metrology for Phototransistor Gain: A Hierarchical, Uncertainty-Aware Approach for Small Production Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11868)
*Mahshid Amirabgir,Lorenza Ferrario,Paolo Conci,Mahdieh Amirabgir,Giancarlo Orengo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A small-sample, hierarchical study predicting silicon bipolar phototransistor gain from process recipes, decomposing variance between/within runs and providing forward prediction, inverse recipe search, and multi-level data-quality assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fabricating a silicon bipolar phototransistor requires months of cleanroom time before measurement, so a model predicting device gain from process parameters before a run is highly valuable even without perfect accuracy. The real fabrication history (13–14 process runs of a single device) is a small-sample, hierarchically structured setting, unlike conventional large-corpus virtual metrology.

Method: Variance decomposition of device gain shows roughly half lies between process runs rather than within them, bounding recipe-only prediction. The authors build a forward gain predictor with a relative, uncertainty-aware signal; an inverse search returning recipes for a target gain; and a multi-level data-quality assessment tailored to nested physical entities (batch, wafer, die) with an explicit cross-level linkage score. Normalized dataset and analysis code are released.

Result: Roughly half of the variance in device gain lies between process runs, so recipe-only prediction is inherently bounded. The framework yields a forward gain predictor with relative uncertainty, an inverse recipe search for target gains, and a multi-level data-quality assessment with cross-level linkage scoring.

Conclusion: The hierarchical, small-sample approach provides practically useful gain prediction, inverse recipe search, and data-quality assessment for fabrication, with full reproducibility via released normalized data and code.

Abstract: The customization, optimization and stabilization of the process flow of a silicon bipolar phototransistor commits months of cleanroom time before a finished device can be measured, so a model that predicts device gain from process parameters before a run has value out of proportion to its accuracy. We study this problem on a real fabrication history, thirteen to fourteen process runs of a single device: a small-sample, hierarchically structured setting unlike the large-corpus regime of conventional virtual metrology. Decomposing the variance of device gain, we find that roughly half of it lies between process runs rather than within them, so recipe-only prediction is bounded by construction. Building on these findings we provide a forward gain predictor with a relative, uncertainty-aware signal, an inverse search that returns recipes for a target gain, and, as the foundation for all of it, a multi-level data-quality assessment tailored to the nested physical entities of fabrication (batch, wafer, die) with an explicit cross-level linkage score. The normalized dataset and analysis code are released for full reproducibility.

</details>


### [177] [DCM Bandits: Multiplayer Information Asymmetric Cascading Bandits for Multiple Clicks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11873)
*Andy Wang,Charlton Shih,William Chang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper extends Dependent Click Model (DCM) bandits to a multiplayer, information-asymmetric setting, providing sublinear-regret algorithms for asymmetric actions/rewards and showing termination-rank knowledge is unnecessary for small termination probabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world ranked-list interactions often involve multiple agents sharing a list with asymmetric information, where some agents act on different parts or receive different feedback (actions or rewards). Prior DCM bandit work focused on single agents or symmetric settings, motivating the study of selection strategies under asymmetry.

Method: The authors model multiple agents interacting with a shared ranked list under the Dependent Click Model, allowing multiple clicks per session. They formalize asymmetry in (1) actions and (2) rewards, then design algorithms with sublinear regret guarantees for three settings where at least one asymmetry is present. They also analyze the case of unknown termination rankings for small termination probabilities.

Result: The work provides sublinear regret guarantees for three asymmetric settings and improves prior single-agent results by showing the termination ranking need not be known when termination probabilities are small. Experiments confirm strong performance across asymmetric environments and show that feedback structure—full vs. first-click feedback—critically affects exploration coordination and regret.

Conclusion: The proposed algorithms achieve sublinear regret in multiplayer, information-asymmetric DCM bandits, with experiments underscoring the importance of feedback structure for coordination. Establishing matching information-theoretic lower bounds remains an open problem for future work.

Abstract: In this work, we extend the Dependent Click Model (DCM) Bandits to a multiplayer information-asymmetric setting, where multiple agents interact with a shared ranked list and may observe multiple clicks per session, introducing new challenges for selection strategies. We study asymmetry in (1) actions and (2) rewards, providing sublinear regret guarantees for three settings where at least one asymmetry is present. Establishing matching information-theoretic lower bounds for these settings is left as an open problem. We further show that for small termination probabilities, the termination ranking need not be known, improving on prior single-agent results. Experiments confirm that our algorithms perform well across asymmetric environments and highlight the critical role of feedback structure, specifically the distinction between full versus first-click feedback, in coordinating exploration and minimizing regret.

</details>


### [178] [Disentangling the Expressivity of RoPE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11909)
*Selim Jerad,Anej Svete,Jiaoda Li,Ryan Cotterell*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formally analyzes Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) in uniform finite-precision soft-attention transformers. It shows that fully periodic RoPE recognizes exactly the languages of Past Temporal Logic with modular predicates, whereas conventional RoPE (whose rotations never repeat) instead yields a precision-dependent bounded simulation of fixed-offset look-back operators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two competing explanations for RoPE's success exist in the literature: expressivity studies (linking periodic positional information to modular predicates) and mechanistic/long-context studies (emphasizing positional anchors and local offsets). The authors aim to reconcile these by formalizing both accounts and determining which characterization actually holds for the RoPE variant used in practice.

Method: The authors formalize both accounts within the framework of fully uniform, finite-precision soft-attention transformers. They distinguish ideal fully periodic RoPE (every rotary component is periodic) from conventional RoPE (whose computed rotations never repeat). They derive a formal language-theoretic characterization for each, connecting periodic RoPE to Past Temporal Logic with modular predicates and conventional RoPE to a precision-dependent bounded simulation of fixed-offset look-back operators. They then validate the theoretical separation with controlled experiments on constructed periodic schedules and modular languages.

Result: Fully periodic RoPE transformers recognize exactly the languages definable in Past Temporal Logic with modular predicates. By contrast, conventional RoPE does not yield an all-length modular characterization; it provides only a precision-dependent bounded simulation of fixed-offset look-back operators. Experiments confirm the separation: constructed periodic schedules length-generalize on modular languages, while conventional RoPE behaves like a bounded locality bias and can impair tasks requiring position-invariant access to distant context.

Conclusion: The study shows that standard RoPE behaves more like a bounded locality bias than a modular-predicate mechanism, and it can even impair position-invariant long-context tasks. The findings bring theoretical expressivity characterizations of RoPE transformers closer to the behavior of models used in practice.

Abstract: Two accounts recur in explanations of the success of rotary position embeddings (RoPE). Expressivity studies associate periodic position information with modular predicates, whereas mechanistic and long-context studies emphasize positional anchors and local offsets. We formalize both accounts for fully uniform, finite-precision soft-attention transformers. We find that, if every rotary component is periodic, RoPE transformers recognize exactly the languages definable in past temporal logic with modular predicates. Conventional RoPE is different: The rotations it computes never repeat. This yields a precision-dependent bounded simulation of fixed-offset look-back operators, rather than an all-length modular characterization. Controlled experiments match this separation: Constructed periodic schedules length-generalize on modular languages, while conventional RoPE behaves more like a bounded locality bias and can impair tasks requiring position-invariant access to distant context. Altogether, our findings shed light on RoPE transformers, bringing theoretical expressivity characterizations closer to models used in practice.

</details>


### [179] [A Factor Graph Approach to Scalable Multi-Output Gaussian Process Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11917)
*Wouter W. L. Nuijten,Esther G. van Pelt,Albert Podusenko,İsmail Şenöz,Wouter M. Kouw*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper reformulates multi-output Gaussian process regression as a Forney-style factor graph along a nearest-neighbor chain over candidate inputs, enabling exact Gaussian message passing at linear cost in data samples while tolerating missing observations without matrix restructuring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard multi-output Gaussian process regression scales cubically in observations times outputs, and dense kernel-matrix methods require bespoke handling when different outputs are observed at different inputs. The authors seek a scalable formulation that handles missing observations naturally and scales linearly in the number of data points.

Method: The approach expresses multi-output GP regression as a Forney-style factor graph. A nearest-neighbor chain orders a fixed candidate set of C inputs into a one-dimensional sequence; latent Matérn processes evolve via linear-Gaussian transition factors along this chain; a linear model of coregionalization mixes L latent processes into D outputs through a deterministic mixing factor and per-output scalar observation factors. Posterior inference reduces to exact Gaussian message passing on the chain at cost O(C(DL^2 + L^3)) after chain construction. Missing observations simply omit their local factor.

Result: At low input dimension the factor-graph posterior tracks the exact kernel-matrix posterior closely, with the gap growing gradually as input dimension increases while remaining competitive with sparse-variational and nearest-neighbor baselines. On electricity time series forecasting, the formulation matches all three baselines (exact kernel-matrix, sparse-variational inducing-point, nearest-neighbor) in accuracy while scaling linearly in data points, where the exact method becomes infeasible and the inducing-point baseline remains substantially slower.

Conclusion: The factor-graph formulation offers a scalable multi-output GP regression method that scales in data samples and missing-observation rate, is best suited to low-dimensional candidate sets, and achieves competitive accuracy with strong scaling behavior compared to exact and approximate baselines.

Abstract: Multi-output Gaussian process regression scales cubically in the number of observations times outputs, and dense kernel-matrix methods need bespoke handling whenever different outputs are observed at different inputs. We express multi-output Gaussian process regression as a Forney-style factor graph in which a nearest-neighbor chain orders a fixed candidate set of $C$ inputs into a one-dimensional sequence. Along this chain, latent Matérn processes evolve through linear-Gaussian transition factors, while the linear model of coregionalization mixes $L$ latent processes into $D$ outputs through a deterministic mixing factor and per-output scalar observation factors. Posterior computation reduces to exact Gaussian message passing on the chain at cost $\mathcal{O}(C(DL^2 + L^3))$ after chain construction, and missing observations omit their local factor without any covariance-matrix restructuring. The formulation therefore scales in the number of data samples and in the rate of missing observations, while remaining best suited to candidate sets in low input dimension.We compare the factor-graph formulation against an exact kernel-matrix baseline, a sparse-variational inducing-point baseline, and a nearest-neighbor baseline on a synthetic input-dimension sweep and on electricity time series forecasting. At low input dimension the factor-graph posterior tracks the exact kernel-matrix posterior closely, and the gap grows gradually as input dimension increases while staying competitive with both approximate baselines. On the electricity time series our factor-graph formulation matches all three baselines in forecast accuracy while scaling linearly in the number of data points, where the exact kernel-matrix method becomes infeasible and the inducing-point baseline remains substantially slower.

</details>


### [180] [Distillation of Foundation Models for Time-dependent PDEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11937)
*Daniel Musekamp,Boshra Ariguib,Andrei Manolache,Mathias Niepert*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TREX is a knowledge distillation method that compresses large pretrained PDE foundation models into small, fast student models by augmenting limited downstream data with long synthetic trajectories generated via teacher rollouts (optionally with noise injection), yielding students that match or exceed teacher accuracy with orders-of-magnitude fewer parameters and faster inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PDE foundation models generalize well after fine-tuning on few trajectories, but they are large and computationally expensive, making them impractical as fast surrogates for numerical solvers. The goal is to transfer their predictive power into compact, efficient models suitable for low-data, fast-inference settings.

Method: TREX distills a fine-tuned teacher foundation model into a compact student. It augments limited downstream data by running long teacher rollouts to generate synthetic trajectories (optionally with periodic noise injection), sampling from the teacher-induced rollout distribution without needing the initial-condition distribution and exposing the student to long-horizon states and local recovery behavior. The student can also add task-specific inductive biases (e.g., equivariance) not enforced by the teacher.

Result: On multiple PDE benchmarks, TREX-trained students match or surpass teacher accuracy while reducing parameter count by several orders of magnitude and achieving more than an order-of-magnitude inference speedup.

Conclusion: TREX enables effective compression of PDE foundation models into fast, accurate surrogates, making them practical for low-data regimes where the original large models are too costly, while allowing the student to incorporate beneficial inductive biases.

Abstract: Foundation models for time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) are trained on large and diverse collections of physical systems and can generalize effectively to new downstream tasks. After fine-tuning on only a few trajectories from a target domain, they can achieve strong accuracy in low-data regimes. However, these models are typically large and computationally intensive, limiting their usefulness as fast surrogates for numerical solvers. We propose Teacher Rollout Extension (TREX), a knowledge distillation framework that transfers the predictive capability of a pretrained foundation model into a compact and efficient student. Starting from a fine-tuned teacher, TREX augments limited downstream data by generating long synthetic trajectories through teacher rollouts, optionally with periodic noise injection. This procedure samples from the teacher-induced rollout distribution without requiring explicit knowledge of the initial-condition distribution, while exposing the student to long-horizon states and local recovery behavior around states encountered during autoregressive prediction. The student can further incorporate task-specific inductive biases, such as equivariance, that the teacher does not necessarily enforce. We evaluate TREX on multiple PDE benchmarks. The resulting students can match or surpass the teacher's accuracy while reducing the number of parameters by several orders of magnitude and achieving more than an order-of-magnitude speedup in inference.

</details>


### [181] [TailBooster: A Dual-Layer Generative Framework for Extreme Value Augmentation with Operational Validity Enforcement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11951)
*Karim Aly,Alexei Sharpanskykh,Jacco Hoekstra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TailBooster is a dual-layer generative framework that augments rare extreme events in air transport data using a statistical tail-extraction layer plus Tabular VAE generation, followed by an autoencoder-based cleaning layer to enforce operational validity; it substantially improves extreme-event prediction accuracy over conventional synthetic data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extreme events (severe arrival delays, abnormal air times) are rare and provide insufficient training signal. Conventional generative models under-represent distribution tails and may produce operationally infeasible records (e.g., short air time with long distance), with no existing method addressing both issues for mixed-type tabular data.

Method: A dual-layer framework: (1) a statistical layer extracts extremes via interquartile range to feed tail-concentrated signal to dedicated generative models (Tabular Variational Autoencoder); (2) a deep learning layer applies autoencoder-based cleaning to discard synthetic records violating the operational envelope learned from historical data.

Result: On US flight records, data-driven cleaning markedly improved operational validity and targeted augmentation enhanced utility. Across six regression algorithms, training on TailBooster records reduced MAE by 47-49% on extreme air time and 29-57% on extreme arrival delay compared to conventional synthetic data, with comparable gains when real records were enriched with synthetic extremes.

Conclusion: TailBooster is fully data-driven and model-agnostic, extending to domains requiring extreme-event prediction where domain-specific rules are unavailable, addressing both tail under-representation and operational infeasibility in mixed-type tabular synthesis.

Abstract: Extreme events in air transport, such as severe arrival delays and abnormal air times, cause cascading network disruptions with substantial operational, economic, and safety costs. Such events are rare in historical records, leaving insufficient training signal for machine learning models. Synthetic data augmentation offers a principled solution, but conventional generative models under-represent distributional tails and give no guarantee against operationally infeasible instances, such as a short air time paired with a long flight distance. No existing approach addresses both limitations for mixed-type tabular records. We propose TailBooster, a dual-layer generative framework combining generative modelling with two anomaly detection layers. A statistical layer extracts extremes via the interquartile range, supplying tail-concentrated training signal to dedicated generative models, here a Tabular Variational Autoencoder. A deep learning layer then applies autoencoder-based cleaning, discarding synthetic records that violate the operational envelope learned from historical data. The framework was evaluated on US flight records across five dimensions: diversity, statistical similarity, fidelity, operational validity, and utility, the latter two being the primary improvement targets. Data-driven cleaning markedly improved operational validity, while targeted augmentation enhanced utility for extreme-event prediction. Across six regression algorithms, training on the framework's records reduced Mean Absolute Error by 47-49% on extreme air time and 29-57% on extreme arrival delay prediction relative to conventional synthetic data, with comparable gains when real records were enriched with synthetic extremes. Being fully data-driven and model-agnostic, TailBooster extends to domains where extreme-event prediction is critical and domain-specific rules are unavailable.

</details>


### [182] [LoongReflect: Boosting Long-Horizon Reflection in Search Agents via Global Perspective Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11967)
*Zhixin Zhang,Xinke Jiang,Zhibang Yang,Weixuan Xu,Guohong Qiu,Xu Chu,Junfeng Zhao,Yasha Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LoongReflect frames reflection in long-horizon LLM agents as a memory-control policy over a reversible trajectory tree, trained with a two-channel (fast distillation + slow GRPO) mechanism to overcome the local-global credit assignment problem of reflection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon agent tasks require reflection (assessing progress, spotting missing evidence/unreliable states, deciding whether to continue, revise, or abandon). However, reflection decisions are made locally within a branch while their value is determined only by final trajectory outcome, creating a local-global mismatch. Outcome-based RL thus gives only local, sparse, and delayed supervision for reflective decisions, making reflection hard to learn.

Method: LoongReflect models reflection as a memory-control policy over a reversible trajectory tree with explicit "reflect" and "backtrack" actions. Reflection consolidates verified facts, missing evidence, and branch-specific risks into working memory; backtracking removes an unreliable branch and stores a concise corrective lesson. Training combines two complementary signals via a look-ahead, extragradient-style coordination: (1) a fast channel distills globally informed reflective behavior from a privileged teacher, supervising only reflection and backtracking tokens; (2) a slow channel optimizes full trajectories with outcome-based GRPO to align local control with final task success.

Result: On multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, LoongReflect consistently improves over outcome-only reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines.

Conclusion: Treating reflection as a learnable memory-control policy and jointly training with privileged-teacher distillation (local control signals) plus outcome-based GRPO (global success signal) effectively resolves the local-global supervision mismatch, yielding stronger long-horizon reasoning agents.

Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on long-horizon reasoning to solve complex tasks involving planning, tool use, and memory. A critical capability in such settings is reflection: assessing trajectory progress, identifying missing evidence and unreliable intermediate states, and deciding whether to continue, revise, or abandon the current branch. Learning effective reflection, however, is challenging because reflection is performed locally within the current branch, whereas its utility can only be determined by its contribution to the final trajectory outcome. This local-global mismatch makes outcome-based reinforcement learning provide only local, sparse and delayed supervision for reflective decisions. To solve these, we propose LoongReflect, a training framework that formulates reflection as a memory-control policy. The agent operates over a reversible trajectory tree using explicit reflect and backtrack actions. Reflection consolidates verified facts, missing evidence, and branch-specific risks into working memory, while backtracking removes an unreliable branch from the active context and preserves a concise corrective lesson. To learn this policy, LoongReflect combines two complementary signals through a look-ahead, extragradient-style coordination mechanism. A fast channel distills globally informed reflective behavior from a privileged teacher, with supervision restricted to reflection and backtracking tokens. A slow channel optimizes complete trajectories using outcome-based GRPO, aligning local control decisions with final task success. Experiments on multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation and mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over outcome-only reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines.

</details>


### [183] [TESLA: Taylor Expansion of Sinusoidal Learnable Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11970)
*Daehwa Ko,Jaehyeon Kim,Seunghyun Ham,Jay Hoon Jung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TESLA is a learnable sine-cosine activation that controls polynomial degree and amplifies high-order components, enabling neural networks to solve the parity problem efficiently, tolerate heavy label noise, and transfer to vision tasks like ImageNet-100.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard neural networks struggle with parity due to linear inseparability and the need for global interactions across inputs. The authors seek an activation-level mechanism that can expose and emphasize high-order frequency structure to overcome this limitation.

Method: TESLA is an activation defined as a learnable combination of sine and cosine terms. Its coefficients constrain the effective polynomial degree and selectively amplify high-order components. Theoretical analysis connects these coefficients to Lipschitz/Rademacher complexity bounds and shows the training dynamics favor higher-frequency structure.

Result: On parity with n=32 inputs, TESLA achieves strong generalization using only 100K training samples (~0.002% of the 2^32 space) and stays robust with up to 30% label noise. It outperforms SIREN, SNAKE, and Fourier feature baselines on parity and Forrelation, and achieves comparable ImageNet-100 performance.

Conclusion: Activation-level control over polynomial degree transfers beyond synthetic structure to general vision workloads, offering a practical route to address global, high-order problems while maintaining competitive real-world performance.

Abstract: The parity problem--deciding whether the number of ones in a binary vector is odd or even--remains challenging for standard neural networks due to linear inseparability and the need for global interactions. We propose TESLA, an activation defined as a learnable combination of sine and cosine terms, enabling explicit control over polynomial degree and selective amplification of high-order components. Theoretically, we show that constraining TESLA's coefficients yields Lipschitz/Rademacher complexity bounds and shapes the training dynamics to emphasize higher-frequency structure. Empirically, on parity with input length n = 32, TESLA attains strong generalization with 100K training samples (approximately 0.002% of the 2^32 input space) and remains robust under heavy corruption, retaining high accuracy with up to 30% label noise. We also compare against periodic and frequency-based baselines (SIREN, SNAKE, and Fourier feature embeddings) on parity and Forrelation. Beyond synthetic structure, TESLA delivers comparable performance on ImageNet-100, indicating that activation-level degree control transfers to more general vision workloads. Code: https://github.com/KAU-QuantumAILab/TESLA

</details>


### [184] [Remote Sensing and Machine Learning-Based Analysis of Land Use and Vegetation Change in Dhaka District, Bangladesh](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12001)
*Muhammad Masud Tarek,Md. Alamgir Hossain,Md. Samiul Islam,Muntasir Hasan Kanchan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Using Sentinel-2, Landsat 8 imagery and machine learning classifiers (Decision Tree, KNN, Random Forest) in Google Earth Engine, this study tracked land cover and vegetation changes in Dhaka District from 2019 to 2024, finding a 59.5% rise in built-up areas alongside declines in vegetation (-8.46%) and water bodies (-7.77%), with Random Forest achieving the highest accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rapid urbanization in Dhaka District has caused major shifts in land use and environmental conditions, creating a need for systematic, data-driven monitoring to support informed urban planning and ecological sustainability.

Method: The study used Sentinel-2 MSI and Landsat 8 high-resolution imagery to classify land cover and compute spectral indices (NDVI, NDBI, NDWI). A supervised machine learning approach with Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Random Forest classifiers was applied using labeled geospatial training points within Google Earth Engine, with accuracy evaluated via confusion matrices and kappa statistics.

Result: Urban built-up areas increased by 59.5%, while vegetation declined by 8.46% and water bodies by 7.77% between 2019 and 2024. Land conversion from vegetated and aquatic areas to urban infrastructure was the dominant trend. Random Forest yielded the highest classification accuracy among the tested models.

Conclusion: The findings reveal growing environmental pressures from unregulated urban expansion in Dhaka and highlight the value of remote sensing combined with machine learning for delivering timely, actionable data to support sustainable urban development, land-use regulation, and ecosystem conservation policies.

Abstract: Rapid urbanization in Dhaka District, Bangladesh has triggered substantial alterations in land use and environmental conditions, necessitating systematic monitoring for informed urban planning and ecological sustainability. This study employs remote sensing data and machine learning techniques to analyze spatiotemporal changes in land cover and vegetation dynamics between 2019 and 2024. High-resolution satellite imagery from Sentinel-2 MSI and Landsat 8 was utilized to classify land cover types and compute spectral indices including the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Built-up Index (NDBI), and Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI). A supervised machine learning approach incorporating Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Random Forest classifiers was applied using labeled geospatial training points within Google Earth Engine. Accuracy assessments were conducted using confusion matrices and kappa statistics. Results indicate a 59.5% increase in urban built-up areas and a significant decline in vegetation (-8.46%) and water bodies (-7.77%) over the five-year period. Land conversion from vegetated and aquatic areas to urban infrastructure was identified as a dominant trend. Among the models, Random Forest demonstrated the highest classification accuracy. These findings underscore the growing environmental pressures driven by unregulated urban expansion in Dhaka. The study highlights the potential of remote sensing and machine learning tools in providing timely, actionable data to support sustainable urban development, land-use regulation, and ecosystem conservation policies.

</details>


### [185] [Dual-Model Sentiment Analysis of Consumer Reviews in the Retail Coffee Sector Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Approaches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12007)
*Muntasir Hasan Kanchan,Md. Alamgir Hossain,Md. Samiul Islam,Muhammad Masud Tarek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares classical machine learning and deep learning models for sentiment analysis of Starbucks customer reviews, finding SVM (91.0% accuracy) best among ML models and Bidirectional LSTM best among deep learning models, while highlighting the impact of class imbalance on positive sentiment recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Consumer reviews significantly influence brand perception and business strategy in service industries like retail coffee, so there is a need for reliable, comparative evaluation of sentiment analysis techniques on real-world review data.

Method: Sentiment labels were generated by binarizing star ratings (4-5 = positive, 1-3 = negative), creating an imbalanced dataset of 700+ Starbucks reviews from ConsumerAffairs. After preprocessing and exploratory data analysis (temporal/geographic), five ML classifiers (Logistic Regression, SVM, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Naive Bayes) and five deep learning models (LSTM, RNN, Bidirectional LSTM, GRU, CNN) were evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.

Result: SVM achieved the highest accuracy among machine learning models at 91.0%, and Bidirectional LSTM performed best among deep learning models with good generalization on unseen data. Class imbalance (skewed toward negative sentiment) negatively affected positive sentiment recall across several models.

Conclusion: Appropriate model selection and preprocessing are critical for real-world consumer sentiment analysis in the retail coffee sector; the study offers a practical comparative benchmark of ML and deep learning approaches for customer experience analytics.

Abstract: Consumer reviews play an important role in shaping brand perception and business strategies, particularly in service-driven industries such as retail coffee. This study presents a comparative sentiment analysis framework for Starbucks customer reviews using classical machine learning and deep learning approaches. The dataset, collected from ConsumerAffairs, contains more than 700 reviews and was analyzed through preprocessing and exploratory data analysis to identify temporal and geographic patterns. Sentiment labels were generated by binarizing star ratings, with ratings of 4 and 5 classified as positive and ratings of 1 to 3 as negative. The resulting dataset was substantially imbalanced toward negative sentiment. Five machine learning classifiers, including Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Naive Bayes, were evaluated alongside five deep learning models: LSTM, RNN, Bidirectional LSTM, GRU, and CNN. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. SVM achieved the highest accuracy among the machine learning models at 91.0 percent, while Bidirectional LSTM showed the strongest performance among the deep learning models and demonstrated good generalization on unseen data. The findings also show that class imbalance negatively affected positive sentiment recall across several models. Overall, this study provides a comparative evaluation of machine learning and deep learning approaches for real-world consumer sentiment analysis and highlights the importance of appropriate model selection and preprocessing for customer experience analytics in the retail coffee sector.

</details>


### [186] [Reducing Symmetry Increase in Equivariant Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12010)
*Ning Lin,Jiacheng Cen,Anyi Li,Wenbing Huang,Hao Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Equivariant neural networks can over-symmetrize symmetric inputs, reducing expressivity. This paper characterizes this symmetry-increase phenomenon, proves the increased symmetry has an infimum determined by the feature space, gives a computable algorithm to derive it, and proposes feature-design guidelines that provably reduce the issue for most equivariant maps under standard regularity assumptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Equivariant Neural Networks lose expressivity on symmetric inputs because their outputs become invariant to transformations beyond the input's symmetries. Prior work only documented this symmetry increase in specific cases, lacking a rigorous account of its causes and general reduction strategies.

Method: The authors prove that for any feature space and input symmetry group, the increased symmetry admits an infimum determined by the feature-space structure (a Galois-type correspondence between equivariant maps and symmetry groups). They then develop a computable algorithm to derive this infimum and propose practical feature-design guidelines. Under standard regularity assumptions, they show that for generic (most) equivariant maps the guidelines effectively reduce symmetry increase.

Result: The theoretical framework yields a computable infimum for symmetry increase and feature-design guidelines that provably reduce symmetry increase for most equivariant maps. Visualizations and experiments on synthetic datasets and the QM9 dataset validate the theoretical predictions.

Conclusion: Symmetry increase in ENNs is governed by a feature-space-determined infimum that can be computed, and principled feature design can mitigate harmful symmetry increase, with theory confirmed by experiments on synthetic and QM9 data.

Abstract: Equivariant Neural Networks (ENNs) have empowered numerous applications in scientific fields. Despite their remarkable capacity for representing geometric structures, ENNs suffer from degraded expressivity when processing symmetric inputs: the output representations are invariant to transformations that extend beyond the input's symmetries. The mathematical essence of this phenomenon is that a symmetric input, after being processed by an equivariant map, experiences an increase in symmetry. While prior research has documented symmetry increase in specific cases, a rigorous understanding of its underlying causes and general reduction strategies remains lacking. In this paper, we provide a detailed and in-depth characterization of symmetry increase together with a principled framework for its reduction: (i) For any given feature space and input symmetry group, we prove that the increased symmetry admits an infimum determined by the structure of the feature space; (ii) Building on this foundation, we develop a computable algorithm to derive this infimum, and propose practical guidelines for feature design to prevent harmful symmetry increases. (iii) Under standard regularity assumptions, we demonstrate that for most equivariant maps, our guidelines effectively reduce symmetry increase. To complement our theoretical findings, we provide visualizations and experiments on both synthetic datasets and the real-world QM9 dataset. The results validate our theoretical predictions.

</details>


### [187] [SoftWater: Class-Aware Rate Allocation for Softmax Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12026)
*Joao V. Cavalcanti,Ashia C. Wilson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SoftWater quantizes the softmax output head of small LLMs by framing it as a rate-distortion problem under KL divergence, exploiting class-aware geometry to allocate fine grids to frequent classes and coarse grids to rare ones, outperforming prior quantizers at matched rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training quantization pipelines typically leave the softmax head in high precision, but in small LLMs with modern vocabularies the head holds 15–30% of all parameters, so a nominal "2-bit" model with an fp16 head stores several times more bits per weight than claimed. The goal is efficient quantized head storage without large output-distribution distortion, challenging because prior linear-layer quantizers (e.g., WaterSIC) are near-optimal under weight MSE but not under output KL divergence.

Method: The paper poses softmax-layer quantization as a rate-distortion problem minimizing KL divergence between original and quantized output distributions. A second-order analysis reveals class-aware geometry where quantization error is weighted jointly by feature covariance and class-specific softmax curvature. A separability approximation replaces the Kn×Kn Cholesky factorization with a single n×n factorization rescaled per class, enabling lattice encoding via successive interference cancellation. Both statistics are obtained from a single forward pass. The method, SoftWater, assigns fine grids to frequent, low-variance classes and coarse grids to rare ones.

Result: Across five models (1B–32B), SoftWater outperforms the released WaterSIC quantizer on 59 of 60 test points at matched head rates, without WaterSIC's refinements, cutting head-induced KL by 6.5×–8.3× at 2 bits. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct with quantized bodies, a 2-bit head removes 45–60% of stored bytes for a 2.9–3.7% perplexity increase. Matching calibration data to the deployment domain yields the lowest KL. On a tied model, a 4-bit head is near-lossless and a 2-bit head costs under 4% perplexity.

Conclusion: Quantizing the softmax head is practically important for small LLMs since it stores a large fraction of parameters. By optimizing under output KL with class-aware geometry, SoftWater substantially reduces head-induced distortion at low bit rates, making 4-bit heads near-lossless and even 2-bit heads practical on tied models, while calibration-domain matching proves important for deployment.

Abstract: Post-training quantization pipelines routinely leave the softmax output layer in high precision. Yet in small LLMs with modern vocabularies, the head holds 15--30\% of all parameters, so a nominal ``2-bit'' model with an fp16 head can store several times as many bits per weight. We pose softmax-layer quantization as a rate-distortion problem under the KL divergence between the original and quantized output distributions. A second-order analysis reveals a class-aware geometry: quantization error is weighted jointly by feature covariance and class-specific softmax curvature. A separability approximation replaces the $Kn\times Kn$ Cholesky with one $n\times n$ factorization rescaled per class, making the lattice encodable by successive interference cancellation, with both statistics from a single forward pass. The resulting method, SoftWater, gives fine grids to frequent, low-variance classes and coarse grids to rare ones, a large gap under Zipfian token distributions. Across five models from 1B to 32B, SoftWater outperforms the released WaterSIC quantizer (near-optimal under linear-layer WMSE but not output KL) at matched head rates on 59 of 60 test points, using none of that pipeline's refinements and cutting head-induced KL by $6.5\times$--$8.3\times$ at 2 bits. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct with quantized bodies, a 2-bit head removes 45--60\% of stored bytes for a $2.9$--$3.7\%$ perplexity increase. Because the class-side statistic comes from calibration data, matching calibration to the deployment domain gives the lowest KL on that domain throughout. On a tied model, a 4-bit head is near-lossless and a 2-bit head costs under 4\% perplexity, making head quantization of such models practical.

</details>


### [188] [Uncertainty-Aware Probabilistic Constrained Clustering from Entangled Pairwise Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12027)
*Shaojie Zhang,Ke Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper formalizes probabilistic (soft) constrained clustering as uncertainty-aware probabilistic constrained clustering (UPCC), proposes the ProbPair angular objective for probabilistic pairwise relations, and introduces ECI-PP, an estimator–corrector–integrator framework that refines imperfect supervision, outperforming state-of-the-art deep constrained clustering methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Realistic pairwise supervision is often real-valued and entangled with ambiguity, expert judgment, and noise, yet existing deep constrained clustering (DCC) methods target hard, expert-agnostic constraints and treat soft labels purely numerically rather than semantically. This motivates a principled uncertainty-aware treatment of probabilistic constraints.

Method: The authors formalize UPCC by defining a canonical aleatoric target via a heterogeneous observation process and analyze its conditional identifiability. They propose ProbPair, an angular pairwise objective for probabilistic relations, and build ECI-PP, an estimator–corrector–integrator framework that refines imperfect supervision through belief estimation, correction, and reliability-aware integration.

Result: Across challenging probabilistic supervision settings on diverse benchmarks, ECI-PP outperforms state-of-the-art DCC methods and remains robust using a shared default configuration.

Conclusion: Probabilistic constrained clustering can be effectively addressed by modeling supervision uncertainty explicitly; the ECI-PP framework with the ProbPair objective yields superior and robust performance over existing DCC approaches under soft, imperfect pairwise supervision.

Abstract: Pairwise constrained clustering typically relies on hard must-link/cannot-link labels, whereas realistic pairwise supervision may be real-valued and entangle intrinsic ambiguity, expert judgment, and stochastic corruption. Existing deep constrained clustering (DCC) methods mainly target hard, expert-agnostic constraints, treating soft labels mostly numerically rather than semantically. We formalize this setting as uncertainty-aware probabilistic constrained clustering (UPCC), defining a canonical aleatoric target through a heterogeneous observation process and analyzing its conditional identifiability. We introduce ProbPair, an angular pairwise objective for probabilistic relations, and build ECI-PP, an estimator--corrector--integrator framework that refines imperfect supervision via belief estimation, correction, and reliability-aware integration. Across challenging probabilistic supervision settings, experiments on diverse benchmarks show that ECI-PP outperforms state-of-the-art DCC methods and remains robust with a shared default configuration.

</details>


### [189] [Clustered Randomized Smoothing for Stochastic Prediction Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12037)
*Eduardo Figueiredo,Frederik Mathiesen,Julian Schumann,Jens Kober,Arkady Zgonnikov,Luca Laurenti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces clustered α-smoothing, a randomized-smoothing framework for stochastic multi-modal regression that partitions noisy samples, applies α-smoothing within each cluster, and combines results into a mixture distribution, avoiding the mode-collapse problem of standard randomized smoothing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern stochastic predictors model rich multi-modal distributions, but ensuring robustness (especially adversarial robustness via randomized smoothing) is critical in safety-critical domains. However, randomized smoothing fails in stochastic multi-modal regression because it averages modes together (mode collapse), producing predictions that do not reflect the true underlying distribution.

Method: The proposed clustered α-smoothing framework: (1) partitions noisy samples using an arbitrary clustering algorithm, (2) applies α-smoothing locally within each cluster, and (3) combines the resulting predictions into a mixture distribution. The authors interpret the smoothing distribution as a mixture of α-smoothers and derive a lower bound on the probability that the smoothed prediction lies within a union of compact regions corresponding to distinct modes.

Result: On a stochastic trajectory prediction benchmark (driving simulator), the approach achieves on average a 27% lower Wasserstein distance to the ground-truth distribution compared to α-smoothing. In quadrotor control (modes = distinct feasible paths), it reduces the collision rate by 81% relative to state-of-the-art randomized smoothing.

Conclusion: Clustered α-smoothing effectively addresses mode collapse in randomized smoothing for multi-modal regression, providing substantial robustness and distributional-accuracy gains over state-of-the-art methods in both trajectory prediction and quadrotor control tasks.

Abstract: Modern stochastic predictors can model rich, multi-modal outcome distributions. However, this expressive power comes with challenges in ensuring robust predictions $-$ a critical requirement in safety-critical domains. Randomized smoothing is a leading technique for improving robustness, particularly against adversarial perturbations. Yet, in stochastic multi-modal regression settings, randomized smoothing often fails due to mode collapse, yielding averaged predictions that do not reflect the underlying distribution. To address this limitation, we propose clustered $α$-smoothing, a framework that (1) partitions noisy samples using an arbitrary clustering algorithm, (2) applies $α$-smoothing locally within each cluster, and (3) combines the resulting predictions into a mixture distribution. By interpreting the smoothing distribution as a mixture of $α$-smoothers, we derive a lower bound on the probability that the smoothed prediction lies within a union of compact regions corresponding to distinct modes. We empirically evaluate our framework on two benchmarks, demonstrating substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods. In stochastic trajectory prediction on a driving simulator dataset, our approach achieves, on average, a $27\%$ lower Wasserstein distance to the ground-truth distribution compared to $α$-smoothing. In quadrotor control, where modes correspond to distinct feasible paths to a target, our method reduces the collision rate by $81\%$ relative to the state-of-the-art randomized smoothing.

</details>


### [190] [AI4AI at Test-Time: Strong-to-Weak Capability Transfer via Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12307)
*Cheng Qian,Wenting Zhao,Liangwei Yang,Heng Wang,Jielin Qiu,Heng Ji,Silvio Savarese,Huan Wang,Shelby Heinecke*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies "strong-to-weak scaffolding": whether a stronger builder model can construct inference-time harnesses (no parameter updates) that let a weaker target model solve tasks more reliably. On four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks, builders refine harnesses iteratively using 5% validation data, nearly doubling average target performance from 0.49 to 0.91. Gains come from offloading unstable reasoning to deterministic code, benchmark-specific routing, and answer-format enforcement rather than extra sampling; builder reasoning effort improves harness quality, and weaker targets benefit most.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional distillation transfers large-model capabilities to small models via training-time parameter updates (teacher forcing, on-policy distillation). The authors ask whether such capability transfer can instead happen at test time, i.e., without any retraining of the weaker model.

Method: Strong-to-weak scaffolding: a strong builder model receives 5% of each benchmark's data as a validation set and iteratively designs/refines an inference-time harness over multiple rounds. The finalized harness is then applied to the weak target model on the full test set, with no updates to the target's parameters. Evaluated across four representative Theory-of-Mind benchmarks.

Result: Test-time capability transfer is highly effective, nearly doubling average target-model performance from 0.49 to 0.91. Gains derive mainly from (1) offloading unstable model reasoning into deterministic code, (2) benchmark-specific routing, and (3) strict answer-format enforcement—not from more extensive reasoning or broader sampling. Builder-model reasoning effort improves harness quality monotonically; platform effects are modest relative to builder capability; weaker target models gain the most.

Conclusion: Inference-time harness design is an important complement to conventional training-time distillation, letting strong models transfer cognitive structure to weaker models without any retraining.

Abstract: Recent work on distillation transfers the capabilities of large models to smaller ones often by updating the latter's parameters, through teacher forcing, on-policy distillation, and related training-time methods. In this paper, we ask whether such transfer can instead occur at test time. We study strong-to-weak scaffolding: whether a stronger builder model can construct inference-time harnesses that help a weaker target model solve tasks more reliably without any parameter updates. Using four representative Theory-of-Mind benchmarks, each builder model uses 5% of the data as a validation set to iteratively refine its harness over multiple rounds, after which the finalized harness is evaluated on the full test set. Empirically, this form of test-time capability transfer is highly effective, nearly doubling average target-model performance from 0.49 to 0.91. Our analysis shows that the gains come primarily from offloading unstable model reasoning into deterministic code, benchmark-specific routing, and strict answer-format enforcement, rather than from encouraging the target model to reason more extensively or sample more broadly. We further find that builder-model reasoning effort improves harness quality monotonically, platform effects are modest relative to the builder model's own capability, and weaker target models receive the largest gains. These results suggest that inference-time harness design is an important complement to conventional training-time distillation, enabling strong models to transfer cognitive structure to weaker models without retraining.

</details>


### [191] [Towards Truly Unsupervised Evaluation of Feature Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12057)
*Hafiz Saud Arshad,Muhammad Rajabinasab,Arthur Zimek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper critiques existing "unsupervised" evaluation methods for feature selection as being secretly supervised, and proposes a truly unsupervised framework based on Principal Component Analysis and optimal transport to measure feature selection quality without labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most methods used for unsupervised evaluation of feature selection algorithms contain critical design flaws, meaning they are not truly unsupervised but are effectively supervised evaluation under an unsupervised downstream task. The authors seek to correct this by providing a genuinely label-free evaluation framework.

Method: A novel evaluation framework that combines unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with optimal transport to assess the quality of feature selection methods without any label information.

Result: The proposed framework provides a truly unsupervised way to measure feature selection quality, addressing the flaws identified in conventional allegedly-unsupervised evaluation techniques.

Conclusion: Established unsupervised evaluation techniques for feature selection are not truly unsupervised, and the PCA + optimal transport framework offers a valid, label-free alternative for measuring feature selection algorithm quality.

Abstract: Feature selection is one of the most important and fundamental tasks in data mining, tackled by a family of methods with an established set of evaluation techniques to measure the quality of a specific method. Most of the methods commonly used for the unsupervised evaluation of feature selection algorithms suffer from critical design flaws which question their unsupervised nature. In this paper, we provide a critical discussion on the established allegedly unsupervised evaluation techniques, and shed light on the reasons why they are not truly unsupervised but, at best, supervised evaluation under an unsupervised downstream task. We also propose a novel, truly unsupervised evaluation framework to measure the quality of the feature selection algorithms without any form of information about the labels. The proposed framework utilizes unsupervised Principal Component Analysis, and optimal transport to measure the quality of the feature selection methods in a truly unsupervised manner.

</details>


### [192] [Faithful, Sufficient and Understandable: Rethinking Graph Counterfactual Explanations via Discrete Diffusion Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12083)
*David Bechtoldt,Sidney Bender*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes GDCE-I, a diffusion-based method for generating counterfactual explanations on graphs that produces minimal, valid, in-distribution edits by using a discrete denoising diffusion model with a novel discrete inversion scheme. It also introduces a unified evaluation framework of explanation desiderata and shows GDCE-I outperforms prior explainers across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNNs lack intrinsic explanations, limiting their use in high-stakes settings. Counterfactual explanations require minimal structural edits that flip predictions, but graph edits are discrete and combinatorial and must respect categorical node/edge types and domain rules (e.g., chemical valency). Existing explainers either generate edits that are not on the data manifold or do not search the full edit space. The authors aim to overcome both limitations and to fix the field's incomplete and inconsistent evaluation practices.

Method: GDCE-I uses a discrete denoising diffusion model combined with a novel discrete inversion scheme to generate distribution-aware counterfactual edits that exploit the entire domain edit space while keeping edits on the data manifold. The authors also derive a framework of explanation desiderata (validity, proximity/distance, sparsity, and other criteria) and apply it uniformly to all methods under a shared evaluation protocol.

Result: Across four benchmarks, GDCE-I outperforms related work by a large margin on the defined evaluation framework. Qualitative analysis on molecular data shows GDCE-I attains interpretable, in-distribution counterfactual solutions that respect domain constraints.

Conclusion: GDCE-I closes the gap left by prior graph counterfactual explainers by simultaneously staying on the data manifold and searching the full discrete edit space, yielding superior performance and interpretable solutions, while also establishing a standardized, principled framework for evaluating graph counterfactual explanations.

Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) achieve strong predictive performance on graph-structured data across domains such as chemistry, biology, and network analysis, yet they provide no intrinsic explanation of their predictions. This limits their adoption in high-stakes and safety-critical settings. Counterfactual explanations address this by revealing the minimal structural modifications that would change a model's prediction. On graphs, however, such a modification is hard to produce. The search space is discrete and combinatorial, and a valid answer must respect categorical node and edge types together with domain rules such as chemical valency in the case of molecular graphs. Existing explainers give up one of two things. Either edits are not held on the data manifold, or the search does not span the full edit space. We propose Graph Diffusion Counterfactual Explanation via Inversion (GDCE-I), which gives up neither. A discrete denoising diffusion model with a novel discrete inversion scheme enables distribution-aware edits leveraging the whole domain edit space. We further address the incomplete and inconsistent evaluation of graph counterfactuals by deriving a framework of explanation desiderata and applying it to every method under one shared protocol. Across four benchmarks, GDCE-I outperforms related work by a large margin on the defined framework. For the molecular domain, we further qualitatively show that GDCE-I attains interpretable in-distribution solutions.

</details>


### [193] [NAE: Normalizing AutoEncoder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12084)
*Muhammad Abdur Rafae,Niels Landwehr*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper analyzes flow autoencoders (normalizing flows with approximate inverses) and shows their standard loss is suboptimal, then proposes Normalizing Autoencoder (NAE) with a conditional loss aligning surrogate and reconstruction gradients, achieving state-of-the-art generation results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing flow autoencoders, which handle both full-dimensional and bottleneck settings, use a loss that is theoretically suboptimal because the encoder and decoder surrogates are not optimized in alignment with the reconstruction loss. The authors aim to correct this misalignment to improve training dynamics and generation quality.

Method: The authors present a theoretical analysis of training dynamics in flow autoencoders and prove the existing loss is suboptimal. Guided by this, they propose the Normalizing Autoencoder (NAE), which introduces a novel conditional loss that aligns the surrogate loss gradient with the reconstruction loss gradient.

Result: Extensive experiments on molecule generation, tabular data, and image benchmarks show that NAE achieves state-of-the-art performance, validating the importance of loss alignment in flow autoencoders.

Conclusion: Loss alignment between surrogate and reconstruction objectives is crucial for flow autoencoders; the proposed NAE framework establishes a powerful generative model and sets a new state of the art across multiple domains.

Abstract: We consider the setting of Normalizing flows with approximate inverses, an established paradigm spanning both full-dimensional ($d=D$) and bottleneck ($d<D$) settings, and group these models under the term flow autoencoders. We present a theoretical investigation into their training dynamics and prove that the proposed loss used by existing approaches is suboptimal; specifically, both encoder and decoder surrogates must be optimized in alignment with reconstruction loss. Guided by these insights, we propose Normalizing Autoencoder (NAE), which employs a novel conditional loss that aligns the surrogate loss gradient with that of reconstruction loss, directly improving upon the current standard. Extensive experiments across molecule generation, tabular data, and image benchmarks demonstrate that NAE achieves state of the art performance. Our work highlights the importance of loss alignment in flow autoencoders and establishes NAE as a powerful generative framework.

</details>


### [194] [Task- and dataset-specific information in protein language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12090)
*Roman Joeres,Ilya Senatorov,Olga V. Kalinina*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The study analyzes 13 protein language models (PLMs) across 15 downstream tasks to understand where informative embeddings reside, finding that the last layers rarely produce the best results and that task type and dataset characteristics determine which layer's embeddings are most useful.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A common practice is to use embeddings from a PLM's last layer for downstream tasks, but the models' internal behavior is poorly understood. The authors aim to investigate whether intermediate layer embeddings are more informative and what factors determine where task-relevant information is distributed across layers.

Method: The authors analyzed 13 PLMs across 15 downstream tasks from 11 datasets. They trained probe models on embeddings extracted from each layer of each PLM, compared their performance on downstream tasks, and computed characteristics of the latent spaces to estimate the information they contain.

Result: Last layers rarely contained embeddings giving the best downstream performance. A connection exists between task type and the distribution of relevant information across layers: residue-level property prediction shows steadily increasing understanding across layers (matching the pre-training objective), while whole-protein tasks are governed more by the dataset. Shallow-layer embeddings perform better for deep mutational scan (DMS) datasets, while deeper layers are more useful for datasets of diverse natural proteins. PLM performance drops significantly on artificial proteins.
