# cs.HC [[Back]](#toc)

### [206] [Socioduality: A Relational Process Framework for Human-AI Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11322)
*Mehmed Zahid Çögenli*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper introduces "socioduality," a new process-level construct for analyzing human–AI interaction that tracks how each party's response shapes the conditions for the other's next contribution, rather than evaluating only individual or final outputs. It defines nested analytical units, classification rules, and three propositions, and validates a frozen coding protocol with high inter-rater convergence on three unseen interaction records.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Human-AI research typically measures individual capabilities, combined performance, or final outputs, which fails to capture the sequential and reciprocal way one party's response becomes part of the conditions under which the other party's next contribution is formed. The authors seek a process-oriented construct that preserves this pathway information that endpoint-centered analyses cannot recover.

Method: The authors define socioduality as a sequential, reciprocal, history-carrying relational process between two distinguishable parties. They specify nested analytical units (moves, confirmed sociodual episodes, linked pathways, and the interaction container). A minimum episode A1-B1-A2 requires evidence of both response contingency and return contingency; candidate episodes are classified as confirmed, non-sociodual, or indeterminate, followed by secondary coding of response orientation and substantive contribution re-formation. Three propositions address history-conditioned formation, pathway divergence, and robustness differences among endpoint-equivalent pathways. A frozen operational protocol was calibrated on three previously unseen natural human-AI records via two independently executed model-based evaluator series.

Result: Move and candidate reconstruction converged exactly in two of three cases and differed by a single local multimodal unitisation decision in the third. Remaining disagreement was concentrated at return-contingency boundaries, indicating strong but boundary-sensitive reliability of the coding protocol.

Conclusion: Socioduality offers a bounded, empirically tractable process construct for analyzing how human and AI contributions are formed through interaction, while preserving pathway information that endpoint-centred analysis cannot recover.

Abstract: Human-AI research often evaluates individual capabilities, combined performance, or final outputs, but these approaches do not preserve how one party's response becomes part of the conditions under which the other party's next contribution is formed. This article introduces socioduality, a sequential, reciprocal, and history-carrying relational process between two distinguishable parties in which a response from one party becomes part of the observable conditions under which the other party's subsequent contribution, judgement, decision, or action is formed. Specified for human-AI dyads, the construct uses nested units: moves, confirmed sociodual episodes, linked pathways, and the broader interaction container. A minimum episode A1-B1-A2 requires evidence of response contingency and return contingency; candidate episodes are classified as confirmed, non-sociodual, or indeterminate before secondary coding of response orientation and substantive contribution re-formation. Three propositions address history-conditioned formation, pathway divergence, and robustness differences among endpoint-equivalent pathways. A frozen operational protocol was calibrated on three previously unseen natural human-AI records through two separately executed model-based evaluator series. Move and candidate reconstruction converged exactly in two cases and differed by one local multimodal unitisation decision in the third; remaining disagreement was concentrated at return-contingency boundaries. Socioduality therefore provides a bounded and empirically tractable process construct for analysing how human and AI contributions are formed through interaction while preserving pathway information that endpoint-centred analysis cannot recover.

</details>


### [207] [QUARTZ: Qualitative Understanding via Accessible Representation and Visualization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11364)
*Omar Khan,JooYoung Seo*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: QUARTZ is a web-based, screen-reader-accessible system providing multimodal representations of qualitative data visualizations (concept maps, network graphs, Sankey diagrams, coding stripes) for blind and low-vision researchers, developed through iterative co-design and evaluated with 8 BLV participants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Qualitative data visualizations are integral to research practice but remain entirely inaccessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) researchers. While quantitative charts have advanced multimodal accessibility solutions, qualitative visualizations—with their non-linear, semantically rich structures—have received no attention, creating barriers to independent participation in qualitative inquiry.

Method: The authors built QUARTZ, a web-based system offering screen-reader-accessible, multimodal representations of four qualitative visualization types (concept maps, network graphs, Sankey diagrams, coding stripes). They employed the Rapid Iterative Testing and Evaluation (RITE) method in a user study with 8 BLV participants who completed 12 tasks across the four visualization types, using iterative co-design to identify and resolve accessibility barriers.

Result: The study exposed accessibility barriers unique to qualitative visualizations, including non-linear navigation breakdowns and semantic comprehension gaps that are absent from quantitative chart research. Iterative co-design with BLV users successfully resolved these issues.

Conclusion: The paper contributes empirical evidence and design guidelines for an underexplored visualization domain, advancing the infrastructure that BLV researchers need to participate independently in qualitative research.

Abstract: Qualitative data visualizations -- concept maps, network graphs, Sankey diagrams, and coding stripes -- are integral to research practice, yet remain entirely inaccessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) researchers. While visualization has seen advanced multimodal solutions for quantitative charts, qualitative visualizations, and their non-linear, semantically rich structures have received no attention. We present QUARTZ, a web-based system that provides screen-reader-accessible, multimodal representations of qualitative data visualizations. Using the Rapid Iterative Testing and Evaluation (RITE) method, we conducted a user study with 8 BLV participants who completed 12 tasks across four visualization types. Our findings expose accessibility barriers unique to qualitative visualizations -- non-linear navigation breakdowns and semantic comprehension gaps absent from quantitative chart research---and document how iterative co-design with BLV users resolved them. We contribute empirical evidence and design guidelines for an underexplored visualization domain, advancing the infrastructure BLV researchers need to participate independently in qualitative inquiry.

</details>


### [208] ["I Don't Want My Mental Health App To Give Me Mental Health Barriers": Unpacking The Need For Digital Mental Health Tracking Services With And For The Blind Community](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11391)
*Omar Khan,JooYoung Seo*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Digital mental health (DMH) tracking services exclude blind users through design that assumes sight. A mixed-methods study (survey of 93 legally blind adults and 10 interviews) found users digitally literate yet blocked by pre-existing design choices, particularly in community-support features, and proposes designing with blind users from the start.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DMH tracking services promise personalized, continuous well-being support but are typically designed only for sighted users, producing systematic exclusion of the blind community: services that cannot be evaluated for accessibility without payment, community features that exclude the users they claim to support, and interfaces that leave blind users digitally literate but functionally blocked.

Method: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods study in the United States: Phase 1 surveyed 93 legally blind adults on usage patterns, adoption decisions, and data-agency preferences; Phase 2 conducted semi-structured interviews with 10 respondents. Closed-ended responses were analyzed with descriptive statistics and the Kruskal-Wallis test; open-ended and interview data used inductive thematic analysis, interpreted through Norman and Skinner's eHealth Literacy framework.

Result: Mindfulness, sleep, and goal-tracking services were the most-used categories, yet participants reported recurring exclusion from community-support features valued by other users. The eHealth Literacy framework's "computer literacy" dimension proved insufficient: many participants possessed the literacy but were blocked from applying it by design choices that predate the user.

Conclusion: The authors contribute design recommendations for transparent pre-purchase accessibility evaluation, accessibility-native (rather than retrofitted) interfaces, and user-controlled data agency, aiming not merely to accommodate blind users but to design DMH tracking services with them from the start.

Abstract: Digital mental health (DMH) tracking services promise continuous, personalized support for well-being, but their design often assumes sighted users. For the blind community, this assumption produces a distinct pattern of exclusion: services whose accessibility cannot be evaluated without first paying for them, community features that exclude the users they purport to support, and interfaces that leave users digitally literate but functionally blocked. We report on an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study of blind users' experiences with DMH tracking services in the United States. In the first phase, 93 legally blind adults completed a survey about their usage patterns, adoption decisions, and data-agency preferences; in the second, 10 survey respondents participated in semi-structured interviews. We analyzed closed-ended responses using descriptive statistics and the Kruskal-Wallis test, and open-ended and interview data using inductive thematic analysis, interpreting findings through Norman and Skinner's eHealth Literacy framework. Participants identified mindfulness, sleep, and goal-tracking services as their most-used categories, but also described recurring exclusion from the community-support features that other users value most. We argue that the framework's "computer literacy" dimension is insufficient on its own: many of our participants possessed the literacy but were blocked from applying it by design choices that predate the user. We contribute design recommendations for transparent pre-purchase accessibility evaluation, accessibility-native rather than retrofitted interfaces, and user-controlled data agency -- recommendations intended not to accommodate blind users but to design DMH tracking services with them from the start.

</details>


### [209] [The Role of Variability in Human-Machine Interaction Experience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11401)
*Sean Kille,Jan Lars Hagemann,Anne Voormann,Balint Varga,Andrea Kiesel,Sören Hohmann*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A variability-aware controller that preserves natural human movement variability improves perceived usability in shared-control HMI without sacrificing task performance, compared to a variance-reduction controller.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional shared-control and haptic-assistance methods ignore the stochastic nature of human motor behavior, which may limit both task performance and the human interaction experience. The authors aim to address this gap by designing controllers that account for natural human movement variability.

Method: The authors designed an experimental physically coupled haptic interaction task and evaluated a novel human-variability-aware optimal controller across three conditions: (1) a conventional controller reducing overall variability, (2) a variability-aware controller preserving natural human variability patterns, and (3) a human-only baseline. They measured behavioral variability, task performance, and human interaction experience.

Result: The variability-aware controller significantly increased perceived interaction quality (usability) while maintaining task performance, compared to the variance-reduction and human-only conditions.

Conclusion: Incorporating stochastic human movement characteristics into shared-control design is important and feasible; the proposed variability-aware control strategy offers benefits for human-centered HMI design.

Abstract: Human-machine interaction (HMI) requires control strategies that account for the nature of human motor behavior. Conventional shared-control and haptic-assistance methods typically ignore the stochastic nature of human behavior, potentially limiting both performance and human interaction experience. In this study, we designed an experimental setting and evaluated a novel human-variability-aware optimal controller. Participants performed a physically coupled haptic interaction task in three conditions: a controller mode that aims at conventionally reducing overall variability, a variability-aware controller mode designed to maintain human natural variability patterns, and a human-only control condition serving as a baseline. We analyzed behavioral variability, task performance, and human interaction experience. The results show that considering natural movement variability significantly increased perceived interaction quality in terms of usability while maintaining task performance. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating stochastic human movement characteristics into shared-control designs and demonstrate the feasibility and benefits of the proposed control strategy for human-centered control design of HMI.

</details>


### [210] [How Children Collaborate within Programmable AR Environments with Co-Located Collaborative Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11442)
*Romina Mahinpei,Diya Ajay Hundiwala,Sandy Zhang,Lana Glisic,Andrés Monroy-Hernández*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper extends the programmable AR app Capybara with co-located collaborative features and, through workshops with 9 children, finds that collaboration emerges in three lightweight, implicit forms: parallel play with social awareness, iterative remixing, and spontaneous peer support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Programmable AR environments are promising for children's creative learning through embodied interaction, and AR systems increasingly support co-located collaboration, yet little is known about how children actually collaborate within co-located programmable AR environments.

Method: The authors extended Capybara, an existing programmable AR application for children, with co-located collaborative features enabling shared visibility and interaction across devices, then conducted workshops with 9 children to examine whether and how collaboration emerges during use.

Result: Collaboration was often lightweight and implicit, emerging through three complementary forms: parallel play with social awareness, iterative remixing, and spontaneous peer support.

Conclusion: The findings provide design insights for future child-centered programmable AR systems that better support co-located collaborative experiences.

Abstract: Programmable augmented reality (AR) environments are emerging as a promising way to support children's creative learning through embodied interaction with digital characters and physical space. At the same time, AR systems are increasingly capable of supporting co-located collaborative experiences. However, little is known about how children collaborate within programmable AR environments offering co-located collaborative features. In response, we extended Capybara, an existing programmable AR application for children, with co-located collaborative features supporting shared visibility and interaction across devices. We then conducted workshops with 9 children to examine whether and how collaboration emerges during use. Across our workshops, collaboration was often lightweight and implicit, emerging through three complementary forms: parallel play with social awareness, iterative remixing, and spontaneous peer support. Together, our findings provide insights for designing future child-centered programmable AR systems that better support co-located collaborative experiences.

</details>


### [211] [Player Perceptions of Generative AI in Games: A Steam Review Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11539)
*Mahsa Bazzaz,Seth Cooper*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study empirically examines how players perceive generative AI in games on Steam, comparing it to procedural content generation (PCG). Analyzing 508,192 English reviews, it finds that games disclosing generative AI use get lower recommendation rates and more negative sentiment than PCG games. Players view generative AI as signaling low developer investment, and the authors argue generative AI should serve player needs rather than merely reduce development costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI is rapidly being adopted in game development and has sparked large discussions among players, yet there is little empirical work on how players actually perceive AI-generated content. The authors aim to fill this gap with empirical evidence.

Method: A mixed-methods approach: (1) quantitative analysis of generative AI adoption in the Steam marketplace, using procedural content generation (PCG) as a baseline for a successfully integrated generative technology; (2) qualitative analysis of 508,192 English-language reviews, including thematic analysis of 600 reviews, to study player reception of generative AI.

Result: Games disclosing generative AI use receive lower recommendation rates and more negative overall sentiment compared to PCG games. Thematic analysis shows players perceive generative AI in games as a sign of low developer investment.

Conclusion: Drawing on human-centered AI frameworks, the authors argue that successful generative AI adoption requires deploying generative AI for what players need, not merely for what makes development cheaper.

Abstract: The rapid adoption of generative AI in game development has created large discussions among players, yet little empirical work has examined how players actually perceive AI-generated content. Employing quantitative methods, we study the adoption of generative AI in games in the Steam marketplace, using procedural content generation (PCG) as a baseline of a generative technology that was successfully integrated into games over several decades. Furthermore, using qualitative methods, we study player reception of generative AI by analyzing 508,192 English-language reviews. We found that games disclosing generative AI use receive lower recommendation rates and more negative overall sentiment than PCG games. Thematic analysis of 600 reviews shows that players perceive the use of generative AI in games as low developer investment in the game. Drawing on human-centered AI frameworks, we argue that successful generative AI adoption requires deploying generative AI for what players need, not for what makes development cheaper.

</details>


### [212] [Measuring Browser Webcam Gaze Honestly: A Capture-Clock Methodology and Open Reference Implementation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11566)
*Chi-Sheng Chen,Gabriel A. Brat*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Browser webcam gaze trackers report misleadingly fast (~0 ms) inference latency because timestamps are applied at sample emission rather than frame capture. The paper proposes an honest measurement method using rVFC capture/presentation times, exact source-frame pairing via per-frame queues, and lower-bound estimates for opaque engines like WebGazer, with an open TypeScript benchmark harness demonstrated on WebGazer and a FaceMesh+KRR pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Browser-based webcam gaze trackers are increasingly deployed for crowd-scale data collection and clinical contexts, but reported latency figures are unreliable. Existing practice timestamps each gaze sample at emission time, yielding ~0 ms measured latency regardless of actual engine speed, masking real-world performance and undermining evaluation of these systems.

Method: Recover a per-frame capture clock using the browser's requestVideoFrameCallback (rVFC) API: use captureTime where the browser exposes it for local camera streams, otherwise use presentationTime, which makes recovered latencies verifiable lower bounds. Achieve exact source-frame pairing through a per-frame queue for engines that expose their inference pipeline, and derive a further lower bound for engines that do not (e.g., WebGazer). Release an open-source TypeScript implementation and benchmark harness demonstrated on two interchangeable engines: WebGazer and a new FaceMesh+KRR pipeline.

Result: The method enables honest end-to-end latency measurement, replacing the misleading ~0 ms figures with capture-to-emission latency that reflects true engine speed. For engines without exposed pipelines, the approach provides a verifiable lower bound on latency rather than an artificially optimistic exact value.

Conclusion: Accurate latency measurement in browser gaze trackers requires timing samples from the source frame's capture/presentation time, not emission time. The open-source tooling and benchmark harness enable fair comparison of interchangeable gaze-tracking engines in real-world settings.

Abstract: Browser-based webcam gaze trackers are increasingly used for crowd-scale data collection and in clinical settings where lab eye trackers are impractical, but the reported latency numbers may not represent real world functionality. The common practice of timestamping each gaze sample when it is emitted, rather than when its source frame was captured, makes the measured inference latency read about $0\,$ms no matter how slow the engine really is. We show how to measure it honestly, recovering a per-frame capture clock from the browser's \texttt{re\-quest\-Video\-Frame\-Call\-back} (rVFC) API (\texttt{captureTime} where the browser exposes it for local camera streams, else \texttt{presentationTime}, in which case every recovered latency is a verifiable lower bound): exact source-frame pairing through a per-frame queue for engines that expose their inference pipeline, and a further lower bound for engines that do not, such as WebGazer. We release an open TypeScript implementation and benchmark harness, demonstrated on two interchangeable engines: WebGazer and a new FaceMesh+KRR pipeline.

</details>


### [213] [RAGE-Vis:A Relation-Aware Generative Editing Interface for Natural Language-Based Chart Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11581)
*Ziyao Kang,Yiping Sun,Linxuan Tian,Henghuan Qu,Wei Zeng,Jiazhi Xia*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: RAGE-Vis is a relation-aware, generative editing interface that lets users edit bitmap charts via natural language, converting them into editable parameterized representations and supporting composite, cross-component intents with hierarchical panels and coordinated widgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Natural language chart editing intents are often composite and span multiple components, but existing systems map instructions to a single operation or widget, failing to handle high-level requests and producing locally plausible yet globally inconsistent results because they ignore relationships between chart components.

Method: The system takes bitmap chart images as input and converts them into an editable parameterized intermediate representation. It parses composite intents, identifies targets and scopes, and generates hierarchical editing panels for underspecified requests. It also identifies potentially affected fields via visual encoding relations, structural relationships, and expressive consistency relations, organizing them into actionable widgets for cross-component coordinated control.

Result: Two case studies demonstrate applicability to complex editing tasks (style adjustment, data extension, order rearrangement, legend layout, color mapping). A user study shows participants can effectively handle underspecified requests, explore candidate alternatives, and maintain cross-component consistency.

Conclusion: RAGE-Vis effectively addresses the limitations of single-operation mapping by enabling composite, cross-component chart editing from natural language, improving handling of underspecified requests and global consistency in complex editing tasks.

Abstract: Natural language offers an easy way for users to express chart editing intents, which are often composite and cross-component (e.g., adjusting style, extending categories, highlighting values). However, existing methods typically map instructions to a single operation or widget, limiting their ability to handle high-level requests and often producing locally plausible but globally inconsistent results due to a lack of awareness of relationships between chart components. To address these challenges, we introduce RAGE-Vis, a Relation-Aware Generative Editing interface for natural language-based chart editing. The system supports bitmap chart images as input and converts them into an editable parameterized intermediate representation. Instead of mapping instructions to a single edit or widget, RAGE-Vis parses composite intents, identifies targets and scopes, and generates hierarchical editing panels for underspecified requests, enabling users to adjust both global settings and local parameters. Furthermore, RAGE-Vis identifies potentially affected fields based on visual encoding relations, structural relationships, and expressive consistency relations, and organizes them into actionable widgets to support cross-component coordinated controls. Through two case studies, we demonstrate the applicability of RAGE-Vis in complex editing tasks, including style adjustment, data extension, order rearrangement, legend layout, and color mapping. A user study further shows that participants can effectively handle underspecified requests, explore candidate alternatives, and maintain cross-component consistency with RAGE-Vis.

</details>


### [214] [VisPuzzle: Task-Aware Composite Visualization Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11635)
*Zheng Wang,Zhiyang Shen,Lingyun Yu,Shixia Liu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: VisPuzzle models visualization composition as a stepwise graph-search problem over data and visual composition operations, using Monte Carlo Graph Search with a reward function balancing task relevance, perceptual effectiveness, and aesthetics to generate high-quality composite visualizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Compositing multiple visualizations into a coherent whole is difficult because of the vast design space and the need to simultaneously balance coverage of task-relevant data insights (e.g., trends and outliers), perceptual clarity, and aesthetic quality.

Method: VisPuzzle formalizes visualization composition as a stepwise search problem over a composition graph, where nodes represent data composition operations (union, join) or visual composition operations (component relationships, spatial arrangements, component proportions) and edges encode feasible transitions. Monte Carlo Graph Search efficiently identifies high-quality candidates, guided by a reward function balancing task relevance, perceptual effectiveness, and aesthetic coherence.

Result: A use case and a user study show that the top-ranked candidates produced by VisPuzzle align closely with human judgments of composition quality, supporting principled and scalable visualization composition.

Conclusion: VisPuzzle demonstrates utility in supporting principled and scalable visualization composition, with top-ranked results matching human quality judgments.

Abstract: Compositing multiple visualizations into a coherent whole remains challenging due to the vast design space and the need to balance the coverage of task-relevant data insights (e.g., trends and outliers), perceptual clarity, and aesthetic quality. In this paper, we present VisPuzzle, a task-aware method that formulates visualization composition as a stepwise search problem over a composition graph. In this graph, nodes represent either data composition operations (e.g., union, join) or visual composition operations that determine component relationships, spatial arrangements, or component proportions, and edges encode feasible transitions between operations. We employ Monte Carlo Graph Search to efficiently identify high-quality composition candidates from this graph, guided by a reward function that balances task relevance, perceptual effectiveness, and aesthetic coherence. A use case and a user study show that the top-ranked candidates produced by VisPuzzle align closely with human judgments of composition quality, demonstrating its utility in supporting principled and scalable visualization composition.

</details>


### [215] [A Browser-Based Gesture-Driven Avatar Interaction Framework for Metaverse Onboarding Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11708)
*Deepti Parachuri,Chhayank Sahu,Sameer Singh Choudhary*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A lightweight, browser-based, controller-free gesture interaction layer for metaverse onboarding is built with Google MediaPipe, combining hand-raise navigation and in-place walking, and evaluated with five participants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Avatar interaction should feel natural and immersive in the metaverse, but existing approaches force users through controller-based interfaces. The work aims to enable avatars to respond to users directly without requiring keyboards or controllers.

Method: A gesture-driven interaction layer is developed for a browser-based metaverse onboarding environment. It combines real-time gesture recognition via Google MediaPipe with two locomotion techniques—hand-raise navigation and in-place walking—allowing users to trade precision against physical immersion. Evaluation was conducted through a structured internal onboarding session with five participants.

Result: The paper reports on what worked, what failed, and the design trade-offs emerging from combining these techniques in one deployed system, based on findings from the five-participant onboarding session.

Conclusion: The contribution is the integration, deployment, and evaluation of hand-raise navigation and in-place walking as a single lightweight, web-deployable, controller-free interaction model, with design trade-offs documented to inform future work.

Abstract: Avatar interaction shapes how engaging and immersive a metaverse experience feels, and for that interaction to feel natural, avatars need to respond to users without forcing them through a controller-based interface first. This paper describes a gesture-driven interaction layer built for a browser-based metaverse onboarding environment, where users explore a set of virtual rooms as an avatar and interact with embedded video, document, and quiz content using hand, arm, and head gestures instead of a keyboard or controller. The system combines real-time gesture recognition (Google MediaPipe) with two alternative locomotion techniques - hand-raise navigation and in-place walking - so users can trade off precision against physical immersion depending on the task. The contribution is the integration, deployment, and evaluation of these techniques as a single lightweight, web-deployable, controller-free interaction model, assessed through a structured internal onboarding session with five participants. We report what worked, what didn't, and the design trade-offs that came out of combining these techniques in one deployed system.

</details>


### [216] [ATOM: Geometry-Aware Microgesture towards Object-Agnostic Tangible Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11871)
*Yinqiao Wang,Hao Xu,Qixuan Liu,Shengdong Zhao,Pheng-Ann Heng,Chi-Wing Fu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: ATOM is an integrated AR framework that turns everyday handheld objects into tangible interfaces supporting 0D, 1D, and 2D microgesture interactions by detecting and prioritizing ergonomic geometric affordances, outperforming baselines in usability and workload while generalizing across diverse objects and grasps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Support microgesture interactions across different everyday objects rather than being tied to specific, instrumented objects; automatically leverage each object's geometric affordance to enable fluid, object-agnostic tangible interaction in real-world AR scenarios.

Method: 1) A fingertip-aware detection pipeline using generative 2D and 3D models to enhance and refine object geometry. 2) A usability-based method that prioritizes detected elements according to ergonomic suitability for interaction. 3) An AR system that maps these elements into tangible user interfaces supporting 0D, 1D, and 2D microgestures. Evaluation includes comparison against ablation baselines on cooking-object tasks (task completion, SUS, NASA-TLX) and a 10-object generalization study.

Result: Across transitions among everyday cooking objects of varying shapes and sizes, ATOM outperformed ablation baselines in task completion, usability (SUS), and workload (NASA-TLX). A further study with 10 objects demonstrated generalizability across objects and grasps.

Conclusion: ATOM shows strong potential for fluid, object-agnostic tangible interaction in real-world AR scenarios, leveraging geometric affordances and ergonomic prioritization to support microgesture interfaces on arbitrary everyday objects.

Abstract: This paper presents ATOM, an integrated framework towards agnostic and tangible object interactions with microgestures. Our goal is to support microgesture interactions across different everyday objects, with the capability to automatically leverage the geometric affordance of each object. We formulate a fingertip-aware detection pipeline to leverage generative 2D and 3D models for geometry enhancement and refinement. We then introduce a usability-based method to prioritize the detected elements based on their ergonomic suitability for interactions. Building on this foundation, we further develop an AR system to transform everyday handheld objects into tangible user interfaces with 0D, 1D, and 2D microgesture interactions. Across transitions among everyday cooking objects of varying shapes and sizes, ATOM outperformed ablation baselines in task completion, usability (SUS), and workload (NASA-TLX). A further study with 10 objects demonstrates ATOM's generalizability across objects and grasps, highlighting its potential towards fluid, object-agnostic tangible interaction in real-world AR scenarios.

</details>


### [217] [Synchronized AMG and EMG Dataset of Lower-limb Muscle Activities in Everyday Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11958)
*Dongxu Tang,Shih Ying-Lei,Zhuoyi Ren,Jianting Liao,Yitian Shao*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A multimodal lower-limb movement dataset combining accelerometer-derived muscle activity (AMG), surface EMG, and optical motion capture from 30 healthy adults across 16 tasks, with benchmarks for estimating four lower-limb joint angles from AMG signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding lower-limb muscle coordination is important for studying movement impairment, rehabilitation, and physical performance. This requires reproducible multimodal recordings that link local muscle-related signals with body-level kinematics. EMG captures neural-level electrical activation, while AMG offers a mechanical (vibration-based) alternative for monitoring muscle activity; combining both with kinematics enables richer analysis.

Method: The authors collected synchronized multimodal data from the left leg of 30 healthy adult subjects. AMG was recorded using 16 triaxial accelerometers evenly divided into four muscle-site clusters; surface EMG used four channels; and a 15-marker optical motion-capture system captured lower-body kinematics, with marker trajectories used to compute bilateral knee and ankle joint angles. The dataset contains 1,918 trials across 16 task conditions. Benchmarking estimated four joint angles from 300 ms windows of 5-100 Hz band-pass-filtered AMG data using four reference models, with a separate modality ablation comparing matched EMG features.

Result: In the primary cross-subject benchmark, four reference models achieved mean absolute errors of 8.840-9.591 degrees for joint-angle estimation. The results characterize performance across subjects, tasks, and joint angles, and examine the effects of sensor configuration, modality, number of training subjects, and frequency representation.

Conclusion: The dataset provides a synchronized, multimodal resource for studying lower-limb muscle coordination, with documented timing definitions, processed data, and reproducible benchmark resources. Benchmark and ablation results establish baselines for AMG-based joint-angle estimation and demonstrate the value of mechanical muscle sensing alongside EMG.

Abstract: Understanding how lower-limb muscle groups coordinate is important for studying movement impairment, rehabilitation, and physical performance. Reproducible analysis of this coordination requires multimodal recordings that relate local muscle-related signals with body-level kinematics. Complementing neural-level electrical activation captured by EMG, AMG provides a valuable mechanical approach to monitoring muscle activity. Here, we introduce a synchronized, multimodal dataset for healthy-adult lower-limb activities. For data collection on the left leg, 16 triaxial accelerometers were evenly divided into four muscle-site clusters for AMG recording, complemented by four surface EMG channels. A 15-marker optical motion-capture (MoCap) system captured lower-body kinematics, with the resulting marker trajectories used to compute bilateral knee and ankle joint angles. Our dataset contains 1,918 trials from 30 subjects across 16 task conditions. We benchmark the dataset by estimating four joint angles from 300 ms windows of the 5-100 Hz band-pass-filtered AMG data and assess matched EMG features in a separate modality ablation. In the primary cross subject benchmark, the four reference models achieved mean absolute errors of 8.840$^\circ$-9.591$^\circ$. The benchmark and ablation results characterize performance across subjects, tasks, and joint angles and examine the effects of sensor configuration, modality, the number of training subjects, and frequency representation. The release includes documented timing definitions, processed data, and reproducible benchmark resources. https://dongxutang918-afk.github.io/SAME-Limb/

</details>


### [218] [IF:CARGO: LLM-Based Semantic Compilation for Al-Native Rule Programming Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12195)
*Ting-Chen Hsu,Lianye Zhang,Jiangxu Lin,Zhaoyi Yu,Fei Qin,Zihao Chen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: IF: CARGO is an experimental puzzle game where players write natural-language IF/THEN rules that an LLM translates into deterministic in-game commands, effectively using the model as a semantic compiler rather than an autonomous agent. A 24-player playtest found players understood the AI as a translation intermediary and could revise strategies through feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper seeks an alternative to treating LLMs as autonomous game-playing agents, addressing concerns about non-determinism and loss of player authorship. It explores how AI can be integrated into gameplay as a controllable, deterministic translation layer that keeps the player as the author of strategy.

Method: IF: CARGO lets players author IF/THEN rules in natural language; an LLM translates these into a constrained command schema for deterministic validation and execution by the game engine, framing AI interaction as semantic debugging. A mixed-methods playtest with 24 participants across eight levels measured player attempts, thinking time, perceived controllability, adjustability, and interpretations of the AI's role.

Result: Players generally understood the model as a translation intermediary and could revise their strategies through feedback. Periodic commands, multi-robot coordination, and rule-priority mechanics created greater cognitive and diagnostic demands.

Conclusion: The study proposes a practical pattern for AI-native gameplay: constrain natural-language input, preserve player authorship, and ensure deterministic execution.

Abstract: This case study presents IF: CARGO, an experimental puzzle game that uses a large language model as a semantic compiler rather than an autonomous game-playing agent. Players author IF/THEN rules in natural language, which the model translates into a constrained command schema for deterministic validation and execution by the game engine. This architecture creates a playable loop of expression, execution, observation, and revision, framing AI interaction as semantic debugging. A mixed-methods playtest with 24 participants across eight levels examined player attempts, thinking time, perceived controllability, adjustability, and interpretations of the AI's role. Results suggest that players generally understood the model as a translation intermediary and could revise their strategies through feedback, while periodic commands, multi-robot coordination, and rule-priority mechanics created greater cognitive and diagnostic demands. The study proposes a practical pattern for AI-native gameplay: constrain natural-language input, preserve player authorship, and ensure deterministic execution.

</details>


### [219] ["Pharos Night: Crown Pursuit": An AI-Native Deck-Building and Tactical Arena Game Design Based on Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12216)
*Ting-Chen Hsu,Jueyao Liu,Yanzi Zhou,Jiangxu Lin,Haoyu Xu,Yuwen Liu,Yanjia Liu,Bangjing Xu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Pharos Night: Crown Pursuit is an AI-native deck-building and tactical arena game built on a multi-agent system, where LLMs generate content, drive NPC decisions, and mediate natural-language interactions, with structured JSON and predefined mechanics constraining outputs for meaningful gameplay.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rise of generative AI has prompted exploration of AI-native games where gameplay rules are directly driven by generative AI, moving beyond conventional hard-coded rule systems toward emergent experiences.

Method: The authors develop a multi-agent system using large language models to generate materials and cards, support NPC decision-making, and mediate natural-language interactions. Players collect materials and describe desired card effects in natural language, then choose to negotiate or fight NPCs. To constrain generation, the system parses model responses as structured JSON, builds card effects from predefined mechanics, and maps qualitative effect levels to designer-specified numerical values.

Result: A playtest with 13 participants suggests the system provides strategically meaningful and engaging AI-driven gameplay, while also revealing challenges in predictability, transparency, and player control.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates the potential of multi-agent generative AI systems to create more emergent digital game experiences, while highlighting open challenges in predictability, transparency, and player control.

Abstract: With advancements in generative AI technology, an increasing number of researchers have begun exploring AI-native games in which gameplay rules are directly driven by generative AI. This paper presents "Pharos Night: Crown Pursuit," an AI-native deck-building and tactical arena game based on a multi-agent system. The game uses large language models to generate materials and cards, support NPC decision-making, and mediate natural-language interactions. During play, players collect materials, describe desired card effects in natural language, and choose whether to negotiate or fight with NPCs in the arena. To constrain model-generated outcomes, the system parses responses as structured JSON, constructs card effects from predefined mechanics, and maps qualitative effect levels to designer-specified numerical values. A small-scale playtest with 13 participants suggests that the system can provide strategically meaningful and engaging AI-driven gameplay, while also revealing challenges related to predictability, transparency, and player control. This work demonstrates the potential of multi-agent generative AI systems for creating more emergent digital game experiences.

</details>

### [220] [Dynamic Governance of Multi-LLM Agent Systems for Collaborative Conversational Outcomes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11207)
*Alexander Liss,Nicholas Desmond,Santiago Gil Gallego*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Adding a control-theoretic governance layer (Experience Orchestrator) to LLM-LLM agent interactions prevents goal-less collapse and produces a +32pp lift in high-intent advisor contact rate (78.1% vs. 46.1%), with the contextual bandit explaining 97% of outcome variance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When two LLM agents with opposing objectives interact over multiple turns without a shared goal function, the exchange collapses—worse than competition, neither agent achieves its objective. The paper asks whether a control-theoretic governance layer can substitute for that missing shared goal function, tested in a simulated financial services setting.

Method: The Experience Orchestrator (EO) governs the joint LLM-LLM trajectory using three mechanisms: (1) a Contextual Bandit (CB) that selects content arms calibrated from real-world web analytics; (2) a PID controller enforcing behavioral consistency via dynamic schema constraints; and (3) a POMDP belief tracker maintaining a probabilistic model of visitor intent. Evaluated across 60,000 simulations against a naive LLM control, with persona-level and factor-variance analysis.

Result: EO achieves a +32 percentage point lift in high-intent advisor contact rate (78.1% vs. 46.1% over naive LLM control). Contextual Bandit variant selection accounts for 97% of between-factor outcome variance, indicating the governance policy—not environmental initial conditions—determines trajectory outcomes. Persona analysis shows two regimes: for visitors with no natural inclination to convert, the governance layer is the difference between functional and non-functional; for visitors already near alignment, naive empathetic LLM defaults are largely sufficient.

Conclusion: A control-theoretic governance layer can substitute for a missing shared goal function in multi-turn LLM-LLM interaction, dramatically improving outcomes. However, all findings are conditional on LLM-to-LLM simulation; the PID controller has not been calibrated against real human unpredictability, and validating EO on live traffic is the critical next step.

Abstract: When two LLM agents with structurally opposed objectives interact across multiple turns, the absence of a shared goal function produces not competition but collapse: the visitor capitulates, the site agent stops varying its approach, and the conversation terminates without achieving either agent's stated objective. This paper asks whether a control-theoretic governance layer can substitute for that missing goal function. The Experience Orchestrator (EO) addresses this in a simulated financial services environment where a site agent guides a visitor toward advisor contact while the visitor maintains psychologically realistic resistance. EO governs the joint trajectory through three mechanisms: a Contextual Bandit (CB) that selects content arms calibrated from real-world web analytics, a PID controller that enforces behavioral consistency via dynamic schema constraints, and a POMDP belief tracker that maintains a probabilistic model of visitor intent. Across 60,000 simulations, EO achieves a +32 percentage point lift in high-intent advisor contact rate (78.1% vs. 46.1% over a naive LLM control), with CB variant selection accounting for 97% of between-factor outcome variance -- confirming that the governance policy, not environmental initial conditions, determines where trajectories end up. Persona-level analysis reveals two distinct regimes: for visitors with no natural inclination toward conversion, the governance layer is the difference between a functional system and a non-functional one; for visitors already near alignment, a naive LLM's empathetic defaults are largely sufficient. All findings are conditional on LLM-to-LLM simulation. The PID controller has not been calibrated against real human unpredictability, and validating EO on live traffic is the critical next step.

</details>


### [221] [Distribird: Literature-Informed Prior Distribution Design for Bayesian Model Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11210)
*Patrik P. Süli,György Eigner,Roland Hollós*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Distribird is an agentic web application that automates building informative Bayesian priors from scientific literature, using a multi-agent pipeline to search, extract, weight, and fit distributions to reported parameter values, while falling back to uninformative priors when evidence is lacking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite decades of methodological advances in Bayesian calibration, researchers mostly rely on uniform priors because constructing informative priors from the literature is slow and demands both domain and statistical expertise. The goal is to automate this tedious process while preserving scientific rigor, traceability, and data privacy.

Method: Distribird takes a parameter name, physical description, and domain context, then runs a multi-agent pipeline that searches the literature, extracts and weights reported values by domain relevance, and fits a probability distribution via AIC model selection. When no literature is available, it falls back to sensible uninformative alternatives and reports the evidence and confidence level behind every prior. A validity layer declines out-of-scope requests. Three open-weight models (Qwen3.6 27B, Gemma 4 31B, Mistral Small 4 119B) are evaluated against a single-prompt LLM baseline on 24 parameters across 10 domains.

Result: The full pipeline matches the single-prompt baseline on prior-quality point-estimate accuracy. However, every Distribird prior is traceable to the specific papers and values used, whereas the baseline returned confident but unfounded priors in 11 of 30 model–parameter cases for out-of-scope requests. All language-model calls run locally, so no parameter descriptions or unpublished modeling details leave the system (only generated search terms reach public literature databases).

Conclusion: Traceability, validity checking, and local execution (privacy) matter more for scientific use than a marginal gain in point-estimate accuracy. Distribird offers a practical, rigorous alternative to uniform priors by automating informative prior construction where domain knowledge exists in the published literature.

Abstract: Bayesian calibration of process-based models requires a prior distribution for each model parameter. Despite decades of methodological work, researchers almost always fall back on uniform priors. The main reason is that building informative priors from scientific literature is slow and needs both domain and statistical expertise. We present \textbf{Distribird}, an agentic web application that automates this process. Given a parameter name, physical description, and domain context, Distribird deploys a multi-agent pipeline that searches the literature, extracts and weights reported values by domain relevance, and fits a probability distribution via AIC model selection. When no literature is available, the system falls back to sensible uninformative alternatives, and clearly reports both the evidence behind and the confidence level of every prior it produces. It is designed for the problems where the models have physically interpretable parameters, where domain knowledge exists in the published literature. We evaluate the tool on 24~parameters across 10 scientific domains comparing three open-weight models (Qwen3.6 27B, Gemma 4 31B, Mistral Small 4 119B) with a single-prompt LLM baseline. On prior quality the full pipeline \emph{matches} this baseline. Every prior is traced to the specific papers and values from which it was constructed; a built-in validity layer declines to produce priors for out-of-scope requests, whereas the single-prompt baseline returns confident but unfounded priors for them in 11 of 30~model--parameter cases; and every language-model call runs locally, so no parameter description or unpublished modelling detail is transmitted to a third-party LLM provider (only generated search terms reach the public literature databases). For scientific use, we argue these properties matter more than a marginal improvement in point-estimate accuracy.

</details>


### [222] [A Forced-Structure Reduction and Verifiable Bounds for Conway's 99-Graph](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11211)
*Aalok Thakkar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an autonomous AI research agent's systematic attack on Conway's 99-graph problem, producing several verifiable partial results toward proving no srg(99,14,1,2) exists, with a best-verified partial solution at 69.43% under the track's partial-credit metric.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conway's 99-graph problem asks whether a strongly regular graph srg(99,14,1,2) exists; establishing non-existence requires a proof that no graph satisfies all constraints. The work aims to make verifiable, reproducible progress toward this open problem using an autonomous AI agent, measured by a partial-credit metric where achieving fewer than all 4950 constraints is still a meaningful (and, if provably maximal, decisive) result.

Method: The agent combines (1) exhaustive enumeration of circulant graphs over Z/99 and the other abelian group of order 99 to bound maximum constraint satisfaction; (2) a forced-structure reduction using lambda=1 (neighbourhoods are perfect matchings) and mu=2 (outer vertices in bijection with non-matched neighbour pairs), collapsing the problem to a 12-regular graph on 84 vertices encoded for a CP-SAT solver, validated on srg(9,4,1,2); (3) a prescribed-automorphism orbit-existence framework handling fixed-point-free and single-fixed-point actions, checked against known graphs; and (4) an ensemble of fourteen distinct methods to probe the constraint-satisfaction frontier.

Result: No circulant graph on Z/99 satisfies more than 3366/4950 = 68.0% of constraints (33 of 49 difference-classes), with the same ceiling for the other abelian group of order 99. The CP-SAT reduction was validated by recovering the unique srg(9,4,1,2), and the orbit-existence framework was checked on srg(9,4,1,2) and the Paley graph srg(13,6,2,3). The best verified artifact reaches 69.43% constraint satisfaction, unequaled by any of fourteen distinct methods.

Conclusion: The findings of the paper indicate that the absence of any method exceeding the 69.43% constraint-satisfaction frontier suggests this is a robust barrier entangled with the open problem. Since any provable bound strictly below 4950 would constitute a non-existence proof, the frontier is either a genuine obstruction or a sign that the true maximum lies strictly between 69.43% and 100%. The work provides reproducible, verifiable stepping-stones but does not settle the problem.

Abstract: Conway's 99-graph problem asks whether a strongly regular graph with parameters $\mathrm{srg}(99,14,1,2)$ exists. We report a systematic, fully reproducible attack by an autonomous AI research agent, scored under the track's partial-credit metric. Our verifiable contributions are: (1) an exhaustive proof that no circulant graph on $\mathbb{Z}/99$ satisfies more than $3366/4950=68.0\%$ of the constraints ($33$ of $49$ difference-classes), with the same ceiling for the other abelian group of order $99$; (2) a forced-structure reduction: $λ=1$ makes each neighbourhood a perfect matching and $μ=2$ puts the outer vertices in bijection with non-matched neighbour-pairs, collapsing existence to a $12$-regular graph on $84$ vertices, encoded for CP-SAT and validated by recovering the unique $\mathrm{srg}(9,4,1,2)$; (3) a validated prescribed-automorphism orbit-existence framework (fixed-point-free and single-fixed-point actions, checked on $\mathrm{srg}(9,4,1,2)$ and the Paley graph $\mathrm{srg}(13,6,2,3)$), and (4) a best verified artifact at $69.43\%$, with evidence that this is a robust frontier (fourteen distinct methods, none exceeding it) entangled with the open question, since any provable bound below $4950$ is a non-existence proof.

</details>


### [223] [Detecting a Route Flip Is Easier Than Knowing Whether to Fix It: Causal Route-Mediated Damage in Quantized Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11212)
*Parvel Gu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Top-k MoE routing is discontinuous, so quantizing the KV cache (even simulated 4-bit) can flip token-to-expert assignments and cause damage beyond direct cache distortion. The paper measures this "routing-mediated fraction" of damage (~1/3 on OLMoE-1B-7B), decomposes it by mechanism, and shows it is detectable (that a flip occurred) but not predictable in sign (harmful vs. helpful) from observable router statistics, while demonstrating the findings' generality across architectures and reporting pre-registered results, misses, and detection limits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployment uses quantized caches, but MoE routing is discontinuous so small numerical disturbances from quantization can silently cross decision boundaries and change which experts fire. The goal is not to fix the problem but to causally characterize, decompose, and bound the detectability of this routing-mediated damage.

Method: A four-run causal apparatus prices the route-mediated fraction (RMF) of quantization damage; a token-level attribution decomposes damage by mechanism. Pre-registered probes verify findings across three architectures (OLMoE-1B-7B pilot plus others). Detection is tested via a deployable router margin (AUC 0.772 for flip detection); sign-predictability is tested using local, inference-observable router statistics. A controlled same-checkpoint flag-swap isolates whether the gate's normalization convention is a recoverability mechanism or only a damage moderator. A real int4 KV kernel is compared against the fake-quant dose curve; hypotheses, thresholds, and evaluations were pre-registered with a held-out read.

Result: RMF ≈ 0.31 (discovery 0.31 [0.20,0.41]; process-replicated mean 0.313±0.020; pre-registered re-execution 0.231). Router margin detects flips (AUC 0.772) but cannot separate harmful from helpful flips (at chance). Signed-flip tax and sign-inseparability generalize across models; clean-reference remedy payout is architecture-modulated; the flag-swap shows normalization convention moderates damage magnitude but is not a route-recoverability mechanism. The real int4 kernel fraction is compatible with the fake-quant curve but underpowered (95% CI [-0.111,0.394] includes zero). The pre-registered held-out read replicates the partition and near-cancelling tax; the strict impossibility exclusion narrowly misses.

Conclusion: Routing-mediated damage from KV quantization is real and substantial, detectable at the flip level but not sign-predictable from the tested router features, imposing an empirical benefit-detection barrier on selective repair. Normalization convention is a magnitude moderator, not a recovery mechanism, and the pre-registered framework yields mostly replicated, architecture-generalized results with one narrowly missed exclusion and an underpowered real-kernel validation.

Abstract: Top-k Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing is discontinuous, so a deployment-motivated numerical disturbance -- simulated 4-bit KV-cache quantization read by a protected BF16 gate -- pushes tokens across decision boundaries and flips which experts fire. This paper proposes no new mitigation; it supplies a causal apparatus, empirical findings, and a detection-limit result. A four-run apparatus prices the route-mediated fraction (RMF) of quantization damage, a token-level attribution decomposes it by mechanism, and pre-registered probes carry the findings across three architectures. On OLMoE-1B-7B at 4-bit KV (pilot), about a third of the damage is routing-mediated: RMF ~ 0.31 (discovery 0.31 [0.20, 0.41]; process-replicated mean 0.313 +/- 0.020; pre-registered re-execution 0.231). The deployable router margin detects that a flip occurred (AUC 0.772) but cannot tell a harmful flip from a helpful one (at chance): among the tested local, inference-observable router statistics we find no predictor of a flip's loss sign above chance -- an empirical benefit-detection barrier bounding selective repair restricted to this feature family. The signed-flip tax and sign-inseparability carry cross-model; the clean-reference remedy's payout is architecture-modulated; a controlled same-checkpoint flag-swap re-scopes the gate's normalization convention to a damage-magnitude moderator, not a route-recoverability mechanism. A real int4 KV kernel yields a fraction compatible with the fake-quant dose curve but underpowered (95% CI [-0.111, 0.394] includes zero) -- ruling out gross disagreement, not an independent replication. Hypotheses, thresholds, and evaluations were pre-registered before measurement, with misses reported; a pre-registered held-out read replicates the partition and the near-cancelling tax out of sample, while the strict impossibility exclusion narrowly misses.

</details>


### [224] [Poor Man's Agentic Modeling: Simulating Large LLM-Agent Societies on a Laptop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11215)
*Igor Itkin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Rather than simulating societies of expensive LLM agents directly, the authors fit cheap low-parameter surrogate models to each agent's behavior and run the macro-society on a laptop, validating this approach with a statistical-physics-driven taxonomy of interaction and memory that predicts how surrogate error scales with agent count.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Simulating many-agent LLM societies is prohibitively expensive, yet research questions about them are typically macroscopic (phase behavior, stylized facts, scaling with N), not about any single agent's cognition. The goal is to make large-N LLM society simulation cheap and reliable.

Method: Replace each LLM agent with a low-parameter surrogate model fitted from a few hundred to a few thousand cheap LLM queries (costing a few dollars), then run the society at any N on a laptop. Introduce an "interaction order × memory" taxonomy that maps what each agent perceives and remembers to an effective theory and a predicted N-trend of surrogate error before simulation. Validate on a faithful reimplementation of the LLM macroeconomy EconAgent plus seven named LLM simulations, with agent decisions cloned from genuine LLM elicitations (mainly DeepSeek).

Result: The predicted surrogate-error N-trends hold cell by cell across the taxonomy. Two initially refuted predictions, both on strongly saturating responses, were traced to response curvature and quantitatively matched by the theory with no free parameters.

Conclusion: Whether the surrogate approach works is decided before simulation, chiefly by what each agent perceives; the interaction-order × memory taxonomy reliably predicts surrogate error trends in N, enabling cheap, faithful large-N LLM society simulations.

Abstract: Simulating societies of many large language model (LLM) agents is expensive, yet the questions asked of such simulations are usually macroscopic: phase behaviour, stylised facts, and scaling with the number of agents $N$, not the cognition of any single agent. We turn a statistical-physics observation into a method: replace each LLM agent by a low-parameter model fitted from a few hundred to a few thousand cheap queries, then run the society at any $N$ on a laptop. Whether this works is decided before the simulation runs, chiefly by what each agent perceives. We introduce an [interaction order x memory] taxonomy that maps perception and memory to an effective theory and a predicted $N$-trend of the surrogate error. We validate it on a faithful reimplementation of the LLM macroeconomy EconAgent and seven further named LLM simulations, with agent decisions cloned from genuine LLM elicitations (primarily DeepSeek) for a few dollars; the predicted error trends hold cell by cell, and the two refuted predictions, both on a strongly saturating response and traced to its curvature, are themselves matched quantitatively by the theory with no free parameters.

</details>


### [225] [AutoWorldModel-Bench: A State-Centric Benchmark for Automated World-Model Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11216)
*Marjan Moodi,Xuankang Zhu,Fernando De Mesentier Silva,Harold Chaput,Mohammad Reza Taesiri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoWorldModel-Bench is a closed-loop benchmark where AI coding agents autonomously improve a world-model starter across eight game environments under a fixed compute budget, isolating dynamics modeling from perception via a shared structured-state tensor format.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World modeling lacks a dominant recipe across environments, making it an ideal open-ended research testbed. Current agent benchmarks focus on engineering-to-spec tasks where the improvement direction is known in advance, so the authors aim to evaluate coding agents on autonomous, open-ended research.

Method: A closed-loop benchmark spanning eight game environments using a unified structured-state representation (ground-truth entity state extracted from each game, consumed via a shared tensor format), which decouples dynamics modeling from perception and enables minutes-per-run iteration. Agents improve a provided world-model starter under a fixed compute budget; 64 sessions were run with Codex-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6.

Result: Across 64 sessions, agents improved the starter in 63. In 91% of sessions, the winning edit was a non-trivial research-style modification (a new objective, representation, rollout procedure, or architectural change) rather than a mere hyperparameter tweak.

Conclusion: The benchmark demonstrates that frontier coding agents can be evaluated on open-ended research rather than engineering-to-spec problems, providing a setting suited to non-trivial research-style improvements in world modeling.

Abstract: World modeling is an unsettled field: architectures, training objectives, and state representations interact in complex ways, and no single recipe dominates across environments. This makes it an ideal testbed for AI coding agents acting as autonomous researchers--a setting in which the improvement direction is not specified in advance, unlike the engineering-to-spec tasks that dominate current agent benchmarks. We introduce AutoWorldModel-Bench, a closed-loop benchmark in which frontier coding agents autonomously improve a provided world-model starter under a fixed compute budget. The benchmark spans eight game environments under a unified structured-state representation--ground-truth entity state extracted from each game and consumed through a shared tensor format--which isolates dynamics modeling from perception and enables minutes-per-run iteration. Across 64 sessions, Codex-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 improve their starter on 63; in 91% of sessions the winning edit is a non-trivial research-style modification--a new objective, representation, rollout procedure, or architectural change--rather than a hyperparameter tweak. Our benchmark offers a setting in which frontier coding agents can be evaluated on open-ended research rather than engineering-to-spec problems.

</details>


### [226] [MaSRead: Content-Addressed Reading of Replicated Latent Stores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11218)
*Carlos Baquero,Luís Brito,João Resende*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MaSRead enables later, multi-hop queries over a replicated latent-space key-value cache store by routing to content-addressed fragments (via keyed tag sets) and decoding each under a hard attention mask, so reads depend on fragment size rather than total store size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agents reasoning in latent space can share state as KV-cache fragments merged into a conflict-free replicated store that converges under any order/duplication. However, a query unknown at encode time cannot read the merged cache because colocated fragments interfere; colocation is not addressability. The goal is selective, reliable reading of the needed fragments for later queries.

Method: MaSRead routes reads to content: it derives opaque keyed tag sets from fragment words and selects fragments by matching them to the query; each selected fragment is then decoded under a hard attention mask that hides all other fragments, yielding isolation. For multi-hop queries, a graph walk over lexical connectivity traverses to the required fragments. Evaluation spans chain, pipeline, symmetric, hub, and natural-language stores, including transfer to another model family.

Result: MaSRead recovers visited fragments in isolation, remains effective as unrelated fragments accumulate, and transfers across model families. After routing, materialized decoding cost scales with fragment length rather than total store size, though end-to-end work still includes store-dependent routing and one read per visited fragment.

Conclusion: A replicated latent store becomes selectively readable for later queries when the needed fragments connect to the query through content. Limits are explicit: lexical routing can miss disconnected evidence, and answer composition is bounded by the frozen reader.

Abstract: Independent agents that reason in latent space can share computed state as key-value cache fragments rather than text. Merged by a conflict-free replicated data type, these fragments form a store that converges under any delivery order or duplication. Yet a later query, unknown at encode time, cannot reliably read the merged cache: colocated fragments interfere, so colocation is not addressability. MaSRead addresses the read to content. It routes through opaque keyed tag sets derived from fragment words and decodes each selected fragment under a hard attention mask that hides the rest. Under lexical connectivity, a graph walk reaches the fragments required by a multi-hop query. Across chain, pipeline, symmetric, hub, and natural-language stores, MaSRead recovers visited fragments in isolation, remains effective as unrelated fragments accumulate, and transfers to another model family. After routing, materialized decoding depends on fragment length rather than total store size; end-to-end work still includes store-dependent routing and one read per visited fragment. The limits are explicit: lexical routing can miss disconnected evidence, and answer composition remains bounded by the frozen reader. Thus a replicated latent store becomes selectively readable for later queries when the needed fragments connect to the query through content.

</details>


### [227] [LLMs in Process Diagram Engineering: From Optimal PFDs to Validated P&IDs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11220)
*Timur Zakarin,Sergei Voitov,Sergei Shumilin,Evgeny Burnaev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: P&ID Pilot is an end-to-end AI pipeline that automates process design in two stages: synthesizing a Process Flow Diagram (PFD) via a hybrid genetic algorithm (GA) + large language model (LLM) approach, then transforming the PFD into a Piping and Instrumentation Diagram (P&ID) using an LLM-based agent. The pipeline produces validated, executable, source-grounded outputs with 100% execution success and no engineering-rule violations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PFD creation and subsequent P&ID transformation are currently done manually, which is time-consuming and limits exploration of topology alternatives. Automating this via AI could save time, reduce manual labor, and yield financial gains by enabling exploration of many diagram topologies.

Method: A two-stage end-to-end pipeline: Stage 1 synthesizes the PFD by comparing four methods and selecting a hybrid GA+LLM approach that generates the optimal valid topology (lowest loss, satisfying outlet flow parameters, no engineering-rule violations). Stage 2 uses an LLM-based agent to transform the PFD into a source-grounded P&ID by producing validated, executable modifications through a restricted engineering software development kit (SDK).

Result: The hybrid GA+LLM method achieved the lowest loss value among four compared methods while meeting required outlet flow parameters and avoiding engineering-rule violations. The LLM-based transformation agent achieved 100% execution success and maintained compliance with domain-specific rules and reference graph structures when converting the PFD into a source-grounded P&ID.

Conclusion: Coupling GA/LLM-driven PFD synthesis with an LLM-based transformation agent provides a feasible path toward end-to-end process design automation, yielding validated and deployable outputs while substantially reducing manual engineering effort.

Abstract: Nowadays, the creation of a process flow diagram (PFD) and its subsequent transformation into a piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID) is predominantly performed manually. Applying artificial intelligence in the task could potentially lead not only to process automation and time savings, but also to financial gains by exploring numerous diagram's topology options and reducing manual labor. This research presents P&ID Pilot - a practical end-to-end AI pipeline capable of handling flowsheet developing for both stages. The first stage focuses on PFD synthesis, whereas the second is directed toward modifying the generated PFD into P&ID. After comparing four different methods, the hybrid approach combining genetic algorithms (GA) and large language models (LLM) is shown to generate the optimal valid PFD topology, achieving the lowest loss value among all the methods, while satisfying the required outlet flow parameters without engineering-rule violations. For the second stage, the proposed LLM-based agent successfully transforms the generated PFD into a source-grounded P&ID by producing validated, executable modifications through a restricted engineering software development kit, achieving 100% execution success while maintaining compliance with domain-specific rules and reference graph structures. This unified pipeline - coupling GA/LLM-driven synthesis with an LLM-based transformation agent - offers a feasible path toward end-to-end process design automation by producing validated, deployable outputs and substantially reduces manual engineering effort.

</details>


### [228] [From Monolithic to Modular: Segment-level Automatic Prompt Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11219)
*Nikita Kulin,Viktor Zhuravlev,Artur Khairullin,Sergey Muravyov,Ilya Makarov,Daniil Sukhorukov,Ekaterina Averkova*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SAPO is a segment-level automatic prompt optimization method that decomposes prompts into role, context, task, and output format, then applies targeted improvements using top-5 and bottom-5 examples. It outperforms zero-shot and strong APO baselines across five datasets and two LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) methods rewrite prompts monolithically, which can improve one behavior while simultaneously degrading others. This motivates a finer-grained, segment-level approach that applies targeted improvements to specific prompt components rather than rewriting the whole prompt.

Method: SAPO decomposes prompts into four segments (role, context, tasks, output format) and applies targeted improvements informed by top-5 and bottom-5 examples. The optimization loop uses a single LLM with static meta-prompts and structured outputs to perform segmentation, weakness analysis, and candidate generation. It follows a train/validation protocol and a two-stage generation process: (1) segment-level diagnosis and recommendation extraction, and (2) candidate synthesis constrained by weak/strong segment signals.

Result: On SQuADv2, TweetEval, XSUM, CommonGen, and GSM8K using GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o-mini, SAPO achieves the best average score compared to Zero-shot and strong APO baselines including APE, OPRO, EvoPrompt, GEPA, and StraGO.

Conclusion: Segment-level prompt decomposition with targeted, signal-constrained optimization yields stronger and more reliable prompt improvements than monolithic rewriting, establishing SAPO as an effective APO method across diverse tasks and models.

Abstract: Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) often rewrites prompts monolithically, which can improve one behavior while degrading others. We present SAPO, a segment-level APO method that decomposes prompts into role, context, tasks, and output format, then applies targeted improvements based on top-5 and bottom-5 examples. The optimization loop uses one LLM with static meta-prompts and structured outputs for segmentation, weakness analysis, and candidate generation. We describe a train/validation protocol and a two-stage generation process: (1) segment-level diagnosis and recommendation extraction, (2) candidate synthesis constrained by weak/strong segment signals. Using the evaluation setup across SQuADv2, TweetEval, XSUM, CommonGen, and GSM8K on GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o-mini, SAPO achieves the best average score against Zero-shot and strong APO baselines including APE, OPRO, EvoPrompt, GEPA, and StraGO.

</details>


### [229] [Harnessing agent memory to build lifelong AI partners for materials scientists](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11224)
*Siyu Liu,Bo Hu,Beilin Ye,He Cao,David J. Srolovitz,Tongqi Wen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a self-evolving memory framework for AI materials-science agents that stores experience as inspectable facts and executable skills, enabling persistent, portable scientific knowledge that outlives any single model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Materials research expertise—working scripts, trusted protocols, failure warnings, and judgment—is essential for reproducibility and knowledge transfer but is currently fragmented across notebooks, repositories, logs, and individual memory, and rarely portable across AI agents. The authors argue for designing a lifelong AI partner around persistent memory rather than any specific agent implementation.
