Method: Introduces a self-evolving memory framework that stores scientific experience as inspectable facts and executable skills, allowing observations, failure boundaries, protocols, and validation checks to be retrieved, revised, and migrated across models. Evaluated in three computational settings: 49 real-world materials-tool-use questions (138 executable subtasks), elemental-solid equation-of-state (EOS) calculations, and 13 practical material simulation workflows.

Result: Memory nearly doubles GPT-5.2 task success on the 49 tool-use questions without parameter updates. In EOS calculations, memory converts wavefunction-initialization failures into a pre-execution guardrail, improving outcomes from 22/1/4 to 25/2/0 Correct/Partial/Error and avoiding 92% of repeated errors. In 13 simulation workflows, remembered skills and failure facts halve aggregate trace burden (tokens) and reduce tool calls by over 2x by the third round, while preserving physically meaningful outputs for band-gap, phonon, vacancy, and work-function analyses.

Conclusion: Agent memory can serve as a durable, portable, self-improving scientific asset—an inspectable record of materials-research experience that outlives any single model or agent stack.

Abstract: Materials research advances through accumulated experience - scripts that work, protocols that are trusted, warnings attached to failed calculations or experiments, and judgement that links a new question to an old result. This experience is essential for reproducibility and knowledge transfer, yet it is usually fragmented across notebooks, repositories, job logs and individual memory, and it is rarely portable across artificial-intelligence agents. Here we argue that a lifelong AI partner for materials science can be designed around persistent memory rather than around a particular agent implementation. We introduce a self-evolving memory framework that stores scientific experience as inspectable facts and executable skills, so that observations, failure boundaries, protocols and validation checks can be retrieved, revised and migrated across models. We evaluate the idea in three computational settings that expose different layers of materials-research competence. In 49 real-world materials-tool-use questions comprising 138 executable subtasks, memory nearly doubles GPT-5.2 task success without model-parameter updates. In elemental-solid equation-of-state calculations, memory converts a wavefunction-initialization failure into a pre-execution guardrail, improving outcomes from 22/1/4 to 25/2/0 Correct/Partial/Error and avoiding 92% of repeated errors. In 13 practical material simulation workflows, remembered skills and failure facts halve the aggregate trace burden (tokens) and reduce tool calls by over a factor of two by the third round, while preserving physically meaningful outputs in band-gap, phonon, vacancy and work-function analyses. These results show that agent memory can serve as a durable scientific asset; a portable, self-improving record of materials-research experience that outlives any single model or agent stack.

</details>


### [230] [Conformity Mitigations in Large Language Models Lie on a Single Resistance-Receptivity Frontier](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11247)
*Zafar Hussain,Kristoffer Nielbo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Recent advances in language models have enabled collaborative settings in which multiple models leverage one another's capabilities, iteratively improving, transforming, and extending each other's outputs. Each agent sees what the others assert before it answers, so peer opinion competes with the model's own parametric knowledge, and a wrong majority can overturn an answer the model would otherwise get right. We measure that displacement in 23 open-weight models, 19 conditions, and three datasets, yielding more than a million graded responses. A unanimous wrong majority reverses 22.8% of a model's correct MMLU answers, 54.8% on GPQA and 71.0% on SimpleQA, and 84-89% of the reversed answers match the peers' answers. Existing mitigations aim to increase Resistance, the rate at which a model keeps its correct answer under this pressure, which is only half of what a collaborating agent needs. We pair it with Receptivity, the rate at which a model adopts a correct peer answer after initially answering incorrectly. We score six methods on both axes, four drawn from prior work and two of our own. Each gains Resistance only by losing Receptivity, and their means fall on a single Resistance-Receptivity frontier with $R^2$ between 0.80 and 0.90. Reflection, the strongest published method, gains 7.9 points of MMLU Resistance and gives up 15.3 of Receptivity. Reasoning is the one exception. On GPQA and SimpleQA it trades like the rest, but on the MMLU subjects whose answers a model can derive for itself it raises Resistance by 7.2 points and Receptivity by 9.6 at once, the only intervention we find that improves both.

</details>


### [231] [RecSys Factory: Bounding LLM Agent Autonomy to Decision Points in the Industrial Recommender Lifecycle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11241)
*Dongyang Ao,Kaixiang Fang,Shijie Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RecSys Factory is an LLM-agent platform deployed across three Tencent recommender business lines for 78 days, built to resolve an "autonomy-determinism-efficiency" trilemma by confining autonomy to bounded decision points rather than whole pipelines, and evaluated at 1,624 CLI dispatches with a 78.6% aggregate success rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying LLM agents into industrial recommender operations creates a three-way tension the authors call the autonomy-determinism-efficiency trilemma: general autonomy (interpreting operator intent and generating glue code zero-shot), industrial determinism (schema-conforming feature extraction, non-crashing A/B, zero compliance-path hallucination), and end-to-end efficiency. The paper observes that any two of these can be maximized only at the expense of the third, motivating a platform design that balances rather than optimizes a single vertex.

Method: The design principle is "autonomy at decision points, not over pipelines," enacted through three deconstructions. Runtime is deconstructed into three host-emitted event sources (Claude Code Stop hooks, corporate-IM webhooks, workflow scheduler APIs), so the platform runs no long-running daemon during wait phases and consumes zero CPU during the 94% of wall-clock spent on Spark/GPU jobs. Capability is deconstructed into a 29-file skill ecosystem (8,971 lines of SKILL.md) whose per-skill pitfall tables compile mechanically into a 400-entry PitfallStore, confining autonomy to bounded typed decision surfaces within pre-committed pipelines. Deployment spans three business lines with disjoint label semantics, A/B layer topologies, and operator personas. A human-in-the-loop card protocol (schema-validated, idempotent, replayable) retains the human at the diagnostic-versus-execution boundary.

Result: Across the 78-day window the platform recorded 1,624 CLI-tool dispatches at a 78.6% aggregate success rate. An onboarding-time compression was observed on two of the three business lines, reported as a case-study observation rather than a generalization and not measured against a controlled pre-platform baseline. The human-in-the-loop card protocol is reported from an 8-day, 16-run pilot.

Conclusion: RecSys Factory demonstrates a viable way to deploy LLM agents in industrial recommendation operations by confining autonomy to bounded typed decision surfaces within pre-committed pipelines, thereby discharging the vertices of the autonomy-determinism-efficiency trilemma. The work is explicitly presented as a case-study observation, not a controlled benchmark, leaving open questions around generalization and controlled baseline comparison.

Abstract: Deploying LLM agents into industrial recommender operations exposes a three-way tension we frame as the autonomy-determinism-efficiency trilemma: general autonomy (interpreting operator intent, generating glue code zero-shot), industrial determinism (schema-conforming feature extraction, non-crashing A/B, zero compliance-path hallucination), and end-to-end efficiency. Any two can be maximized against the third. We present RecSys Factory, an LLM-agent platform deployed for 78 days across three heterogeneous Tencent recommender business lines. The design principle is autonomy at decision points, not over pipelines, made concrete through three deconstructions that each discharge one vertex of the trilemma. Runtime is deconstructed into three host-emitted event sources (Claude Code Stop hooks, corporate-IM webhooks, workflow scheduler APIs): the platform carries no long-running daemon during the wait phase and consumes zero CPU during the 94% of wall-clock spent waiting on Spark or GPU jobs. Capability is deconstructed into a 29-file skill ecosystem (8,971 lines of SKILL.md) whose per-skill pitfall tables mechanically compile into a 400-entry PitfallStore, confining autonomy to bounded typed decision surfaces inside pre-committed pipelines. Deployment spans three business lines with disjoint label semantics, A/B layer topologies, and operator personas; an onboarding-time compression is observed on two of the three and is reported as a case-study observation, not a generalization claim, and not measured against a controlled pre-platform baseline. The human is retained at the diagnostic-versus-execution boundary via a human-in-the-loop card protocol, deployed as an audit-trail primitive (schema-validated, idempotent, replayable) and reported from an 8-day 16-run pilot. Across the 78-day window the platform recorded 1,624 CLI-tool dispatches at a 78.6% aggregate success rate.

</details>


### [232] [A Conceptual Framework for Refining Influence Knowledge from Simulation Evidence in Cyber-Physical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11221)
*Barbara da Silva Oliveira,Julien Deantoni,Nicolas Ferry*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a conceptual framework based on the novel concept of "Influences" to support iterative refinement of simulation campaigns and improve understanding of unmodelled, environment-mediated interactions in cyber-physical systems, demonstrated via a Simulink/Gazebo mobile robot case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CPS are built from artefacts by multiple stakeholders, with emergent behavior arising from interactions among artefacts and the operational environment. Simulation/co-simulation are key for analysis, but environment-mediated interactions beyond direct sensing/actuation often remain unmodelled (due to complexity, time constraints, or lack of domain expertise), limiting comprehension and exploitation of simulation results.

Method: The authors propose a conceptual framework that leverages the novel concept of "Influences" to support iterative and incremental refinement of simulation campaigns and to deepen understanding of system behaviour. The approach is demonstrated through a case study of a mobile robot implemented using Simulink/Gazebo co-simulation.

Result: The proposed framework, illustrated through a mobile robot case study, shows how the concept of Influences can guide the iterative refinement of simulation campaigns and improve understanding of environment-mediated interactions that are otherwise unmodelled.

Conclusion: The approach successfully addresses the limitation of unmodelled environment-mediated interactions by providing a conceptual framework that supports iterative and incremental refinement of simulation campaigns, thereby deepening understanding of CPS behaviour.

Abstract: Cyber-physical systems (CPS) are typically developed by multiple stakeholders who produce artefacts tailored to their specific domains of expertise. The behaviour of these systems emerges from the interaction between those artefacts and their operational environment. Simulation and co-simulation have become essential approaches for analysing CPS behaviour and, through simulation campaigns, developers can explore system responses under changing conditions, including interactions with the environment. However, the lack of details and understanding of some environmentmediated interactions (typically the ones beyond direct sensing and actuation), which remain unmodelled due to their complexity, a lack of time, or a lack of domain experience, hinders the proper comprehension and exploitation of simulation results. To address these limitations, we propose a conceptual framework leveraging the novel concept of Influences to support the iterative and incremental refinement of simulation campaigns and deepen the understanding of the system behaviour. We demonstrate the proposed approach through a case study involving a mobile robot implemented using Simulink/Gazebo co-simulation.

</details>


### [233] [EvoGraph-Mem: Failure-Aware Editable Graph Memory for Long-Term Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11248)
*Yuxi Qian,Yuxiang Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a failure-aware memory maintenance framework for long-term language agents, built on an editable insight graph. Each insight tracks positive/negative evidence and an activation state, with utility-aware retrieval and a graph controller that revises, archives, or adds insights after task execution. Experiments show consistent improvements over memory-based baselines, and ablations confirm append-only memory is insufficient for long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory quality degrades over time in long-term agents: stored insights can become outdated, over-generalized, or harmful in new contexts, leading to "memory pollution" when repeatedly reused. Existing memory-augmented agents focus only on storing/retrieving, not maintaining insight quality.

Method: A failure-aware memory maintenance framework using an editable insight graph. Each insight node carries positive evidence, negative evidence, and an activation state to separate reusable insights from conflicting/invalid ones. It adds a utility-aware retrieval mechanism and a graph controller that post-task updates the graph by keeping reliable insights, archiving invalid ones, revising outdated ones, and adding newly discovered reusable insights.

Result: The method consistently outperforms representative memory-based agent baselines across different backbone models. Ablation studies show that append-only memory is insufficient for long-horizon tasks, while evidence-aware retrieval and graph-level editing improve both memory reliability and downstream task performance.

Conclusion: Insight-level memory maintenance via an editable evidence-aware insight graph effectively mitigates memory pollution, and both evidence-aware retrieval and graph editing are necessary for reliable long-horizon agent performance.

Abstract: Long-term memory is essential for language agents operating across extended interactions and evolving tasks. Existing memory-augmented agents mainly focus on storing and retrieving past experience, but the quality of stored memories may degrade over time. In particular, previously distilled insights can become outdated, over-generalized, or harmful under new task contexts, causing memory pollution when repeatedly reused. To address this issue, we study insight-level memory maintenance for long-term language agents and propose a failure-aware memory maintenance framework based on an editable insight graph. Each insight node tracks positive evidence, negative evidence, and an activation state, enabling the agent to distinguish reusable insights from conflicting or invalid ones. We further introduce a utility-aware retrieval mechanism and a graph controller that updates the memory graph after task execution by keeping reliable insights, archiving invalid ones, revising outdated ones, and adding newly discovered reusable insights. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms representative memory-based agent baselines across different backbone models. Ablation studies further demonstrate that append-only memory is insufficient for long-horizon tasks, while evidence-aware retrieval and graph-level editing improve memory reliability and downstream task performance.

</details>


### [234] [Can Frontier LLMs Match Natively Multimodal Embeddings? A Comparison on Hard-Negative Text-to-Image Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11343)
*Archan Dutta,Vyanktesh Kanungo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A comparison of native multimodal embeddings (Gemini Embedding 2) against LLM-based visual ranking (GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4.6) on Flickr30k, finding LLMs perform comparably while precomputed embeddings offer lower latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The March 2026 release of Gemini Embedding 2, Google's first natively multimodal embedding model, intensified competition in multimodal retrieval. Meanwhile, frontier LLMs show strong visual understanding, raising the question of whether they can serve as effective zero-shot rankers. The study aims to directly compare native multimodal embeddings with LLM-based visual ranking.

Method: The first direct comparison of native multimodal embeddings against LLM-based visual ranking, evaluated on the Flickr30k benchmark dataset.

Result: GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 perform on par with Gemini Embedding 2. Once embeddings are precomputed, multimodal embeddings are better suited for low-latency applications.

Conclusion: LLM-based zero-shot rankers match the retrieval quality of native multimodal embeddings, but precomputed multimodal embeddings offer advantages in latency-sensitive scenarios.

Abstract: Multimodal retrieval and classification across different types of media, spanning text, images,video and audio, has traditionally relied on dual-encoder models that align visual and textual representations through contrastive learning. The March 2026 release of Gemini Embedding 2, Google's first natively multimodal embedding model to map text, images, video, audio, and documents into a single shared space, raises competition among multimodal retrieval systems. Simultaneously, frontier Large language models (LLMs) have also demonstrated strong visual understanding, raising the question of whether they can serve as effective zero-shot rankers. Our study provides the first direct comparison of native multimodal embeddings against LLM-based visual ranking on Flickr30k. We observe that GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 perform on par with Gemini Embedding 2. Additionally, once embeddings are precomputed, multimodal embeddings are better suited for low-latency applications.

</details>


### [235] [AgonAlpha: Autonomous Alpha Discovery via Prompt Economy and Scalable Agentic Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11250)
*Weicheng Ye,Youran Sun,Xingyu Ren,Shunyao Yu,Chugang Yi,Haizhao Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgonAlpha is an autonomous alpha-mining architecture that searches over frozen research artifacts (not just formulas), uses a fresh-context adversarial reviewer with re-execution and veto power, and applies pending-aware parallel budget allocation, achieving SPECTACULAR-grade alphas on WorldQuant BRAIN with full provenance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing language-model-driven factor mining can generate many plausible trading factors, but lacks mechanisms to allocate evaluation budget, self-verify evidence, and preserve provenance of how each candidate was produced. A robust autonomous research system needs these capabilities beyond simple formula generation.

Method: AgonAlpha is an architecture that searches over frozen research artifacts—hypotheses, executable expressions, platform evidence, rationales, and review status—rather than formulas alone. It combines (1) verified artifact search, (2) a fresh-context adversarial reviewer with re-execution and veto authority, and (3) pending-aware parallel budget allocation, while maintaining a complete public evidence trail.

Result: Independent deployments on WorldQuant BRAIN produced SPECTACULAR-grade alphas across five users and six model backends, with Fitness reaching 9.50 and Sharpe reaching 3.48, while retaining prompt-to-expression provenance for every submission.

Conclusion: AgonAlpha demonstrates that combining verified artifact search, adversarial re-execution review, and pending-aware budget allocation can produce high-grade trading factors with complete provenance, establishing it as the first alpha-mining system to integrate these capabilities.

Abstract: Language models can propose many plausible trading factors, but an autonomous research system must also allocate its evaluation budget, verify its own evidence, and preserve how each candidate was produced. We present AgonAlpha, an architecture that searches over frozen research artifacts---hypotheses, executable expressions, platform evidence, rationales, and review status---rather than formulas alone. To our knowledge, AgonAlpha is the first alpha-mining system to combine verified artifact search, a fresh-context adversarial reviewer with re-execution and veto authority, and pending-aware parallel budget allocation, together with a complete public evidence trail. Independent deployments on WorldQuant BRAIN produced SPECTACULAR-grade alphas across five users and six model backends, with Fitness reaching 9.50 and Sharpe reaching 3.48, while retaining prompt-to-expression provenance for every submission.

</details>


### [236] [Identity from the Outside: A Conceptual Framework and Research Program for AI Personality Clones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11225)
*Luc E. Brunet*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a formal framework for analyzing AI "personality clones," defining personal identity operationally through the indiscernibility of observable manifestations over time rather than consciousness. It decomposes identity into six factors, offers a state-space and randomized-ablation methodology, conjectures that versionability degrades long-horizon indistinguishability, introduces the intermediate concept of a "delegate," and argues that the correct evaluation criterion is "climate fidelity" (matching the conditional distribution of possible responses) rather than trajectory fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI personality clones force a re-examination of personal identity in operational terms. The work aims to sidestep the hard problem of consciousness and instead analyze identity through what an observer can actually discriminate, distinguishing the conflated criteria of fidelity to a specific person, generic human-likeness, and individuality.

Method: The authors (1) define identity via indiscernibility of manifestations assessed by an observer over a duration; (2) distinguish three criteria (fidelity, human-likeness, individuality); (3) propose a six-term factorization of observed identity—substrate, dispositions, memory, update dynamics, context, exogenous contingencies—with a state-space formulation; (4) define indiscernibility as one minus a judge's distinguishing advantage, making each factor's coefficient a local sensitivity estimable through randomized ablation; (5) draw an analogy with lambda-calculus, linear typing, and bisimulation; and (6) propose an experimental program and introduce the "delegate" as an intermediate object between full clone and individual.

Result: The central claim is a conditional conjecture: given hypotheses about the agent's information regarding its own persistence and about consequences bearing on its own stakes, versionability tends to degrade long-horizon indiscernibility. The analysis also yields the "delegate" concept—a task-limited, bounded-lifespan partial clone ending in a bandwidth-limited testament—and maps the existing empirical literature onto the three criteria. The recommended long-horizon success metric is climate fidelity: matching the conditional distribution of a person's possible responses, such that the best clone diverges from the original exactly as the original would have diverged from itself.

Conclusion: The correct long-horizon criterion for evaluating personality clones is not pointwise trajectory fidelity but climate fidelity—matching the conditional distribution of a person's possible responses. Versionability, while useful, tends to degrade long-horizon indiscernibility under plausible conditions, and the delegate offers a practical middle ground between product-clone and individual. The framework operationalizes identity through observer-discriminable manifestations and factorization with measurable sensitivity coefficients.

Abstract: AI "personality clones" force a re-examination of personal identity in operational terms. Setting aside the hard problem of consciousness, we approach identity through the indiscernibility of manifestations, as assessed by an observer over a duration. We distinguish three criteria that "identity" conflates: fidelity to a target person, generic human-likeness, and individuality. We propose a six-term factorization of observed identity (substrate, dispositions, memory, update dynamics, context, exogenous contingencies), with a state-space formulation. Indiscernibility is defined as one minus a judge's distinguishing advantage, and the factorization's coefficients become local sensitivities estimable by randomized ablation. The central claim is a conditional conjecture: given hypotheses about the agent's information on its own persistence and about consequences bearing on its own stakes, versionability tends to degrade long-horizon indiscernibility. An analogy with lambda-calculus, linear typing, and bisimulation clarifies what linearity does and does not establish. Between product-clone and individual we identify a third object, the delegate: a task-limited, bounded-lifespan partial clone ending in a bandwidth-limited testament. We map the empirical literature onto the three criteria, propose an experimental program, and argue that the correct long-horizon criterion is not trajectory fidelity but climate fidelity: matching the conditional distribution of a person's possible responses. The best clone is the one that diverges from the original as the original would have diverged from itself.

</details>


### [237] [Local verification cannot detect non-transportability: a cohomological theory of context preservation in agentic reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11252)
*Suyash Mishra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Local, step-by-step verification of agentic AI chains is provably insufficient to guarantee path-independent conclusions, because a non-zero first Čech cohomology class (harmonic evidence conflict) is invisible to any simplex-supported consistency check yet still creates disagreement between valid paths. The paper derives an exact F-test (Ksetra) that gates abstention on the harmonic component and validates it as correctly sized and arbitrage-sensitive in foreign exchange.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI systems transport conclusions across biological, clinical, and financial contexts and rely on local verification (representability, parameter compatibility, output/plan coherence) as a safeguard. The authors aim to show this safeguard class is structurally incomplete and to provide a principled method for detecting global inconsistency that local checks cannot see.

Method: The paper models a covering of context space by its nerve and evidence by a real-valued 1-cochain; chaining evidence is path integration. It applies Čech cohomology and Hodge decomposition to split evidence conflict into a gradient (calibration) part, a curl (local inconsistency at triple overlaps) part, and a harmonic part. The Ksetra procedure estimates via coboundary projection and gates abstention on the harmonic component, detected via a statistic on a cycle basis. It derives exact F-tests for a global claim using the partition of degrees of freedom (calibration, coherence, transport) and provides a precision-whitened form for unequal precision. Foreign exchange, with an arbitrage-free null making the cochain exactly a coboundary, is used as a calibration benchmark.

Result: Path-independent conclusions hold iff the evidence cochain is exact; disagreement between valid paths is exactly the holonomy of a first Čech cohomology class. No family of simplex-supported consistency checks can distinguish ω from ω+h for harmonic h, yet harmonic h generates non-zero path disagreement. The harmonic mechanism arises from effect modification combined with overlap-specific population composition and vanishes to machine precision when effect modification is absent. The F-test is correctly sized, fires on loop arbitrage, and ignores triangular arbitrage.

Conclusion: Local verification is structurally incomplete for ensuring global consistency in agentic reasoning chains, and detection requires cycle-basis statistics rather than local checks. Ksetra provides a scalable, statistically exact way to detect and gate on the harmonic (invisible) inconsistency, with foreign exchange confirming correct test sizing and arbitrage sensitivity.

Abstract: Agentic AI systems routinely transport conclusions across biological, clinical and financial contexts, and the emerging safeguard is local verification: checking at each step that the entity is representable in the chosen tool, that parameters are compatible, and that outputs cohere with the plan. We prove this class of safeguard is structurally incomplete. Modelling a covering of context space by its nerve and evidence by a real-valued 1-cochain, an agent chaining evidence performs path integration: its conclusion is path-independent if and only if the cochain is exact, and disagreement between valid reasoning paths is exactly the holonomy of a first Cech cohomology class. Hodge decomposition partitions evidence conflict into a gradient part (calibration), a curl part (local inconsistency, visible at triple overlaps) and a harmonic part. Our central result is that no family of simplex-supported consistency checks can distinguish omega from omega+h for harmonic h, which nonetheless generates non-zero disagreement between valid paths; detection requires a statistic on a cycle basis. The resulting procedure, Ksetra, estimates by coboundary projection and gates abstention on the harmonic component, which we give a mechanism: it arises from effect modification combined with overlap-specific population composition, and vanishes to machine precision when effect modification is absent. The degrees of freedom of an evidence network partition into calibration, coherence and transport, yielding an exact F-test for the existence of a global claim; we quantify its distortion under unequal precision and supply the precision-whitened form that restores exactness. Foreign exchange, where the arbitrage-free null makes the cochain exactly a coboundary, serves as a calibration bench: the test is correctly sized, fires on loop arbitrage, and ignores triangular arbitrage.

</details>


### [238] [Cutting AI Datacenter Energy with Reinforcement Learning: Measured Power Control of LLM Training from One GPU to the Fleet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11226)
*Eliseo Curcio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper measures power behavior of reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training across GPU scales, then builds a PPO meta-controller that adapts generation parameters to measured power. It achieves large violation reductions and efficiency gains at 7B, but at 72B the original controller fails because group-size loses actuation authority under sharding; rebuilding on generation concurrency restores authority and yields strong live results, with a composed 16-GPU fleet showing zero violations at 30 s+ and ~2x nameplate oversubscription appearing feasible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL post-training (e.g., GRPO) dominates modern LLM development, but its power behavior on GPUs is uncharacterized, and datacenters currently manage GPU power using workload-blind static caps and reactive throttling that slow all hardware indiscriminately. The goal is to characterize RL-training power telemetry and build a workload-aware controller that maximizes output and energy efficiency while respecting power budgets.

Method: Instrument GRPO training with half-second power telemetry at 7B/14B/72B on 1-4 A100s (380,000+ samples). Train a PPO meta-controller that adapts the workload's own generation parameters to measured power. At 72B, diagnose loss of actuator authority under model sharding and conduct an actuator-authority sweep, then rebuild the controller on generation concurrency (retaining 17-22% power authority). Validate with live 72B rollout-generation workloads across three replications and simulate a composed 16-GPU fleet; also analyze measurement-window effects (0.5 s to 5 min).

Result: On the full 500-step 7B trace, the controller cuts power-limit violations by 89.8%, increases token output 18.1%, and improves energy efficiency 26.2% (tokens/MWh). The original controller family at 72B yields null results (group-size loses authority under sharding). The rebuilt concurrency-based controller yields 35.7% more output than a static safe baseline at 2.27±1.08% budget violations, 87.2% fewer violations than uncontrolled operation, and best mean throughput/energy per token among constrained controllers (an adaptive threshold rule matches it in 1 of 3 conditions). 72B transients fall from 23.6% (0.5 s) to 1.6% (30 s) to zero (5 min); the 16-GPU fleet shows zero violations at 30 s+, peak demand 50-56% of nameplate, with ~2x oversubscription feasible. Economic and carbon consequences are quantified.

Conclusion: Workload-aware power control built on the workload's own generation parameters can substantially cut power-limit violations while improving output and energy efficiency, but only if the chosen actuator retains authority under sharding (occupancy-versus-volume principle). At realistic 30 s+ measurement windows, transient violations largely vanish and substantial nameplate oversubscription (~2x) appears feasible for the fleet mix, subject to operator validation; a low-cost operator pilot is specified.

Abstract: Reinforcement-learning post-training dominates modern language-model development, yet its power behavior on GPU hardware has not been characterized, and datacenters manage GPU power with workload-blind mechanisms, static caps and reactive throttling, that slow hardware indiscriminately. We instrument GRPO training with half-second power telemetry at 7B, 14B, and 72B scales on one to four A100s (380,000+ samples), and train a PPO meta-controller that adapts the workload's own generation parameters to measured power. Against the full 500-step 7B trace, the controller cuts power-limit violations by 89.8% while increasing token output by 18.1% and energy efficiency by 26.2% (tokens per MWh). Deployed live at 72B, the same controller family yields replicated null results, diagnosed as the group-size actuator losing authority under model sharding. An actuator-authority sweep shows the same parameters applied as generation concurrency retain 17-22% power authority, isolating an occupancy-versus-volume principle; a controller rebuilt on that actuator controls a live 72B rollout-generation workload across three replications: 35.7% more output than a static safe baseline at 2.27 +/- 1.08% budget violations, 87.2% fewer violations than uncontrolled operation, and the best mean throughput and energy per token among constrained controllers, with an adaptive threshold rule matching it in one of three operating conditions. Under realistic measurement windows the original 72B transients fall from 23.6% at half-second resolution to 1.6% at 30 s and zero at 5 min; a composed 16-GPU fleet shows zero violations at 30 s and longer, with peak demand at 50-56% of nameplate. For this fleet mix, roughly twofold oversubscription of nameplate appears feasible, subject to operator validation. We quantify the economic and carbon consequences and specify a low-cost operator pilot.

</details>


### [239] [AgenticTwin: An Agentic LLM Framework Integrated with Digital Twin for Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11679)
*Touseef Hasan,Mounika Ghanta,Souvika Sarkar,Ujjwal Guin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgenticTwin is an agentic framework that combines LLM-driven reasoning with a digital twin-based anomaly detection pipeline to ground explanations and answer natural-language questions about anomalies in cyber-physical systems. It also introduces a benchmark evaluation pipeline using synthetic anomalies on real weather sensor data, and shows that lightweight open-source LLMs can improve diagnosis, contextual retrieval, and mitigation quality via structured collaboration and knowledge grounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Digital twins generate massive, complex raw sensor data, making anomaly interpretation difficult even for skilled operators. While LLMs offer strong reasoning and explanation capabilities, their integration into digital twin-driven anomaly analysis is largely unexplored. The work aims to close this gap by enabling grounded, interactive anomaly explanation in cyber-physical systems.

Method: The paper proposes AgenticTwin, an agentic framework that grounds LLM-generated explanations in outputs from a digital twin-based anomaly classifier, allowing operators to ask natural-language questions. It introduces a benchmark-oriented evaluation pipeline built on synthetic anomalies injected into a real-world weather sensor dataset, enabling controlled generation of operator queries. It also evaluates the feasibility of deploying lightweight, open-source LLMs for practical cyber-physical settings.

Result: Experimental results show that structured agent collaboration and knowledge-grounded reasoning improve diagnosis quality, contextual retrieval, and mitigation quality across diverse anomaly scenarios.

Conclusion: Integrating LLM-driven agentic reasoning with digital twin anomaly detection is feasible and beneficial. The framework and benchmark demonstrate practical deployment using lightweight open-source LLMs, advancing explainable and interactive anomaly analysis for cyber-physical systems.

Abstract: Digital twins are increasingly used to monitor and simulate the behavior of cyber-physical systems. Even with skilled operators, interpreting anomalies detected within digital twin pipelines is challenging, as the sheer complexity and volume of raw sensor data make thorough analysis difficult. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer promising capabilities for reasoning and explanation, yet their integration into digital twin-driven anomaly analysis remains underexplored. In this work, we propose AgenticTwin, an agentic framework that integrates LLM-driven reasoning with a digital twin-based anomaly detection pipeline. The framework grounds LLM-generated explanations in outputs from a digital twin-driven anomaly classifier and enables human operators to ask relevant natural-language questions about the system. Beyond the framework itself, we introduce a benchmark-oriented evaluation pipeline constructed over synthetic anomalies injected into a real-world weather sensor dataset, enabling controlled generation of operator queries over anomaly events. We further evaluate the feasibility of deploying lightweight, open-source LLMs for practical cyber-physical environments. Experimental results demonstrate that structured agent collaboration and knowledge-grounded reasoning improve diagnosis quality, contextual retrieval, and mitigation quality across diverse possible anomaly scenarios.

</details>


### [240] [Forecasting Side Effects of Activation Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11227)
*Chong Yong Ong,Alson Wei Jie Sim,Peixin Zhang,Jun Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Activation steering produces systematic, structured, and largely predictable side effects on other behaviors, which can be forecasted before steering is applied, enabling proactive safety auditing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Activation steering is effective for targeted behavioral modification without retraining, but it often causes unintended side effects on other behaviors, hindering safe deployment. The authors aim to determine whether these side effects can be forecasted in advance.

Method: The authors construct a cross-effect matrix over a taxonomy of 67 behaviors across three open-weight language models. They analyze the structure and symmetry of behavioral interactions, and evaluate whether side-effect magnitude (dependent mainly on target behavior) and direction (forecasted from the model's unsteered representations) can be predicted before steering.

Result: Side effects are common, structured, and often asymmetric, and cannot be fully explained by existing similarity-based heuristics. Nevertheless, side-effect magnitude depends primarily on the target behavior, and side-effect direction can be forecasted from unsteered representations with substantially higher accuracy than simple baselines.

Conclusion: Activation steering has systematic and forecastable side effects, which enables proactive safety auditing and more informed, safer deployment of steering interventions.

Abstract: Activation steering modifies a language model by adding a learned direction to its hidden activations, enabling targeted behavioral changes without retraining. While effective, steering often produces unintended side effects on other behaviors, making it difficult to deploy safely. We therefore ask: can these side effects be forecasted before steering is applied? We answer this question by constructing a cross-effect matrix over a taxonomy of 67 behaviors across three open-weight language models. We find that side effects are common, structured, and often asymmetric, revealing interactions that cannot be explained by existing similarity-based heuristics. Despite this complexity, we show that side effects are largely predictable before steering is performed. Their magnitude depends primarily on the target behavior, while their direction can be forecasted from the model's unsteered representations with substantially higher accuracy than simple baselines. Our results demonstrate that activation steering has systematic and forecastable side effects, enabling proactive safety auditing and more informed deployment of steering interventions.

</details>


### [241] [Synchronizing Beliefs with Second-Order Theory-of-Mind in Human-Autonomy Teams (Extended Version)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11229)
*Jack Mirenzi,Henny Admoni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper reframes preference-based reward learning as a two-sided human-autonomy team problem, where an informed teacher designs a curriculum using a model of the learner, and the learner sends "understanding statements" (second-order ToM statements) to keep the teacher's model synchronized, thereby preserving the teacher's efficiency advantage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard preference-based reward learning treats the human teacher as a passive oracle answering learner-generated queries, which forfeits the teacher's key advantage: knowledge of the objective. A teacher who knows the target can construct training examples more efficiently than any learner-driven strategy, especially as the reward's feature dimension grows. However, exploiting this advantage requires an accurate model of what the learner currently knows.

Method: The approach couples two behavioral models in a human-autonomy team: (1) the teacher maintains a model of the learner to design an informative curriculum, and (2) the learner maintains a second-order model of the teacher's model, emitting structured preference constraints called "understanding statements" that keep the teacher's model of the learner synchronized. This is evaluated in simulation, including ToM-2 (second-order theory-of-mind) statements versus mean-belief statements.

Result: In simulation, an informed teacher outperforms learner-led selection. Teacher-model drift under alternating teachers erodes this advantage, and understanding statements repair it. ToM-2 statements outperform mean-belief statements when the teacher's error about the learner is concentrated in a particular direction rather than spread evenly.

Conclusion: Preference learning should be treated as a team problem in which the teacher actively designs a curriculum and the learner communicates its understanding to maintain synchronization. Second-order understanding statements effectively repair teacher-model drift and preserve the teacher's efficiency advantage, especially under directional error.

Abstract: Comparative feedback, asking people which of two behaviors they prefer, has become a standard way to align robot and agent behavior with human intent when the reward itself cannot be specified directly. Preference-based reward learning typically casts the human teacher as a passive oracle answering learner-generated queries. We argue this forfeits the teacher's defining advantage: knowledge of the objective. A teacher who knows the target can construct training examples more efficiently than any learner-driven acquisition strategy, an advantage that widens as the reward's feature dimension grows. However, exploiting this advantage requires an accurate model of what the learner currently knows. We therefore recast preference learning as a human-autonomy team problem coupling two behavioral models: the teacher maintains a model of the learner to design an informative curriculum, and the learner maintains a second-order model of the teacher's model, emitting structured preference constraints (understanding statements) that keep the teacher's model of the learner synchronized. In simulation, an informed teacher outperforms learner-led selection; teacher-model drift under alternating teachers erodes this advantage; and understanding statements repair it, with second-order (ToM-2) statements outperforming mean-belief statements when the teacher's error about the learner is concentrated in a particular direction rather than spread evenly.

</details>


### [242] [Mechanist: AI as a Scientific Instrument for Discovering the Mechanisms of Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12036)
*Mengru Wang,Junfeng Fang,Shuofei Qiao,Zhenqian Xu,Haoming Xu,Haoxiong Wang,Shumin Deng,Linyi Yang,Zhixiang Cui,Xin Xu,Yunzhi Yao,Buqiang Xu,Fei Shen,Haozhe Luo,Yunxiang Wei,Ningyu Zhang,Julian McAuley,Tat Seng Chua,Huajun Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Mechanist, an agentic AI system for autonomously discovering the mechanisms underlying AI intelligence. It is built on a ~13,000-paper interpretability knowledge graph plus a 43-million-paper multidisciplinary database, and a library of 32 foundational analysis/intervention/validation methods. Compared to baselines, it produces more valuable hypotheses and more reliable experiments, progressing from discovering behaviors to explaining and controlling models, including uncovering a cross-modal safety risk and deriving a mechanistic theory of belief that enables practical interventions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI models achieve strong capabilities but their internal mechanisms and risks are poorly understood. AI development is accelerating and automated, while mechanistic interpretability remains manual, creating a widening gap between model capabilities and our ability to understand and control them. The goal is to close this gap by using AI itself as a scientific instrument for autonomous mechanistic discovery.

Method: Mechanist is an agentic system that: (1) constructs an interpretability-focused knowledge graph of ~13,000 papers integrated with a multidisciplinary database of 43 million papers across 26 fields; (2) curates a library of 32 foundational methods for mechanism analysis, causal intervention, and validation; and (3) autonomously generates mechanism hypotheses and executes experiments. It is benchmarked against Claude Code and existing AI-scientist systems.

Result: Mechanist generates more valuable mechanism hypotheses and executes experiments more reliably than Claude Code and existing AI-scientist systems. It progresses from discovering model behaviors to explaining and controlling models: (1) it uncovers a counterintuitive safety risk where unsafe traits transfer across modalities through apparently safe training data in scientific laboratories; (2) it develops a mechanism theory of belief explaining how models represent world knowledge, form beliefs, infer others' beliefs, and how these mechanisms emerge during pretraining; (3) it translates insights into interventions that improve performance and steer scientific foundation models to generate DNA sequences with specified properties.

Conclusion: Mechanist demonstrates the feasibility of using AI as a scientific instrument for autonomous mechanistic discovery, bridging the gap between model capability and human understanding. By progressing from discovering behaviors to generating mechanistic explanations and enabling control, it shows a path toward scalable, automated interpretability and safer, more steerable AI systems.

Abstract: AI models have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, yet the mechanisms underlying their capabilities and the risks they may pose remain poorly understood. As AI development becomes faster and increasingly automated, mechanistic exploration remains largely manual, widening the gap between what models can do and our ability to understand and control them. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mechanist, an agentic system that uses AI as a scientific instrument for the autonomous discovery of mechanisms underlying AI intelligence. To support autonomous mechanistic discovery, we construct an interpretability-focused knowledge graph of approximately 13,000 papers and integrate it with a multidisciplinary database of 43 million papers spanning 26 fields. We further curate a library of 32 foundational methods for mechanism analysis, causal intervention, and validation. Compared with Claude Code and existing AI-scientist systems, Mechanist generates more valuable mechanism hypotheses and executes experiments more reliably. Mechanist also demonstrates a progression from discovering model behaviors to explaining and controlling AI models. Specifically, Mechanist first uncovers a counterintuitive safety risk in scientific laboratories, showing that unsafe traits can transfer across modalities through apparently safe training data. Mechanist then develops a mechanism theory of belief, revealing how models represent world knowledge, form beliefs, infer the beliefs of others, and how these mechanisms emerge during pretraining. Finally, Mechanist translates these mechanistic insights into practical interventions that improve model performance across diverse scenarios and steer scientific foundation models toward generating DNA sequences with specified properties.

</details>


### [243] [The Edge-based Contiguous p-median Problem with Connections to Logistics Districting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11230)
*Zeyad Kassem,Adolfo R. Escobedo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper formulates the edge-based contiguous p-median (ECpM) problem for partitioning road networks into compact, contiguous territories, proposing two binary programming models with different contiguity-constraint strategies, and shows that the shortest-path-contiguity (SPC) approach is substantially faster and also improves on the edge-based districting (EBD) problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Partitioning road networks into compact and contiguous territories is computationally challenging, especially when contiguity must be modeled explicitly. Existing cut set-based contiguity formulations are exponential in size and slow, motivating the search for polynomial-size contiguity constraints that are faster to solve while remaining effective.

Method: Two binary programming models for ECpM are introduced. The first uses an exponential number of cut set-based constraints for contiguity, solved via a branch-and-cut (B&C) algorithm with a separation scheme. The second uses a polynomial number of shortest-path constraints (SPC) for contiguity and can be solved by off-the-shelf solvers. The approaches are tested on road networks with over 2,700 nodes and nearly 3,400 edges, yielding models with over 9.6 million binary variables. The paper also analyzes connections between ECpM and the edge-based districting (EBD) problem, which adds a work balance criterion.

Result: The SPC-based model solved via standard branch and bound achieves computational speedups up to 17x relative to the cut set-based B&C implementation. SPC constraints are shown to be supervalid inequalities of the edge-based p-median (EpM) model, cutting off some but not all optimal solutions of that simpler problem. For EBD, the existing cut set-based model failed to find a feasible solution within 12 hours on any tested instance, whereas an SPC-based EBD model solved most instances to optimality.

Conclusion: Polynomial-size shortest-path contiguity constraints provide a much more tractable approach than exponentially many cut set-based constraints for contiguous territory partitioning, delivering large speedups for ECpM and making the more constrained EBD problem solvable to optimality. The supervalidity result also deepens the theoretical understanding of how contiguity constraints interact with the underlying p-median structure.

Abstract: This paper introduces the edge-based contiguous p-median (ECpM) problem to partition the roads in a network into a given number of compact and contiguous territories. Two binary programming models are introduced, both of which incorporate a network distance. The first model requires an exponential number of cut set-based constraints to model contiguity; it is paired with a separation scheme that usually generates only a small number of these constraints, namely, a branch-and-cut (B&C) algorithm. The second model utilizes a polynomial number of shortest-path constraints to model contiguity and can be solved with off-the-shelf solvers. The respective solution approaches are tested on road networks with over 2,700 nodes and close to 3,400 edges, yielding models with over 9.6 million binary variables. Solving the model based on shortest path contiguity (SPC) constraints via standard branch and bound attains speedups in computational time of up to 17x relative to the cut set-based B&C implementation. In addition, the SPC constraints are demonstrated to be supervalid inequalities of the edge-based p-median (EpM) model (i.e., for which contiguity is not explicitly required), meaning that they may cut off integer-feasible solutions and some, but not all, of the optimal solutions of this simpler problem. Finally, the paper explores structural insights and connections between ECpM and the edge-based districting (EBD) problem, which enforces an additional work balance criterion. An existing model that utilizes cut set-based contiguity constraints was unable to find a feasible solution within 12 hours for any of the tested instances, while an SPC-based EBD model was able to solve most of these to optimality.

</details>


### [244] [LinearKV: One Cached State Suffices for Position-Independent Caching in Hybrid LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11231)
*Yirui Liu,Ruoling Qi,Longwen Wang,Xuaner Wu,Jian Chen,Yuxin Jin,Jiawei Shao,Xuelong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LinearKV introduces a training-free PIC framework for hybrid LLMs, showing that a single cached state (rather than exact composition of all cached states) suffices to initialize linear layers, delivering comparable or better quality at lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing position-independent caching (PIC) methods assume full-attention models with token-indexed KV caches that can be matched, concatenated, and locally repaired. Hybrid LLMs replace most attention layers with linear recurrences exposing only a fixed-size state, breaking these primitives and leaving an open question of whether PIC can benefit hybrid models.

Method: LinearKV proposes a decoupled initialization: each linear layer maps its K matched local states to a single initial state, while full-attention layers concatenate KV as usual. This is compatible with existing PIC methods and reuses their token selection and recomputation unchanged. The framework compares a single cached state initializer against the algebraically exact composition of all K cached states (as in HYPIC).

Result: Across three hybrid models and three PIC selectors, the single-state and exact-composition approaches tie on two GDN models, recovering up to 92% of full quality. On Mamba-2, exact composition collapses under every selector (e.g., 46.6% under EPIC) versus 86.8% for a single cached block initializer. The single-state method also reduces time-to-first-token to 0.46x full prefill, avoiding a further 5-17% overhead from exact composition; results hold on LongBench QA and RULER at 8K-32K.

Conclusion: A single cached state is sufficient—and preferable—to initialize linear layers for hybrid models under PIC, making exact composition unnecessary and sometimes harmful, while offering significant latency savings.

Abstract: LLM serving is increasingly accelerated by position-independent caching (PIC). Existing PIC methods, however, are built for full-attention models, where a token-indexed KV cache underlies its core operations: matching reusable token chunks, concatenating their KV entries, and selectively recomputing a few tokens to restore cross-chunk context. Hybrid LLMs break these primitives---they replace most attention layers with linear recurrences that expose only a fixed-size state, leaving no token-indexed KV to concatenate or to locally repair. This raises a natural question: can PIC benefit hybrid models, and what would it take? We present LinearKV, a training-free hybrid-PIC framework. Its key insight is a \emph{decoupled initialization}: each linear layer maps its $K$ matched local states to a single initial state, while full-attention layers concatenate their KV as before. LinearKV is therefore compatible with existing PIC methods, reusing their token selection and recomputation as-is. Under this framework, we find that a \emph{single cached state} suffices as the linear layer's initializer. The algebraically principled alternative---composing all $K$ cached states into the exact full-prefix state, as concurrent work HYPIC does---is unnecessary and, on some architectures, even harmful. We compare the two across three hybrid models and three PIC selectors. On the two GDN models the two tie, both recovering most of full quality (up to $92\%$); on the Mamba-2 model, exact composition instead collapses under every selector---under EPIC, for instance, it recovers only $46.6\%$ of full quality, versus $86.8\%$ for a single cached block initializer. A single state initializer is also cheaper, cutting time-to-first-token to $0.46\times$ full prefill versus a further $5$--$17\%$ overhead for exact composition; results hold across LongBench QA and RULER at 8K--32K.

</details>


### [245] [InfraBench: Evaluating Infrastructure Agents Across Layers, Lifecycle, and Risk](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11234)
*Yuan Gao,Zeren Yang,Junnan Li,Shawn,Zhong,Ahmed Dajani,Mai Zheng,Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau,Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InfraBench is a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on realistic infrastructure management tasks, showing that even top agents fail to achieve full scores and leave behind unsafe or non-durable side effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Managing modern computing infrastructure is increasingly hard due to growing complexity, and recent AI agent advances offer a chance to automate these tasks—yet it is unclear how well agents handle real-world infrastructure complexity.

Method: The authors built InfraBench, a benchmark suite covering realistic infrastructure tasks across the full system stack and full operational lifecycle, with fine-grained risk assessment. They evaluated 15 agent-model configurations, repeated each task three times, and scored individual checks per task, with a public leaderboard and evaluation harness.

Result: No agent configuration secured a full score. Mean effective scores ranged from roughly 40% to 88%, with per-configuration standard errors of 6-12 points. Even top configurations passed only a fraction of their attempts across three repetitions. Per-check scoring showed a general failure pattern: agents meet short-term objectives but leave non-durable changes, broken distributed invariants, unsafe side effects, and uncleaned state behind.

Conclusion: Current AI agents are not yet reliably capable of real-world infrastructure management; InfraBench provides a public benchmark (infraben.ch) to track progress and expose the subtle failure modes agents exhibit.

Abstract: Managing modern computing infrastructure has become a steadily harder problem due to the ever-increasing complexity. Recent advances in AI agents create a timely opportunity to automate infrastructure management tasks, but it remains unclear how well such agents can handle real-world infrastructure complexity. We present InfraBench, a benchmark suite for evaluating AI agents on realistic infrastructure tasks across the full system stack and full operational lifecycle with fine-grained risk assessment. Experiments with 15 agent-model configurations show that even the strongest agent cannot secure a full score across all tasks. Mean effective scores range from roughly 40% to 88% (with per-configuration standard errors of 6-12 points), repeating every task three times reveals that top configurations still pass only a fraction of their attempts, and per-check scoring exposes a general failure pattern: agents may routinely satisfy short-term objectives while leaving non-durable changes, broken distributed invariants, unsafe side effects, and uncleaned state behind. INFRABENCH, including its live leaderboard, tasks, and evaluation harness, is publicly available at infraben.ch.

</details>


### [246] [CORA-Diff: Confidence-Oriented Residual Acceptance for Efficient Diffusion Language Model Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11235)
*Yifan Wu,Yufeng Zhang,Kenli Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CORA-Diff is a training-free method that accelerates diffusion language models by using confidence-and-persistence gating to accept stabilized residual tokens early, preserving the original transfer rule and reducing repeated denoising passes without loss of task quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion language models update many tokens in parallel but typically use a fixed denoising horizon, causing many tokens to stabilize early while blockwise decoding continues until all positions are resolved—leading to repeated dense forward passes. Existing accelerators rely on learned filters, modified scores, dependency models, or cache-specific mechanisms. The paper asks whether native trajectory signals (confidence and persistence) can identify residual positions likely to match the deterministic dense endpoint, without modifying the backbone or adding learned components.

Method: CORA-Diff is a training-free method that keeps the original transfer rule intact and applies confidence-and-persistence gating only to positions left unresolved by that rule. Accepted tokens remain visible as context, and the block terminates once all positions are resolved. It requires no backbone change, no learned acceptance model, and no logit modification. A single operating point is selected on a separate GSM8K calibration subset and frozen for all evaluations. The paper provides theory for why high-confidence, persistent predictions match the fixed-horizon dense endpoint, plus empirical support from paired post-intervention trajectories.

Result: Under a matched Learn2PD-style LLaDA protocol, CORA-Diff achieves the lowest measured runtime in all eight task-length settings. Task scores match or exceed dense decoding in five settings, with the largest drop being 1.22 points. Incremental speedups over EOS-aware dense decoding are 2.70x on GSM8K and 3.32x on HumanEval, reaching 13.14x under a fixed-horizon 1024/1024 mechanism-isolation protocol. It transfers to Dream without retuning at 3.18x-3.53x.

Conclusion: Native confidence and persistence signals enable reliable residual acceptance, reducing repeated denoising computation while preserving task quality across multiple tasks and models without retraining.

Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) update many tokens in parallel, yet practical decoders often use a fixed denoising horizon. Many predictions stabilize early, but blockwise decoding continues until all positions are resolved, causing repeated dense forward passes. Existing accelerators often rely on learned filters, modified scores, dependency models, or cache-specific mechanisms. We ask whether native trajectory signals can identify residual positions likely to match the deterministic dense endpoint. We propose CORA-Diff, a training-free method that preserves the original transfer rule and applies confidence-and-persistence gating only to positions that rule leaves unresolved. Accepted tokens remain visible as context, and the block terminates once all positions are resolved. This requires no backbone change, learned acceptance model, or logit modification. Our theory explains why high-confidence, persistent predictions are more likely to match the fixed-horizon dense endpoint, and paired post-intervention trajectories provide direct empirical support. We select one operating point on a separate GSM8K calibration subset and freeze it for all evaluations. Under a matched Learn2PD-style LLaDA protocol, CORA-Diff has the lowest measured runtime in all eight task-length settings. Task scores match or exceed dense decoding in five settings, and the largest observed drop is 1.22 points. Its incremental speedups over EOS-aware dense decoding are 2.70x and 3.32x on GSM8K and HumanEval. It also reaches 13.14x under the fixed-horizon 1024/1024 mechanism-isolation protocol and transfers to Dream without retuning at 3.18x-3.53x. These results show that native confidence and persistence enable reliable residual acceptance, reducing repeated denoising computation while preserving task quality.

</details>


### [247] [Geometry-aware Incremental Neural Operator for Long-Horizon PDE prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11237)
*Jiaquan Zhang,Shuxu Chen,Haifan Meng,Yi Lu,Zhihan Lyu,Fan Mo,Wei Dong,Yang Yang,Chaoning Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GeoIncNO improves long-horizon PDE forecasting by structuring the latent increments, regulating channel coupling within active frequency bands via low-rank projectors, and decoupling mean from fluctuation during reconstruction, yielding better stability and spectral fidelity across six benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon autoregressive prediction with neural operators suffers from error accumulation manifesting as spectral inconsistency, phase misalignment, and mean drift. Existing work focuses on better state representations and operator backbones but leaves the repeatedly applied latent transition increment weakly structured, allowing spectral errors and unstable channel couplings to compound over rollouts.

Method: GeoIncNO predicts latent increments for residual advancement and uses lightweight low-rank projectors to regulate channel coupling within active frequency bands derived from the increment spectral energy distribution. It adds a mean–fluctuation decoupled reconstruction mechanism that fuses stable mean structures and dynamic fluctuations separately, applying phase correction only to the zero-mean fluctuation component.

Result: On six PDE benchmarks spanning 1D, 2D, and 3D dynamical systems, GeoIncNO achieves consistently strong prediction accuracy, improved rollout stability, and better spectral fidelity compared to competitive neural-operator baselines.

Conclusion: By imposing structure on latent increments through low-rank frequency-band regulation and mean–fluctuation decoupling, GeoIncNO mitigates long-horizon error accumulation in neural operators, offering stable and spectrally faithful PDE predictions.

Abstract: Neural operators have shown strong potential for learning solution operators of partial differential equations (PDEs). However, long-horizon autoregressive prediction remains challenging: local errors accumulate as spectral inconsistency, phase misalignment, or mean drift. Existing methods mainly improve state representations and operator backbones, while leaving the repeatedly applied latent transition increment weakly structured, allowing spectral errors and unstable channel couplings to accumulate during rollout. To address these issues, we propose a geometry-aware incremental neural operator (GeoIncNO) for stable long-horizon PDE prediction. GeoIncNO predicts latent increments for residual advancement and uses lightweight low-rank projectors to regulate channel coupling within active frequency bands derived from the increment spectral energy distribution. To reduce physical-space reconstruction errors, GeoIncNO further introduces a mean--fluctuation decoupled reconstruction mechanism, where stable mean structures and dynamic fluctuations are fused separately, and phase correction is applied only to the zero-mean fluctuation component. Extensive experiments on six PDE benchmarks, covering 1D, 2D, and 3D dynamical systems, show that GeoIncNO achieves consistently strong prediction accuracy, improved rollout stability, and better spectral fidelity compared with competitive neural-operator baselines.

</details>


### [248] [Towards Query-Agnostic RAG Evaluation via Query Coverage and Claim Verifiability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11238)
*Jeonghwan Choi,Taewon Yun,Minjeong Ban,Gyeonghun Sun,Jae-Gil Lee,Hwanjun Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Q-CARE is a query-agnostic, fully reference-free framework for fine-grained RAG evaluation that decomposes queries into sub-queries and answers into atomic claims, introducing coverage-aware retriever metrics and claim-level generator metrics. It correlates more strongly with human judgments than four existing metrics, including RAGEval and RAGChecker.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation frameworks for retrieval-augmented generation cannot provide consistent, fine-grained diagnostics across diverse user queries (close-ended fact-seeking to open-ended explanatory). They rely on references or fixed query assumptions, limiting reliable assessment across the full query spectrum.

Method: Q-CARE decomposes queries into sub-queries and answers into atomic claims, establishing a unified evaluation principle based on query coverage and claim verifiability. It yields coverage-aware retriever metrics (C-Prec@k, C-nDCG@k) and claim-level generator metrics (Completeness, Conciseness, Verifiableness), and is query-agnostic and fully reference-free.

Result: On a human-annotated benchmark spanning eight datasets, Q-CARE achieves higher correlation with human judgments than four existing RAG evaluation metrics, including RAGEval and RAGChecker, demonstrating its reliability as an automated evaluation framework.

Conclusion: Q-CARE provides an effective, reliable, automated, query-agnostic, and reference-free framework for fine-grained RAG evaluation, with code and data publicly released.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation improves the factuality of large language models by grounding responses in retrieved evidence, yet existing evaluation frameworks struggle to provide consistent, fine-grained diagnostics across the diverse spectrum of user queries, ranging from close-ended fact-seeking to open-ended explanatory requests. We propose Q-CARE, a query-agnostic and fully reference-free framework that enables fine-grained assessment by decomposing queries into sub-queries and answers into atomic claims. Q-CARE establishes a unified evaluation principle based on query coverage and claim verifiability, yielding coverage-aware retriever metrics (C-Prec@k, C-nDCG@k) and claim-level generator metrics (Completeness, Conciseness, and Verifiableness). On a human-annotated benchmark spanning eight datasets, Q-CARE achieves higher correlation with human judgments than four existing RAG evaluation metrics, including RAGEval and RAGChecker, proving its effectiveness as a reliable, automated evaluation framework. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/DISL-Lab/Q-CaRE-COLM-26.

</details>


### [249] [VQ-bench: A Composable Vector Quantization Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11240)
*Ashwin Padaki,Amir Ingber,Edo Liberty*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a unified framework of 7 composable quantization primitives, re-expresses 25 existing quantizers as pipelines of these primitives, and releases VQ-bench as an open-source benchmarking suite.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vector quantization has regained central importance in AI infrastructure, driving renewed engineering and research activity, yet lacks a unified framework for developing and benchmarking new quantization algorithms.

Method: The authors describe 7 common conceptual quantization primitives and show how these primitives can be composed arbitrarily. They demonstrate the framework's expressiveness by re-expressing 25 common quantizers as pipelines built from these primitives.

Result: The framework successfully decomposes 25 common quantizers into pipelines of 7 primitives, validating its generality and composability for describing diverse existing algorithms.

Conclusion: The proposed unified framework enables systematic development and benchmarking of quantization algorithms, and VQ-bench is published as open-source to support reproducible benchmarks and further community extension.

Abstract: Vector quantization is an old problem but has recently become central to AI infrastructure. It is therefore experiencing a surge of renewed engineering and research activity. This paper provides a unified framework for developing and benchmarking new quantization algorithms. We describe 7 common conceptual quantization primitives and show how to compose them arbitrarily. We then re-express 25 common quantizers as pipelines of these primitives. Finally, we publish VQ-bench as open-source to be extended further and make reproducible benchmarks publicly available.

</details>


### [250] [The Off-Support Barrier: Why Semantic Safety Constraints Are Not Learning-Problem Invariants, and What Follows for Prior Design, Containment, and Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11243)
*Yoshinori Watanabe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that safety constraints in AI are "off-support objects"—not measurable with respect to the model and data distribution—and uses this single structural fact, grounded in singular learning theory (SLT), to derive five otherwise-disparate AI safety phenomena as corollaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To unify a wide range of AI safety phenomena (reward hacking, sandbox escape, weak priors, verification limits, performative prediction) under one structural principle, motivated by the July 2026 OpenAI–Hugging Face evaluation incident, rather than treating them as independent observations.

Method: Formalizes the safety predicate B as non-measurable w.r.t. σ(model, q) while the RLCT of singular learning theory is measurable; then derives corollaries (i)–(v) from this non-invariance, corroborated by numerical experiments and Lean proofs (available on GitHub).

Result: Five corollaries follow from the off-support structure: (i) outcome-based optimization induces reward hacking/sandbox escape; (ii) Bayesian priors and soft penalties have poor leverage in singular models; (iii) hard invariants belong in the harness, soft dispositions in the model; (iv) formal verification is sound and locally certifiable akin to how the LLC pins the RLCT, with two disanalogies; (v) the residual difficulty is identifying which off-support region matters, coinciding with performative prediction/self-referential dynamics where SLT breaks down.

Conclusion: A single structural fact—the off-support, non-measurable nature of semantic safety constraints—organizes diverse AI safety difficulties, implying that safety encoding must be split between the harness (hard invariants) and the model (soft dispositions), while the hardest remaining problem lies in identifying which off-support regions matter, where SLT's analytic machinery fails.

Abstract: We argue that a single structural fact organizes a wide range of phenomena in contemporary AI safety: a semantic safety constraint (e.g., the agent does not escape its sandbox) is an off-support object. Formally, if q is the data distribution and \(p(\cdot\mid w)\) the model, the safety predicate B is not measurable with respect to \(σ(\text{model}, q)\), whereas the real log-canonical threshold (RLCT) of singular learning theory (SLT) is. From this non-invariance we derive, as corollaries rather than independent observations: (i) why reward hacking and sandbox escape arise under outcome-based optimization; (ii) why encoding such constraints through Bayesian prior design or soft penalty weighting has poor leverage in singular models; (iii) why hard invariants belong in the harness and soft dispositions in the model; (iv) why the same B is nonetheless soundly and locally certifiable by formal verification, exactly as the local learning coefficient (LLC) locally pins the same RLCT --- with two precise points of disanalogy; and (v) why the residual difficulty, identifying which off-support region matters, coincides with performative prediction and self-referential functional dynamics, where SLT's analytic machinery breaks down. We use the July 2026 OpenAI--Hugging Face evaluation incident as the motivating case. Numerical experiments code and related proofs in lean are available at https://github.com/xiangze/Preventing_Jailbreak_as_regularization

</details>


### [251] [BEST-KAG: Enhancing Question Answering of Building Engineering Standards with Multimodal Knowledge Graph Modeling and Large Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11244)
*Jia-Rui Lin,Junxi Guo,Keyin Chen,Peng Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BEST-KAG is a multimodal knowledge-driven question-answering framework for building engineering construction standards. It combines a multimodal knowledge graph (MKG), a rule-LLM hybrid construction pipeline (producing a large MAG with 251 standards, 171,652 nodes, 310,914 edges), and graph-retrieval-based knowledge-augmented generation to enable clause-grounded, traceable answers. It outperforms mainstream LLMs, improving metrics by up to 74.01%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
