To train CLAIM, we formulate the clarification process as a structured decision generation problem and adopt a training paradigm that combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). Experimental results demonstrate that CLAIM can learn stable and generalizable clarification strategies without relying on manually labeled data, offering a low-cost and robust solution for proactive understanding in real-world open-domain interactions with LLMs.

</details>


### [274] [XBridge: Entity-Grounded Latent Bridge for Heterogeneous LLM Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11676)
*Wooseong Yang,Wei-Chieh Huang,Weizhi Zhang,Yu Wang,Philip S. Yu,Junhyun Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: XBRIDGE is a decode-free communication protocol for heterogeneous multi-agent LLM systems that combines discrete lexical entity anchors with a latent enrichment bridge to transfer cross-architecture information, avoiding rare-token compression collapse while achieving lower latency and stronger task performance than text-based baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Heterogeneous multi-agent LLM systems reduce redundant reasoning, but existing communication either works only through text (discarding internal representations) or requires architectural homogeneity for latent transfer. The core obstacle is the entity grounding problem: cross-attention bridges transferring continuous representations across different LLM families suffer rare-token compression collapse, where entity identity is lost in the continuous bottleneck (bridge-only F1 ~30%).

Method: XBRIDGE uses two mechanisms: (1) Lexical Anchor Mapping (LAM), which maps the sender's original context tokens to the receiver's vocabulary to provide discrete entity anchors, and (2) a Latent Enrichment Bridge (LEB), which lets the receiver query the sender's hidden states for contextual enrichment. The entity anchors ground the bridge's contextual signals to specific entities through the receiver's own self-attention.

Result: Across three model families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral), seven benchmarks, and both communication directions, XBRIDGE outperforms text-based communication on all seven tasks for every model pair with 11x lower latency. In a same-architecture setting it exceeds a KV-sharing baseline on six of seven tasks. LEB requires only 264M trainable parameters (3.8% of the receiver), is trained on a small balanced sample set, and adds negligible inference overhead.

Conclusion: XBRIDGE solves the entity grounding problem in cross-architecture communication by combining discrete lexical anchors with a latent enrichment bridge, enabling efficient, high-performance latent-level transfer across heterogeneous LLM families without requiring text decoding or architectural homogeneity.

Abstract: Heterogeneous multi-agent LLM systems, where agents are powered by different model families, can outperform homogeneous configurations by reducing redundant reasoning patterns. Yet existing communication protocols either operate through text, discarding the sender's internal representations, or require architectural homogeneity for latent-level transfer. We identify the entity grounding problem in cross-architecture communication: cross-attention bridges that transfer continuous representations across different LLM families suffer from rare-token compression collapse, where entity identity is lost in the continuous bottleneck (bridge-only F1 ~30%). We propose XBRIDGE, a decode-free communication protocol that addresses this through two mechanisms. Lexical Anchor Mapping (LAM) maps the sender's original context tokens to the receiver's vocabulary, providing discrete entity anchors. A Latent Enrichment Bridge (LEB) lets the receiver query the sender's hidden states for contextual enrichment. The entity anchors ground the bridge's contextual signals to specific entities through the receiver's own self-attention. Across three model families (Llama, Qwen, and Mistral), seven benchmarks, and both communication directions, XBRIDGE outperforms text-based communication on all seven tasks for each model pair while achieving 11x lower latency, and in a same-architecture setting it also exceeds a KV-sharing baseline on six of seven tasks. LEB requires only 264M trainable parameters (3.8% of the receiver), is trained on a small balanced sample set, and adds negligible inference overhead.

</details>


### [275] [FrontierFinance: A Challenging Benchmark for Measuring Frontier Intelligence of Finance Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11683)
*Yuhao Zhang,O. Ozan Koyluoglu,Thejas Venkatesh,Richard Diehl Martinez,Vishank Bhatia,Arash Alidoust,Ashwin Paranjape*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FrontierFinance is a new open benchmark of 220 expert-crafted queries and 11,543 source-attributed rubrics spanning six use cases across the full investor workflow, showing that tool harnesses shape agent quality/efficiency more than models alone and that open-weight models approach proprietary performance at much lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing financial AI benchmarks focus narrowly on data extraction (a largely saturated task) and rely on reference-based metrics or generic LLM-as-a-judge scoring that cannot adequately evaluate the open-ended, long-form answers real investor queries require. There is no benchmark capturing the complexity of the full investor workflow, so the authors built FrontierFinance to fill this gap.

Method: The authors created FrontierFinance, a fully open benchmark of 220 expert-crafted queries and 11,543 source-attributed rubrics covering six use cases across the complete investor workflow. They evaluated frontier models and agent systems under a common harness restricted to publicly available data, comparing quality, efficiency, and cost across proprietary and open-weight systems.

Result: The tool harness (not the model alone) strongly shapes quality and efficiency. Samaya's in-house system leads at 56.0%, ahead of the strongest frontier model (Claude Fable 5, 49.2%) at roughly 2.2x lower cost. The best open-weight model (Kimi K3, 46.4%) nearly matches the best proprietary model at 4.5x lower cost. Screening & Discovery and Sector, Industry & Macro remain the hardest use cases, where even the best systems reach only 33% and 39%, respectively.

Conclusion: FrontierFinance provides a broader and harder benchmark than existing public finance benchmarks, demonstrating that system design (tool harness) is a key lever for performance and cost, and that open-weight models are becoming competitive with proprietary models. The dataset and grading code are publicly available to support further research.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed for professional investment research, yet no benchmark captures the complexity of the full investor workflow. Existing benchmarks mainly target financial data extraction, a narrow slice that current models have largely saturated, while reference-based metrics and generic LLM-as-a-judge scoring fall short on the open-ended, long-form answers that real analyst queries demand. We introduce FrontierFinance, a fully open benchmark of 220 expert-crafted queries and 11,543 source-attributed rubrics spanning six crucial use cases across the full investor workflow. FrontierFinance is both broader and harder than existing public finance benchmarks. Evaluating frontier models and agent systems under a common harness restricted to publicly available data, we find that the tool harness, not the model alone, strongly shapes quality and efficiency; that Samaya's in-house system leads at 56.0%, ahead of the strongest frontier model (Claude Fable 5, 49.2%) at roughly 2.2x lower cost; and that the best open-weight model (Kimi K3, 46.4%) nearly matches the best proprietary model at 4.5x lower cost. Screening & Discovery and Sector, Industry & Macro remain the hardest use cases across all systems, where even the best systems reach only 33% and 39%. We make the dataset and grading code publicly available.

</details>


### [276] [HUGIN: Enhancing Vision-Language Planning for Autonomous Logistics Sorting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11692)
*Xikai Sun,Cangtian Zhou,Kebin Liu,Ke Ma,Xu Wang,Zaishu Chen,Haotian Wang,Li Liu,Yunhao Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces HUGIN, a training framework that equips vision-language models (VLMs) for Joint Multi-Scene Understanding (JMSU) in autonomous logistics sorting, improving accuracy substantially and validating real-world viability through deployment over 15,000 packages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous logistics sorting systems require joint planning across spatially disjoint camera views, a setting formalized as Joint Multi-Scene Understanding (JMSU). VLMs are promising for this open-world visual understanding and planning task, but direct application is hindered by (1) scarce cross-scene supervision and (2) attention dispersion caused by long visual context.

Method: The authors propose HUGIN, a training framework with two complementary components: (1) Endogenous Data Augmentation, which recombines verified atomic facts under operating constraints to generate training data, and (2) Global Context Ranking, which aligns instruction representations more strongly with the complete visual context than with partial visual context. They also construct SortingBench, a high-quality industrial sorting dataset and benchmark built from four layouts of autonomous logistics sorting systems.

Result: Across five open VLMs, HUGIN consistently outperforms matched baselines; for example, Qwen3-VL-8B accuracy on SortingBench improves from 63.6% to 78.8%. Ablation experiments verify each component's effectiveness, and additional experiments show JMSU yields spillover benefits in embodied tasks. Deployment tests over more than 15,000 packages confirm practical viability of VLM-based planning for autonomous logistics sorting.

Conclusion: HUGIN effectively addresses cross-scene supervision scarcity and attention dispersion in JMSU, enabling VLMs to perform reliable joint multi-scene planning for autonomous logistics sorting, with strong benchmark improvements and evidence of real-world deployability.

Abstract: Autonomous logistics sorting systems (ALSS) are an important industrial application of embodied AI, which requires joint planning over spatially disjoint camera views. We formulate this setting as Joint Multi-Scene Understanding (JMSU). With open-world visual understanding and task-planning capabilities, vision-language models (VLMs) are promising candidates for JMSU. However, directly applying existing VLMs to JMSU is non-trivial due to scarce cross-scene supervision and attention dispersion caused by long visual context in JMSU. To address these challenges, we propose HUGIN, a training framework with two complementary components. Endogenous Data Augmentation recombines verified atomic facts under operating constraints, while Global Context Ranking aligns the instruction representation more strongly with the complete visual context than with a partial visual context. To support ongoing research, we construct a high-quality industrial sorting dataset and benchmark named SortingBench from four layouts of autonomous logistics sorting systems. Across five open VLMs, HUGIN consistently outperforms matched baselines; for example, the accuracy on SortingBench of Qwen3-VL-8B increases from 63.6% to 78.8%. Additional experiments verify the effectiveness of each component and JMSU's spillover benefits in embodied tasks. Deployment tests involving more than 15,000 packages support the practical viability of VLM-based planning for autonomous logistics sorting.

</details>


### [277] [Making Your LLMs More Objective: Stabilizing LLM Safety Behavior Across Traits with Trait-Invariant Safety Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11705)
*Lang Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Assigning different traits in the system prompt can flip an LLM's safety decisions on the same request (trait-induced safety variation). The authors analyze this at the representation level, then introduce Trait-Invariant Safety Tuning (TIST) and its instantiation TraSN, which neutralize the trait subspace to make safety behavior stable across traits while improving harmful-request refusal without hurting general capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aligned LLMs should make safety decisions based solely on request content, but the authors show that trait assignments in the system prompt cause inconsistent safety behavior. This motivates measuring and mitigating trait-induced safety variation to achieve robust, stable model behavior.

Method: The authors define two refusal-based metrics (Trait-Induced Deviation and Trait-Induced Flip Rate) to quantify trait-induced safety variation. They conduct a representation-level analysis showing traits perturb safety representations within a low-dimensional subspace. They then propose Trait-Invariant Safety Tuning (TIST), a self-distillation framework aligning trait-conditioned behavior with no-trait behavior, and Trait-Subspace Neutralization (TraSN), which enforces invariance only in the identified trait subspace.

Result: Experiments show that TraSN improves trait-invariant safety and strengthens harmful-request safety while preserving general capability. The representation analysis confirms traits perturb safety representations in a low-dimensional subspace.

Conclusion: Traits are an important factor in LLM safety and robust model behavior; neutralizing the trait subspace via TraSN effectively mitigates trait-induced safety variation while maintaining capabilities.

Abstract: Aligned large language models (LLMs) are expected to exhibit safety behavior based on the content of the user request: they should refuse unsafe requests and comply with safe ones. However, we show that the same request can elicit substantially different safety decisions under different traits assigned in the system prompt, a failure mode we call trait-induced safety variation. To measure this failure, we introduce refusal-based metrics: Trait-Induced Deviation measures dataset-level deviation from the no-trait baseline, while Trait-Induced Flip Rate measures whether the same request receives different safety decisions across traits. We then provide a representation-level analysis of the mechanism behind trait-induced safety shifts and find that traits perturb the model's safety representations within a low-dimensional subspace. To achieve trait-invariant safety, where safety behavior remains stable across traits, we introduce Trait-Invariant Safety Tuning (TIST), a simple yet effective self-distillation framework that aligns an LLM's trait-conditioned behavior with its no-trait behavior. Guided by our analysis, we further propose Trait-Subspace Neutralization (TraSN), an instantiation of TIST, which enforces invariance only within the identified trait subspace. Experiments show that TraSN improves trait-invariant safety and strengthens harmful-request safety while preserving general capability. Our results highlight traits as an important factor in LLM safety and robust model behavior.

</details>


### [278] [Proportional Analogies on Probability Distributions via Bayesian Updating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11724)
*Pierre-Alexandre Murena*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper formalizes proportional analogies ("A is to B as C is to D") for probability distributions by defining the relationship between distributions in terms of Bayesian updating with suitable observations, studying this for exponential-family distributions and extending it via Gaussian mixtures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Proportional analogies provide a rigorous axiomatic framework for analogical reasoning, but while they are well studied over Boolean, symbolic, and real-valued domains, their extension to probability distributions remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap.

Method: The authors introduce a notion of proportional analogy for probability distributions based on Bayesian updating: two distributions are considered related if one can be transformed into the other via Bayesian updating induced by a suitable set of observations. They investigate this framework for standard members of the exponential family and extend the approach to arbitrary distributions through Gaussian mixture approximations.

Result: The paper establishes a Bayesian-updating-based framework for proportional analogies over probability distributions, characterizes it for several standard exponential-family members, and shows a natural extension to arbitrary distributions via Gaussian mixture approximations.

Conclusion: Proportional analogies can be meaningfully extended to probability distributions by grounding the "is to" relation in Bayesian updating, with the framework applying cleanly to exponential-family distributions and generalizing through Gaussian mixture approximations.

Abstract: Analogies are quaternary relations of the form "A is to B as C is to D". Among the various formalizations of analogical reasoning, proportional analogies provide an important axiomatic framework by characterizing valid analogies through a set of postulates. While proportional analogies have been extensively studied over Boolean, symbolic, and real-valued domains, their extension to probability distributions remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce a notion of proportional analogy for probability distributions based on Bayesian updating. Our approach builds upon the idea that two distributions are related whenever one can be transformed into the other through Bayesian updating induced by a suitable set of observations. We investigate this framework for several standard members of the exponential family and discuss how it naturally extends to arbitrary probability distributions through Gaussian mixture approximations.

</details>


### [279] [Harness-IF: Evaluating Instruction Following Across Instruction Surfaces in Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11727)
*Zining Huang,Haoran Que,Hong Zeng,Ge Zhang,Zuo Wang,Jin Chen,Haodong Wang,Zhongfei Hou,Changxin Pu,Shen Yan,Wenhao Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Harness-IF, a benchmark that evaluates whether coding agents genuinely follow operational rules rather than simply doing what they would have done anyway, and finds that all frontier models overstate rule compliance due to prior-confounded defaults.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing instruction-following benchmarks place rules in the user turn and coding-agent benchmarks focus on final task success, so neither can distinguish genuine rule-following from an agent merely behaving as it would have regardless of the rule. The authors need a way to measure compliance with operational rules purely from execution evidence while separating coincidence from actual adherence.

Method: Harness-IF scores one operational rule at a time from execution evidence, using 60 realistic multi-turn coding items drawn from a 642-rule library, with 256 rules receiving verdicts placed on five configurable surfaces read by deployed agents. It introduces Against-Prior Accuracy (AP-Acc), which scores only rules labeled as opposing the agent's unprompted defaults, identified by re-running tasks with the rule withheld across nine probe builds. It also runs a counterbalanced conflict pilot on nine separate builds to test precedence among rule sources.

Result: Across 12 frontier models, accuracy spans 72.1-85.9% and AP-Acc 66.1-78.6%. Every model performs worse on against-prior rules by 3.6 to 7.4 points (mean 5.81), a direction that survives a common-support analysis with item-clustered intervals. Prior control leaves the top build unchanged but exchanges three adjacent rank pairs. A conflict pilot finds pooled precedence does not follow prompt depth: system prompts, project files, and user instructions rank ahead of tool and skill descriptions.

Conclusion: Aggregate scores overstate compliance by a model-specific margin because some apparent compliance is merely prior alignment. Accounting for this prior control reorders several adjacent model ranks, and rule precedence among competing sources does not track prompt depth.

Abstract: When a coding agent obeys a rule, it may simply have been going to do that anyway. Existing instruction-following benchmarks cannot tell the difference: they concentrate rules in the user turn, while coding-agent benchmarks emphasize final task success. We introduce Harness-IF, which scores operational rules one at a time from execution evidence: 60 realistic multi-turn coding items drawn from a 642-rule library, 256 rules receiving verdicts, placed on the five configurable surfaces a deployed agent reads. To separate compliance from coincidence we introduce Against-Prior Accuracy (AP-Acc), which scores only rules labeled as opposing unprompted defaults, observed by re-running tasks with the rule withheld across nine probe builds and curated otherwise. Across 12 frontier models, accuracy spans 72.1-85.9% and AP-Acc 66.1-78.6%; every model is worse on against-prior rules, by 3.6 to 7.4 points (mean 5.81), and the direction survives a common-support analysis with item-clustered intervals. Aggregate scores therefore overstate compliance by a model-specific margin: prior control leaves the top build unchanged and exchanges three adjacent rank pairs. A counterbalanced conflict pilot on nine separate builds adds a second result: pooled precedence does not follow prompt depth, with system prompts, project files, and user instructions ahead of tool and skill descriptions.

</details>


### [280] [HyperANFIS: Enhancing Rule Representation and Interpretability in Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Systems via Hyperbolic Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11768)
*Haoran Pei,Zhao Su,Zetao Lin,Haoran Li,Jun Shen,Qi Zhu,Lan Guo,Qingguo Zhou,Binbin Yong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyperANFIS extends the adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system by moving rule-prototype learning, rule activation, and consequent aggregation into hyperbolic space, preserving fuzzy IF-THEN interpretability while improving accuracy and rule quality over standard ANFIS and its variants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ANFIS models build rule antecedents and perform inference in Euclidean space, which limits representational capacity and predictive performance. The goal is to overcome these limitations while retaining ANFIS's transparent, interpretable IF-THEN reasoning.

Method: The authors propose Hyperbolic ANFIS (HyperANFIS), a hyperbolic extension of ANFIS that keeps the fuzzy semantics and core architecture but performs rule-prototype learning, rule activation, and consequent aggregation in hyperbolic space. It uses hyperbolic geometry's representational properties to strengthen the fuzzy inference process while preserving interpretable rule generation.

Result: HyperANFIS consistently outperforms the standard ANFIS baseline and various ANFIS variants across all tested datasets, achieving higher predictive accuracy, better inter-rule collaboration, and greater credibility of its interpretable rules.

Conclusion: Embedding ANFIS inference in hyperbolic space enhances predictive performance and yields higher-quality, more credible fuzzy rules, confirming that HyperANFIS is an effective interpretable reasoning framework.

Abstract: The adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) is an interpretable reasoning framework capable of generating explicit IF-THEN fuzzy rules, making it suitable for tasks requiring transparent reasoning. However, existing ANFIS models generally construct rule antecedents and perform inference in Euclidean space, limiting their representational capacity and predictive performance. To address this issue, we propose Hyperbolic ANFIS (HyperANFIS), a hyperbolic extension of ANFIS. HyperANFIS preserves the fuzzy semantics and core architecture of conventional ANFIS while performing rule-prototype learning, rule activation, and consequent aggregation in hyperbolic space. It also retains the ability to generate interpretable IF-THEN rules. By exploiting the representational properties of hyperbolic geometry, HyperANFIS strengthens the fuzzy inference process, thereby improving predictive accuracy, inter-rule collaboration, and the credibility of its interpretable rules. Experimental results show that HyperANFIS consistently outperforms the standard ANFIS baseline and various ANFIS variants across all datasets, while also generating higher-quality fuzzy rules.

</details>


### [281] [Reproducing and Stress-Testing Two Approaches to LLM Reasoning Reliability: Test-Time Probability Aggregation and Logic-Representation Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08514)
*Minhan Cho,Jimin Kweon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An independent reproduction and stress-test of two LLM-reasoning-reliability methods (RPC and LCF) across new domains and models finds that neither method's claimed benefits survive rigorous evaluation: RPC's edge over self-consistency is never significant on new domains and its best result reverses with a larger sample, while LCF's logic-validity direction is weak and its only positive effect is insignificant (and harmful on two other models).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliability claims for LLM reasoning methods are typically evaluated only by their own authors and have never been independently reproduced or stress-tested across models and domains (and LCF released no public code), so the authors seek to verify whether these methods' reported improvements generalize beyond the original narrow evaluations.

Method: The authors reproduce RPC's published-path aggregation (inference-time aggregation of token probabilities and self-consistency) and re-implement LCF's projector, contrastive, and intervention pipeline (splitting hidden states into content/logic and editing the logic part). They extend both to four new task domains (text-to-SQL, legal extraction, fallacy identification, precedent grading), test RPC across Qwen3-8B and LCF across four 7-8B models, run paired significance tests, vary the sampling budget on BIRD (K) with enlarged samples (n=200), and directly probe LCF's representation via separability analysis.

Result: RPC reproduces the original grid exactly on the authors' released reasoning paths, but on four new domains its edge over self-consistency is never significant (ties or small mixed differences, paired p >= 0.28); on BIRD its gap grows with K but the largest (+2.5 accuracy at K=32, p=0.16) reverses to -0.25 with n=200. LCF's logic-validity direction is real but weak (0.82 separability at the best sub-layer vs 0.95 for a semantic-attribute control); its one positive effect (Qwen3 ΔProb) is not significant (p=0.56) and it significantly reduces ΔProb on two of the other three models.

Conclusion: The claimed reliability improvements of both RPC and LCF fail to generalize under independent replication and stress-testing; RPC's gains over self-consistency are not significant or even reverse on a larger sample, and LCF's logic-validity direction is weak with its only positive effect insignificant while actively hurting two other models. This underscores the need for independent reproduction, cross-model/cross-domain stress-testing, and released code before reliability claims are accepted.

Abstract: We independently reproduce two recent methods for making large language model (LLM) reasoning more reliable, and stress-test them across domains and models (RPC across four new task domains with Qwen3-8B, LCF across four 7-8B models). The first, RPC, aggregates token probabilities and self-consistency at inference; the second, LCF, trains projectors that split hidden states into "content" and "logic" and edits the logic part toward a valid region. Validating such reliability claims matters because the original evaluations are run by each method's own authors and were never independently reproduced or stress-tested across models and domains, and LCF shipped no public code. We re-run RPC's published-path aggregation and re-implement LCF's projector, contrastive, and intervention pipeline, then extend both to text-to-SQL, legal extraction, fallacy identification, and precedent grading, and probe LCF's representation directly. RPC reproduces the original grid exactly on the authors' released reasoning paths; on four new domains its edge over self-consistency is never significant (ties or small mixed differences, paired p >= 0.28), and on BIRD, the one domain where we vary the budget, the edge grows with K as predicted but its largest gap (+2.5 accuracy at K=32, p=0.16) reverses to -0.25 when we enlarge the sample to n=200. LCF's logic-validity direction is real but weak (0.82 separability at the single best sub-layer versus 0.95 for a semantic-attribute control); its one positive effect (Qwen3 $Δ$Prob) is not significant (p=0.56), while it significantly reduces $Δ$Prob on two of the other three models.

</details>


### [282] [The Sleeping Agent: What Gist-Based Context Compression Loses and Why](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11775)
*Nicholas E. Kyrkewood*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper uses a biologically-inspired gist compression framework (SWC) to probe how context compression affects memory retrieval in long-horizon language model agents, finding that compression helps multi-hop/factual questions but hurts temporal questions due to discarding dates, a failure fixable with a one-sentence prompt change.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gist-based context compression is widely used to summarize long conversation histories, but its differential effect on various memory retrieval types is poorly understood. The work seeks to diagnose when compression helps versus hurts retrieval performance.

Method: The authors use Salience-Weighted Consolidation (SWC), a sleep-inspired compression framework that scores history by salience, partitions content into priority tiers, and applies structured gist abstraction to mid-priority content. They evaluate four conditions across all ten LoCoMo conversations with 1,935 matched text-only questions (1,501 in the primary aggregate after excluding adversarial Category 5) at temperature 0, and perform a preservation analysis of temporal expressions, named entities, and events.

Result: Gist compression significantly outperforms truncation on multi-hop reasoning and single-hop factual questions, but temporal questions remain much harder under compression, scoring well below the full-context reference. The failure is traced to the abstraction prompt discarding dates/times. A one-sentence prompt modification yields an ~20-fold increase in temporal expression preservation (3.05% to 62.39%) while named entity and event preservation barely change (x1.02 and x1.11), recovering +0.314 [0.254, 0.375] judge accuracy on temporal (Category 2) questions.

Conclusion: Gist compression has task-type-dependent effects: it aids relational/factual retrieval but degrades temporal retrieval by dropping temporal information. However, a targeted, precise prompt modification restores temporal performance without harming other retrieval types, demonstrating that compression failures are diagnosable and correctable.

Abstract: Gist-based context compression---summarising older conversation history into compact representations---is a common approach in long-horizon language model agents, yet its effect on different types of memory retrieval is poorly understood. We use Salience-Weighted Consolidation (SWC), a biologically-inspired compression framework motivated by sleep-based memory consolidation, as a diagnostic probe to study when gist compression helps and when it hurts. SWC scores conversation history by salience, partitions it into priority tiers, and applies structured gist abstraction to mid-priority content. Evaluating four conditions on all ten LoCoMo conversations---1,935 matched text-only questions in total, 1,501 used in the primary aggregate after excluding Category 5 (adversarial) questions---at temperature 0, we find a consistent task-type interaction: gist compression substantially outperforms truncation on multi-hop reasoning and single-hop factual questions, but temporal questions remain substantially harder under compression, with compressed conditions scoring well below the full-context reference on the conversations where both are evaluated. We trace this failure to a specific mechanism: the gist abstraction prompt preserves relational and event structure while discarding dates and times. A preservation analysis across all ten conversations confirms the mechanism: an approximately 20-fold increase in temporal expression preservation (3.05% to 62.39%) with a one-sentence prompt modification, while named entity and event preservation rates barely change (x1.02 and x1.11), demonstrating that the fix is a precision instrument. The prompt modification recovers +0.314 [0.254, 0.375] judge accuracy on category-2 (temporal) questions in the matched set. Code and results: https://github.com/kyrkewood/sleeping-agent.

</details>


### [283] [Agent Skills Can Be Harmful: An Empirical Study of Skill-Induced Failures in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11888)
*Gen Dong,Yanjie Gao,Liqun Li,Tianyin Xu,Yu Hua,Fan Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper analyzes how agent skills cause LLM agent failures, introducing a differential attribution framework that pinpoints task failures and efficiency regressions to specific skills, applied to produce 307 skill-induced failures and a taxonomy-guided triage tool.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent skills are widely used to extend LLM agents with reusable guidance, but prior work reports mixed outcomes: some skills improve success, while others have no effect or even increase token cost, execution time, and reduce success rates. The lack of systematic understanding of why skills fail motivates a rigorous analysis of skill-induced failures and regressions.

Method: The authors introduce a differential analysis framework that attributes a failure or regression to a specific skill by comparing a target skill-guided run against a reference run (either no-skill or a semantically matched skill) that solves the same task or solves it more cheaply. The framework is instantiated on SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench, and they build SkillTriage, a taxonomy-guided attribution tool that normalizes paired cases, extracts differential evidence, and produces triage reports.

Result: The analysis yields 307 skill-induced failures: 125 functional failures and 182 efficiency regressions. Key findings: (1) functional failures are rarely caused by obviously irrelevant skills—instead, seemingly relevant skills lead the agent to incorrectly implement or omit required elements; (2) efficiency regressions are not explained by prompt length alone; (3) within the Excessive Procedure category, excessive verification and heavy implementation pipelines are the largest sources, contributing 67 and 30 cases respectively, showing skills often turn checklists and recipes into mandatory work.

Conclusion: The paper proposes research topics and tooling improvements for safer and more cost-aware skill reuse, based on the insight that skill-induced failures stem largely from seemingly relevant skills imposing mandatory procedures and validation overhead.

Abstract: Agent skills are the de facto mechanism for extending LLM agents with reusable guidance. A skill can shape the agent's task execution, including planning, tool use, problem-solving, and validation. Prior work reported mixed results of agent skills: some skills improve task success rates, while others have no effect, increase token use and execution time, and even reduce success rates. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of skill-induced agent failures by attributing task failures and cost regressions to specific loaded skills. We introduce a differential analysis framework that attributes a failure or regression to a skill by comparing a target skill-guided run against a no-skill or semantically matched skill reference run that solves the same task, or solves it more cheaply. We instantiate this framework on SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench, yielding 307 skill-induced failures, including 125 functional failures and 182 efficiency regressions. We also build SkillTriage, a taxonomy-guided attribution tool that normalizes paired cases, extracts differential evidence, and produces triage reports. Our major findings include: (1) Skill induced functional failures are rarely caused by obviously irrelevant skills; instead, seemingly relevant skills often make the agent incorrectly implement or omit task-required implementation elements. (2) Skill-induced efficiency regressions are not explained by prompt length alone. (3) The largest sources within Excessive Procedure are excessive verification and heavy implementation pipelines, contributing 67 and 30 cases, respectively. This shows that skills often turn validation checklists and construction recipes into mandatory work. Based on our findings, we propose research topics and tooling improvements for safer and more cost-aware skill reuse.

</details>


### [284] [Policy-as-logic for robust reasoning over rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11905)
*Rahul Nair,Bastian Lipka,Elizabeth Daly*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hybrid symbolic approach for policy-compliant query answering that separates fact extraction (via language models) from logical reasoning (via answer set solvers), achieving higher accuracy, robustness, and ~10x lower token usage than policy-as-prompt or policy-as-code methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI systems used in practical applications (e.g., tax rules, airline baggage policies) must produce responses that respect written policies or rules. Existing approaches rely on either prompting models with the policy or encoding it as code, both of which struggle with interpretability, auditability, accuracy, and robustness under input perturbations.

Method: A hybrid symbolic approach: policies are expressed in formal logic. At inference time, a language model performs fact extraction to ground predicates from natural language queries, and an answer set solver performs the reasoning step. This cleanly separates extraction from reasoning.

Result: The separation of extraction and reasoning outperforms policy-as-prompt and policy-as-code methods in most cases, with approximately a 10x reduction in token usage, while producing interpretable, auditable, accurate, and perturbation-robust responses.

Conclusion: Structured reasoning combined with symbolic solvers and generative models offers a valuable approach for making robust, objective, policy-compliant decisions.

Abstract: In many practical applications of generative AI systems, from tax rules to airline baggage allowance, responses to natural language queries must respect written policies or rules. We present a hybrid symbolic approach that expresses policies in formal logic and at inference time exploits the representation power of language models for fact extraction to ground predicates, and an answer set solver for reasoning such that responses are interpretable, auditable, and as we show, accurate and robust under input perturbations. Specifically, we show this separation of extraction and reasoning steps outperforms policy-as-prompt and policy-as-code methods in most cases with ~10x reduction in token usage. The results point to the value of structured reasoning and symbolic solvers in conjunction with generative models to make robust decisions involving objective criteria.

</details>


### [285] [OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11941)
*Tom Adamczewski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents OEIS Open, an open-source benchmark of 492 formalized open mathematical conjectures from OEIS, which current LMs with minimal tools resolve 30% of at $50/attempt, and 44% on a 100-conjecture Lite subset at $200/attempt; adding arXiv literature access or sophisticated agent loops did not help.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work only tested OEIS conjectures with a bespoke agent and non-reusable evaluation. The authors seek a general, open-source, secure benchmark that any language model can be run against, enabling standardized and fair measurement of whether LMs can autonomously resolve open mathematical research conjectures.

Method: They build OEIS Open from 492 open OEIS conjectures formalized in Lean, with evaluation code that is open-source, generic across LMs, and hardened against LM cheating. They evaluate LMs equipped with a minimal tool set under fixed budgets ($50 and $200 per attempt). As ablations, they give LMs access to 476,000 arXiv papers and test more sophisticated agent loops, plus a random 100-conjecture "Lite" subset for cheaper evaluation.

Result: With minimal tools and $50 per attempt, LMs resolve 147 of 492 conjectures (30% on OEIS Open). On OEIS Open Lite (100 random conjectures) with $200 per attempt, the best LM scores 44%. Providing arXiv literature access or more sophisticated agent loops did not improve performance.

Conclusion: Despite the conjectures being of uncertain mathematical significance and likely little studied, LMs can resolve open research conjectures autonomously and at modest cost, demonstrating meaningful autonomous math-research capability under secure, open, and generalizable evaluation.

Abstract: We construct OEIS Open, a benchmark based on 492 open mathematical conjectures from the OEIS, formalized in Lean by Tsoukalas et al. Whereas these conjectures had previously been attempted only with a bespoke agent, our open-source evaluation code runs any generic language model (LM) against them, and is secure against LM cheating attempts. We find that LMs equipped with a minimal set of tools resolve 147 of these conjectures with a budget of \$50 per attempt, scoring 30% on OEIS Open. OEIS Open Lite is a random subset of 100 conjectures for cheaper evaluation. When evaluated with a budget of \$200 per attempt, the best current LM scores 44% on OEIS Open Lite. Giving LMs access to the mathematics literature via 476,000 papers from arXiv did not increase performance on OEIS Open Lite, and nor did using more sophisticated agent loops. The conjectures covered in this work are of uncertain mathematical significance, and most have likely received little previous attention. Nevertheless, our results show that LMs can resolve open research conjectures autonomously and at modest cost.

</details>


### [286] [ExRole: From Team Trajectories to Executable Roles in Multi-Agent Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11949)
*Zhou Liu,Chaoyang Han,Zewei Pan,Zeli Su,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes ExRole, a framework that learns future-aware role prototypes from team trajectories, turning roles from hand-written labels into executable control variables (readable instructions + token-aligned markers + optionally routed LoRA slots). It substantially outperforms single-agent and non-ExRole baselines on multi-hop QA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most multi-agent systems treat roles as hand-written prompt labels disconnected from learned behavior and parameter updates. The authors argue a useful role should be an executable control variable that (1) summarizes behavior predictive of future utility, (2) guides subsequent interaction, and (3) identifies the trainable capacity responsible for that behavior.

Method: ExRole is a trajectory-to-role framework that learns future-aware role prototypes from prefix-local team traces, resolves them into readable instructions and token-aligned role markers, and optionally routes shared LoRA rank slots with turn-aligned credit. It also supports Role-Agent-Turn interventions to test transferability of learned roles.

Result: On MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, ExRole improves over single-agent search by 15.0/14.4 and 13.5/16.1 EM/F1 points, respectively. Against the strongest non-ExRole controls, gains are 11.5/11.6 and 7.7/9.7 points. Controlled results across both benchmarks consistently favor trajectory-induced role conditioning over role-free, manual, random, and shuffled alternatives.

Conclusion: Trajectory-induced roles serve as effective executable control variables, capturing transferable behavioral specialization beyond fixed agent identities or turn positions, and significantly outperform both single-agent and strong non-ExRole baselines on multi-hop QA.

Abstract: Roles provide an interpretable interface for organizing language-model agents, yet most multi-agent systems treat them as hand-written prompt labels disconnected from learned behavior and parameter updates. We argue that a useful role should instead be an executable control variable: it should summarize behavior predictive of future utility, guide subsequent interaction, and identify the trainable capacity responsible for that behavior. We introduce ExRole, a trajectory-to-role framework that learns future-aware role prototypes from prefix-local team traces, resolves them into readable instructions and token-aligned role markers, and optionally routes shared LoRA rank slots with turn-aligned credit. Across MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, ExRole improves over single-agent search by 15.0/14.4 and 13.5/16.1 EM/F1 points, respectively. Against the strongest non-ExRole controls, the corresponding gains remain 11.5/11.6 and 7.7/9.7 points. Across both benchmarks, the controlled results consistently favor trajectory-induced role conditioning over role-free, manual, random, and shuffled alternatives. Role-Agent-Turn interventions further show that the induced roles capture transferable behavioral specialization beyond fixed agent identities or turn positions.

</details>


### [287] [Retry, Switch, or Abstain? Learning Strategy-Aware Tool-Use Policies via Controlled Error Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11977)
*Chaoran Chen,Vy Nguyen,Ziji Zhang,Abhinav Gullapalli,Ziyi Wang,Yuxuan Lu,Dakuo Wang,Jing Huang,Zhou Yu,Jin Lai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BENCH2ROBUST converts failure-free tool-use benchmarks into stochastic environments with controlled solvability to study robust recovery. Combining Bayesian Tool Memory (BTM) with curriculum RL yields up to 45.5% success under tool-failure injection while preserving failure-free performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-using LLM agents are trained/evaluated under reliable tool calls, but deployed tools can fail transiently, persistently, or silently. Robust recovery needs more than retries: agents must retry, switch, or stop. This motivates a controlled framework to study and improve recovery behavior.

Method: BENCH2ROBUST converts failure-free benchmarks into stochastic environments with scenario-controlled solvability (requiring retry, switch, or stop). Two interventions are studied: (1) Bayesian Tool Memory (BTM) providing structured runtime recovery context, and (2) curriculum-controlled reinforcement learning. Evaluated across 7 models from 4 families and two multi-turn benchmark families.

Result: Tool failures create a near-universal robustness gap. BTM improves robustness by up to 16.8 points without retraining; RL learns complementary recovery behavior beneficial even without inference-time BTM. Combined, they reach 40.8-45.5% under injection while preserving failure-free performance.

Conclusion: Robust tool use benefits from combining environment-specific recovery knowledge (BTM) with learned recovery behavior (curriculum RL), suggesting a complementary pairing of memory-based and learned strategies.

Abstract: Tool-using LLM agents are commonly trained and evaluated in environments where tool calls succeed reliably, yet deployed tools can fail transiently, persistently, or silently. Robust recovery therefore requires more than repeated retries: an agent may need to retry the same path, switch to an alternative, or recognize that no viable path remains. We present BENCH2ROBUST, a framework that converts failure-free tool-use benchmarks into controlled stochastic environments with scenario-controlled solvability, where episodes explicitly require retrying, switching, or stopping after available paths are exhausted. We use BENCH2ROBUST to study two complementary interventions: structured runtime recovery context through Bayesian Tool Memory (BTM), and curriculum-controlled reinforcement learning. Across 7 models from 4 families and two multi-turn benchmark families, tool failures produce a near-universal robustness gap. On held-out Retail tasks, BTM improves robustness by up to 16.8 percentage points without retraining, while RL learns complementary recovery behavior that remains beneficial without inference-time BTM. Combining the two reaches 40.8-45.5% under injection while preserving failure-free performance. These results suggest that robust tool use benefits from combining environment-specific recovery knowledge with learned recovery behavior.

</details>


### [288] [Claim-Level Reliability Assessment for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11994)
*Sen Xu,Wei Wang,Shixi Liu,Jixin Min,Yingwei Dai,Zhibin Yin,Yirong Chen,Junlin Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CLR is a training-free test-time scaling framework that verifies reasoning traces by isolating "decision-critical claims" and searching for refuting evidence, improving accuracy over pass@1 and self-consistency while using fewer tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Whole-trace evaluation obscures decisive errors due to signal dilution from routine tokens; additionally, generating entirely correct solutions is fundamentally difficult under fixed model capabilities. The authors seek to reallocate test-time compute from extra sampling toward targeted verification that exploits an asymmetry between constructing valid solutions and refuting incorrect claims.

Method: CLR (Claim-Level Reliability Assessment) condenses each reasoning trace into a compact set of decision-critical claims to isolate logical anchors, then performs semantic falsification: it searches for a single decisive flaw that refutes a claim rather than requiring a flawless solution path. This negative-evidence search compresses the survival space of high-confidence incorrect traces and suppresses erroneous consensus via nonlinear reliability scoring.

Result: Across four LLMs and four reasoning benchmarks under matched compute budgets, CLR generally improves upon pass@1 and self-consistency. On GPT-OSS-20B/CMIMC25, CLR beats pass@1 by 27.15 percentage points and lifts self-consistency accuracy from 77.50% to 82.19% while using 37.0% fewer tokens.

Conclusion: Claim-level falsification is an effective principle for test-time scaling, enabling targeted verification that outperforms naive sampling budgets and self-consistency by focusing compute on refuting decision-critical claims rather than generating more solutions.

Abstract: We propose claim-level falsification as a principle for test-time scaling and instantiate it through Claim-Level Reliability Assessment (CLR), a training-free framework that reallocates test-time compute from additional solution sampling to targeted verification. Since whole-trace evaluation often obscures decisive errors due to signal dilution from routine tokens, CLR condenses each reasoning trace into a compact set of decision-critical claims, thereby isolating its logical anchors. Furthermore, recognizing the inherent difficulty of generating entirely correct solutions under fixed model capabilities, CLR shifts the focus to semantic falsification. This approach exploits a fundamental asymmetry between solution construction and claim refutation. Constructing a valid solution requires a flawless reasoning path, whereas refuting an incorrect claim requires identifying only a single decisive flaw. This targeted search for negative evidence systematically compresses the survival space of high-confidence incorrect traces, effectively suppressing erroneous consensus via nonlinear reliability scoring. Across four LLMs and four reasoning benchmarks under matched budgets, CLR generally improves upon pass@1 and self-consistency. On GPT-OSS-20B/CMIMC25, for instance, CLR exceeds pass@1 by 27.15 percentage-points and raises self-consistency accuracy from 77.50\% to 82.19\% with 37.0\% fewer tokens.

</details>


### [289] [CTBench: Evaluating Troubleshooting Capabilities of AI Agents in Realistic Telecom Network Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12002)
*Xingyu Yan,Tingting Dai,Antonio De Domenico,Mohamed Sana,Nicola Piovesan,Changchang Li,Bowen Liu,Kun Jiang,Mengjie Zhang,Dingcheng Shan,Jing-Cheng Pang,Chenwei Wu,Sijie Wu,Lianying Chao,Haoran Cai,Jiantao Ye,Xubin Li,Simon Mark Lucas,Xin Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CTBench is a public benchmark for evaluating whether AI agents can behave like competent telecom troubleshooting engineers, focusing on root cause analysis and path restoration. It uses expert-constructed tasks with golden evidence steps and evidence-grounded metrics. Results show state-of-the-art agents excel at endpoint identification in path restoration but underperform on root cause analysis, especially on interface, link-layer, and service-management faults, and often fail to provide evidence-grounded diagnoses despite plausible final answers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agents are increasingly used to automate network operations and maintenance, but existing evaluations fail to accurately model real network characteristics or assess agents under partially observable telecom environments with diverse vendors, devices, protocols, and interfaces. There is a need for a benchmark that tests whether agents can act as competent telecom troubleshooting engineers.

Method: CTBench is constructed by experts with tasks annotated with rich metadata, including golden evidence steps. It focuses on root cause analysis and path restoration, and uses expert-grounded metrics that evaluate both the final answers and the diagnostic evidence provided by agents. Experiments test representative harness-model combinations to assess agent performance and resource usage.

Result: State-of-the-art agents perform very well at identifying endpoints in path-restoration tasks but underperform in root cause analysis overall. They particularly struggle with interface state, link-layer, service-management, and other operational faults. Critically, even when agents produce plausible or correct final answers, they often fail to provide evidence-grounded diagnoses required in operational practice. Path restoration is generally more resource expensive, yet larger resource usage does not necessarily translate into better diagnosis.

Conclusion: Current state-of-the-art agents are insufficient for operational network troubleshooting, particularly for root cause analysis, and fail to provide evidence-grounded diagnoses. The benchmark reveals the gap between plausible final answers and defensible, evidence-based reasoning, and highlights that increased resource usage alone does not improve diagnosis quality.

Abstract: Agents are increasingly considered for automating network operations and maintenance, where engineers must diagnose network faults, optimize configurations to enhance services, and reduce operational costs while acting under strict constraints. However, existing evaluations fail to accurately model real network characteristics or assess agents under partially observable telecom environments with diverse vendors, devices, protocols, and interfaces. In this paper, we introduce CTBench, a public benchmark for assessing whether an agent behaves like a competent telecom troubleshooting engineer. CTBench focuses on root cause analysis and path restoration. Each task is constructed by experts and annotated with rich task metadata, including golden evidence steps. CTBench uses expert-grounded metrics that evaluate both final answers and the diagnostic evidence. Experiments with representative harness-model combinations show that state-of-the-art agents perform very well at identifying endpoints in path-restoration tasks but, more generally, underperform in root cause analysis. In particular, agents struggle with interface state, link-layer, service-management, and other operational faults. Most importantly, even when agents produce plausible or correct final answers, they often fail to provide the evidence-grounded diagnoses required in operational practice. Our results further show that path restoration is generally more resource expensive, yet larger resource usage does not necessarily translate into better diagnosis.

</details>


### [290] [Graph-Structured Rubrics: Compiling Rubrics into Typed Evaluation Graphs for LLM Judges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12097)
*Xi Chen,Jie Mu,Mo Xuan,Qun Shao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents Graph-Structured Rubrics (GSR), a method that compiles rubrics into a typed evaluation graph with explicit composition operators, improving LLM-based evaluation accuracy for both pointwise scoring and pairwise preference tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing rubric-based evaluators treat rubrics as prompt context or flat criteria, specifying what to judge but leaving criterion composition implicit even when natural-language rules define how to combine them. This implicit composition limits evaluation reliability and accuracy.

Method: GSR compiles a rubric into a response-independent typed evaluation graph before observing responses. Criterion nodes elicit judgments; transformation, reduction, and gating operators compose them through named ports; and a task-specific Readout mapping converts the unique sink node into a score or preference. Compilation statically rejects malformed or type-incompatible graphs. Pointwise evaluation judges rubric dimensions separately before graph aggregation, while pairwise evaluation reuses the graph with one judgment per candidate under each criterion.

Result: Under GPT-OSS-120B, GSR improves exact score agreement by 0.62–6.75 percentage points over Prometheus-style scoring on four pointwise datasets, and achieves the numerically highest end-to-end pairwise accuracy on two preference benchmarks under native tie and abstention policies.

Conclusion: Making criterion composition explicit through a typed evaluation graph yields measurable gains in both score agreement and pairwise preference accuracy, demonstrating the value of structured rubric compilation over flat or prompt-embedded rubric usage.

Abstract: Rubric-based evaluators commonly treat rubrics as prompt context or flat criteria: they specify what to judge but leave criterion composition implicit, even when natural-language rules state it. We introduce Graph-Structured Rubrics (GSR), which compiles a rubric into a response-independent typed evaluation graph before observing responses. Criterion nodes elicit judgments; transformation, reduction, and gating operators compose them through named ports; and a task-specific output mapping, termed Readout, converts the unique sink into a score or preference. Compilation rejects malformed or type-incompatible graphs. Pointwise evaluation judges rubric dimensions separately before graph aggregation; pairwise evaluation reuses the graph with one judgment for each candidate under every criterion. Under GPT-OSS-120B, GSR improves exact score agreement by 0.62--6.75 percentage points over Prometheus-style scoring on four pointwise datasets and achieves the numerically highest end-to-end pairwise accuracy on two preference benchmarks under native tie and abstention policies.

</details>


### [291] [GUIDE: Governed Unified Intelligence for Document-to-Artifact Generation in Enterprise Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12133)
*Shivali Dalmia,Sumukha Thoppanahalli,Mohammadreza Sediqin,Abhishek Mukherji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GUIDE is a governed multi-agent framework for processing heterogeneous, multimodal enterprise guideline documents (text, tables, images), delivering 96% document success, 3,896 rules extracted (71.4% auto-approved), 812 deployment-ready artifacts, and reducing turnaround from 2-3 days to 40-125 minutes per document.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise guideline documents are heterogeneous and multimodal (narrative text, complex tables, embedded images), but existing LLM/VLM systems suffer from hallucinated content, table structure degradation, and lack governed workflows covering validation and artifact generation. Enterprises currently handle this manually, spending 2-3 days per document.

Method: GUIDE uses a governed multi-agent framework built on a shared versioned rule store with schema-validated inter-agent contracts and end-to-end provenance tracking. Six specialized agents handle parsing, VLM-driven extraction, consistency checking, evaluation, human-in-the-loop (HITL) escalation, and persona-tailored artifact synthesis.

Result: On 120 real-world enterprise guideline documents, GUIDE achieves 96% document success, extracts 3,896 rules with 71.4% auto-approved, produces 812 deployment-ready artifacts, and reduces turnaround to 40-125 minutes per document.

Conclusion: GUIDE demonstrates a governed multi-agent approach that reliably extracts, validates, and synthesizes artifacts from complex multimodal guideline documents, dramatically reducing manual effort and turnaround time for enterprises.

Abstract: Enterprise guideline documents are heterogeneous and multimodal, combining narrative text, complex tables, and embedded images. Existing LLM and VLM systems face hallucinated content, table structure degradation, and lack governed workflows extending beyond extraction to validation and artifact generation. This leaves enterprises to perform this manually, consuming 2-3 days per document. To address this, we introduce GUIDE, a governed multi-agent framework built on a shared versioned rule store with schema-validated inter-agent contracts and end-to-end provenance tracking. Six specialized agents handle parsing, VLM-driven extraction, consistency checking, evaluation, human-in-the-loop (HITL) escalation, and persona-tailored artifact synthesis. Evaluated on 120 real-world enterprise guideline documents, GUIDE achieves 96% document success, extracts 3,896 rules with 71.4% auto-approved, produces 812 deployment-ready artifacts, and reduces turnaround to 40-125 minutes per document.

</details>


### [292] [Who Thinks Best Depends on How Long You Let Them: Budget-Dependent Rankings in LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12150)
*Rodrigo Guedes de Souza,Alison R. Panisson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Model rankings on reasoning benchmarks are unstable across token generation budgets: accuracy can be non-monotone, rankings reverse, and budget-aware routing/conditioned evaluation is needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard LLM evaluation assumes stable model rankings regardless of inference conditions. The authors challenge this by showing that the token generation budget (max output tokens) materially affects model accuracy and relative standing, motivating budget-conditioned evaluation protocols.

Method: They vary the token generation budget across seven levels (64–4,096) and evaluate four models on three reasoning benchmarks, totaling 56,476 inferences. They analyze non-monotone behavior (controlling for truncation), ranking reversals via McNemar tests, oracle complementarity, and a budget-aware router (with within-domain and cross-domain transfer experiments).

Result: (i) 3–19% of items show non-monotone accuracy (decreasing with larger budget) even after controlling for truncation, with model-specific effects (cross-model overlap 6–14%). (ii) Rankings reverse across budgets on all benchmarks (p < 0.01, McNemar). (iii) Oracle analysis shows model complementarity up to +27.8pp, strongest at constrained budgets. (iv) A budget-aware router captures 14.1% of the oracle gap cross-domain; budget features help within-domain (+1.6 to +5.7pp) but are domain-specific and hurt transfer (−1.2pp).

Conclusion: Model rankings are not stable across token budgets, so evaluation should be budget-conditioned. Budget-aware routing is promising but current budget features do not transfer across domains.

Abstract: Standard evaluation of large language models assumes stable model rankings across inference conditions. We challenge this assumption by varying the token generation budget, i.e., the maximum tokens a model may produce, across seven levels (64--4,096), evaluating four models on three reasoning benchmarks (56,476 inferences). We report four findings: (i) 3--19% of items exhibit non-monotone behavior (accuracy decreasing with more budget), even after controlling for truncation, and this phenomenon is model-specific (cross-model overlap: 6--14%). (ii) Model rankings reverse across budgets on all benchmarks ($p {<} 0.01$, McNemar). (iii) Oracle analysis reveals model complementarity up to $+27.8$pp, most pronounced at constrained budgets. (iv) A budget-aware router captures 14.1% of the oracle gap cross-domain; budget features help within-domain ($+1.6$ to $+5.7$pp) but are domain-specific and hurt transfer ($-1.2$pp). These results argue for budget-conditioned evaluation protocols.

</details>


### [293] [How to Spend Your Oracle Budget: Practical Guidance for Protein Structure Prediction Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12192)
*Aleksandra Kalisz,Jack Simons,Krisztina Sinkovics,Noam Ghenassia,Shikha Surana,Henry Moss,Paul Duckworth*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper benchmarks oracle-budget-aware guidance methods (FK-steering, DPO, Best K-of-N, and O3) for protein structure prediction, extending O3 to this domain and showing that no method dominates across all budgets, with O3 best at low budgets and FK-steering/DPO improving as budget grows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation models for protein structure prediction are unreliable on certain targets, and external oracles can flag/correct failures but are expensive, making oracle budget a critical constraint. Existing guidance methods differ in budget usage yet lack a systematic comparison to inform method selection.

Method: The authors benchmark FK-steering, DPO, and Best K-of-N sampling alongside Optimisation Over Outputs (O3), extending O3 to protein structure prediction by applying off-the-shelf optimisers within a generative model's latent subspace. They evaluate on two protein targets: calmodulin (1CLL) and E. coli aspartate transcarbamoylase (9EEH).

Result: No single method consistently dominates across all oracle budgets and oracle types. O3 is most effective at low oracle budgets, while FK-steering and DPO show improved performance as the budget increases.

Conclusion: The work provides the first practical reference for oracle budget-aware guidance, distilling findings into actionable recommendations for practitioners operating under real-world oracle-budget constraints.

Abstract: Foundation models for protein structure prediction remain unreliable on certain targets. External oracles can flag and correct these failures, but biological oracles are expensive, making oracle budget a critical constraint. Existing guidance methods, such as FK-steering, DPO, and Best K-of-N sampling, differ in how they spend this budget, yet no systematic comparison exists to guide method selection. To bridge this gap, we benchmark these methods alongside the recently proposed Optimisation Over Outputs (O3), which applies off-the-shelf optimisers within a generative model's latent subspace. We extend the usage of O3 to protein structure prediction models. Overall, our work provides the first practical reference for oracle budget-aware guidance. Our evaluation on two protein targets, calmodulin (1CLL) and E. coli aspartate transcarbamoylase (9EEH), reveals that no single method consistently dominates across all budgets and oracles. Specifically, O3 proves most effective at low oracle budgets, while FK-steering and DPO demonstrate improved performance as the budget increases. We distil these findings into actionable recommendations for practitioners operating under real-world oracle-budget constraints.

</details>


### [294] [An Agentic Workflow for Legacy HPC Modernization: Converting the Two-Electron-Integral Core of GAMESS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12249)
*Yuzhong Shen,Masha Sosonkina,Peng Xu,Mark S. Gordon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An agentic workflow using prompt-specialized AI roles under a version-controlled, agent-authored specification is applied at production scale to convert 56,448 lines of Fortran 77 code in GAMESS to free-form Fortran 2008, validated by bit-for-bit reproduction of canonical test energies with zero differences across 612 runs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modernizing legacy Fortran is routinized but enormous in volume, so the work often goes undone across computational science. The paper seeks to determine how far safe delegation of such mass transformation to AI agents can reach.

Method: Three prompt-specialized Claude Code agent roles operate in isolated worktrees under a version-controlled specification that the agents themselves authored and revised, with humans holding a small number of gates. Safety is enforced by an exact verification oracle from the domain (bit-for-bit reproduction of printed energies), which defines the boundary of safe delegation. The work spanned four Claude model generations.

Result: Twelve source files (56,448 lines, 225 subroutines) were converted from fixed-form Fortran 77 to free-form Fortran 2008. All twelve files pass a 51-test validation battery (49 standard GAMESS tests plus two additional calculations), with zero chemistry-relevant differences across 612 test runs, and every file passes Jenkins continuous-integration tests.

Conclusion: The agentic workflow successfully handles production-scale legacy Fortran modernization, with safe delegation bounded exactly by where the domain's exact verification oracle stops seeing, demonstrating that such delegation can reach large, mature scientific codebases with bit-for-bit correctness guarantees.

Abstract: Modernizing legacy Fortran is a problem of volume: the transformations are individually routine, but the codebases can be enormous, and across much of computational science the work simply goes undone. We propose an agentic workflow that takes this work on at production scale, and we set out to measure how far such delegation can reach. In this work, three prompt-specialized agent roles operate under a version-controlled specification that the agents themselves authored and revised, while humans hold a small number of gates. The arrangement is kept safe by an exact verification oracle inherited from the domain, and the boundary of safe delegation lies exactly where that oracle stops seeing.
  We apply the proposed workflow in a case study, converting the two-electron-integral routines of GAMESS (General Atomic and Molecular Electronic Structure System), a mature quantum-chemistry package with a 48-year development history, from fixed-form Fortran 77 to free-form Fortran 2008. The scope of this work was twelve source files, 56,448 lines, and 225 subroutines for computing electron repulsion integrals. The agents ran as three Claude Code roles in isolated worktrees, and the work spanned four Claude model generations. Because the GAMESS group ships a standard test suite whose printed energies its user community treats as canonical, we could adopt bit-for-bit reproduction of those energies as the merge criterion, where a deviation in the twelfth decimal place counts as a failure rather than drift. All twelve source files pass a 51-test validation battery comprising the 49 standard GAMESS tests and two additional calculations, and across 612 test runs the number of chemistry-relevant differences is zero, and every file also passes the Jenkins tests that are used for continuous integration.

</details>


### [295] [VAKRA: Evaluating Multi-Hop Reasoning Across APIs and Retrieval Under Tool-Use Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12282)
*Ankita Rajaram Naik,Anupama Murthi,Benjamin Elder,Siyu Huo,Raavi Gupta,Abhinav Jain,Praveen Venkateswaran,Abdulhamid Adebayo,Danish Contractor*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VAKRA is a benchmark of 8,000+ executable APIs across 62 domains for evaluating agents that combine API and knowledge retrieval. It features three increasingly difficult task settings, uses live-API re-execution for correctness verification (allowing multiple valid paths), and evaluates models under a fixed ReAct harness. Frontier models reach only ~70% on single-hop tasks, ~50% on compositional APIs, and degrade sharply with reasoning depth and policy constraints; failures stem mainly from language-mediated reasoning rather than tool mechanics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise agents must jointly reason over structured APIs and document collections, but existing benchmarks evaluate these abilities in isolation, leaving a gap in assessing combined API-and-knowledge retrieval with realistic policy constraints.

Method: Introduces VAKRA, a benchmark of over 8,000 executable APIs across 62 domains. Tasks span three settings of increasing difficulty: (1) diverse API interaction styles, (2) multi-hop reasoning over structured APIs, and (3) multi-source reasoning with natural-language tool-use policy constraints. Correctness is verified by re-executing predicted tool calls against live APIs, which accommodates multiple valid solution paths. Evaluation uses a fixed ReAct harness to isolate model capability from agent architecture, applied to both frontier and open-weight models.

Result: The best model achieves only 70.4% on single-hop endpoint-style tasks and drops to 50–51% on compositional APIs. Performance degrades by over 50% as reasoning depth increases. Policy-constrained questions expose severe failures, reaching as low as 2.4% on unanswerable queries. Trace analysis shows failures concentrate in language-mediated reasoning (entity disambiguation, cross-source grounding) rather than tool invocation mechanics.

Conclusion: Current frontier and open-weight models remain far from reliable performance on joint API-and-knowledge retrieval tasks. The main bottleneck is language-mediated reasoning (disambiguation and cross-source grounding) rather than tool-use mechanics, and policy constraints drastically degrade reliability. VAKRA provides the code and dataset to drive further research in enterprise agent reasoning.

Abstract: Agents deployed in enterprise settings must reason across structured APIs and document collections, yet existing benchmarks evaluate these capabilities in isolation. We introduce VAKRA (e\textbf{V}aluating \textbf{A}PI and \textbf{K}nowledge \textbf{R}etrieval \textbf{A}gents), a benchmark of over $8{,}000$ executable APIs across $62$ domains with tasks spanning three settings of increasing difficulty: diverse API interaction styles, multi-hop reasoning over structured APIs, and multi-source reasoning with natural-language tool-use policy constraints. Correctness is verified by re-executing predicted tool calls against live APIs, accommodating multiple valid paths. Using a fixed ReAct harness to isolate model capabilities from agent architecture, we evaluate frontier and open-weight models and find that even the best model achieves only 70.4\% on single-hop endpoint-style tasks and drops to 50--51\% on compositional APIs; performance degrades by over 50\% as reasoning depth increases, and policy-constrained questions expose severe failures (as low as 2.4\% on unanswerable queries). Trace analysis shows failures concentrate at language-mediated reasoning - entity disambiguation, cross-source grounding, rather than tool invocation mechanics. Code is available https://github.com/IBM/VAKRA. Dataset is available https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/VAKRA

</details>


### [296] [Constructing Dynamic Master Logic Models as Knowledge Graphs for Complex System Diagnostics Using Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12304)
*Saman Marandi,Yu-Shu Hu,Mohammad Modarres*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an automated framework for building Dynamic Master Logic (DML) models as Knowledge Graphs (KG-DML) from technical documentation, using Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Large Language Models, and validates it on a complex nuclear reactor system.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DML construction traditionally requires expert manual interpretation of technical documentation, which limits scalability for complex systems. The work aims to automate this process to enable large-scale functional modeling for diagnostics and reliability analysis.

Method: The framework uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Large Language Models to automatically construct KG-DML from system descriptions. It builds models hierarchically across the DML structure using targeted retrieval, preserving functional dependencies and explicit logical relationships. Validation employs a multi-level methodology assessing layer-specific precision and recall, logical gate consistency, and structural integrity. The approach is applied to the Low-Pressure Coolant Injection system of a decommissioned Boiling Water Reactor.

Result: The framework produced consistent KG-DML reconstructions across repeated runs on a substantially larger and more complex system than prior work. The resulting models support diagnostic reasoning, safety assessment, upward failure propagation, and downward dependency tracing. Multi-level validation confirmed precision/recall, gate consistency, and structural integrity.

Conclusion: Automated KG-DML construction can transform technical documentation into executable functional models, demonstrating that RAG and LLM-based methods are viable for scalable, complex-system diagnostic and reliability analysis.

Abstract: Dynamic Master Logic (DML) provides a hierarchical framework for representing system behavior by linking functional objectives to underlying structural elements. However, DML construction typically relies on expert interpretation of technical documentation, limiting scalability for complex systems. This study presents a framework for automated construction of DML models from system descriptions and their representation as Knowledge Graphs (KG-DML), using Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Large Language Models as enabling tools. Building on prior work with small-scale systems, the framework extends automated KG-DML construction and evaluation to substantially larger and more complex systems. Model construction proceeds across the DML hierarchy using targeted retrieval while preserving functional dependencies and explicit logical relationships. The resulting KG-DML supports diagnostic reasoning, safety assessment, upward failure propagation, and downward dependency tracing. A multi-level validation methodology evaluates layer-specific precision and recall, logical gate consistency, and overall structural integrity. Application to the Low-Pressure Coolant Injection system of a decommissioned Boiling Water Reactor demonstrates consistent reconstruction across repeated runs. The results show that automated KG-DML construction can transform technical documentation into executable functional models for diagnostic and reliability analysis.

</details>
